title: ‘Friend to everyone' honored for hard work, drive
description: Working to be the best person he can be hasn't gone unnoticed by those who know Palatka resident Jonathan Hurt. 'He is always happy and ready to help,' his dad, Cliff Hurt, said. 'When he has money,…
content: Working to be the best person he can be hasn't gone unnoticed by those who know Palatka resident Jonathan Hurt. 'He is always happy and ready to help,' his dad, Cliff Hurt, said. 'When he has money, he has no problem spending it on others. He is a friend to everyone.' Cliff Hurt said his son is developmentally disabled, has a low mentality and suffers from Milroy disease, a condition that affects the normal function of the lymphatic system, where he retains fluid in one leg. But Jonathan Hurt doesn't let that stop him from getting up and staying active. 'Even though Jonathan has a painful medical condition and flare-ups while working, he works with no complaints and never wants to miss work,' said Patty Dame, the manager of administrative services for the Arc of Putnam County Inc. And that determination and drive is why Jonathan Hurt was given the 2023 James 'Eddie' Mooney Leadership Award during a banquet and fundraiser March 7 at the Roy E. Campbell Civic Center inside Ravine Gardens State Park in Palatka. The Arc hosted the 26th annual event. 'He was caught completely off guard since he was not told about getting the award but he was very happy,' Cliff Hurt said. Submitted photo – Jonathan Hurt, left, is pictured with his dad, Cliff Hurt, at a March 7 banquet, where Jonathan was given the James 'Eddie' Mooney Leadership Award. Each year, the Arc's board of directors honors an Arc client with the Eddie Mooney Award based on the individual's courage and determination, which has long served as an example for people with developmental differences. According to a news release from the Arc of Putnam County, the award has been established to recognize the accomplishments of people with disabilities within the community. Mooney, a member of the former St. James United Methodist Church in Palatka, was well-liked with an outgoing personality. Mooney was also known to invite other Arc clients to church. He died Jan. 8, 1998, after a short illness at the age of 43, according to findagrave.com. He is buried at Oak Hill West Cemetery in Palatka. 'The annual award is a chance to recognize an individual who displays the qualities of leadership, independence and courage,' Dame said. 'These were hallmarks of Eddie Mooney's life.' Other award winners at the banquet included Russell Washington, who won the Employment Excellence Award, Michelle Huffman, who won the Peter Prater Self-Advocacy Award, and Kevin Spence, who won the Community Contributions Award. Submitted photo – From left, Sharon Betts, direct service provider; Elethyia Cruz, group home manager; award winner Michelle Huffman; Patty Dame manager of administrative services; and award winner Russell Washington gather for a picture at the banquet. Beck Automotive Group was also recognized at the award ceremony, receiving the Lucille Flint Volunteerism Award. 'We are so thankful for everything that they have done and continue to do for the people we serve,' Dame said. 'All of our winners have worked so hard and are very deserving of their awards.' Jonathan Hurt has an extensive history with the Arc. Prior to moving to Palatka, he worked for 17 years through the Arc in Columbus, Ohio, securing employment as a packager at a warehouse in the area. He and his father moved to Palatka in 2018. Once in Putnam County, Jonathan Hurt decided he wanted to learn more and entered Project SEARCH, a program Beck hosts that educates and trains adults with disabilities to learn life skills and job skills to obtain marketable employment in an integrated setting, according to a news release from the Arc of Putnam County. 'He did great in the classroom, where he was very encouraging to all of his classmates, always trying to lift up those who might be having a bad day,' Dame said. 'He also did well at all of his internships.' Upon graduation, Jonathan Hurt was hired by Goodwill Industries of Palatka, where he still works and continues to do well, Dame said. 'Jonathan is very deserving of this prestigious award,' she said. Cliff Hurt is proud of his son, the advancements he's made and the recognition he's received. Submitted photo – Kevin Spence was named the winner of the Community Contributions Award. 'I got emotional at the ceremony even though I knew he was getting the award,' he said. 'I am very proud of him.' Jonathan Hurt said he enjoys working at Goodwill. 'I love it,' he said. 'I look forward to going to work every day, and Candace and my coworkers are very nice.' Jonathan Hurt lives with his dad in Palatka but hopes to find his own housing soon. Cliff Hurt said his son loves anything that deals with their religion, going to meetings and watching religious videos. He also enjoys going to Disney on Ice and to Disney plays. 'Since being here, he has worked in the community, and everywhere we go, someone knows him,' Cliff Hurt said. Dame agrees. 'He is a friend to everyone he meets,' she said. 'He makes your day brighter just by saying, ‘Good morning.''

title: Numerous species, varieties to be at plant sale
description: Joy A. McGuirl-Hadley is calling for all hands on deck when the Putnam County Master Gardeners has its annual plant sale on Saturday. As the event chairwoman for the past three years and a Master…
content:
Joy A. McGuirl-Hadley is calling for all hands on deck when the Putnam County Master Gardeners has its annual plant sale on Saturday.
As the event chairwoman for the past three years and a Master Gardener, McGuirl-Hadley is excited about this year's event, which will be from 9 a.m. – 1 p.m. under the pavilion at the Putnam County Fairgrounds, 118 Fairgrounds Road in East Palatka.
More than 1,500 plants, including citrus, blueberry bushes, herbs, pollinators, cacti, succulents, vegetables and flowering plants, will be available at the sale while they last. More than a third of the plants are native to Florida and about 800 come from local Master Gardeners' gardens. Prices will range from $2 to $55, with the higher price for the star of the sale, the Sugar Belle orange trees the University of Florida developed and premiered at last year's event.
'The orange trees were developed by the university to be tolerant of citrus greening disease if properly cared for,' McGuirl-Hadley said. 'We sell them with their nets, which the university recommends stay on the tree for two years.'
According to McGuirl-Hadley, the nets let the plants get big and strong before being exposed to the insects in people's gardens that carry the disease.
'The two I bought last year are now about 5 feet tall and beautiful in their safe-netted cocoons for one more year,' she said.
A Welaka resident McGuirl-Hadley said she has more than 100 plants coming out of her own garden this year alone.
'Some of them include three different types of bromeliads, night blooming Cereus, ground orchards, Christmas cactus, aloe, and rhizomes of edible ginger and turmeric,' she said.
Admission to the sale is free. The public is invited. No pets are allowed and shoppers are invited to bring their own wagons.
TRISHA MURPHY/Palatka Daily News – Joy A. McGuirl-Hadley stands next to a wagon filled with some of the Sugar Belle orange trees that will be available at the Putnam County Master Gardeners plant sale Saturday. For details, contact Julio Perez, horticulture agent for the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension of Putnam County, at pjulio@ufl.edu or 386-329-0318.
McGuirl-Hadley said most of the local Master Gardeners will be working the sale and answering questions about plant care, optimum planting locations and conditions, and what to do about pests in the garden.
'I have learned that natively grown plants make the best transition into local gardens,' she said. 'They are already proven winners that are familiar with the local growing cycles and weather conditions. Lots of the plants are native to Florida and we never sell invasive plants.'
McGuirl-Hadley said last year's sale attracted more than 400 in attendance.
'We have a steady following of folks that come every year and hope for some first-timers to join us this year,' she said. 'This is our only fundraising event.'
According to McGuirl-Hadley, proceeds from the sale will go to fund group operations such as training new Master Gardener volunteers and horticultural programs for the community, schools and nonprofits.
McGuirl-Hadley added there are several new types of plants for sale because Master Gardeners have different interests and focus on growing different types and varieties of plants.
McGuirl-Hadley said she has two favorite plants, one flowering and one herb, that will be at the sale.
'Some angel trumpets with their big, beautiful coral flowers are one of my favorites while the other is my African basil,' she said. 'They have beautiful, pink flowers that attract pollinators and, of course, make the best pesto sauce.'
McGuirl-Hadley said her garden is currently alive with spring color.
'I love the lush growth and harvesting my own herbs, blueberries and citrus for cooking and eating,' she said. 'We are hoping the public will come to the sale and take home a new friend for their porch or garden.'

title: Hog Waller crash leaves child, 7, dead
description: A 7-year-old died Sunday after the all-terrain vehicle on which he was riding overturned in a well-known mudbogging park, authorities reported. The boy succumbed to his injuries following a single…
content:
A 7-year-old died Sunday after the all-terrain vehicle on which he was riding overturned in a well-known mudbogging park, authorities reported. The boy succumbed to his injuries following a single-vehicle vehicle crash at Hog Waller, 454 County Road 310 in Palatka, according to a Florida Highway Patrol report. The child's father, 32, was driving the ATV through Hog Waller Campground & ATV Resort around 2:06 p.m. Sunday when the vehicle made a sharp turn and flipped, the report reads. The ATV overturned onto the boy, who had been seated behind his father, the report states. When the ATV flipped over, the boy also struck a tree stump, according to the agency. The boy was transported to HCA Florida Putnam Hospital in Palatka, where he later died. His father sustained only minor injuries, FHP reported. The two, who were from Reddick, hadn't been wearing seatbelts or helmets, authorities said. Sunday's death is at least the fifth reported to FHP since 2019, and there were other crashes where victims sustained critical injuries. Before operating ATVs at Hog Waller, guests must sign consent waivers, which warn of the dangers they face and absolve the park of liability if crashes occur. The waivers to enter Hog Waller, also listed as Magnolia Dunes in court papers, state a parent gives up their and their child's right to sue even if death happens. The park's limited liability waivers cover the possible endangerment of children and adults. People who do not sign the waivers are not allowed to enter, according to the forms. 'You are agreeing that, even if Magnolia Dunes, LLC, uses reasonable care in providing this activity, there is a chance your child may be seriously injured or killed by participating in this activity because there are certain dangers inherent in the activity which cannot be avoided or eliminated,' the waiver a parent or guardian must sign states.

title: Putnam teachers recognized for academic tenacity
description: School officials are celebrating two local teachers, one of whom learned this week she'd been selected to attend a teaching program and the other who is the first educator from Florida to receive a…
content:
School officials are celebrating two local teachers, one of whom learned this week she'd been selected to attend a teaching program and the other who is the first educator from Florida to receive a literary award.
Interlachen Junior-Senior High School teacher Katie Hess was selected Tuesday to attend the Georgia Council on Economic Education summer program, a partnership with Georgia-Pacific.
The economics teacher and girls weightlifting coach will spend four days in June learning about better practices for teaching economics in high schools, according to the council. Hess said she will travel around Atlanta to learn about monetary policies, entrepreneurship and personal finance from economics experts.
'I've taught economics for three years now at IHS,' Hess said. 'It's one of those classes that you want to make more real for the students. And I figured, when I looked at the itinerary, there were a lot of things on there that piqued my interest, and so I thought, ‘Why not go ahead and apply for (the program)?''
Other parts of the program include learning about economics through trivia nights, hearing from speakers from Georgia-Pacific and touring the Waffle House Museum, according to the itinerary.
Hess has taught for 15 years and thought she could learn much from the program. She said she wants to make her economics classes fun, and this program could amplify her efforts.
Georgia Council officials selected just 25 people nationwide, and Hess said she is one of only two people chosen from Florida.
'I'm really looking forward to it,' she said.
Superintendent Rick Surrency said he's proud of Hess and the opportunity she has been presented. He believes the four-day excursion will significantly benefit her students.
'Mrs. Hess is a superb educator and spends many hours planning lessons and collaborating with her peers,' he said in an email. 'I have no doubt she will use this learning experience to share with her colleagues in our district-wide learning communities.'
Principal Amber Symonds called Hess a lifelong learner who always looks for ways to grow.
'She is a teacher that is truly in the profession for the betterment of kids,' Symonds said.
Hess, who taught middle school in Putnam County before junior and senior high schools merged, has supported her students from their middle school years to their senior year, Symonds said.
Interlachen is blessed to have Hess as a teacher, said Symonds, who wishes every student could learn from someone like Hess.
'She is a very, very intelligent lady that has the skill of sharing knowledge with kids on a level that they can understand,' Symonds said. 'To me, she's the total package because not only does she have the content and has that desire to know the content. She has a great rapport with kids. So, she can bring it all together.'
Over in Florahome, Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School officials are celebrating English teacher Catelyn Boze.
The Dante Society of America awarded Boze the Robert M. Durling Prize for being the best classics teacher in the country. The prize, named after a distinguished literature professor at the University of California, recognizes educators who teach Italian poet Dante Alighieri.
Alighieri is best known for authoring 'The Divine Comedy,' which Boze teaches in her 11th and 12th grade classes.
She said the award is special because she wrote her undergraduate thesis on 'The Divine Comedy' at the University of Florida.
'It's a real kind of honor to get this award because, first of all, I think it represents really positive things about our school and the level of teaching that we're aspiring to,' Boze said. 'And it's a book that means a lot to me.'
Photo submitted by Rick Surrency – Catelyn Boze, Leah Zabad, Gavin Miles, Audrey Redman and Superintendent Rick Surrency visit Bass Capital Radio on Wednesday to talk about the students' fourth-place ranking at the recent Florida Commissioner's Academic Challenge. Boze is the first recipient from Florida and the first public school teacher to receive the award since its inception in 2016, according to the society's website.
'Our teaching is at that level,' she said. 'Our kids are at that level. We just have to have that belief in what kids are capable of.'
Boze is in her 10th year of teaching at Q.I. Roberts and said she wouldn't want to be anywhere else.
Principal Joe Theobold said Boze is driven to make students think hard about how past literature is still relevant.
Boze, who has been teaching Alighieri's work for four years, said students like it because it teaches them about persistence, how other literature relates to Alighieri and why people study literature, culture and history.
'Mrs. Boze is a fascinating teacher,' Theobold said. 'While she has the knowledge to be a researcher or professor, her pedagogy is so remarkably technical she gets great results and deep engagement from her students.'
Surrency said Boze is a teacher who continues to excel and contributes to the success of Q.I. Roberts. She recently spoke on a radio program about her students and some of the accolades they recently won, the superintendent said.
'While listening to Mrs. Boze talk about her students and their experiences, it is obvious that she has a heart for teaching,' Surrency said. 'The Durling Prize is a prestigious and well-deserved honor for Catelyn Boze.'

IN THE CHANCERY COURT FOR GRAINGER COUNTY, TENNESSEE No. 2022-CH-20 WOODS R. RUSSELL A/K/A RUSSELL WOODS Plaintiff, v. JASON FAULKNER, DENNIS FAULKNER, AND GEORGE FAULKNER Defendants. NOTICE OF ENTRY REQUESTED ORDER ALLOWING SERVICE BY PUBLICATION IN LIEU OF PERSONAL SERVICE Plaintiff, Woods R. Russell A/K/A Russell Woods, has filed a Motion for an Order allowing service of process upon defendant, Dennis Faulkner, by publication in lieu of personal service. Plaintiff has demonstrated by affidavit that the residence of the defendants are unknown and cannot be ascertained based on diligent inquiry. It is therefore ORDERED, that the Clerk and Master shall: 1. Forthwith cause a copy of this order to be published, for four (4) consecutive weeks in the Palatka Daily News, which newspaper is the newspaper of general circulation in Putnam County, Florida. 2. The copy of this order that is to be published shall include the names of the parties to this action, the name of this Court, and the location at which this Court is held. 3. The copy of this Order that is published shall further notify the defendant, Dennis Faulkner, that he must answer or otherwise respond to the complaint in this action within 30 days of the fourth weekly publication of this order, and if he does not answer or otherwise respond a default judgment shall be entered against him at a future date. ENTERED this the 9 day of May, 2024. /s/ Chancellor Telford Forgety Chancellor Telford Forgety, Special Judge Approved for Entry: /s/ Pepper C. Bowser Peper C. Bowser, BPR # 025081 P.O. BOX 35 Rutledge, TN 37861 (865) 828-3533 Pep540@msn.com CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE Pursuant to Rule 58 off the Tenn. Rules of Civil Procedure, I, Vickie Greenlee, hereby certify that a true and exact copy of the foregoing ORDER has been delivered to Pepper Bowser, Esq., attorney for Plaintiff, at P.O. Box 35, Rutledge, Tennessee 37861, Mr. Jason Faulkner at 1289 Indian Creek Road, Thorn Hill, Tennessee 37881, and Mr. Dennis Faulkner at 211 Beaver Lane, Palatka, FL 32177 within five (5) days of its entry, by placing same in the U.S. Mail with sufficient postage to carry it to its destination This the 13 day of May, 2024. /s/ Vickie B Greenlee Clerk Legal No. 00102687 05/18, 05/25, 06/01, 06/08/24

title: Putnam Celebrates Independence
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Putnam County residents turned out in their best red, white and blue outfits Thursday to wish America a happy birthday.
content:
Putnam County residents turned out in their best red, white and blue outfits Thursday to wish America a happy birthday.
The town of Interlachen and the city of Palatka hosted Independence Day festivities that drew in hundreds, if not thousands, of spectators.
People packed the streets of Interlachen early for kids activities, games and the popular parade downtown. State Rep. Bobby Payne, R-Palatka, served as the parade's grand marshal and led a series of items, including horses, candy and blow-up rubber ducks decorated for the Fourth of July.
Vendor booths wrapped around Atlantic Avenue and Washington Street while children cooled off colorful water slides or played putt-putt golf next to the town's famous caboose.
Interlachen resident Kathie Kelley joined in on the celebrations while watching over the West Putnam Pop Warner. Kelley, who has been attending Interlachen's Independence Day celebrations for 45 years, enjoyed carrying on the patriotic vibe of the day while informing spectators about the area's youth sports scene.
'It was awesome this year,' Kelley said after the parade. 'I would have liked to have seen a lot more children involvement within the parade, but it was awesome.'
Putnam County Board of Commissioners Chairman Larry Harvey has spent nearly 40 years organizing the town's Independence Day events. Kelley commended him for always putting a lot of effort into the event.
'Larry does a great job on getting this together, works very, very hard,' Kelley said.' 'Always has. This year, it was great.'
The city of Palatka hosted its Fourth of July bash later in the day. Families from Putnam County and surrounding areas set up chairs and blankets from Riverfront Park, 100 Memorial Parkway, to River Street. Kids played with sparklers as the sun went down, and boats dotted the St. Johns River to get a different view of the fireworks show.
While waiting for the pyrotechnics to begin, some people visited the St. Johns River Center, 102 N. First St. in Palatka, to learn about the river and the local ecosystem.
Attendees Shelby and Brian Boswell don't live in Palatka, but they visited her family and stayed to watch the fireworks with their daughters.
'I get to be with my family,' she said. 'It's the Fourth of July, and it's my hometown.'

title: Group debuting new exhibit, hopes to boost art scene
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Being an artist is in Marty Johnson's DNA and is a trait she believes everyone has in common.
content:
Body
Being an artist is in Marty Johnson's DNA and is a trait she believes everyone has in common.
'I think we are all born artists and possess creativity,' the East Palatka resident said. 'Along the way as we navigate through life, we find a way to express ourselves.'
Johnson will be exhibiting those expressions along with the works of 19 other area artists beginning today during the Gathering Artists of Putnam's next exhibit at its new location, 712 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka. The exhibit is titled 'New Beginnings.'
The opening reception will be from 5–8 p.m. today with free refreshments and drinks for guests. The exhibit will be on display through Sept. 8, with exhibit hours from 10 a.m. – 5 p.m. on Mondays through Saturdays and from 11 a.m. – 3 p.m. on Sundays.
Attendance on Mondays and Tuesdays is by appointment only. For details, call any GAP member, call Shelley Schenker at 561-635-9399 or visit gatheringartistsofputnam.com.
According to Johnson, GAP's mission is to showcase visual artists and artisans of Putnam County, promote a visionary community spirit and become a creative force in the revitalization of the city of Palatka and Putnam County through the arts.
'GAP formed a little over a year ago to fill a need in Putnam County and in particular showcase local artists in the Palatka downtown area,' she said. 'This allows for artists to network, show their work and help revitalize the Palatka downtown area.'
The exhibit will include jewelry, hanging mobiles, abstract paintings, acrylic, oil and watercolors, landscapes, figures and animal friends.
'We want to get the word out that we would love to have ceramic and or sculpture artwork, too,' Johnson said. 'If there's an artist out there wanting to show their work, we'd love to meet with them.'
Johnson said her art medium of choice is cattle markers, but her work is primarily intuitive. She enjoys collaging and allowing the materials to dictate the process and experience.
'I find this method to be both exciting and never quite know where I'm going with it, but the end result has been extremely rewarding,' she said.
Johnson has discovered through her own creative journey that people express themselves in different ways.
'The writer through his or her words and the musician through their melodies and lyrics,' she said. 'My mother was very creative and she allowed us the freedom to explore making art and at times making quite a mess.'
Johnson said she has been an artist since I could hold a pencil or crayon.
'My real start happened when I returned to college and studied fine arts, which gave me a strong base for techniques and craftsmanship,' she said. 'Also studying art history was very inspirational. My first painting sold during my student art exhibit and shortly after I started a small business leasing artwork created by several local artists to local businesses and vacant office space, which led me to network with the city of Spokane, Washington, to help revitalize their downtown area.'
Johnson said the weekend show is particularly special to her, especially since it's the group's first showing as the newly formed Gathering Artists of Putnam LLC.
'There was a lot of thought, conversations and work involved in making this a reality,' she said. 'We want to be an integral part of Putnam County and the city of Palatka's art community.'
Johnson hopes visitors to the exhibit will enjoy the ambiance and art experience, and have an opportunity to speak with the artists about their work and art in general.
'We hope there will be an opportunity to educate the public on the visual arts and the diversity in mediums and styles,' she said.
GAP vice president Hollis Ellis hopes the exhibits and the 'Art on the Avenue' storefront window project are important to local artists.
'Until recently, there were very few brick-and-mortar options for artists to show work in Putnam County and specifically Palatka,' said Ellis, who primarily works in acrylics on recycled wood panels or natural craft paper. 'At the same time, there were few opportunities for the wider Putnam County community to view and purchase technically excellent original artwork without traveling outside the county. We hope Gathering Artists of Putnam will continue to be a win-win experience for all. In fact, in the future, we hope to become more involved in art education for youth as well as adults in the community, and several of our artists are already providing creative educational experiences within Putnam County.'

title: Student 1 of 20 selected for national reading honor
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Bryan Jenkins of Palatka is top-notch when it comes to working hard and reaching goals.
content:
Body
Bryan Jenkins of Palatka is top-notch when it comes to working hard and reaching goals.
Anyone who doubts that can ask those involved with the Read 180 program at Putnam Academy of Arts and Sciences, where he will be starting eighth grade Aug. 12.
'The program is a research-based, intensive reading program designed for students who are reading one or more years below grade level,' said Sharon Merwin, his teacher.
Jenkins, 13, was one of 20 students in the nation who were recognized by textbook publishing company Houghton Mifflin Harcourt during the 18th annual 180 Awards this year. Jenkins was the only student in Florida who received the honor thanks to the help of his teachers and his own hard work in the program.
'Bryan started off as a student who was disruptive at times,' said Merwin, who has been teaching Read 180 for two years and has been an educator in Putnam County for 11 years. But during his sixth grade year, he started to make achievements in reading, which led to less frustration and better behavior.'
Merwin said Jenkins' positive behavior carried over into his other academic subjects and inspired him to strive to be a better student.
According to Jenkins, Merwin's goal is to set a positive example for other students who are having a hard time and to show compassion to the needs of others at the school.
'I was really surprised that I was the only student in Florida that got the award,' he said.
Victoria Gibbs, Jenkins' mom, gives credit to her son for working hard and to the staff at Putnam Academy of Arts and Sciences for using the Individual Educational Program to offer him the extra help he needed.
'It gave him a sense of responsibility,' she said. 'He began to take more notice of himself at school. It was a different environment for him. He had discipline issues at elementary school because he needed one-on-one attention, and when he went to Putnam Academy of Arts and Sciences, he got it.'
Gibbs said her son receiving the Read 180 recognition has given him a feeling of accomplishment, and she attributes that recognition to Merwin.
'She has been there tremendously from Day 1,' she said. 'She is like a school mom. She has been very, very supportive.'
When describing the Read 180 program, Merwin said it was through the comprehensive intervention curriculum that includes age-appropriate, teacher-led, adaptive instruction that incorporates foundational literacy, vocabulary, language, comprehension and writing to achieve reading proficiency for students in grades three through 12.
Merwin said Jenkins experienced such growth in reading during his seventh grade year that he started to help other students, and, as a result, his behavior problems in class decreased.
'We are thrilled that Bryan's reading improvement was recognized,' Putnam Academy Principal Curtis Ellis said. 'With the help of his teachers and because of his efforts, he has blossomed from a misbehaving, non-reader to a school leader who now reads on grade level and volunteers to help others improve as well.'
Merwin believes Jenkins had not been academically challenged until he learned the school's staff would not only hold him accountable but would also push him to his full potential.
'He then began to strive for success,' she said. 'He was mentored by staff on appropriate behaviors, and small successes were celebrated throughout his growth journey. His success and improvement is from his hard work, support and the Read 180 curriculum.'
Students who receive the 180 Award are nominated by educators, coaches, intervention specialists, administrators or individuals familiar with students' exceptional work using HMH's Read 180 programs. They are then evaluated on academic growth, personal growth, innovative projects and other criteria.
Jenkins, who met all of the requirements, was nominated by Merwin.
Houghton Mifflin Harcourt representative Janette Sangster presented the award to Jenkins at Putnam Academy's end-of-year ceremony in May.
Merwin said everyone who knows Jenkins is proud of his accomplishments.
'He is a student who exemplifies hard work and dedication to his academic growth,' she said. 'His success allows other students to see that if he can do this, so can they.'
During his spare time, Jenkins enjoys playing video games, helping out with his animals, playing with his dog and spending time with his brother playing basketball.
Jenkins has learned to work hard at school, enjoy reading and stop playing around. He plans to carry his previous success and build upon it when he starts eighth grade in less than two weeks.
'I had to get serious with it,' he said of his studies and behavior. 'I've heard my mom and teachers say, 'Hard work pays off.' It definitely does.'

title: Health department warns of algae in South Putnam
author: News Staff
description: Local health officials are encouraging people to take caution around Crescent Lake because of the algae blooms that have been detected.
content:
Local health officials are encouraging people to take caution around Crescent Lake because of the algae blooms that have been detected.
In a press release Friday, the Florida Department of Health in Putnam County said a water sample taken Wednesday alerted the agency to blue-green algae toxins in the lake.
The toxins were found at the mouth of Dunns Creek, according to the health department.
'Blue-green algae are a type of bacteria that is common in Florida's freshwater environments,' the health department stated in a press release. 'A bloom occurs when rapid growth of algae leads to an accumulation of individual cells that discolor water and often produce floating mats that emit unpleasant odors.'
People should not drink, swim or use watercraft in areas of the water where they can see algae blooms, according to a health department press release. Pets and livestock should stay away from the area, and people should not cook with water that has algal contaminations, according to the release.
People who come into contact with possibly contaminated water should wash their clothes and skin thoroughly, the press release states.
'Do not cook or clean dishes with water contaminated by algae blooms. Boiling the water will not eliminate toxins,' health officials said in the statement. 'Eating fillets from healthy fish caught in freshwater lakes experiencing blooms is safe. Rinse fish fillets with tap or bottled water, throw out the guts, and cook fish thoroughly. Do not eat shellfish in waters with algae blooms.'
If people have questions, they can call the health department at 386-326-7189.

title: Putnam welcomes students back on first day of school
author: Carter Mudgett
description: Crescent City was full of change on Monday, both in the present and on the horizon.
content:
Body
Crescent City was full of change on Monday, both in the present and on the horizon.
Teachers and administrators at Middleton-Burney Elementary School and Crescent City Junior-Senior High School welcomed around 2,000 students with open arms.
At Middleton-Burney, parents lined up to walk their child to class around 7:10. The line stretched far down the sidewalk, with parents still trickling in even after the Pledge of Allegiance at 8 a.m.
Principal Tiffany Scranton called it 'a wonderful start' to the year.
'We had a huge turnout with families walking students to class,' she said. 'We've had a great outpouring of district support and volunteers helping us make sure everything is handled in a safe and efficient way. And we are grateful that our parents understand that it takes a little more time but it's worth it to make our babies safe.'
Teachers stood outside classroom doors, reconnecting with old students, meeting new ones and helping guide each one to their first class.
It was all smiles, albeit some stress too, as students steadily made their way through the front gate.
'(I'm) super excited,' said Shauntie McLeod, a new paraprofessional at Middleton-Burney. 'I'm gonna be the (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) teacher so we're going to be doing a lot of cool projects this year.'
Less than an hour after the start-of-school bell rang at Middleton-Burney, Crescent City High students were already getting packed into the gymnasium and cafeteria before the first bell set them loose in the hallways.
'Even after my 25th year, I still get nervous the very first day of school,' Principal Tim Adams said. 'I'm nervous because I want things to run well. I want my kids to have a great day. I want my teachers to have a great day. … It's natural to be nervous.'
'The sky's the limit'
There's a lot of change coming down the pipe and some already set in motion at both South Putnam schools.
For those at Middleton-Burney, Monday was potentially their last first day of school at 1020 Huntington Road. Less than a mile away, district officials are preparing to break ground on a new elementary school Friday afternoon.
If all goes to plan, officials hope to move into the new building either before or during the 2025-2026 school year, said Superintendent Rick Surrency, who was at both Crescent City schools Monday morning to greet parents and welcome back students.
Middleton-Burney's principal is looking forward to moving into the new building, specifically because it means having more space.
'Our current campus limits activities and gatherings because we just don't have the space. With our new campus, the sky is the limit,' Scranton said with relief. 'Until then, we will continue to clean and Band-Aid what we have because we take pride in where we serve but can't wait for the new campus.'
It's a similar story at Crescent City High, where the school is undergoing a gradual expansion to add more room to what's already there.
School leaders are emphasizing flexibility for students, faculty and staff.
'Flexibility because as we are going through the process,' Adams said. 'There might be buildings that are torn down and so we change to other areas or temporary venting going up to help support safety of students. Knowing that there's change because by next August, we should have at least 25 classrooms to move into.'
Building student achievement
In total, over 10,000 students walked through the front doors of Putnam County School District buildings Monday, according to the district. Always striving for improvement, district leaders hope it will be a pivotal year.
Beyond literal construction, the school year began after it was announced the district was reaccredited in STEM instruction and taking a harder focus on that curriculum.
The district is also looking to achieve a B grade from the Florida Department of Education. That's not just a district-wide goal. It's an individual school goal too.
Crescent City High is just 7% away from being a B school, said Adams, who marks his fourth year at the helm this year.
Starting from the ground up, he said improving student learning is all about building true relationships with each student.
'The more relationships you build, the more comfortable the kids get,' he said. 'And the more comfortable the kids get, the more effort they want to put in, not just for themselves and their family but also the school and the teachers.'

title: District breaks ground on new elementary school
author: Carter Mudgett
description: By Carter Mudgett and Sarah Cavacini
content:
Body
Middleton-Burney Elementary School Principal Tiffany Scranton wasn't afraid to get her hands dirty Friday morning. In fact, she had been looking forward to it for a while.
The Putnam County School District broke ground at the site of a new elementary school in Crescent City early Friday morning. Eleven Middleton-Burney students tossed the first shovelfuls of dirt to mark the start of construction on the $68 million elementary school.
Scranton took a bag of that dirt from 1282 Huntington Road back to her school to act as a reminder of what is to come.
'We have 1,081 students right now and I was only able to bring 11 with me this morning,' she said. 'But I told them before I left I was bringing a piece of our new home to our current home. So this dirt is going to go in a jar and be displayed in our front office with the Tonka truck (from the groundbreaking ceremony) just to remind everyone that new is coming and we're ready to grow.'
District officials hope to move Middleton-Burney students and staff into the currently-unnamed facility sometime before or during the 2025-2026 school year, Superintendent Rick Surrency said.
The Crescent City Commission last week approved the final land rezoning cases required for the district to begin construction, and district officials were hot on their heels to get the project in motion.
'Most importantly, it's a great day for our youth because what all of us have done is we've put an investment in their futures,' said Crescent City Mayor Michele Myers, calling Friday a great day for South Putnam. 'We've told them how important they are and how important their futures are.'
The new school is part of the school district's 10-year revitalization plan, the planning process for which began in 2020. Surrency likened the process to a tightrope walker traversing a line between two tall buildings and how once they had one foot on the rope, there was no turning back.
'Folks, we've been on the tightrope for a long time now, for the last four years, and we are walking across that tightrope,' he said. 'And I'm very happy that through all thick and thin and through all the people that have second-guessed things, we are building a school.'
The day brought on a sense of deja vu for Scranton, who said she remembered being a student and helping plant the azaleas at Browning-Pearce Elementary School when it first opened.
'We're talking about generations of prayers and hopes coming to reality right now,' she said.
Friday's groundbreaking was a full-circle moment, said Scranton, who called herself a 'product of Putnam County.'
As of Friday, the total cost of the project is $68,657,691, according to James Marini, the project manager from Ajax Building Corp., the company contracted to construct the school.
District officials thanked taxpayers who trusted the district enough to vote for the general obligation bond referendum in the November 2022 general election.
'You're going to see evidence of those funds being spent for the betterment of this community right here today,' Surrency said.
Friday's groundbreaking is part of the first phase of the district's revitalization plan, which also includes the construction of a Palatka elementary school already in progress.
Phase 2 will see the district build a second Palatka elementary school and an elementary school in Melrose. During Phase 3, extensive renovations will be carried out at Browning-Pearce Elementary School in San Mateo and Robert H. Jenkins Jr. Elementary School in Interlachen.
In addition to building new elementary schools, the district is using state funds to construct a replacement for Crescent City Junior-Senior High School. A groundbreaking ceremony for that project took place earlier this year.
In Phases 2 and 3 of the junior-senior high school builds, the district will be applying for state funds to build new facilities in Interlachen and Palatka, respectively.
'It is a new day in Putnam County, and these precious children here deserve the best that we can provide for them,' said Surrency. 'And I don't care what anybody else is doing in any other county. Putnam County's children deserve the best.'
Editor Brandon D. Oliver contributed to this story.

'We are so excited about having this band coming to play and I know guests will not be disappointed with the great lively music they perform,' said Denise Aiken, executive director of the Arts Council of Greater Palatka.
The concert will be from 7–9 p.m. Friday at the Scarlett-Hill Theater inside the Larimer Arts Center, 216 Reid St. in Palatka. Doors will open at 6:30 p.m. The cost is $15 at the door. Light refreshments will be served.
Janine Rainville, a member of the band who plays the upright bass, said The New Hoppers play a blend of bluegrass intertwined with the old country sound as well as originals.
Other band members include Mike Elias on guitar, Brian Lappin on banjo and Bob Parsons on the mandolin.
'We have been entertaining for many years across North Florida,' she said.
Some of those places include festivals, private parties and restaurants among other places.
Aiken hopes the public will come out and show their support for the performers.
'The band members have collaborated to create and give an enjoyable experience to those who come to the show to have fun and enjoy themselves while they play their toe-tapping music,' Aiken said. 'We want everyone to come out and have a great evening with us.'
The Arts Council is the state-designated local arts agency for Putnam County and is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit.
The Arts Council is partnering with Ramicah Johnson, the executive director of the Putnam Habitat for Humanity for the concert.
Arts Council supporters are the Putnam County Tourist Development Council, the city of Palatka and other patrons. Volunteers are always welcome. For details, email artsinputnam@aol.com.
Rainville, who lives in Pomona Park, can't wait for her first time performing at the Larimer with The New Hoppers.
'I'm looking forward to connecting with the people,' she said. 'It's a beautiful building and we are hoping for many more visits to come.'

title: Top 2 judge hopefuls to compete in November
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: The contest to become a Putnam County judge was narrowed down to two contenders after the unofficial primary results were tallied Tuesday.
content:
Body
The contest to become a Putnam County judge was narrowed down to two contenders after the unofficial primary results were tallied Tuesday.
Judge Anne Marie Gennusa, who won 6,014 votes (45.62%), and challenger Alex Sharp, who received 5,062 votes (38.4%), will compete in a runoff in the Nov. 5 general election. The two were in the primary race Constance Daniels, who earned 2,106 votes (15.98%).
Had a competitor won 50% of the vote plus at least one additional vote, that candidate would have won Tuesday's primary outright and a runoff would not have been unnecessary.
Although she has more campaigning in her future, Gennusa said she was grateful for Putnam voters showing her such support in the primary.
'I am so grateful that I have been entrusted as much as I have by the people of Putnam County,' she said after the final results were posted.
This was the first time Gennusa, who was appointed to the bench in April 2023, had run for office. She said she made sure to not let campaigning get in the way of her full-time job in the courtroom, but she is looking forward to getting back out there to meet more potential voters.
With a little over two months left before the general election, she knows time will fly by. But she is looking forward to hitting the campaign trail once again while still fulfilling her judicial duties.
'Time has flown by pretty quickly,' Gennusa said. '… We're going to still do what we did (leading up to the primary): meeting people, seeing the voters. For me, it's business as usual.'
Although he did not win the most votes, Sharp was thankful for his supporters and hopes to come out on top in November.
The general election will be a different beast, he said, mainly because of the increased number of people expected to vote in November. The Elections Office website showed Putnam County had a 31.23% voter turnout, but the turnout for previous presidential elections has averaged around 70% or higher.
'I want to thank all of my family and supporters who got us to that point,' Sharp said about his primary performance. 'Obviously, we have some more work to do. Hopefully, we can get the word out and win over those voters.'
Sharp commended Gennusa and Daniels for running clean races and said he looks forward to the contest against Gennusa in November.
Despite not being the outright winner Tuesday, Sharp still looked on the bright side.
'It was a great experience,' he said. 'We went against an incumbent judge and survived the primary.'
Tuesday's results are expected to be official Aug. 27, according to Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III.

title: 3-year-old found dead in Satsuma waterway
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The search for a missing child ended Tuesday after two hours when his body was discovered in a canal near his home, authorities said.
content:
Body
The search for a missing child ended Tuesday after two hours when his body was discovered in a canal near his home, authorities said.
Gabriel Paguio, 3, was located around 5:30 p.m. Tuesday after going missing from his Clearwater Road home at about 3:30 p.m., Putnam County Sheriff's Office spokeswoman Allison Waters-Merritt said.
Paguio is believed to have been autistic, she said. His family had been looking into getting an official diagnosis but had not yet received it, Waters-Merritt said.
Paguio's family had been searching for the child for about 20 minutes before they called 911, the spokeswoman said.
'At this time, we ask for you to say a prayer for the family,' Sheriff Gator DeLoach said in a Facebook statement. 'No family should undergo the tragedy of losing their child, and we ask for comfort from our community to support them as they navigate the difficult journey ahead.'
Authorities are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the boy's death.

title: Schools to close Thursday as Helene to make landfall
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Tuesday afternoon's weather update predicted the tropical storm charging toward the Gulf Coast might spare Putnam County from severe damage, but local officials are taking precautions to be prepare
content:
Tuesday afternoon's weather update predicted the tropical storm charging toward the Gulf Coast might spare Putnam County from severe damage, but local officials are taking precautions to be prepared in case the path changes.
Meteorologists from the National Weather Service predicted Tropical Storm Helene to make landfall Thursday in Florida.
Deputy County Administrator J.R. Grimes said it's still unknown exactly what time Helene, which elevated to a tropical storm only Tuesday, will make landfall, but government officials are working to make sure the county is as prepared as possible.
'The issue we're going to have with this one is we don't have a lot of time to act once it hits the Gulf of Mexico,' he said Tuesday during the Board of County Commissioners meeting.
In preparation, county officials have opened eight sandbag sites:
– 5226 Silver Lake Drive in Palatka.
– 341 Paradise Circle in San Mateo.
– 51 Sportsman Drive in Welaka.
– Jonas Road in Crescent City.
– 145 W. Washington St. in Hawthorne.
– 114 S. 11th St. in Palatka.
– 223 Putnam County Blvd. in East Palatka.
– 107 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka.
The sites are self-serve and people should bring a shovel, Putnam County Emergency Management officials posted on Facebook.
Putnam County School District Superintendent Rick Surrency said Kelly Smith Elementary, 141 Kelley Smith School Road in Palatka, will open for people with special needs after school dismisses today.
All district schools will be closed Thursday and all activities will be canceled, he added.
'Decisions will be announced tomorrow about the opening of other shelters,' Surrency said Tuesday via text. 'We will make a decision about school for Friday on Thursday.'
St. Johns River State College posted Tuesday on Facebook to say all classes will be closed Thursday and Friday, and athletic events will be canceled Thursday.
The county was not under a storm watch Tuesday afternoon, according to The Weather Channel, but the agency said people near the St. Johns River basin might see storm surges of up to 3 feet Thursday. Meteorologists expect Helene to make landfall in the Big Bend area of Florida late Thursday before moving into the Panhandle and up to Southeast Georgia.
The Weather Channel said Gilchrist, Suwannee, western Alachua and western Marion counties were under a Hurricane watch Tuesday evening.
While Putnam may not see the worst of the storm, Grimes said he just wants everyone to stay safe.
'We have to prepare for the worst in this and hope for the best,' he said. 'I would much rather have everything ready to go and not need it than need it and not have it all set up and ready to go.'

title: Shelters to open as Helene strengthens to a hurricane
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Helene's intensifying Wednesday from a tropical storm to a hurricane incited school and extracurricular activity cancellations and government office closures across Putnam County.
content:
Body
Helene's intensifying Wednesday from a tropical storm to a hurricane incited school and extracurricular activity cancellations and government office closures across Putnam County.
The Board of County Commissioners placed Putnam under a state of emergency Tuesday evening because of Hurricane Helene, which is expected to make landfall on the Gulf Coast Thursday.
The county opened four shelters Wednesday, canceled school through Friday and shuttered government offices until Monday.
The following shelter opens 6 p.m. Wednesday:
– Kelley Smith Elementary School, 141 Kelly Smith School Road in Palatka.
The following shelters open 8 p.m. Wednesday:
– Ochwilla Elementary School, 299 State Road 21 in Hawthorne.
– Middleton-Burney Elementary School, 1020 Huntington Road in Crescent City.
– Browning-Pearce Elementary School, 100 Bear Blvd. in San Mateo.
The Ochwilla shelter is pet-friendly, while the Kelley Smith shelter is for people with special medical needs.
People can call the Putnam County Emergency Management call center at 386-329-1904 to get more information about when shelters are expected to close.
Officials at the call center said they would be monitoring the storm and its effects on the area to determine how long shelters should remain open.
Putnam was under a tropical storm warning by Wednesday evening, with winds of 25-35 mph and gusts of 55 mph expected, according to The Weather Channel. Emergency Management officials said the county could receive up to 4 inches of rain.
The county and city of Palatka set up eight sandbag locations Wednesday. The sites, which require people to bring their own shovels and pack their own bags, will remain available until Friday.
The locations are at:
– 5226 Silver Lake Drive in Palatka.
– 341 Paradise Circle in San Mateo.
– 51 Sportsman Drive in Welaka.
– Jonas Road in Crescent City.
– 145 W. Washington St. in Hawthorne.
– 114 S. 11th St. in Palatka.
– 223 Putnam County Blvd. in East Palatka.
– 107 Johns Road in the Bardin area.
The Putnam County School District canceled school and extracurricular activities through Monday.
Interlachen Junior-Senior High School and Crescent City Junior-Senior High School football games have been rescheduled to Monday. There had not been a makeup game date announced for Palatka Junior-Senior High School by Wednesday afternoon.
St. Johns River State College has canceled classes Thursday and Friday at all of its Palatka, Orange Park, St. Augustine and online campuses. The college's sporting events are canceled on Thursday but will continue Friday.
City Hall in Palatka will be closed until Monday and residential garbage pickup in the city will be stopped Thursday, according to a press release. City officials hope to resume trash pickup Friday.
'In preparation for the storm's forecasted impacts, the city of Palatka is urging residents to prepare for high winds by securing outdoor containers and materials, such as trash cans, plants, furniture and anything that could cause potential damage or loss of property,' officials stated in a Wednesday evening press release.

title: Exercising in the Sunshine
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: INTERLACHEN – Elected officials showcased six new exercise stations Wednesday morning in the hopes of promoting more workouts and better health among local residents.
content:
Body
INTERLACHEN – Elected officials showcased six new exercise stations Wednesday morning in the hopes of promoting more workouts and better health among local residents.
A ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new equipment took place in Jenkins Park in downtown Interlachen. Town Clerk Joni Payne said this is the first time the town has had workout equipment at one of its parks.
'It represents our commitment to promoting healthy living and active lifestyles,' she said. 'We hope the community gets a lot of use out of our new additions to Jenkins Park.'
Interlachen Town Council Vice Chairwoman Joni Conner presented the idea to her colleagues in October 2023. After months of discussion, the council unanimously approved funding the project in April, according to council meeting minutes.
Conner, who lived in South Florida for 30 years, said she remembers all the opportunities to work out in the fresh air but had never seen those same options when she moved to Interlachen.
The equipment is positioned along the 0.7-mile park trail, which Conner said would add more to people's workouts.
'If you were to park down at the other end (of the park) and walk up and do all the equipment, and then, you know, jog or walk in between and do it back, you'd get a pretty good workout,' Conner said.
Payne and County Commissioner Larry Harvey, who represents Interlachen and other areas of West Putnam, tried out the ab press equipment Wednesday. Payne said the town's maintenance crew also installed a chest press, step-up, leg press, sit-up and bench dip equipment along the trail.
If enough people take advantage of the new workout gear, she said, the park has plenty of room to add more.
The equipment cost $19,998 and was funded using American Rescue Plan Act money the federal government gave to local and state governments during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Maintenance employees installed the equipment in July, but town leaders wanted to wait until now to officially debut the new additions to avoid scorching summer temperatures.
'I think the improvements that the town of Interlachen has made for the residents of West Putnam (allows them) to take advantage of this tremendous opportunity for better health (and) to get out and enjoy the community and take care of your health at the same time,' Harvey said.

title: Superintendent cites student improvement in reelection bid
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, answers that went over the limit were cut to be as close to 100 words as possible.
The incumbent and a challenger are vying to be elected as the superintendent of the Putnam County School District.
Competing are Superintendent Rick Surrency and write-in candidate Pat Wilson.
The Palatka Daily News asked local candidates whose names are on the ballot why they should be elected.
Surrency stated below why he would be the best person for the job:
What are some of the goals you hope to accomplish once taking office if you are elected?
Surrency: Our students showed great improvement in learning gains throughout the district. Increasing learning gains year after year is how we increase the number of students meeting proficiency. Our goal is to continue those practices that create learning gains and improve district achievement scores. We need 678 points to be a 'B' district and we earned 630 points in 2024. In 2016, we earned 467 points, which was barely in the 'C' grade range. What we are doing is working, and consistent systems and leadership at the district and school levels will be key in meeting this goal.
The obligation bond to build new elementary schools with taxpayer dollars is already in effect. What are your thoughts on the bond, and are there any changes you hope to make in terms of the construction or renovation of elementary schools?
Surrency: I am proud that our community voted to fund the construction, renovation and replacement of public schools, including implementation of safety enhancements and instructional technology upgrades. Our revitalization plan includes bonds for elementary and state special facilities funds for junior-senior high projects to ensure every Putnam County School District student attends a safe and modern school. We will accomplish this by building four and completely renovating two elementary schools. Construction is underway, and two new elementary schools will be ready for 2025-2026. Our students and staff deserve the best, and our community supported that vision by passing the bond referendum.
The Putnam County School District is partnering with the state to build three new junior-senior high schools. What are your thoughts on the partnership?
Surrency: We are grateful to the Florida Department Of Education for awarding the Putnam County School District funds to completely rebuild Crescent City Junior-Senior High School. The process to secure these funds is competitive, and our team successfully navigated that process. Once the CCJSHS project is complete, we will apply for Interlachen and then Palatka Junior-Senior High Schools, thus completing the nine school projects of the revitalization plan. Our team has built a positive partnership with FLDOE, and I believe consistent leadership in the coming years will positively impact future funding, ensuring updated secondary schools in all areas of the county.
What makes you the best candidate to serve as the Putnam County School District superintendent?
Surrency: I am the only candidate with experience to successfully serve as superintendent. I hold the degrees expected for superintendent, and I'm the 2023 Florida Superintendent of the Year. I've served 46 years in education – 38 of those years in Putnam County. I was born and raised in Hawthorne. I know the importance of every employee because I've held positions at every level. The Putnam County School District is Putnam's largest employer, with over 1,500 dedicated staff serving over 10,000 amazing students. I'm trusting our community to choose me – the only candidate with experience to lead this great organization.
How will you work to maintain transparency with district employees and the public?
Surrency: Community collaboration is a significant part of our 2021-2026 Strategic Plan. We've implemented many options to best communicate with our staff, families and community, including the Superintendent's Student Advisory Council, Bond Oversight Committee, Community Forums, online tools to broadcast meetings/events, upgraded apps for families to stay connected and multiple media channels to share district/school news. Maintaining transparency is, and will continue to be, a priority for me. I believe in servant leadership, and I welcome feedback from our students, staff, families and community. This feedback is needed when building a culture of collaboration, which is crucial for success.

title: Mayor, challenger list qualifications for office
author: News Staff
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, answers that went over the limit were cut to be as close to 100 words as possible.
The mayoral incumbent hopes to serve for four more years, but her challenger is keen to take over in the position.
Mayor Michele Myers and challenger Craig Oates, who has run for mayor in the past, are competing in the mayor's race in the general election.
Early voting started last week, but eligible voters have until 5:30 p.m. Saturday to participate in early voting. Election Day hours are from 7 a.m. – 7 p.m. Nov. 5.
The Palatka Daily News emailed a questionnaire to both candidates to find out in their own words why they would be the best choice for the job.
Their answers can be found below:
Why did you decide to run for a seat on the Crescent City Commission?
Myers: Over the past four years, our City Commission has made incredible strides. From strengthening our local economy to stabilizing city government and improving our aging infrastructure, the results are visible and impactful. I am proud of what we've achieved together, including securing legislative appropriations to remodel our fire station, new infrastructure initiatives, and, most recently, not increasing city property taxes for the first time in 10 years. I'm running for re-election because I believe we must keep moving forward — going backwards isn't an option. I'm committed to continuing working hard and making our city a better place for all residents.
Oates: I decided to run for mayor of Crescent City when the entire town realized that the city commission didn't share any ARPA (American Rescue Act Plan of 2021) funds with the citizens directly. Palatka shared a portion of their funds with their citizens, but Crescent City did not. And we'll never forget how this very commission voted to defund our local police department in a closed-door meeting in January of 2021. The commission hasn't considered the feelings of its citizens when making their votes.
*Editor's note: The January 2021 Crescent City Commission meeting in question took place without residents in the audience because of COVID procedures. The meeting was live-streamed on YouTube, and viewers could give input or ask questions in real-time via the streaming platform.
What government experience do you have that would make you an ideal choice for the Crescent City Commission?
Myers: I bring to the mayor's office four years of dedicated service as mayor, extensive experience in state government and a strong entrepreneurship background. I possess a unique blend of skills, including leadership and government operation knowledge, to continue leading our city. In my four years as mayor, we have made significant progress, and I'm running for re-election to keep moving our city forward. I'm committed to balancing city needs with residents' financial well-being – as demonstrated by lowering our city's millage rate this budget year for the first time in 10 years – and building a stronger, brighter future for us all.
Oates: I'm a veteran of the United States Armed Forces.
What do you believe the city commission's main priorities should be and why?
Myers: As we look to the future, the city commission's main priorities are focused on ensuring long-term growth and stability for our community. Our first step will be hiring a new city manager with a clear vision for our city's future and the leadership skills to bring it to life. With our Master Plan as a roadmap, we're committed to continuing infrastructure improvements, securing vital grants and legislative appropriations and providing our city staff with the resources they need to serve our residents effectively. Together, we'll keep our city on the path to progress, building a stronger community for all.
Oates: The main priorities of the city commission should be to be the voice of the people, but instead, they are the voice of a select few citizens.
Crescent City has seen its share of conflict, especially within the past few years. What would you do to bring stability to the city so it can function efficiently?
Myers: Our city has experienced its share of conflict and negativity over the past few years. I recognize the toll this has taken on our community. If re-elected, I will focus on fostering unity and collaboration among residents and city officials. My hope is my continued commitment to transparency, open communication, ensuring every voice is heard, and active community engagement will help rebuild trust. Together, we can create a positive environment where all community members feel valued. I will prioritize initiatives that promote community pride and development, ensuring our city continues to move forward in a constructive and positive way.
Oates: The best way to bring stability to our town is for us to vote these selfish commissioners out of office. When you consider the voice of the citizens before voting, then you, as a commissioner, could bring more stability and less conflict. Another topic that can bring our town together is bringing an emergency room to our town. That is something that every citizen can benefit from. Also, I would like to change the city charter so that big decisions, like defunding a major department like the police department, would be a ballot item so that the citizens can choose.

title: Give Me Something Good to Eat
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: Children of all ages and the adults accompanying them celebrated Halloween on Thursday evening during events in Palatka and Crescent City.
content:
Body
Children of all ages and the adults accompanying them celebrated Halloween on Thursday evening during events in Palatka and Crescent City.
Although trick-or-treating took place throughout Putnam County, the Palatka Police Department hosted its annual Trunk or Treat at the Palatka riverfront. Farther south, the Putnam County Sheriff's Office offered its Trunk or Treat in front of the former Miller Middle School.
Nearly an hour into the Palatka event, there had been about 1,100 people who visited the 24 vendors passing out candy, according to Assistant Police Chief Matt Newcomb. And for most of the event, the line to get to the first candy station extended for an entire city block.
Newcomb said the increasing popularity of Truck or Treat, which is in its ninth year, led to the police moving the event from the Palatka Mall after beautification efforts at the riverfront were completed.
'We'd actually outgrown the mall at that point,' he said. 'It was causing a lot of traffic and stuff up on (State Road) 19, so we moved down here.'
Newcomb said Trunk or Treat was a great opportunity for vendors, which included the police department, other city agencies, and numerous organizations and businesses, to interact with the community.
As part of the police department's outreach efforts, officers were stationed throughout the candy line, and Chief Jason Shaw stood next to the agency's community service trailer to greet families as they received the last of their treats.
'As soon as people come through, they meet at least two of our officers handing out candy,' Newcomb said. 'They get around and see our Police Athletic League. They get to see the other vendors that participate.'
Also passing out candy during Palatka's Trunk or Treat was Mayor Robbi Correa. She arrived at that event after giving out candy during Boo on the Avenue, where downtown businesses handed out sweets to children, many of whom got in line for Trunk or Treat immediately afterward.
The mayor noted how those two events and others like them throughout the county are becoming more prevalent. There are fewer people partaking in traditional trick-or-treating, she said, but Trunk or Treat and fall festivals are safer options, especially for children.
'I know when I first moved here, these events didn't occur, but we had a lot of trick-or-treaters in the South Historic District, where I live,' Correa said. 'I get virtually none there (now). … It's really wonderful to see the community coming together. I know that a lot of these kids are going to be on a sugar high, but it's just a wonderful event.'

title: Crescent City mayor, commission hopeful victorious
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Crescent City's mayor will serve another term, while a political newcomer defeated a former candidate to win a seat on the Crescent City Commission.
content:
Body
Crescent City's mayor will serve another term, while a political newcomer defeated a former candidate to win a seat on the Crescent City Commission.
Mayor Michele Myers will keep her seat after she beat candidate Craig Oates by 105 votes, according to unofficial results from the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections. She received 363 votes while Oates received 258 votes, Elections Office data showed on Election Day.
'I am so honored the citizens have given me the opportunity to serve them for a second term,' Myers said Tuesday in a text message. 'As I promised four years ago, I will continue to work hard for our community.'
Myers beat Oates and former Mayor Brett Peterson in 2020 to win her first term as the mayor of the South Putnam municipality.
'I am very proud of all the winners in Crescent City for running a positive, pro-Crescent City campaign and look forward to working together, moving our city forward,' Myers said.
Another winner was Crescent City Commission candidate Linda Moore, who will occupy the Group 3 seat.
She competed against Jamaad Batts Sr., who unsuccessfully competed for the same position in 2020. Moore took home 336 votes while Batts received 264 votes, according to unofficial election results.
Moore will take over for current Group 3 Commissioner Cynthia Burton, who decided to run in the Group 4 contest in this election cycle. Burton defeated Batts for the Group 3 position in 2020.
'Winning this position gives me the opportunity to make a difference and serve my community,' Moore said. 'I'm ready to work.'
While Burton originally had a competitor in Group 4, Circuit Judge Kenneth Janesk II ruled Friday that challenger Christopher Coleman could not run because his qualification documents did not adhere to Florida statutes.
Coleman had already qualified to run in the Group 3 race, but he changed contests Aug. 9, the day Crescent City's qualification period ended, according to circuit court documents.
Coleman filed a motion Tuesday in the hopes of Janesk rehearing his case. Although a hearing took place on Election Day, Janesk made no decision about whether Coleman would be allowed to run for office.
If he is allowed to run, it is likely a special election will take place.

title: Newbold blows write-in out of the water
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The only candidate on the ballot to represent South Putnam County at the county level handily beat his opponent in the general election.
content:
Body
The only candidate on the ballot to represent South Putnam County at the county level handily beat his opponent in the general election.
Republican J.R. Newbold III won the District 1 Board of County Commissioners seat with 30,814 votes, and write-in candidate Douglas Hays secured only 925 votes, according to the Supervisor of Elections Office's unofficial results.
'I've just been very fortunate in my run,' Newbold said Tuesday night.
Newbold, who said this was his first time running for elected office, will assume his county commissioner duties when he is sworn in later this month.
He said he understands there might be a learning curve when he starts his new job, but he wants to learn on the job and make a difference.
'I'm looking forward to the challenges,' Newbold said.
He spent Tuesday evening celebrating his victory in Crescent City with friends, supporters and family.
'We're very excited,' Newbold said.
During the Aug. 20 primary, he won the Republican nomination by getting 8,348 votes, defeating challenger Jeovanny Palencia, who got 1,130 votes.
Newbold is one of three new Republican faces who will serve on the board. He will be taking over the position currently occupied by Commissioner Bill Pickens, who did not run for reelection.
Republican Josh Alexander won the District 3 contest in the August primary, where his only competitor was Republican Les Sims. Alexander will fill in for outgoing Commissioner Terry Turner, who, like Pickens, decided to not seek reelection.
Former District 5 Commissioner Walton Pellicer II defeated Tim Williams and another former commissioner, Buddy Goddard, in August to secure the Republican nomination. Write-in candidate Tim Grose withdrew from the District 5 race shortly after the primary, handing Pellicer the general election win months ahead of time.
District 5 Commissioner Paul Adamczyk originally filed for reelection but withdrew from the commission race to embark on a school superintendent campaign, which he lost in August.
Putnam County had an 80.45% voter turnout in the general election. All results will be finalized Nov. 15, according to Elections Supervisor Charles Overturf III.
