title: Groups hosting events to observe Veterans Day
author: Trisha Murphy
description: When the Palatka Veterans Day Parade begins its route down St.
content:
Body
When the Palatka Veterans Day Parade begins its route down St. Johns Avenue on Monday, Glenn Wright, the commander of the state Department of Florida Veterans of Foreign Wars, will be near the front as the grand marshal.
The parade will start at 10 a.m. and proceed from 11th Street to the riverfront, where there will be a short ceremony. American Legion Bert Hodge Post 45 and VFW Post 3349, both in Palatka, are organizing the events.
Wright, who lives in Jacksonville, served in the Navy for 22 years. He is a member of VFW Wesconnett Post 7907, where he served as the commander for eight years. He was elected to the Florida VFW office in June and has been awarded All-State and All-American Commander honors numerous times.
While in the Navy, he was awarded four Navy Commendation Medals, four Navy Achievement Medals and numerous other awards.
According to Lester Sheppard, the commander of the American Legion, everyone can participate in the parade as long as whatever they enter is in honor of veterans.
Parade participants should meet at 9 a.m. at the corner of 11th Street and St. Johns Avenue across from the post office.
Following the riverfront ceremony, open house events will take place at the American Legion, 316 Osceola St., and the VFW, 3201 Reid St., from noon – 2 p.m. Hot dogs, hamburgers and desserts will be served at the American Legion. The VFW will provide food as well.
For details call Sheppard at 386-972-2153 or VFW Commander Gerald Donnelly at 717-965-3266.
During the parade, free Buddy Poppies, the official memorial flower of the Veterans of Foreign Wars of the United States, will be handed out and donations will be accepted for the two local military groups.
Sheppard hopes the community will attend the parade on Monday to honor the men and women who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces.
'This is the one day of the year we have the opportunity to honor veterans and their service to our country,' Sheppard said.
Donnelly is looking forward to the parade and hopes Mother Nature will cooperate.
'I think we are going to have a nice parade and we are hoping for good weather,' he said. 'I'm praying for it.'

title: Veterans honored during Palatka parade, service
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Palatka honored veterans near and far Monday as people flocked downtown and along the riverfront to observe Veterans Day.
content:
Body
Palatka honored veterans near and far Monday as people flocked downtown and along the riverfront to observe Veterans Day.
The American Legion Bert Hodge Post 45 and Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 3349 hosted this year's Veterans Day commemorations in Palatka. There was a parade, which traversed along St. Johns Avenue from 11th Street to the riverfront, where there was a ceremony to pay tribute in a quieter setting.
Veteran Lester Sheppard, the commander of the Legion post, asked all his fellow service members in the crowd at the ceremony to raise their hands and asked everyone to think about the words by which he stands.
'It is a veteran, not the reporter, who has given us the freedom of the press,' Sheppard said. 'It is a veteran, not the poet, who has given us freedom of speech. It is a veteran, not the campus organizer, who has given us the freedom to demonstrate.'
Though some of the words changed, Sheppard was reciting parts of a poem written by Army veteran Charles M. Province, often titled 'It Is the Soldier, Not the Minister" or 'It Is the Veteran.'
Schools were out in observance of the holiday, which meant plenty of kids could attend the parade, where they saw combat trucks, a submarine replica, local veterans, cadets from local JROTC programs and other school groups that honor veterans.
While the parade was filled with cheering and frivolity, parade grand marshal Glenn Wright, the commander of the state Department of Florida Veterans of Foreign Wars, reminded everyone during his speech at the riverfront ceremony that Veterans Day is more than a calendar date.
He said the day is a reminder of all the men and women who left their homes, braved unknown dangers and made sacrifices for their country.
'You've defended our freedoms, protected our values and shown us the true meaning of courage,' said Wright, a Jacksonville resident who spent 22 years in the Navy. 'From the beaches of Normandy to the peninsula of Korea, the jungles of Vietnam, the deserts of Iraq and the mountains of Afghanistan, you've faced challenges most of us can only imagine.'
Wright said veterans who returned from duty brought back with them leadership, discipline, a sense of duty and other skills that make their communities better places to live.
Veterans are teachers, first responders, business leaders and neighbors whose presences continue to enrich everyone they meet, he said.
Veterans' families, too, made sacrifices, considering they supported their loved ones in the service during long deployments, experienced many anxious nights and missed precious moments with their family members who served, Wright added.
Veterans Day can honor veterans and their families, said Wright, who acknowledged veterans have paid a debt no civilian could repay.
'As we leave today, let's carry with us a renewed community to honor and support our veterans,' Wright said. 'Whether it's volunteering at a local (Veterans Affairs) hospital, hiring veterans in our businesses or simply taking the time to listen to their stories, there are countless ways we can show our appreciation. Let's make every day Veterans Day by living up to the ideas from which way they fought.'

title: Author's book reflective of her faith in God
author: Trisha Murphy
description: When Tera Hunt started writing, she found herself jotting down her thoughts on anything she could find on which to write.
content:
When Tera Hunt started writing, she found herself jotting down her thoughts on anything she could find on which to write.
'My journal, pieces of paper and in my Bible,' the 71-year-old East Palatka resident said. 'I really felt God's presence in my life so many times over the last few years.'
That time frame includes November 2016 when the wife and mother of eight had open-heart surgery.
'It was a difficult time for me,' she said. 'I remember very early the following morning after my surgery that they wanted me to sit up in a chair, stand up and walk across the room. I thought to myself, 'There is no way.''
But she managed to find a way with the help of God, she said.
'I prayed and asked him to let me feel his presence because I could not do this by myself,' she said. 'I immediately felt God's presence, goodness, grace and peace were with me then and still are today.'
Hunt recently released her first book, 'From My Heart,' a 365-day devotional at the urging of her late brother, Bill Hickman, who passed away in 2020 from COVID.
'My brother strongly encouraged me to put the devotional blogs I started in 2017 into a book,' she said. 'So in 2019, I started compiling my manuscript.'
Hunt said even though her brother never got to see the book come to fruition, he is still a part of her work.
'His encouragement, inspiration, many conversations, tears and prayers inspired me to persevere in my writing,' she said. 'He was my biggest cheerleader. I am thankful for his persistence. I love and miss him every day.'
Hunt, who calls herself a Southern girl with Alabama roots, is a firm believer in Jesus Christ and gives him all the glory for her book.
'When I started writing this book, it was full of challenges and harder than I ever imagined,' she said. 'I owe a great debt of gratitude to so many, especially my family and friends. So many have cared, prayed, encouraged, supported, loved, cried with me and helped nurture my dream of writing this book. I love them all so much.'
Hunt will be featured at a book signing from 10 a.m. – 2 p.m. Dec. 7 at the Now The End Begins Christian Bookstore, 209 N. Fourth St. in Palatka. Her book is available at the bookstore, through amazon.com and at Barnes and Noble.
The softcover books sell for $24.95 and the hardback costs $35.95.
Hunt and her husband, John, have eight children and nine grandchildren between them.
She said God's faithfulness and goodness sustained her through many difficulties and major health issues.
'This book is a way for me to share my thankfulness with others for how God provided,' she said. 'The good is full of God's blessings and rewards. I pray that my book will bring Glory to God, bless people with his presence and peace, and encourage them to live each day with hope and faith in God.'

title: Deadline for decorating contest draws near
description: Time is running out for Putnam County residents to win a total of $300 for the best outdoor holiday decorations.
content:
Time is running out for Putnam County residents to win a total of $300 for the best outdoor holiday decorations.
The Palatka Daily News is hosting its inaugural holiday decorations contest, where the paper's readers will decide the winner.
To compete in the contest, people must email up to two high-quality, in-focus pictures of their outdoor Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa decorations to boliver@palatkadailynews.com. All participants must also submit their first and last name, phone number and municipality of residence.
Three winners will be chosen, with first place receiving $150, second place winning $100 and third place getting $50. Each winner will also receive a plaque.
Contestants have until 5 p.m. Monday to submit up to two pictures of their outdoor holiday decorations. Daily News employees will choose the 10 best pictures – no more than one per contestant – and publish those in the print edition, at palatkadailynews.com and on the Palatka Daily News' Facebook page on Wednesday.
To have a better chance of making the top 10, submitted photos should be of high enough quality to be resized and reproduced.
After the top 10 photos are published, the outcome of the contest will be in the hands of the Daily News' readers. People can vote for their favorite photo via a poll on the Daily News' website or by giving a thumbs up or heart reaction on their favorite photo on Facebook.
Contest winners will be announced Dec. 24, and Daily News employees will reach out to the lucky three afterward.

title: Public asked to select holiday decorations winners
description: The top 10 photos for the Palatka Daily News' first holiday decorations contest are in, and it's now up to the public to determine the winners.
content:
Body
The top 10 photos for the Palatka Daily News' first holiday decorations contest are in, and it's now up to the public to determine the winners.
First-, second- and third-place winners will be selected based on the number of thumbs up and heart reactions each picture receives on Facebook.
The public has until 1 p.m. Dec. 23 to select the photos depicting their favorite decorations.
All three winners will receive a plaque and a cash prize. First place will receive $150, second place will get $100 and third place will win $50.
Putnam County residents had until Monday to submit up to two pictures of their outdoor holiday decorations, and they did not disappoint. Daily News employees chose the best of each entrant's photos to compile the top 10.
Those pictures are being published in today's print edition, at palatkadailynews.com and on the Palatka Daily News' Facebook page.
'We thank everyone who participated in our first decorations contest,' Editor Brandon D. Oliver said. 'We appreciate your willingness to do so and your dedication to holiday cheer. Good luck to all of the contestants.'

title: Author to showcase 3rd book in South Putnam
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Life on the St. Johns and Ocklawaha rivers brings back fond memories of adventure and excitement for author Bob H. Lee.
content:
Body
Life on the St. Johns and Ocklawaha rivers brings back fond memories of adventure and excitement for author Bob H. Lee.
The former lieutenant used to travel those waterways used to travel those waterways throughout his 30 years of work with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.
That's what inspired the 71-year-old author to write his third book, 'Bones in Water,' a contemporary murder thriller he describes as filled with action and adventure. The book, which was released in November, took Lee three years to write.
Lee, who lives in Satsuma with his wife, Karen, will be featured in a book signing from 3–5 p.m. Thursday at the General Federation of Women's Club Crescent City Woman's Club, 604 N. Summit St. The public is invited.
The book sells for $20, with all proceeds benefiting the Fruitland Peninsula Historical Society, where Lee serves as the program coordinator. Cash is preferred for book purchases but payment can be made by check or credit card.
Following the book signing, the Fruitland Peninsula Historical Society's annual potluck dinner will take place from 4–6 p.m. There is no cost to attend, but those who do should bring a covered dish.
Lee said he wanted his book to capture the feeling of life in a working fish camp. There are two fish camps central to the book's storyline.
'One of them is named the Hideaway and would be in the general vicinity of where Bass World Lodge is in Georgetown today,' he said. 'I also write about the blue crab fishery and running commercial trotlines for channel catfish. In short, I try to convey to the reader what life on the river is like.'
Lee remembers when he began his career as a river patrol officer.
'There were 30-plus fish camps south of Dunns Creek, which would include Crescent Lake and the St. Johns River down to Georgetown,' he said. 'Today, there are only a handful of working fish camps left.'
Lee said the characters in his latest book are composites of people he met in the past or are a fabrication of his imagination.
'There is only one character in the book who is real,' he said. 'His name is Kevin Finch.'
Finch, who has lived in Welaka for 20 years, said he and Lee met at a book club signing in Palatka and became friends.
'When Bob was writing this book, he called me and asked if I would mind if he used me as a character,' Finch said. 'My character owns a resort in the book called Steamboat Charlie's Bar & Grill. I'm in there for one chapter.'
Finch admits he and Lee have a mutual admiration for each other, so he was honored when Lee wanted to use him in the book.
'I was flattered,' he said. 'I think the book is excellent and entertaining and I hope he does well with it. This book is so good; I encourage him to write more. He's good at what he's doing.'
Readers who know Lee well may also find signs of him in his latest book's main character, Jake Hawkins.
'I claim a third of Jake Hawkins,' Lee said. 'And the other two-thirds comes from two fellows I worked with. So that makes Hawkins a composite character.'
Lee said in a news release that a puzzling endangered marine mammal's death leads Florida Game Warden Jake Hawkins to investigate a shocking wildlife crime using a backcountry sense of justice that can only end in violence.
'During my career, I caught hundreds of poachers in the act and through complex wildlife investigations,' he said. 'I met some interesting folks. Some wore a badge while others were on the opposite side of the law.'
Lee added that even though his latest book is considered fiction, the foundation of the book is rooted in fact.
'Perhaps we could call it 'faction,'' he said. 'As a writer, I draw on all my past experiences in conservation law enforcement and the thousands of patrol days I spent on the St. Johns and Ocklawaha rivers.
'... I've come to love the rivers and creeks in Putnam County and thought they would make a wonderful backdrop for a book. This is an area I know extremely well, and because of that, it saved me a lot of time that many authors would have had to spend on research.'
Lee is the author of two other fiction books, the award-winning 'Backcountry Lawman,' released in 2013, and 'Bad Guys, Bullets, and Boat Chases,' released in 2017.
For 'Backcountry Lawman, Lee received the 2014 Excellence-In-Craft Award from the Florida Outdoor Writers Association.
Each of Lee's three works will be available for $20 on Thursday.
'Bones in Water' is also available locally at Needful Things, Niko's and Putnam Feed and Farm Supply. The books can be purchased through bobhlee.com or at Amazon.com.
Lee finds most Florida authors of works similar to 'Bones' try to keep things simple and their stories tend to be set in Key West or the Everglades.
'I think it's high time Northeast Florida got its due,' he said. 'The terrain and people here are just as interesting as those who live in South Florida.'

title: Warm Wishes
author: Trisha Murphy
description: With this year's Christmas season came warm wishes for the holidays when area seniors in local assisted living facilities were gifted blankets for Christmas.
content:
Body
With this year's Christmas season came warm wishes for the holidays when area seniors in local assisted living facilities were gifted blankets for Christmas.
The idea for the New Blanket Drive came to Jana Plymel, the care coordinator for Pinnacle Home Care, after seeing a similar project on TikTok.
'I love Christmas,' said Plymel, who coordinates skilled care for patients discharged from the hospital or rehab as well as for residents in assisted living communities. 'Gift-giving is a love language of mine. I love to give.'
The call for blankets went out Nov. 4, and the community responded in a big way.
'We are thankful for Jana,' said Traci Vinson, the sales and marketing director for Vintage Care. 'She worked super, super hard and went out of her way to make sure everyone got a blanket.'
Plymel said this is the first year she has done the New Blanket Drive, but more than 208 blankets were donated.
On Dec. 16, Plymel and other volunteers handed out the blankets to Vintage Care of Palatka, Palatka Center for Rehabilitation and Healing, The Pavilion at Crescent Lake and Five Oaks Rest Home. The remaining 25 blankets were disbursed to several homeless residents around the county.
Various people, businesses and other groups donated blankets, including Putnam County residents, St. Johns County residents, Kelley Smith Elementary School and sixth grade Cambridge classes.
'Our residents are so thankful for their new blankets,' Vinson said. 'The community truly showed up and showed out.'
Volunteer Kathy Fisk helped hand out the blankets dressed as Mrs. Claus.
'Our residents truly enjoyed seeing her,' Vinson said, referencing Fisk.
Plymel said the blanket drive was important to her because oftentimes, seniors in the community get left out.
'Some of these seniors no longer have family or loved ones around,' she said. 'I don't want them to feel as if they've been forgotten about. They deserve a small Christmas gift.'
Plymel is looking forward to Christmas and spending time with her family. She hopes those who received the blankets will know people care.
'What better way to spread holiday cheer than to give someone so deserving a small gift to let them know you're thinking of them,' she said. 'I hope it puts a smile on their face, warmth in their heart and magic of Christmas in their soul.'

title: Snow Day to bring white winter to Putnam
author: Trisha Murphy
description: The Palatka Daily News' latest forecast reports snow is expected Monday in East Palatka.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News' latest forecast reports snow is expected Monday in East Palatka.
This extraordinary turn of events will be a chance for Putnam County residents and visitors to step into a winter wonderland in celebration of the new year.
With further investigation, it turns out the anticipated snow is of the man-made kind. The Daily News' annual Snow Day will take place from 4–7 p.m. Jan. 6 at the Putnam County Fairgrounds, 118 Fairgrounds Road in East Palatka. The event is free to the public.
'Our goal is to give kids in the community a chance to play in the snow, something they may not otherwise have a chance to do,' said Jennifer Moates, publisher of the Palatka Daily News. 'We want to provide a safe, family-friendly event for everyone to enjoy.'
According to Moates, last year's event drew between 1,500 and 2,000 people.
'Every year, Snow Day continues to grow with more fun activities for families to enjoy,' she said. 'The event occurs during the cold weather season so the snow will last and the cold weather makes it feel like real snow weather. The cold air adds to the experience, letting the kids know what playing in the snow is like.'
The Palatka Daily News is sponsoring the event in conjunction with the Putnam County Fairgrounds & Expo Center and the newspaper's Positively Putnam FL sponsors: Beck Automotive Group, the Putnam County School District, Seminole Electric, Georgia-Pacific, Barwick Bank Co., St. Johns River State College and the Putnam County Board of Commissioners.
'Without our Positively Putnam partners, Snow Day would not be possible,' Moates said.
Highlights include two snow play areas, a dual snow slide, face painting, food for purchase and bounced houses with an unlimited bouncing wristband for $7. The Putnam County Sheriff's Office will also have its helicopter on display.
Moates is hoping for a good turnout for the newspaper's third edition of Snow Day.
'This event is designed to give children and families the opportunity to have a fun-filled and unique experience,' she said. 'We hope everyone will come and play in the snow.'

title: One Book swoops into action for premiere event
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: There's a mystery on the horizon in Putnam County as organizers plan for a countywide book club kickoff in Palatka.
content:
There's a mystery on the horizon in Putnam County as organizers plan for a countywide book club kickoff in Palatka.
Board members of One Book One Putnam, a nonprofit that chooses a book each year for Putnam residents to read, are hosting the kickoff event for the 2025 season. This year's book is 'The Maltese Falcon' by Dashiell Hammett.
The public is invited to the One Book event, which will begin at 5:30 p.m. Thursday at the Palatka Golf Club, 1715 Moseley Ave.
For more than two decades, the One Book, One Putnam committee has hosted a series of events each year to encourage residents to read more books, especially the featured book of each season. Board members Joyce Oliver and Lulu Gail Parish said some people think One Book chooses only Florida-based books, but that isn't the case. During One Book's existence, committee members have had to dig deep to find a wide array of inspiring reads.
'It gets a little bit harder because I think a lot of the really good books, we've already done,' Oliver said. '... But we just want something that appeals to just about everybody.'
Whatever book the committee chooses needs to not only be a good read, but it has to inspire activities that will take place during the One Book season, Parish said.
'We do different things to try to involve the community,' Parish said. 'And the more we can do to make them get interested, the more it might promote them to read the book or read (other items.)'
Published in 1930, 'The Maltese Falcon' centers around Detective Sam Spade, criminals, a beautiful woman and a missing statue, according to the publishing group Penguin Random House. It was adapted into two movies, the first starring Bebe Daniels and Ricardo Cortez in 1931 and the second starring Humphrey Bogart and Mary Astor 10 years later.
People don't need to read the book before attending Thursday's gathering, which is an introduction to this year's One Book season. The One Book finale will be in March.
Parish and Oliver said the premiere will include displays about life in Putnam County during the 1930s, film noir, Palatka's Belton Society Syncopators and other topics.
Employees from Palatka bookstore Needful Things, 908 St. Johns Ave., will be selling copies of the book during the event.
One Book organizers have planned a season full of activities to immerse people in 'The Maltese Falcon.'
'We pick books that we can do something with that are still, you know, good to read,' Oliver said. 'I think it's fun because we just let our minds go, and our ideas just kind of really appear. And I love that.'
Throughout the season, participants will get to play the role of private investigator as they hunt for the falcons across Putnam County for a prize, Oliver and Parish said. More details will be announced following the kickoff event.
Azalea City Brewing Co., 120 S. Seventh St. in Palatka, will show the 1941 film at 6:30 p.m. Jan. 30. People can partake in swing dancing during a 1930s-themed dance at 6 p.m. Feb. 21 at Beef 'O' Brady's, 201 N. First St. in Palatka.
More details about this year's One Book events will be released at a later date.
There will be book discussions at different library branches throughout the county. Those events will take place at:
– 10:30 a.m. Jan. 17 at 312 Wynwood Ave. in Melrose.
– 11 a.m. Jan. 22 at 133 County Road 15 in Interlachen.
– 4 p.m. Jan. 30 at 125 Tillman St. in Palatka.
– 5:30 p.m. Feb. 7 at 601 College Road in Palatka.
– 11 a.m. Feb. 12 at 610 Summit St. in Crescent City.

title: Hundreds flock to Putnam for Snow Day
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: EAST PALATKA – There was a 100% chance of snow Tuesday in Putnam County, but it wasn't because of the dipping temperatures.
content:
Body
EAST PALATKA – There was a 100% chance of snow Tuesday in Putnam County, but it wasn't because of the dipping temperatures.
The third annual Snow Day took place at the Putnam County Fairgrounds, where people partook in the Florida version of sledding and snowball fights, got their faces painted and stayed warm in the near-freezing weather with cups of hot chocolate.
More than 1,000 people attended Snow Day – which was hosted by the Palatka Daily News and Positively Putnam, in conjunction with fairgrounds and the Putnam County Sheriff's Office – with attendees coming as far as Clay, Flagler, St. Johns and Duval counties to see Florida snow.
One parent said they wanted to take their kids to the event because they moved from the northern part of the country and hadn't seen snow in a while.
Another mother, Stephanie Strutridge, moved from Canada to Palatka about five years ago. Strutridge said her three young children have never seen snow, and while her children enjoyed Tuesday's event, she doesn't miss white winters.
'I just wanted them to be able to experience some snow since we never get it,' she said. 'We never go anywhere that there is snow. It seems like we always miss where there's snow. Whenever we tried to make a trip to somewhere where there's snow, there ends up being no snow.'
Her daughter, Bella Strutridge, took photos with Flurry the Snowman, Snow Day's mascot, while Bella's brothers played in the snow pits.
Also practicing his snowball-making skills was Jasper Sheptock of Interlachen. He played in the freshly churned snow and showed his mom, Lisa Sheptock, just how far he could throw his snowballs.
'Putnam County doesn't really have a whole lot of fun things for kids to do,' Lisa Sheptock said. 'Some of these kids will never see snow, you know.'
It took Florida Snow Service, a company specializing in bringing snow to Florida, about three hours to lay down the snow for the two snow play areas and the dual sledding slide, which was half metal and half fresh snow.
Plenty of families returned to this week's event after attending in December 2023. It was some children's first time trying the snow slide, but others picked up where they left off from previous years.
But people who wanted a break from the sledding and snowball fights, could play in bounce houses, grab snacks from local vendors or get their faces painted. Sheriff's office deputies brought a special utility vehicle for people to explore and flew in a helicopter for kids to see.
Many people at the event explored and took pictures with the special utility vehicle and helicopter that sheriff's office deputies took to the fairgrounds.
Daily News Publisher Jennifer Moates said she is thankful to the sheriff's office and all other sponsors from Positively Putnam who made the event possible. Although Moates volunteered while trying to stay warm in a full coat, hat and gloves, she thought the 40-degree weather added authenticity.
'What a great time we had at Snow Day,' she said. 'Thank you to everyone who came out to play in the snow, jump in the bouncy houses, check out the sheriff department's helicopter or just throw a snowball or two.'

title: Dental surgery needed before man qualifies for transplant
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Kevin Whitlock doesn't consider himself an unlucky man. Quite the opposite, in fact.
content:
Body
Kevin Whitlock doesn't consider himself an unlucky man. Quite the opposite, in fact.
Despite some unpleasant life experiences, like his mom dying when he was 14 and his fiance' passing away in 2015, he has retained his optimism.
'I've had a lot of bad things happen to me, yet more good things have happened,' the 55-year-old Interlachen resident said. 'I've been blessed in so many ways.'
His most recent challenge, though, was last year when he was diagnosed with Stage 4 cirrhosis of the liver and became in need of a liver transplant.
'I was at work when I started feeling sick with a headache, muscle spasms, nausea and fatigue,' he said. 'I came home and decided to take a nap. When I woke up I couldn't walk or talk properly and was having trouble breathing and pain in my side again. My sister called the ambulance and I was taken to the hospital.'
Whitlock's doctor sent him to a specialist at UF Health in Gainesville, where testing began and he eventually received his diagnosis.
'I thought the doctor had to be crazy,' he said. 'It was the day before my 55th birthday. I've never even had a beer.'
But there's more to Whitlock's story than the need for a transplant.
He has to have major dental surgery to repair damage to his teeth after being hit in the face with a 40-pound weight before he can be added to the transplant list.
The dental damage happened in 2016 when the weight used to tie down a patio umbrella broke loose sending the umbrella into the pool during Hurricane Matthew. Whitlock, trying to avoid damage to the pool, went in after the umbrella when the unthinkable happened.
'It took months for my mouth to heal, and eating anything was difficult,' he said. 'It didn't get much better since I couldn't afford to repair them and they have eventually gotten worse.'
Whitlock was first quoted a price of over $35,000 to have his teeth repaired. He also received a quote of $20,000 to have his teeth removed and get dentures.
Whitlock said his doctor informed him he may have only a year to live unless he gets a new liver.
'He said even a minor tooth infection would destroy or compromise the transplant because of the anti-rejection medicine I would have to take for life,' he said.
Whitlock was thankful his son, Wesley Shawn Whitlock, 32, went with him to the appointment when he got the liver disease diagnosis and asked doctors questions that desperately needed answers.
'He wanted to know what I could do, what medications could be prescribed and what comes next,' Kevin Whitlock said. 'When we got done with my appointment and got on the elevator to leave, my son just grabbed me and hugged me. I didn't ever want to cry in front of my kid. However, I couldn't help it. He said, 'Dad, we will get through this, and if you can use half of my liver, it's yours.''
Kevin Whitlock has been approved for disability but hasn't started receiving it yet. He works part time at the Palatka Daily News as a carrier, a job he's had for four years. He and his sister, who has her own health concerns and was diagnosed with Stage 4 bone and breast cancer last year, share a place and take care of each other.
Kevin Whitlock has applied for help from the Federal Emergency Management Agency because of the accident due to the hurricane but has been denied six times.
'(Former) Rep. Bobby Payne assigned a member of his team to try and assist me,' he said. 'His office sent letters to FEMA on my behalf, where they requested multiple estimates for the teeth repair only to get denied again. Rep. Payne's office did everything they could to assist me. FEMA was simply denying every attempt.'
So far, Kevin Whitlock has raised $5,000 toward getting his teeth fixed and has started a GoFundMe campaign at https://gofund.me/eea8bc1d to help raise the additional $15,000.
'A new liver could get me 20 or 30 more years on this planet and allow me to see and hold my first grandchild, watch my only kid get married and maybe even give me another chance at love after losing the woman I loved 10 years ago,' he said.
Kevin Whitlock realizes times are tough for many people, but he said he would be grateful to anyone who could contribute to his fund – or to a dental surgeon who would donate their services.
He plans to keep working as long as he can because it allows him to keep fighting.
'That's all I have: my family, a few friends and my job,' he said. I'm only missing teeth, getting a new liver and a grandchild.'

title: Vehicular Renaissance
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Royalty will arrive Saturday when 'Queen Victoria' takes her place among the elite motorcade arriving one by one at the Palatka riverfront for the 26th annual Open Car Show-Cruise In.
content:
Body
Royalty will arrive Saturday when 'Queen Victoria' takes her place among the elite motorcade arriving one by one at the Palatka riverfront for the 26th annual Open Car Show-Cruise In.
Sponsored by the Azalea Region Antique Automobile Club of America, the event will be from 8 a.m. – 2 p.m. and will showcase antique, custom, and classic vehicles, vehicles from the 1950s and 1960s, hot rods, muscle cars and other special interest vehicles.
Vehicles will be on display around the clock tower on Memorial Parkway. Admission for vehicles and spectators is free for the non-judged show. The public is invited.
Dash plaques will be awarded to the first 100 vehicles that enter, and there will also be door prizes and a 50/50 drawing. For details or to register, call Art Hall at 386-546-0073 or Clara Cox at 904-553-5303.
One of the featured vehicles during the show will be 'Queen Victoria,' a 1967 Cadillac Superior Coach manufactured in Lima, Ohio. The hearse is owned by Karl N. Flagg, owner of Karl N. Flagg Serenity Memorial Chapel in Palatka and senior pastor at Mt. Tabor First Baptist Church.
According to Flagg, his family appreciates the historical significance of the hearse and its rebirth.
'This hearse or funeral coach has been in active service for several months and is used for initial service calls, funerals and, of course, antique shows,' Flagg said. 'This will be the very first antique show since its renaissance.'
Flagg said he purchased the 58-year-old vintage classic in February 2023 following a nationwide search, during which he found it in a garage in Daytona Beach. Sales manager Brian Freeman facilitated the transaction after it was authorized by Breck Sloan, the general manager and owner of the Beck Automotive Group in Palatka.
Flagg, 65, a lifelong resident of Palatka, said the hearse was used by funeral homes as an ambulance prior to the state offering professional rescue services.
'This vehicle is nostalgic and it speaks volumes about the quality craftsmanship by the General Motors Cadillac division during that era,' he said. 'By a family's special request, we drove in an escorted funeral procession to an interment at a memorial park in St. Augustine several weeks ago.'
Flagg said numerous vendors played an important role in the restoration of his vintage vehicle, including Beck employee Craig Alexander, who rebuilt the engine to include air conditioning, which was not available during 1967. Beck Collision Center also made repairs to the vehicle.
'It's been a year for the restoration, and we are still planning to restore the interior upholstery soon,' Flagg said. 'But we needed to place it on active duty.'
Although Flagg didn't participate in the restoration of the classic himself, he watched and admired the work being done.
'I was amazed at the talented people who work diligently to restore it to its glory days,' he said.
Flagg, who previously served as mayor of Palatka and was a county commissioner, said having a vehicle like Queen Victoria, which has a total of 60,254 miles to date, takes him back to when he was in fifth grade. At the time, he spent six days a week at the Boyd family funeral home in Palatka, something he said prepared him for his lifelong career.
'I actually drove a 1968 Cadillac Miller-Meteor hearse during my teenage years at the Boyd funeral home I served,' he said. 'It takes me all the way back to my middle and high school years when initially I could only wash and wax it. Then I became a licensed driver until it was retired and traded from the active fleet of service vehicles.'
Flagg is looking forward to talking with local residents at this weekend's event and in future shows so long as he doesn't get any service calls and have to leave.
'I hope senior citizens will have moments of reflections, admiration and reminiscing that gives them peace of mind from the past,' he said. 'Younger citizens will remember the model from movies and documentaries.'
Flagg said he would love to see another addition to his fleet – a matching limousine.
'It would be fully sanctioned by families who request it for funerals,' he said.
Art Hall, vice president of the Antique Automobile Club of America, hopes the public will show up to this weekend's car show to see the hearse and other vehicles, for fellowship and to participate in a 50/50 drawing at 1 p.m. There will also be a hot dog food truck.
'We're expecting some of our cars to come from DeLand, Jacksonville, Ocala and St. Augustine as well as local cars,' he said. 'We're hoping for 200 or more spectators.'
Flagg is not sure how he would react if he were to hear, 'All hail the queen,' when he arrives at Saturday's show but said it would be interesting to find out.
'It gives me professional pride to own and operate this hearse,' he said. 'When it brings historical significance and relativity and therapeutic comfort to a grieving family, we are blessed to sincerely share their bereavement and aim to facilitate their healing process.'

title: Mayor, 2 council positions up for grabs Tuesday
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Welaka voters will decide Tuesday which three people will be the next to help oversee the town's government.
content:
Welaka voters will decide Tuesday which three people will be the next to help oversee the town's government.
The Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office will open polling booths from 7 a.m. – 7 p.m. Only the 692 eligible registered voters within the town limits will be allowed to participate in the election, according to Elections Supervisor Charles Overturf III.
Running for mayor are Courtney DeSouza, the fiancée of former Mayor Jamie Watts; Kim Dugger, a current councilmember; Kevin Finch, the ex-husband of acting mayor and council member Jessica Finch; Brad Kay; and Pam Olson, a mayoral candidate in a previous Welaka election.
Hoping to nab the two open council seats are David Jeltes, current Councilwoman Tonya Long and Sandra Walker, who ran for a council seat in 2023.
'They've got some interest as far as candidates,' Overturf said about people's interest in the election.
Usually, he said, at least 300 people turn out for Welaka elections. Overturf hopes this election has a better turnout than the special primary election in January that was open to only Democrat and Republican voters in Putnam County.
Only 9.91% of eligible voters cast a ballot in that primary, according to the Elections Office.
As of 2:15 p.m. Friday, 21 people, or 3.03%, have gotten a head start by voting by mail in the Welaka election, according to the Elections Office's website.
In February, there were well-populated candidate forums for the mayor and council member races on Feb. 5 and 12, respectively, with Welaka residents packing the venue to near capacity. Welaka residents who might not be sure who to vote for can watch the forums on the Friends of Welaka Facebook page.
Overturf said the winners of Tuesday's election will be sworn in on Friday, which will also be the day qualifying opens for residents who want to run for office to replace Jessica Finch on the council.
She confirmed in February her last day will be Tuesday. She took over as acting mayor after Watts resigned following an unsuccessful bid for a seat in the Florida House of Representatives.
Overturf said Jessica Finch could have resumed her role on the council after the town selects a new mayor Tuesday, but she decided after the deadlines for the March 4 election to resign from public office entirely.
Qualifying for her seat ends on March 21, Overturf confirmed, and the special election will be May 6.

title: Council member elected as Welaka's mayor
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: More than half of eligible voters showed up to the polls Tuesday or by mail to elect a new mayor of Welaka and two people to the Welaka Town Council.
content:
Body
More than half of eligible voters showed up to the polls Tuesday or by mail to elect a new mayor of Welaka and two people to the Welaka Town Council.
Kim Dugger, who was elected as a council member in 2023, won the mayor's race with 112 votes. Sandra Walker, who unsuccessfully sought a council seat in 2023, was finally elected to the council with 225 votes, while Councilwoman Tonyal Long was reelected with 253 votes.
While the results won't be official until Friday, Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III told Welaka residents he doubts the winners will change before then.
'I am very excited and humbled at the same time to become the mayor of Welaka,' Dugger said Tuesday night via text message. 'Welaka is a special place, and we face some serious challenges if we want to keep it this way.'
She said overseeing the improvements to the town's wastewater treatment plant is one of her priorities as is getting the town's financial accounting up to date.
In the meantime, however, she expressed her gratitude to her team and the people who voted for her.
'I want to thank those who supported me,' Dugger texted. 'And I am committed to serving all the people of Welaka.'
She defeated Kevin Finch, the ex-husband of acting Mayor Jessica Finch, by six points, according to Elections Office records.
Despite the close count, Overturf said, there will be no recount required. Even if the three provisional ballots are deemed valid and are all for Kevin Finch, there would still not be a difference of less than half of 1%, which is what would necessitate a recount.
'Even if he got all three, it still would not put him ahead,' Overturf said Wednesday.
Courtney DeSouza, the fiancé of former Mayor Jamie Watts, received 81 votes, and Pam Olson and Brady Kay each received 29 votes.
As for the council member race, Long and Walker defeated David Jeltes, who received 177 votes, according to the Elections Office.
Long said everyone loves Welaka and wants to see it succeed. She hopes to work with Dugger and the rest of the council to help the town prosper.
'Once again, I'm just so grateful that the town has placed their trust in me,' Long said Wednesday. 'And moving forward, there is so much work to be done for us to get the ship centered again so we can move forward.
'... I just hope that the new mayor and all of us can come together and get everything ironed out the way it needs to be.'
Walker said she was grateful for all the support she received. Her victory is proof voters have confidence in her, Walker said, and she hopes to live up to their expectations.
'I'm just appreciative of the votes I got from the citizens of Welaka and the confidence they have in me to move forward in getting the town business completed,' she said.
Through mail voting and voting on Election Day, 359 of the 692 eligible voters in Welaka cast a ballot in the election. Overturf said was happy to see the voter turnout climb to 51.88%.
'I was really pleased with that,' he said.
The newly elected officials will be sworn in at 6 p.m. Friday at Town Hall, 400 Fourth St. in Welaka.
While this election is over, qualifying for Welaka's special election will begin at noon Friday and will end at noon March 21, Overturf said. Jessica Finch, who in November announced her plans to resign from the council, will end her time as the acting mayor Friday and will not be returning to her position as a council member.
The special election to find her council successor will be from 7 a.m. – 7 p.m. May 6.

Applicant: The applicant for this project is Certainteed Gypsum Palatka, LLC. The applicant's responsible official and mailing address are: Ms. Debbie Master, Plant Manager, Certainteed Gypsum Palatka, LLC, 886 North Highway 17, Palatka, Florida 32177.
Facility Location: The applicant operates the existing Certainteed Gypsum Palatka, which is located in Putnam County at 886 North Highway 17, Palatka, Florida.
Project: The applicant applied on November 12, 2024 to the Department for an after-the-fact air construction permit modification and a revised Title V air operation permit. The existing facility consists of the following emissions units.
Two FGD surge bins; two cage mill dryer systems; two Imp mill feed silos; two Imp mill flash calciner systems; two Imp mill air cooling systems; two stucco silos; starch silo; sawing systems/dunnage machines; belt conveyors and bucket elevators; emergency live bottom feed hopper; wallboard dryer - with natural gas burners; ball mills; landplaster bin, additive system and pin mixer; reclaim processing and screening; reclaim grinder, two Perkins diesel fired emergency engines; CAT diesel engine and a John Deere water pump. Surge bin filters, fabric filters and baghouses for particulate matter emission control.
This air construction permit modification updates some specific conditions of Permit No. 1070039-033-AC for the as-built emission unit (EU) 039 Reclaim Grinder to change the location from inside to outside the active storage dome, install an after-the-fact wet suppression system control device on EU039 to control fugitive dust emissions from reclaimed wallboard grinding and handling, and to change the operating capacity of the reclaim grinder operating capacity from 100 tons per hour to 38 tons per hour.
This revised Title V air operation permit is to incorporate Permit Nos. 1070039-033-AC and 1070039-037-AC. Permit No. 1070039-033-AC which was extended by permit Nos. 1070039-035-AC and 036-AC.

The proposed project is not exempt from air permitting requirements and a Title V air operation permit is required to operate the facility.

The Permitting Authority will accept written comments concerning the draft Title V air operation permit for a period of 30 days from the date of publication of the Public Notice. Written comments must be received by the close of business (5:00 p.m.), on or before the end of this 30-day period by the Permitting Authority at the above address. As part of his or her comments, any person may also request that the Permitting Authority hold a public meeting on this permitting action. If the Permitting Authority determines there is sufficient interest for a public meeting, it will publish notice of the time, date, and location in the Florida Administrative Register (FAR). If a public meeting is requested within the 30-day comment period and conducted by the Permitting Authority, any oral and written comments received during the public meeting will also be considered by the Permitting Authority. If timely received written comments or comments received at a public meeting result in a significant change to the draft Title V air operation permit, the Permitting Authority shall issue a revised draft Title V air operation permit and require, if applicable, another Public Notice. All comments filed will be made available for public inspection. For additional information, contact the Permitting Authority at the above address or phone number.
Petitions: A person whose substantial interests are affected by the proposed permitting decision may petition for an administrative hearing in accordance with Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S. Petitions filed by any persons other than those entitled to written notice under Section 120.60(3), F.S., must be filed within 14 days of publication of the Public Notice or receipt of a written notice, whichever occurs first. Under Section 120.60(3), F.S., however, any person who asked the Permitting Authority for notice of agency action may file a petition within 14 days of receipt of that notice, regardless of the date of publication. A petitioner shall mail a copy of the petition to the applicant at the address indicated above, at the time of filing. A petition for administrative hearing must contain the information set forth below and must be filed (received) with the Agency Clerk in the Office of General Counsel, 3900 Commonwealth Boulevard, MS 35, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-3000, Agency_Clerk@dep.state.fl.us, before the deadline. The failure of any person to file a petition within the appropriate time period shall constitute a waiver of that person's right to request an administrative determination (hearing) under Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S., or to intervene in this proceeding and participate as a party to it. Any subsequent intervention (in a proceeding initiated by another party) will be only at the approval of the presiding officer upon the filing of a motion in compliance with Rule 28-106.205, F.A.C.
A petition that disputes the material facts on which the Permitting Authority's action is based must contain the following information: (a) The name and address of each agency affected and each agency's file or identification number, if known; (b) The name, address, any email address, telephone number and any facsimile number of the petitioner; the name, address, any email address, telephone number, and any facsimile number of the petitioner's representative, if any, which shall be the address for service purposes during the course of the proceeding; and an explanation of how the petitioner's substantial interests will be affected by the agency determination; (c) A statement of when and how each petitioner received notice of the agency action or proposed decision; (d) A statement of all disputed issues of material fact. If there are none, the petition must so indicate; (e) A concise statement of the ultimate facts alleged, including the specific facts the petitioner contends warrant reversal or modification of the agency's proposed action; (f) A statement of the specific rules or statutes the petitioner contends require reversal or modification of the agency's proposed action including an explanation of how the alleged facts relate to the specific rules or statutes; and, (g) A statement of the relief sought by the petitioner, stating precisely the action the petitioner wishes the agency to take with respect to the agency's proposed action. A petition that does not dispute the material facts upon which the Permitting Authority's action is based shall state that no such facts are in dispute and otherwise shall contain the same information as set forth above, as required by Rule 28-106.301, F.A.C.
Because the administrative hearing process is designed to formulate final agency action, the filing of a petition means that the Permitting Authority's final action may be different from the position taken by it in this written notice of Intent to Issue Air Permit. Persons whose substantial interests will be affected by any such final decision of the Permitting Authority on the application have the right to petition to become a party to the proceeding, in accordance with the requirements set forth above.
Extension of Time: Under Rule 62-110.106(4), F.A.C., a person whose substantial interests are affected by the Department's action may also request an extension of time to file a petition for an administrative hearing. The Department may, for good cause shown, grant the request for an extension of time. Requests for extension of time must be filed with the Office of General Counsel of the Department at 3900 Commonwealth Boulevard, Mail Station 35, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-3000, or via electronic correspondence at Agency_Clerk@dep.state.fl.us, before the deadline for filing a petition for an administrative hearing. A timely request for extension of time shall toll the running of the time period for filing a petition until the request is acted upon.
Mediation: Mediation is not available for this proceeding.
Objections: Finally, pursuant to 42 United States Code (U.S.C.) Section 7661d(b)(2), any person may petition the Administrator of the EPA within 60 days of the expiration of the Administrator's 45-day review period as established at 42 U.S.C. Section 7661d(b)(1), to object to the issuance of any Title V air operation permit. Any petition shall be based only on objections to the permit that were raised with reasonable specificity during the 30-day public comment period provided in the Public Notice, unless the petitioner demonstrates to the Administrator of the EPA that it was impracticable to raise such objections within the comment period or unless the grounds for such objection arose after the comment period. Filing of a petition with the Administrator of the EPA does not stay the effective date of any permit properly issued pursuant to the provisions of Chapter 62-213, F.A.C. Petitions filed with the Administrator of EPA must meet the requirements of 42 U.S.C. Section 7661d(b)(2) and must be filed with the Administrator of the EPA at: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Office of the Administrator, 1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, N.W., Mail Code: 1101A, Washington, DC 20460. For more information regarding EPA review and objections, visit EPA's Region 4 web site at https://www.epa.gov/caa-permitting/florida-proposed-title-v-permits.

St. Johns River State College (SJR State) is soliciting architectural services for the renovation and addition to the Classroom Building (Bldg. T) located on the Palatka Campus, 5001 St. Johns Avenue, Palatka, FL 32177.
To be considered, qualifications must be submitted as prescribed in the RFQ-SJR-01-2025 Specifications Document. The specifications document may be obtained by sending a written request via e-mail to TerryThomas@sjrstate.edu or by clicking on this link to the college's webpage dedicated to this RFQ https://www.sjrstate.edu/012025.
RFQ responses, clearly marked on the outside with the firm name and RFQ-SJR-01-2025, must be received by Mrs. Terry Thomas, AVP of Facilities, Planning, and Capital Projects, St. Johns River State College, Business Office, 5001 St. Johns Ave., Palatka, FL 32177 by 2:00 p.m. on April 16, 2025. Responses received by the deadline will be officially opened and firm names read aloud at 2:30 p.m. on April 16, 2025, in Room A152, Valhalla Hall in the Admin. Bldg. on the campus in Palatka. Information and notices will be posted on the college's web page dedicated to this RFQ at https://www.sjrstate.edu/012025 as the process progresses.

title: Palms harvested ahead of festival
description: Since its start in April 1978, one Putnam County festival has for years provided residents and visitors with a unique cuisine in the form of swamp cabbage. It's not an easy job, according to County…
content: Since its start in April 1978, one Putnam County festival has for years provided residents and visitors with a unique cuisine in the form of swamp cabbage. It's not an easy job, according to County Commissioner Bill Pickens, a member of the Rotary Club of Crescent City, who has been overseeing the swamp cabbage harvesting for about 35 years. He has taken the reins again in preparation for this year's Crescent City Catfish Festival on Saturday. With a generator, saw sharpener, eight chainsaws, a donated dump truck and a back-end loader, Pickens and his crew of nearly 40 volunteers took on the task of harvesting between 500-600 hearts of palm on Wednesday. The size of the palms harvested averaged between 7 to 15 feet tall. 'We usually have eight volunteers sawing the palms and maybe 20 loading it and getting it on the dump truck,' he said. 'That took a good eight-hour day.' BRANDON D. OLIVER/Palatka Daily News – County Commissioner Bill Pickens talks to nearly 40 volunteers who gathered in Bunnell on Wednesday to harvest heart of palm. JROTC students from Crescent City Junior-Senior High School were among those who helped with the harvesting by loading the cabbage heads onto the dump truck. However, Pickens said, the work doesn't end there. 'On Friday, we will spend six hours in two different places booting out the cabbage,' he said. On Saturday, starting at about 5 a.m., the cooking process will begin at the Crescent City Junior-Senior High School cafeteria, according to Pickens. 'We usually will average about 150 gallons of the swamp cabbage in four cookings for the festival,' he said. 'I call this a cracker delicacy.' The swamp cabbage delicacy, Pickens said, has been cooked using the same recipe throughout 42 iterations of the Crescent City Catfish Festival. 'We use about 100 pounds of bacon and sausage and then salt, pepper and a little bit of sugar and vinegar to taste,' he said. BRANDON D. OLIVER/Palatka Daily News – Two volunteers chop down a palmetto in Bunnell to collect heart of palm for swamp cabbage, which will be served Saturday at the Crescent City Catfish Festival. The Catfish Festival returns this weekend after a four-year break due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The festival will be at Eva Lyon Park, 100 S. Summit St., from 10 a.m. – 5 p.m. It will begin with a welcome to festival-goers and vendor booths opening. A DJ will play music from 10 a.m. – noon. 'Because we are restarting the festival, we determined that a one-day event on Saturday would be the best course,' festival Chairman Rodney Phillips said. 'After we see the crowds come back, we may go back to our normal Friday and Saturday event for future festivals.' The Rotary Club of Crescent City is the sponsor for the festival, which will include arts and crafts vendors and a parade at 11 a.m. starting at the flashing light on Summit St. and heading north. A kids zone, a car show sponsored by the Yacht Club of Crescent City and live music from noon – 5 p.m. at the gazebo will also occur at the festival. A variety of food will also be available, including gator tail, quail, frog legs, funnel cakes, hamburgers, hotdogs, chicken fingers, fresh strawberry shortcake, swamp cabbage and, of course, catfish dinners and sandwiches. The music lineup will include the band Frazzled followed by live Latin music starting with the band Clave 386. BRANDON D. OLIVER/Palatka Daily News – Numerous palmettos are situated in a back-end loader before being stripped and loaded Wednesday in Bunnell. Phillips said although the catfish dinners are the staple of the festival and are made fresh and ready to eat, swamp cabbage and strawberry shortcake are big draws, too. 'The festival will be a safe, fun environment for the whole family,' he said. 'We have something to offer for all ages.' Besides that, Phillips said, proceeds from the festival will go to Rotary's 'Dollars for Scholars,' which has raised more than $1 million to benefit high school seniors. Pickens said there will be 15 scholarships of $1,500 each awarded to seniors. Over the years, Phillips said, there have been an estimated 20,000 visitors who have attended the event. 'It's amazing to see the community come together,' he said. 'We have hundreds of volunteers who supply their talents. Without them, we couldn't be successful.' Phillips hopes area residents will come and support the Rotary Club of Crescent City's Catfish Festival. 'We would enjoy seeing our friends and neighbors, and they can be a part of helping kick the Catfish Festival off again,' he said.

title: District warns of potential solar eclipse dangers
description: Putnam County residents on Monday will experience part of the last total solar eclipse in the United States until 2044, but officials are urging caution. A total solar eclipse will be visible in a…
content:
Putnam County residents on Monday will experience part of the last total solar eclipse in the United States until 2044, but officials are urging caution.
A total solar eclipse will be visible in a good-sized portion of the nation, but Florida will see just a partial eclipse. Still, Putnam County School District Superintendent Rick Surrency said there will be precautions in place to protect students' eyes during the event.
'Our concern is always for the safety of our students and a solar eclipse can pose some danger to those who look directly at the sun,' Surrency wrote in an email sent to parents on April 1.
A solar eclipse occurs when the moon passes between the sun and Earth, blocking the face of the sun. Putnam County will experience up to 62% darkness coverage, Surrency said.
The eclipse will occur from 1:46 – 4:18 p.m., with the maximum coverage happening at 3:04 p.m., he said.
People can safely look at the eclipse with special glasses, filters or lenses designed to protect their eyes while looking at the obscured sun, NASA states on its website. Using sunglasses or other unapproved tinted eyewear will result in severe eye damage, officials said.
Surrency said the glasses commonly used need to be up to international standards, but the district has heard reports of counterfeit glasses. Due to the possibility of students getting their hands on faulty eclipse glasses, the school district will not allow students outside from 1:30 – 4:30 p.m. Monday.
'We recognize that students will be transitioning for dismissal during this time, and students will be instructed not to look into the sun,' Surrency wrote in an email.
Looking at the sun 'will instantly cause severe eye injury,' NASA officials confirmed in a safety guide.
Putnam County School Board member David Buckles said he remembers having to look through smoked glass to see an eclipse when he was a child. All safety guidelines for the upcoming eclipse are recognized by state agencies, he said during a school board meeting Tuesday.
'We didn't just make this up willy-nilly out of the sky,' he said. 'I wanted to reassure people that are watching (the school board meeting) that this is an actual event and it's not an April Fools' joke. The intent is to try to protect kids from looking directly at the sun and let parents be parents.'
In his email, Surrency said parents could check their children out of school early or keep them at home Monday and the absence will be excused as long as children provide a note from a parent or guardian.
'(We're) not trying to make (it) a bigger thing than it is, but we feel an obligation to make sure students, educators and parents realize the danger of the solar eclipse,' Surrency said during the board meeting. 'It is a great thing to understand and learn about. … We felt obligated to make sure we sent this (email) out just to make sure if they go out there and just wear any set of sunglasses that are not approved, that could cause damage.'

You are required by section 98.075(7) Florida Statutes, to contact the Supervisor of Elections in Palatka, Putnam County, Florida, no later than Thirty (30) days after the date of the publication. Failure to respond will result in a determination of ineligibility by the Supervisor and your name will be removed from the statewide voter registration system. Within the THIRTY (30) days you may contact the Supervisor of Elections at 386-329-0224 for further assistance or to receive information regarding the potential ineligibility and the procedure to resolve this matter. If you attempt to vote at an early voting site or your normal election day polling place, you will be required to vote a provisional ballot. If you vote by mail, your ballot will be treated as a provisional ballot. In either case, your ballot may not be counted until final determination of eligibility is made. If you wish for your ballot to be counted, you must contact the supervisor of elections office within 2 days after the election and present evidence that you are eligible to vote. Por medio de la presente, se le avisa que su elegibilidad para votar está en duda. En virtud de la sección 98.075(7) de los Estatutos de la Florida, se le exige que se comunique con el Supervisor Electoral en Palatka, Condado de Putnam, Florida, a más tardar Treinta (30) días después de la fecha de la publicación. Si no hay una respuesta, el Supervisor determinará su inelegibilidad y se eliminará su nombre del sistema de inscripción de votantes a nivel de estado. Si desea que se cuente su boleta, debe comunicarse con la oficina del supervisor de elecciones dentro de los 2 días posteriores a la elección y presentar evidencia de que es elegible para votar. title: Actor bidding farewell after final weekend performance
description: Having gotten a taste of musical theater when he was just 12, Matthew Snider has found his happy place on stage. The Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School senior will graduate this year with 12 shows…
content:
Having gotten a taste of musical theater when he was just 12, Matthew Snider has found his happy place on stage.
The Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School senior will graduate this year with 12 shows under his belt with the Palatka Junior-Senior High School Musical Theatre Department, including the spring musical, 'The Drowsy Chaperone, A Musical With A Comedy,' where he plays George, the best man to the groom, Robert, and who is in charge of planning the wedding.
'I have changed tremendously in the six years I have been a part of this program,' said Snider, now 17, who lives in Melrose. 'I learned how you need every single person in the production or anything in life to be fully committed or you will not be able to perform to the best of your ability.'
'The Drowsy Chaperone' opened last weekend and its final performances are set for 7:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday and 2:30 p.m. Sunday at the Jim Pignato Theatre at the C.L. Overturf Jr. District Center, 1100 S. 18th St. in Palatka.
TRISHA MURPHY/Palatka Daily News – Matthew Snider, a senior in the Palatka Junior-Senior High School Musical Theatre Department, will perform his last show, 'The Drowsy Chaperone, A Musical Within A Comedy,' which will start at 7:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday and 2:30 p.m. Sunday. The PHS spring musical is presented through a special arrangement with Music Theatre International. Tickets are $15 in advance at Ralph's House of Flowers, 605 St. Johns Ave., Suite 101, or $20 at the door while available.
Director Jim Pignato said the show, written by Bob Martin and Don Mckellar, won five Tony awards in 2006, including Best Music and Best Book of a Musical.
'The whole show takes place in the apartment of a lonely, eccentric man who shares his favorite Broadway show, ‘The Drowsy Chaperone,' with the audience by playing the soundtrack record,' Pignato said. 'It's a show from 1928 that he's never even seen but it comes to life in his imagination. At the end, he actually crosses over into 1928 with the cast.'
Snider said his first play with the Palatka High group was in 2018 when he was cast as Mike Teavee in 'Willy Wonka.' Then the PHS production 'Newsies' came around and Pignato was in need of many people to play male characters so Snider decided to audition.
According to Pignato, Snider has matured into a fine Christian young man.
'He is coachable, talented and a lot of fun to work with,' he said. 'He has played a great variety of roles. In last year's spring production 'Titanic,' he played Captain Smith, a very dramatic role, which is totally different from this role of George.'
TRISHA MURPHY/Palatka Daily News – Senior Matthew Snider, left, gives a playful wave during rehearsal with castmates Gabrielle Chapman, center, and Andrew McClellan, right, as they prepare for their final bow with the Palatka Junior-Senior High School Musical Theater Department this weekend. Pignato said this year's spring show was selected for his group to perform because 'we all need a good, silly laugh in the world in which we live.'
'Silliness agrees perfectly with Matthew because he is by nature a kidder,' he said. 'He will be missed as he graduates and goes off to (Florida State University).'
Before joining the theater group, Snider said, he had performed three years with the Q.I. Roberts drama class, where he learned a lot. He also was part of two summer musical camps with Florida School of the Arts.
'The Q.I. program helped me grow my skills as an actor,' he said. 'I feel like being with the PHS group has given me training in leadership and in being confident in what I am doing.'
Following graduation, Snider plans to work toward a degree in communications, where he wants to become a broadcaster or a radio host.
'I would love to still do musical theater in college in some form, whether that be for the college or elsewhere,' he said.
Snider admits he always gets a little nervous before every show, but one of his favorite things about live theater is there are never two identical shows because something can always happen.
'There have been many instances of something funny happening on stage,' he said. 'There have been times where someone falls during a dance in a way that they don't hurt themselves and it always provides us with a good laugh afterwards.'
TRISHA MURPHY/Palatka Daily News – Snider, right, and McClellan rehearse a scene from 'The Drowsy Chaperone, A Musical Within A Comedy.' While part of the Palatka High group, Snider has had the opportunity to sing, dance and act. Besides that, Snider said his favorite thing to do though is dance.
'I have spent many times in the ensemble just performing and helping by singing and dancing,' he said. 'I love singing harmonies as it fills in the songs. I greatly fell in love with dancing and I love characters that enable me to act and dance at the same time.'
Snider believes he can't end his time with the theater group without taking the time to thank those who have helped him along the way.
'These past six years have been some of the best moments of my life,' he said. 'I am truly indebted to Mr. P. and I hope he knows how much we care about him and are grateful for him and how much he has helped me grow as a person.'
Snider pauses when considering what his favorite part has been during his time with the theater group.
'It is hard to pick a favorite musical because I love each and every show that I have been a part of,' he said. 'My favorite show to dance in was ‘Hello Dolly' as I loved the number ‘Waiters Gallop' and ‘Hello Dolly.' My favorite show to act in was ‘Titanic' because I greatly enjoyed playing Captain Smith. And my favorite show overall, however, was ‘Newsies' as it was my first big musical and when my heart truly fell in love with theater.'
Snider said what he has loved most about being a part of musical theater is seeing everyone work together.
'You can't do a musical without a dedicated group of people coming together to perform,' he said. 'I have also loved growing myself, especially as a dancer and seeing my own personal improvements. I just love being able to cut loose and be someone other than myself.'

title: Construction phase begins for 1st of 3 new high schools
description: CRESCENT CITY – Local officials and students celebrated Friday as they broke ground at the site of the first of three new high schools to be built in Putnam County. Crescent City Junior-Senior High…
content:
CRESCENT CITY – Local officials and students celebrated Friday as they broke ground at the site of the first of three new high schools to be built in Putnam County.
Crescent City Junior-Senior High School, 2201 S. U.S. 17, will be rebuilt entirely, except for some sports fields, by August 2025.
The new building will replace the current structure that was built in 1968, Putnam County School District Superintendent Rick Surrency said.
'This is truly a momentous occasion,' he said. 'You know, 56 years later, we're here to have a groundbreaking for this community for generations to come.'
The school will cost roughly $95 million to construct, but the money will come from Florida Department of Education funding instead of tax dollars from Putnam residents, district officials said. The guaranteed maximum price has yet to be determined, they said.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – Putnam County School Board member Holly Pickens reminisces Friday on her time teaching and coaching at Crescent City High. State Rep. Bobby Payne, R-Palatka, said Friday he secured $60 million in state funding for the Crescent City school.
'I'm so proud of the fact that we're able to do this,' Payne said. 'I'm proud of the fact that I've worked with Dr. Surrency and others in this community for a long time to finally reach the vision that we see today.'
The school district plans to revitalize eight schools by 2027. Crescent City, Interlachen and Palatka junior-senior high schools are being revamped with state money. Crescent City is the first junior-senior high school for which officials have broken ground.
Five Putnam elementary schools are being upgraded via a $300 million general obligation bond, which 54.53% of Putnam voters approved in the November 2022 general election. The bonds are scheduled to be paid off over 30 years through an additional property tax.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – Superintendent Rick Surrency and Putnam County School Board members break ground Friday morning at Crescent City Junior-Senior High School ahead of the construction of the school's replacement. Construction on a Palatka elementary school currently known as Palatka A broke ground at 156 Horseman Club Road on Oct. 30. The next school scheduled for construction is a Crescent City elementary school located near the intersection of County Road 308 and Union Avenue, but the district has yet to announce a start date.
Crescent City High Principal Tim Adams, other school administrators and five younger students who will see the state-of-the-art building come to fruition were at Friday's groundbreaking ceremony to celebrate the historic moment.
The completion of the new school is something the whole community is looking forward to seeing, Adams said.
'Today started an exciting journey to a new school,' he said. '... At the end of the day, it's really what it's about for our kids.'
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – State Rep. Bobby Payne, R-Palatka, talks about how proud he is to see the first of three new schools enter the construction phase. School Board member Holly Pickens said the construction of a new high school made her emotional for numerous reasons. Pickens taught at Crescent City High for more than 30 years and coached three sports during her time there.
It was at that school, during a school play, that her boyfriend at the time – Bill Pickens, who later married her and became a county commissioner – first told her he loved her.
She said she will keep those memories in her heart.
'Part of me will be really sad when it gets torn down, but I know that the future is bright,' the school board member said. 'I know that the reason we're doing this is to give our kids the best future to reach their full potential and have opportunities that (the current) building just can't give them.'

title: SJRSC softball team victory etched in metal
description: The St. Johns River State College's softball team's National Junior College Athletic Association Division II World Series championship continues to amaze Putnam County elected officials and college…
content:
The St. Johns River State College's softball team's National Junior College Athletic Association Division II World Series championship continues to amaze Putnam County elected officials and college representatives.
The Board of County Commissioners, County Administrator Terry Suggs, and Deputy County Administrator Julianne Young presented the team's coaches, mascot and President Joe Pickens with signs Tuesday commemorating the girls' 2024 National Junior College Athletic Association championship win.
It's the only national championship win in any sport in the college's history.
The signs will be placed at every major entrance to the county, commissioners said.
While none of the softball players could attend the sign unveiling because the girls are out of school for the summer, the team's coaches and Pickens doted on all their hard work and the incredible games they played.
'This is a once-in-a-lifetime occurrence for the college and for Putnam County,' Pickens said.
The state college Vikings secured their history-making win on May 25, beating Kirkwood College of Iowa after a nail-biting seventh inning, 7-5.
People who attended Tuesday's commission meeting saw a video playback of the team's final moments, including a dropped flyball by one Vikings player. At the top of the seventh, the Vikings had been up 4-1, but Kirkwood players came back to change up the game, 5-4, after that.
'At that point, we're just sick,' Pickens said. He said the girl who dropped the ball was in tears on the field, as were the fans who traveled to watch the college play.
However, head coach Joe Pound and assistant coach Britney Purser kept their cool, Pickens said. The last three players up to bat clinched the win, scoring three home runs, and ending the powerful game with the rest of the team piling on top of them after the win.
'We actually think that if Hollywood came up with a script like that, nobody would believe it,' Pickens said.
Photo by SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News.
County Administrator Terry Suggs and Deputy County Administrator Julianne Young reveal a sign Tuesday that will celebrate the St. Johns River State College softball team's 2024 National Junior College Athletic Association championship win for decades to come. Pound called this year a big season for the college beyond the national championship.
'Every record that this program has was broken this year,' he said. 'From the total wins, I think the previous record was 33 wins, we ended with 55. We had the most hits, the most runs, the most doubles, the most home runs, the most stolen bases.'
He thanked everyone for their support, including the community. Of the 19 girls on the team, Pound said 17 families showed up to watch them play for the championship in Spartanburg, South Carolina.
Purser agreed and expressed pride for the players.
'They refused to lose, and I think we said it all year,' Purser said. 'We'd be down, and I think we were down in the sixth or seventh (innings) in about 15 to 20 of our games this year and we have come back to win every single one except for one.
'It just goes to the mindset of the team, and they … battled, they competed, they knew what they were capable of doing.'
