title: Church, nonprofit helping people cool off as temperatures soar
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The summer sun shows no sign of relenting in the next 10 days, but local humanitarians are trying to help disadvantaged people beat the heat.
content:
Body
The summer sun shows no sign of relenting in the next 10 days, but local humanitarians are trying to help disadvantaged people beat the heat.
First Presbyterian Church Pastor Cliff Lyda said the front doors of his church's Westminster Hall, 126 S. Second St., are open for people to go inside to grab a bottle of water and get out of the heat.
'Our intention is to do this until it stops being so ugly out,' he said.
The doors are open from the late morning to about 5 p.m., said Lyda, who acknowledges church officials are figuring out the heat shelter schedule as they go. He said this is one small effort to help people who might not have another way to get cool while temperatures remain in the 90s or above.
'Hopefully, we're going to save people from the heat,' Lyda said. 'We've never done this.'
Westminster Hall also opens in the winter as a cold-weather shelter for people to stay overnight. The summer version of the shelter is only for people to sit inside for a little while, not stay overnight.
Hot-weather shelter efforts began Monday, and Lyda said just a few people stopped by. The hall is scheduled to be open daily, even on the weekends.
'It's the least we can do,' Lyda said.
According to weather.com, temperatures in Palatka are predicted to be in the mid- to low 90s from Saturday through July 16. Scattered thunderstorms are also in that prediction.
The lowest daytime temperature predicted will be Tuesday when the Weather Channel forecasted a high of 88 degrees.
'This is an emergency,' Lyda said.
The church is also seeking water bottle donations and volunteers who can work shifts of two to three hours at Westminster. People can drop water anywhere near the hall and Lyda will bring it inside.
Anyone who wants to volunteer can call the church at 386-328-1435 and leave a message.
Putnam Habitat for Humanity is doing its part to help people vulnerable to the heat.
Director Ramicah Johnson said many elderly and low-income residents need fans during the sweltering conditions because they don't have air conditioning. The organization is seeking larger floor fans even if they are lightly used.
'Whatever people can afford,' she said.
Habitat has been receiving calls requesting fans from all over Putnam County, she added.
Johnson said Habitat received eight fans from Monday to Wednesday. Donors can drop additional fans at Habitat, 2506 Crill Ave. in Palatka, from 9 a.m. – 1 p.m. Mondays through Fridays.
The Habitat headquarters is not where recipients should pick up the fans. Habitat officials will distribute them to other nonprofit organizations across the county, and those organizations will give fans to people in need.
Donors can also take fans to St. Vincent de Paul, 111 N. Francis St. in Interlachen, from 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. on Tuesdays through Fridays and Saturdays; South Putnam Christian Service Center, 223 N. Summit St. in Crescent City, from 9 a.m. – 1:30 p.m. on Tuesdays; and the Palatka Christian Service Center, 2600 Peters St. in Palatka., from 9 a.m. – 1:30 p.m. Mondays through Fridays.
'The important part is just getting them out to the area,' Johnson said.
People can mail cash donations to Putnam Habitat for Humanity, P.O. Box 2433, Palatka, FL 32178. Johnson said donors should write 'fans' on the memo line of the check to specify how the money should be spent.
For questions about the fan donations, call 386-325-5862 or email director@putnamhabitat.org.

title: Column: Looking back on a year in the editor's chair
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: 'Time, time, time 'See what's become of me 'While I looked around for my possibilities' – The Bangles
content:
Body
'Time, time, time
'See what's become of me
'While I looked around for my possibilities'
– The Bangles
What a difference a year makes! It was a year and two days ago when I accepted the challenge of being the editor of the Palatka Daily News. Before informing my publisher I would accept the promotion she'd offered me three days earlier, I weighed the pros and cons of putting myself in such a public-facing, pressure-fueled position.
Obviously, the pros won out.
The days since July 3, 2023, have been filled with personal and professional ups and downs – and a huge gray area I still don't know how to navigate. On one hand, my confidence in my ability to do my job has grown beyond what I thought was possible. On the other, I am almost always wondering if there is more I could be doing or darting awake at 6 a.m. because I'm unsure if I misspelled a simple word in a headline. Problems and surprises I once found daunting now seem easily solvable – or are at least simple enough for me to not break a sweat.
I'm too busy to continually audit my performance. In fact, I'm writing this two days after I intended because there is always something happening. However, there are some lessons and revelations that have stuck with me since occupying this office.
– Some people focus too much on titles. Prior to being promoted, I was the news editor and practically was the interim editor after my predecessor resigned. Much of what I do now, I did then. Imagine my surprise when people who had previously ignored my calls – some blatantly sent me to voicemail before the second ring could finish – began reaching out to me, giving me their personal numbers and encouraging me to call them whenever I needed something. To be fair, those instances were the few that accompanied many other well wishes from people new and familiar. The few continue to stick out, though.
– I had to learn how to accept nice things. For as loud and vain as I can be about certain things, I like to fly under the radar regarding other areas in my life. My intention was to announce the news of my promotion to my family and close friends via text, make posts on different social media platforms to inform the rest of the people in my personal life and write a column to inform the general public. That's when my anxiety-inducing imposter syndrome reared its ugly head and dug in its heels. Did I really deserve this promotion? Could I do this job? Was I the best candidate or was I chosen simply because I was already familiar with the company and community? It took my family celebrating my accomplishment in person and a series of tear-jerking audio notes from a friend and former colleague to make me realize the answers to those questions were 'yes,' 'hell yes' and 'stop being an idiot.'
– I'm great at what I do, but I should always strive to be better. There are days when the tasks ahead of me seem Sisyphean in nature. But the work must get done, so I persist. That persistence, partnered with collaboration, decisiveness and an above-average command of my emotions, gets the job done. And I'm not shy about reaching out to others for assistance, even if they haven't worked here since 2018. No one is an island, so I'm not going to act like one.
– Distractions are necessary. Overseeing coverage of macabre events, playing phone tag with people who don't want to be found and juggling numerous tasks at once can be maddening. Carving out time for myself is vital to me not going insane and taking everyone with me. It's amazing how much calmer I am after a cup of tea, an hour of yoga, gossiping with co-workers or simply taking a series of deep breaths. I can't control what occurs, but I can handle how I react to it.
– I'm going to do it my own way. Rather than trying to fit the mold of how I think an editor should act or present himself, I determined early on – probably before I got promoted – I would be myself. I didn't want to emulate other professionals in the hopes of being taken seriously. If I am going to do this job and be genuine with others, I must be genuine with myself. Therefore, anyone who visits my office will see action figures and a collection of hippos. My writing and how I approach people are unique to the type of person I am. I'm dotted with tattoos and have no qualms about how they affect my professionalism. Spoiler alert: they don't!
The good and fulfilling parts of this job far outweigh the bad and draining. Challenging myself is fun. Becoming more assertive at work has benefitted me in my personal life. I take pride in being responsible, even if that means I have to cut back on my colorful language and general rambunctiousness when I'm out and about in Putnam County.
Year one was a wild ride. Considering the sale of our company was finalized mere days ago, I'm sure year two will be an adventure that will provide even more learning experiences.
What I might learn in the future will not be nearly as valuable as what I learned years ago: Never ever alter the 'Sean of the South' publication schedule. There's a good reason this anniversary column didn't run on my actual anniversary.

Pursuant to Chapter 28-106 and Rule 40C-1.1007, Florida Administrative Code (F.A.C.), the petition must be filed (received) either by delivery at the office of the District Clerk at District Headquarters, P.O. Box 1429, Palatka FL 32178-1429 (4049 Reid St, Palatka, FL 32177) or by e-mail with the District Clerk at Clerk@sjrwmd.com, within twenty-one (21) days of newspaper publication of the notice of District decision (for those persons to whom the District does not mail or email actual notice). A petition must comply with Sections 120.54(5)(b)4. and 120.569(2)(c), Florida Statutes (F.S.), and Chapter 28-106, F.A.C. The District will not accept a petition sent by facsimile (fax). Mediation pursuant to Section 120.573, F.S., may be available and choosing mediation does not affect your right to an administrative hearing.
A petition for an administrative hearing is deemed filed upon receipt of the complete petition by the District Clerk at the District Headquarters in Palatka, Florida during the District's regular business hours. The District's regular business hours are 8 a.m. – 5 p.m., excluding weekends and District holidays. Petitions received by the District Clerk after the District's regular business hours shall be deemed filed as of 8 a.m. on the District's next regular business day. The District's acceptance of petitions filed by e-mail is subject to certain conditions set forth in the District's Statement of Agency Organization and Operation (issued pursuant to Rule 28-101.001, Florida Administrative Code), which is available for viewing at www.sjrwmd.com. These conditions include, but are not limited to, the petition being in the form of a PDF or TIFF file and being capable of being stored and printed by the District. Further, pursuant to the District's Statement of Agency Organization and Operation, attempting to file a petition by facsimile (fax) is prohibited and shall not constitute filing.
The right to an administrative hearing and the relevant procedures to be followed are governed by Chapter 120, Florida Statutes, Chapter 28-106, Florida Administrative Code, and Rule 40C-1.1007, Florida Administrative Code. Because the administrative hearing process is designed to formulate final agency action, the filing of a petition means the District's final action may be different from the position taken by it in this notice. Failure to file a petition for an administrative hearing within the requisite time frame shall constitute a waiver of the right to an administrative hearing. (Rule 28-106.111, F.A.C.).

title: Classes offered to promote home ownership
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Two agencies have teamed up to help residents improve their financial planning and aid them in buying their own homes.
content:
Body
Two agencies have teamed up to help residents improve their financial planning and aid them in buying their own homes.
Employees from Palatka Housing Authority and Ameris Bank in Palatka hosted a Ready, Set, Own class Tuesday evening at the Ragsdale Family Investment Center in Palatka, where bank employees taught financial planning basics.
Carol Coffie, the housing authority's director of resident services, said the agencies are trying to make financial literacy and homeownership a simple journey.
'The whole idea of being a part of the public housing community is not that they're going to stay forever,' she said. 'So, this is kind of like a push and also an acquisition of resources so that they will be able to move forward in the journey and understand the steps along the way.'
Coffie said some people might not strive for homeownership because they do not understand the process.
Another class will take place at 6 p.m. July 23 at the James A. Long Family Investment Center, 601 N. 21st St. in Palatka.
Desireé Akins, the vice president and branch market manager of Ameris Bank, 601 Reid St. in Palatka, said she grew up in a double-wide trailer with her mom, who worked two jobs. But with more resources available, the next generation can more easily improve their and their children's lives, she told the group of about 10 people who attended Tuesday's event.
'The main focus tonight is investing in yourself and investing in your future,' Akins said.
Brittany Dallas, another speaker at Tuesday's class, had previously bounced around from different living spaces with her daughter, but she closed on a home in May after attending the same class last year.
Dallas, a single mom, felt empowered to own a home after attending the meeting and speaking to Ameris Bank representatives.
She said her daughter kept questioning why they kept moving, so it felt good to finally tell her they were settling in a home of their own.
'With us owning our own home, we can make it however we want to make it,' Dallas said. '... She's now a senior in high school. So, it really feels good letting her know that I'm helping her secure her future as well.'
Dallas said she had credit card debt when the home-buying process started, and one home deal fell through along the way. But Ameris employees said she didn't give up, and now, her mortgage payments are less than her rent when she lived in apartments.
'Just because you might have had a bad situation in the past, it does not mean that you won't have a good future,' she told the class attendees. '... To me, this was the hardest step, not even knowing what to do.'
The bank employees want to help people, even those who don't bank with Ameris, save money and take the next step toward homeownership, Akins said.
'You really are in the driver's seat,' the branch manager said. 'Just like Brittany said. Brittany showed up last year. She put herself in the driver's seat. We tossed her the keys. She bought the car. She did the rest.'

title: New college dorms mark shift for SJR State's Palatka campus
author: Carter Mudgett
description: The St. Johns River State College community broke ground on new dorms during a ceremony Thursday morning, an effort 16 years in the making.
content:
Body
The St. Johns River State College community broke ground on new dorms during a ceremony Thursday morning, an effort 16 years in the making.
Construction is already underway at the Palatka campus, 5001 St. Johns Ave., to build the three-floor facility, which will be approximately 60,000 square feet, next to the college's baseball field and batting cage. The project is estimated to cost $20 million, according to the college.
The ceremony, which took place near the institution's Florida School of the Arts, was a moment of pride for SJR State President Joe Pickens.
Bringing student housing to the Palatka campus is an effort Pickens has been pursuing since taking on the presidency in 2008, he told a crowd during the groundbreaking ceremony.
'For 16 years, every minute of my presidency, I have sought an opportunity to bring student housing to this campus,' he said. 'It's going to be a transformational change for this campus … and more importantly, transformational for the nearly twice as many students who will choose to attend the Florida School of the Arts after (its) $11 million renovation and the construction of this student housing project. It will be self-supporting and will be the most vibrant, crucial and critical part of campus life.'
Thursday marked a win for the college and its recruiting efforts, with at least one student saying on-campus housing is more than just a convenience. It's a necessity, said Lillian Johnson, a second-year musical theater student.
'Many FloArts students, me included, commute long distances every day to attend classes and participate in the vibrant artistic community here,' said Johnson, who spoke during the ceremony. 'While this journey is a testament to our dedication and the quality of our program here at the Palatka campus, it presents significant challenges in both terms of time and cost.'
Housing students on campus full time will present its own challenges to a commuter college, Pickens said, but those are challenges leaders say they're ready to tackle.
'With this facility comes a great deal of responsibility,' Pickens told the Daily News. 'We will have as many as 150 to 175 full-time students living on our campus and residing there 24/7. There's a responsibility that goes with those students not coming here, going to class, and going home, but rather considering this home.'
Floor plans presented alongside speakers Thursday outlined 32 four-bedroom units, each about 1,000 square feet with two bathrooms, four vanities, a living room, an eating nook, and a kitchen with a microwave, full-size refrigerator, and range with oven and cooktop.
'This pivotal addition not only meets a crucial need but also significantly raises the attractiveness and the competitiveness of our program,' FloArts Dean Emily Schafer said. 'By offering convenient and modern on-campus housing, we can now better attract talent from across the state.'
Rooms will be accessible from interior corridors with keycard access, and each floor will house one studio unit for a resident assistant, plans show. On-site laundry facilities and a management staff suite will also be included, and students will have access to an activities space, according to the college.
SJR State officials said the dorms will open to students in the fall of 2025.
'The No. 1 question we get from prospective students, but especially parents and families, is, 'Is housing available?'' Schafer said. 'We are delighted to respond with a very excited 'yes.''

title: County prepares for potential tropical storm
author: Carter Mudgett
description: The Putnam County Board of Commissioners declared a local state of emergency Friday morning, as Florida awaits a potential tropical storm to strike over the weekend.
content:
The Putnam County Board of Commissioners declared a local state of emergency Friday morning, as Florida awaits a potential tropical storm to strike over the weekend.
The decision comes on the heels of Gov. Ron DeSantis's declaration of a state of emergency for a majority of Florida counties Thursday night.
The National Hurricane Center has dubbed the storm Potential Tropical Cyclone Four.
'Potential Tropical Cyclone Four is expected to produce rainfall totals of 4 to 8 inches, with maximum rainfall totals up to 12 inches, across portions of Florida and near the Southeast U.S. coast this weekend through Wednesday morning,' the National Weather Service in Miami announced in its 11 a.m. bulletin.
The County's Emergency Management Department has been working with county administrators as well as Public Works and Fire Rescue officials, among others, to ensure they're ready for the storm.
The county also plans to open three self-serve areas for residents to prepare sandbags Friday afternoon: one in the West end of Putnam County, another in East Palatka and one in the South end of the county.
'It brings resources to us that we wouldn't normally be able to access,' board Chairman Larry Harvey said about declaring a state of emergency locally.
Residents are asked to monitor the county's emergency social media pages, the National Weather Service in Jacksonville and the National Hurricane Center for updates.
'I would like for the public to know that we're doing this out of an abundance of caution,' Commissioner Terry Turner said. 'With it being a Friday before a weekend when the possible storm hits, it'll be on possibly Sunday evening. And it would be very difficult to do this with short notice.'

title: Tax collector hopefuls to prioritize efficiency, customer service
author: Brittany Goodson
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Image
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible.
Three political newcomers are competing to be Putnam County's next tax collector and, in doing so, replace the woman who has been doing the job since being elected in 2012.
Republicans Brittany Goodson, Sydney Myers and Brenda Bridges, the deputy tax collector, will square off in the Aug. 20 primary. The three are competing to succeed Linda Myers, who did not run for reelection.
This race is universal, meaning any voter, no matter their political affiliation, can cast a ballot in this contest.
Bridges and Goodson answered questions from the Palatka Daily News ahead of the primary, but Sydney Myers did not respond by the deadline given to all candidates in this race.
Below, the candidates lay out why they think they're the best person for the job.
What are your top goals for the Tax Collector's Office if you are elected?
Bridges: If elected; my number one priority or goal is Customer Service. We have an amazing team that is dedicated to exceeding your expectations. I will continuously look for innovative ways to improve or add services that are a benefit to our community; continue to foster relationships with other offices and local businesses. I will ensure accountability, transparency and will continue to advocate for our citizens, protect your assets and continue a commitment to education and agency partnerships so that our team members are the leaders in our field and faithful stewards of your tax dollars.
Goodson: My goals are to provide enhanced customer service by implementing more efficient, user-friendly systems, including online services, and investing in continuous training for staff to improve quality of service. Maintain transparency and accountability by ensuring clear communication about tax processes, rates, and expenses. Creating cost efficiency by identifying and eliminating wasteful spending. Increase community engagement and information regarding assistance programs. Strengthen internal controls to ensure your tax dollars are being appropriately utilized and distributed.
What are some practices, if any, you would like to change and what aspects are working so well that you wouldn't change them?
Bridges: I have had the pleasure of serving in this office for twelve years, I have been part of the changes that have reduced wait times, improved office culture and worked to find innovative solutions/enhancements to our technology to meet the needs of our customers. I want to hear from you about the improvements you would like to see. We serve you, uphold the law and protect your assets! Our team values and respects our customers and I want to continue to build on that legacy, continue building community partnerships and exceed your expectations. We value your feedback!
Goodson: Implementing a structured training program for new employees to empower them to confidently provide exceptional customer service. Creating an employee development program will allow current employees to expand their knowledge and provide a chance for internal growth, ultimately reducing costly employee turnover. Taking the time to be on the front end of customer service to gain a better understanding of the issues that need to be addressed for residents and employees. Collaborate with local agencies, residents, employees, and businesses to proactively address issues.
What makes you the best choice to be elected as Putnam County's tax collector?
Bridges: The Tax Collector is a Constitutional Officer charged with upholding an Office of Public Trust; charged with understanding and following State Statutes in order to protect your assets. Experience matters and as the only candidate with proven leadership experience in a Tax Collector Office, I understand that your tax dollars are serious business and I am committed to uphold the duties of Tax Collector and provide the citizens with the exceptional customer service they deserve. I am a Certified Florida Collector Assistant, currently serve as your Deputy Tax Collector, and have twenty-three years of local government experience.
Goodson: My education and experience will allow me to successfully lead the Tax Collector's office. I obtained a master's degree in business administration and have years of experience as a Chief Financial and Operations Officer. My decision to run for office is because (I) care deeply for the Putnam County residents and have the desire to provide the outstanding service they deserve. You can count on me to be fiscally responsible, have integrity and do what is best for this county! I am the best candidate because I bring diverse executive-level experience, the highest level of education and a fresh perspective.

title: The Jazzy Belle of the Ball
author: Carter Mudgett
description: When members of the Putnam County School Board convened Tuesday afternoon, they were joined by someone new, someone with four legs instead of two.
content:
Body
When members of the Putnam County School Board convened Tuesday afternoon, they were joined by someone new, someone with four legs instead of two.
Wearing a green Putnam County School District T-shirt and wowing the audience with curious eyes, Jazzy the 14-month-old goldendoodle was celebrated for becoming the school district's first therapy dog. Her handler, Diana Drew, hopes she will help support students' mental health.
Officially certified through the Alliance of Therapy Dogs, an international registry of certified therapy dogs, Jazzy visited a nursing home last week to complete her evaluation.
'It's been something I've kind of dreamed of doing for several years,' said Diana Drew, who is also the district's director of student services. 'When I was a principal at Jenkins Middle School, I started really getting serious about thinking about it and starting to research it. Fast forward, what, three years from Jenkins and here we are with Jazzy.'
Drew said she will start small with Jazzy, bringing her in for individual visits and small groups first. Once Jazzy is comfortable, something Drew told the board she was '100% confident' about, they'll bridge outward to classroom visits.
Although Jazzy may have caused board members' hearts to swoon Tuesday, there are a few more steps that must be completed before the dog can visit Putnam students.
Drew needs to obtain additional insurance and the school board needs to review and approve policy changes. Those changes are expected to be put before the board sometime in the next few weeks, Drew said.
Jazzy is covered under the Alliance of Therapy Dogs' insurance when Drew volunteers somewhere like a hospital or nursing home. But when Jazzy is taken to a school setting, Drew needs to get 'additional liability insurance.'
Once those are secured, 'we are ready to go,' she said.
Drew first got Jazzy when she was just 5 months old. Jazzy has undergone various training for socialization, behavior and temperament. Not all of those training tests are required for Jazzy to become a therapy dog, Drew said, but she wanted the therapy dog to undergo them anyway.
Research has shown the presence of a beloved pet or therapy animal can help a person in numerous ways, like controlling daily anxiety and improving mood, according to the Alliance of Therapy Dogs.
'They provide a lot of emotional support to the kids. They help kids manage emotions,' Drew said. 'If they've gone through something traumatic, she can spend time with them and distract them and, you know, just make them feel better.'
Simply petting a therapy dog 'does things to you physiologically that calm you down and just get you in a better state of mind,' she said.
Beyond the straight-forward benefit for students, introducing Jazzy also goes with the district's strategic plan goal of making each student be a 'whole child' in their pursuit of developing well-rounded graduates ready for life beyond a diploma, Drew explained.
'Today's good mood is sponsored by Jazzy,' she told the board.
Kimberly Simmons, the district's lead clinical mental health counselor, called Jazzy an 'awesome addition' to what they already have.
'Mental health-wise, I think it's going to be a great impact for our students positively,' Simmons said. 'I think they'll be excited about it. I mean, who's not excited about getting to see the puppy?'
Board members were positive about Jazzy and praised the introduction of the therapy dog program.
Board member Phil Leary called it 'a wonderful thing' and asked whether they plan to expand the program. He floated a world where the district had a therapy dog in South Putnam, another in West Putnam and so on.
'That's a dream of mine, to expand it,' Diana said. 'I just want to be very careful to take baby steps. I think you have to be very careful about who is able to do this.'

title: Surrency victorious in tight superintendent's race
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: It was close but the Putnam County School District superintendent emerged with a win Tuesday in the primary.
content:
Body
It was close but the Putnam County School District superintendent emerged with a win Tuesday in the primary.
Incumbent Rick Surrency won with 5,393 votes (54.53%) against challenger Paul Adamczyk, who serves as the District 5 member of the Board of County Commissioners. Adamczyk received 4,497 votes (45.47%), according to unofficial results from the Supervisor of Elections Office.
'Going forward, I think (the win) is just a confirmation of what we're doing,' Surrency said. '... We're creating new opportunities for our kids (that) they never had before, and I think people realize we've made the case that Putnam County's district is on the way up.'
Surrency, who was first elected in 2016, celebrated his triumph at Corky Bell's in East Palatka alongside Putnam County School Board member David Buckles, who won his reelection bid Tuesday.
Surrency was watching with family members, friends and school district staff when the results tipped in his favor.
'We are continuing to improve, and I'm just proud to be a part of it,' Surrency said.
The primary data will be made official Aug. 27, according to Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III.
The Putnam County Canvassing Board will meet at 4:30 p.m. Thursday to review the nine provisional ballots that were reported Tuesday.
Voters whose ballots are in question have until 5 p.m. Thursday to provide proof of identification to the Elections Office.
Surrency's path to victory is still ongoing, as he will face write-in candidate Pat Wilson in November.
However, the superintendent focused only on Tuesday's win. He said he has been part of the school district since 1986 and will mark 50 years with the district at the end of his next term.
'I really do want to leave something for my kids and my grandkids that Putnam County has never had before, and I truly believe that,' Surrency said. '... I do this because I truly believe that we can do some things that have never been done before.'

title: Newbold leaps to victory in commission race
author: Carter Mudgett
description: The contest to see who would serve in the District 1 seat on the Putnam County Board of Commissioners ended in a landslide.
content:
The contest to see who would serve in the District 1 seat on the Putnam County Board of Commissioners ended in a landslide.
J.R. Newbold III won with 8,348 (88.08%) votes, defeating Jeovanny Palencia, who got 1,130 (11.92%) votes, according to unofficial results from the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office.
'It is exciting. I've been appointed to another position and run unopposed, and you know, there's no drama in that,' he told the Daily News. 'This is new, and it's exciting. And I've had just a lot of support from family and friends, and I'm just thankful that all that's come together in a positive way.'
But the battle over the District 1 seat on the Board of County Commissioners isn't done. Newbold will compete against write-in hopeful Douglas Hays during the Nov. 5 general election.
If the results of the primary hold true and Newbold is the victor of the general election, one of his first priorities is digging into the budget to better understand that process.
'I got to get in there and find my bearings,' he said. 'This is my first foray into an office of this state. I want to take that seriously (and) get the technical education that I need.'
Approximately 31% of Putnam County voters participated in the primary, casting a total of 13,987 ballots, according to the Supervisor of Elections Office website.

title: Alexander wins race for District 3 county commissioner
author: Carter Mudgett
description: Putnam County voters decided Tuesday who would be the next person to serve in the District 3 seat on the Board of County Commissioners.
content:
Putnam County voters decided Tuesday who would be the next person to serve in the District 3 seat on the Board of County Commissioners.
Joshua Alexander won out over Les Sims, according to unofficial election results, garnering 8,452 (65.76%) votes compared to Sims' 4,401 (34.24%) votes. Because only Republicans qualified to run as District 3 candidates, Tuesday's contest was a universal race and Alexander will not need to compete in the Nov. 5 general election runoff.
Alexander told the Daily News he's 'really, really excited' to take on the position.
'I have plans to spend time in the field with our people in Public Works, with (Emergency Medical Services), with the sheriff's department,' he said. 'I want to learn what their jobs are (and) learn about them and what I can do to make their lives better.'
His biggest goal is centered around collaborating with Putnam's municipalities, something he summed up in a single phrase: 'We are so much stronger together than we are divided.'
Approximately 31% of Putnam County voters participated in the primary, voting for which closed at 7 p.m. Tuesday, casting a total of 13,987 ballots, according to the Supervisor of Elections Office website.
'This has been the most rewarding adventure of my life,' Alexander said. 'It brought my family together, and to see them coalesce around me and our vision of a better Putnam County has been the best thing I've ever been a part of.'
The votes will be final Aug. 27, Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III told the Daily News.

title: Community gathers to say goodbye
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: Hundreds of family members, friends, classmates and other members of the community went to church Sunday to celebrate the life of a 10th grader who passed away on the second day of school.
content:
Body
Hundreds of family members, friends, classmates and other members of the community went to church Sunday to celebrate the life of a 10th grader who passed away on the second day of school.
The funeral for Palatka Junior-Senior High School sophomore Robert 'RJ' Gillon III, 15, united a grieving community, members of which spoke at Mt. Tabor First Baptist Church in Palatka about Gillon's compassion, generous spirit and never-ending determination to better himself.
Gillon's funeral began at 3:45 p.m., the same time the bell to dismiss classes for the day goes off at Palatka High.
Gillon passed away Aug. 13 from natural causes, but Tyson Lee, Gillon's mentor and former teacher, said the late student-athlete's spirit will always be with his loved ones.
Lee remembered Gillon striving to be the best athlete and brother possible and said his mentee's determination and good nature inspired him to be a better educator and person.
'He didn't allow whatever problems he had to hold him down too long,' Lee said. 'Robert was bright. He had a great personality, and he loved to joke around and make people laugh.
'He taught me to keep pushing. He taught me to stand strong no matter what I've been through. And I will always remember him for the impact he had on my life.'
Gillon was a member of Palatka High's football, wrestling and track teams. Track coach Jarimy Passmore recalled Gillon's actions speaking louder than his words.
Passmore recalled the team being away on a trip, where an elderly woman – who, unbeknown to Gillon, was suffering from dementia – inquired about the team's uniforms. Rather than try to distance himself from the woman like some of his teammates, Passmore said, Gillon engaged the woman and answered every question she asked.
That was one of many moments where Gillon, without knowing it, motivated everyone around him to be better, more compassionate people, Passmore said.
'We coaches … have to have an impact on our athletes,' he said. 'When you have an individual like Robert, you learn easily how an athlete can also have an impact on his coaches. Robert's character embodied loyalty, empathy, humility, commitment, dependability, courage, integrity and, most importantly, resilience.'
The decedent's fathers, Robert Gillon Jr. and William McCormick Jr., spoke of their son's compassion and how he will always live in his loved ones' hearts.
McCormick talked about his child supporting his teammates, caring for his sisters and bringing joy to everyone with whom he came in contact.
Robert III lived with purpose, McCormick said, and used his positive attitude to treat others with kindness.
'Robert's time with us was far too short, but the impact he made in those years will resonate for a lifetime,' McCormick said. 'He had a heart of gold and a genuine desire to help others. His kindness wasn't just reserved for grand gestures. It was the small, everyday actions that truly defined him.'
Robert Jr. said coming to terms with his son's absences filled him with sorrow. Despite the sadness, he said, the tears he sheds will be because of his time with his son and his son's impact on everyone.
While the child's loved ones are hurting, Robert III is smiling down on the community, Robert Jr. said.
'I'm crying because of all the good times that I have had with my son, how impactful and positive that he was with everybody in here,' Robert Jr. said. 'And no matter how weak that I feel, I will make sure that he feels me and he feels all of you.'
The Rev. Karl Flagg – the pastor of Mt. Tabor, where Robert III attended – consoled everyone in the sanctuary and the adjoining overflow room by reminding them that the life a person leads speaks for themselves.
He commended the community for embracing the Gillon family during this devastating time in their lives. The unity throughout Putnam County during this period of bereavement is proof of people's love for Robert III, he said.
'God is so able that he could take a 15-year-old lad and cause him to unite hearts across socioeconomic aisle, across … a political spectrum,' Flagg said. 'Because of the mere 15 years, he has had more (of a) positive impact on a community than some folks who brag about being five times his age.'

title: Child found dead in Satsuma waterway
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The search for a missing child ended Tuesday after two hours when his body was discovered in a canal near his home, authorities said.
content:
The search for a missing child ended Tuesday after two hours when his body was discovered in a canal near his home, authorities said.
Gabriel Paguio, 2, was located around 5:30 p.m. Tuesday after going missing from his Clearwater Road home at about 3:30 p.m., Putnam County Sheriff's Office spokeswoman Allison Waters-Merritt said.
Paguio is believed to have been autistic, she said. His family had been looking into getting an official diagnosis but had not yet received it, Waters-Merritt said.
Paguio's family had been searching for the child for about 20 minutes before they called 911, the spokeswoman said.
'At this time, we ask for you to say a prayer for the family,' Sheriff Gator DeLoach said in a Facebook statement. 'No family should undergo the tragedy of losing their child, and we ask for comfort from our community to support them as they navigate the difficult journey ahead.'
Authorities are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the boy's death.
Editor's note: The Putnam County Sheriff's Office previously reported the child's age as 3, but they have since listed his age as 2. This story has been updated.

NOTICE TO CREDITORS
The administration of the estate of Hoster C. Sepulveda, deceased, whose date of death was July 17, 2024, is pending in the Circuit Court for Putnam County, Florida, Probate Division, the address of which is 410 St. Johns Ave., Palatka, FL 32177. The names and addresses of the personal representative and the personal representative's attorney are set forth below.
All creditors of the decedent and other persons having claims or demands against decedent's estate on whom a copy of this notice is required to be served must file their claims with this court ON OR BEFORE THE LATER OF 3 MONTHS AFTER THE TIME OF THE FIRST PUBLICATION OF THIS NOTICE OR 30 DAYS AFTER THE DATE OF SERVICE OF A COPY OF THIS NOTICE ON THEM.
The personal representative has no duty to discover whether any property held at the time of the decedent's death by the decedent or the decedent's surviving spouse is property to which the Florida Uniform Disposition of Community Property Rights at Death Act as described in ss. 732.216-732.228, Florida Statutes, applies, or may apply, unless a written demand is made by a creditor as specified under s. 732.2211, Florida Statutes.
All other creditors of the decedent and other persons having claims or demands against decedent's estate must file their claims with this court WITHIN 3 MONTHS AFTER THE DATE OF THE FIRST PUBLICATION OF THIS NOTICE.
ALL CLAIMS NOT FILED WITHIN THE TIME PERIODS SET FORTH IN FLORIDA STATUTES SECTION 733.702 WILL BE FOREVER BARRED.
NOTWITHSTANDING THE TIME PERIODS SET FORTH ABOVE, ANY CLAIM FILED TWO (2) YEARS OR MORE AFTER THE DECEDENT'S DATE OF DEATH IS BARRED.
The date of first publication of this notice is August 28, 2024.

title: Officials delighted about visioning survey responses
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The youth of Palatka have something to say about the city's future, with almost half of the people who responded to a survey geared toward the city's vision being 17 or younger.
content:
The youth of Palatka have something to say about the city's future, with almost half of the people who responded to a survey geared toward the city's vision being 17 or younger.
People want Palatka to become a walkable, outdoor-friendly and downtown-oriented city, according to a Northeast Florida Regional Council survey.
'This is the best engagement I've ever seen in a project from folks who are young people,' said Jack Shad, the council's project manager.
Shad read the results during Thursday's Palatka City Commission. The community feedback is set to be finalized in Palatka's vision plan Sept. 26.
Of the 404 people who answered questions about what they want to see Palatka become, 49% were 17 or younger, 10% were between the ages of 18 and 42, 16% were 35-54 and 25% were 55 or older, according to council data.
Shad and other project team members have been surveying people since January to gauge what the community wants Palatka to look like in 10 or 20 years. The results will become the city's road map for development, Shad said.
Some people, who Shad believes were kids, described Palatka as 'boring' or 'lame,' but he said municipal officials always ask how they can get the younger crowd involved in the city's growth.
This survey reached them and is a great step if Palatka wants to keep its young people, Shad insisted
'Most of these responses show folks see the town as growing,' he said. 'They love the small-town feel. Everybody sees the potential.'
While the younger generation may want more modern structures, more seasoned community members are honing in on preserving historic buildings, Shad said.
'Not surprisingly, there's a strong preference for maintaining the historic character of Palatka and even for historic design on new buildings to kind of maintain that feel,' he said.
Nearly all survey-takers think the city needs to improve its street lighting, Shad said. They also want to see pedestrian and bike-friendly pathways in the city.
However, a big focus was on affordable housing.
Shad said survey-takers want to see tiny homes, in-law suites or garage apartments when it comes to housing development.
People want the city to incentivize private developers to build affordable housing in Palatka, he said.
'Big apartment buildings (were) not particularly popular,' he added. 'Manufactured housing (was) not particularly popular.'
Aside from housing, results show residents want more commerce.
People want the city to promote commercial activity and more diverse commerce options, which could increase employment opportunities, according to the council.
While the council didn't include specific comments about what type of commerce people hope to see, Shad said the team saw some recurring requests in the 1,500 comments they received from the 404 respondents.
Residents want to see the Palatka Mall revived with more major retailers, surveyors said.
'We got a lot of comments (that) people would like to see things like a movie theater and those kind of big entertainment options,' he said.
People also hope to have more cultural and art events, according to the council.
The team compared the survey results to the city's existing comprehensive plan, and Shad said the vision plan can help update the plan with the future residents want to see.
Commissioner Rufus Borom said Thursday that he thought the council covered everything, saying it represented the city of Palatka's wants and the benefits the vision could have on Putnam County.
'Man, you covered everything,' Borom said. '... I mean, this is the roadmap for Palatka's future. We just want to at least commend you guys for all the hard work and dedication you put in it. … (I) look forward on how to implement it as best we can.'

title: Pickleball equipment donated to Bostwick library
author: Trisha Murphy
description: An ongoing sports craze is spreading to Bostwick thanks to the donation of new equipment and group members painting an existing court to give people a venue in which to play.
content:
An ongoing sports craze is spreading to Bostwick thanks to the donation of new equipment and group members painting an existing court to give people a venue in which to play.
Pickleball is addictive, according to Jimmi Symonds, a USA Pickleball ambassador, who lives in East Palatka.
'It's a game that's so quick and easy to learn and is a very social game,' she said. 'That's why it's so popular.'
Symonds said it was Bostwick resident Don Holton's idea to bring the growing sport to the North Putnam County community so as many people as possible could take part in the activity.
'I think the two added courts are a great addition to our community of Bostwick,' said Holton, who has lived in Bostwick for 20 years and has been a pickleball player for about nine months. 'I believe it will help bring life to the community.'
Holton said he started playing pickleball when he was one of a handful of people, who set up a net at the church on West River Road in Palatka.
'That was probably about three months ago,' he said. 'Then we saw the court behind the Bostwick Volunteer Fire Station and got permission from the county to use it.'
County Commissioner Leota Wilkinson was instrumental in helping get the permission. He and the commissioner contacted Symonds, a member of the St. Johns River Pickleball Group, to ask for assistance in getting the group to help establish the sport in Bostwick.
The pickleball group members painted court lines on the existing basketball court at Bostwick Community Park, but the paint job won't interfere with people who still want to play basketball on the court.
The group also donated pickleball equipment to the Bostwick library, 125 Tillman St., Building No. 2. The equipment can be checked out free of charge from 9:30 a.m. – 6 p.m. Tuesdays through Fridays and from 9 a.m. – noon Saturdays.
For details, call Branch Manager Bianca Bernardini at 386-326-2750 or email bianca.bernardini@putnam-fl.gov.
'We were happy to partner with Stella Brown, director of the Putnam County Library System, in an effort to enable anyone to play by checking out pickleball equipment from the Bostwick library,' Symonds said.
Symonds said pickleball is still America's fastest-growing sport, with the national average player age having dropped below 38.
'In Palatka, the fastest growing age group is between 15–25,' she said. 'It is a great family and social sport for all ages.'
St. Johns River Pickleball group will host an introductory pickleball clinic to go over rules and techniques from 8:30–10 a.m. Saturday at the Bostwick courts.
Everyone from ages 12 and older is invited to participate.
To play the sport, all players need is something similar to a large ping pong paddle, a hard wiffle ball, a court and a willing opponent. Equipment will be provided, but participants should wear tennis shoes.
For details about the clinic, call Symonds at 386-972-2659. For details on court contacts and schedules for organized play, visit the St. Johns River Pickleball Group on Facebook.
'There are no gender or age barriers,' Symonds said. 'People of any age from 8 to 100 can play. It's one of the reasons it's so popular.'
Holton believes once word gets out about the Bostwick courts, more people will likely start using them and become pickleballers in what many consider the fastest-growing sport in America.
'Now (the courts are) coming to life with people interested in using it,' he said. 'It serves the purpose of our community. People should check out the equipment and go play.'

title: Flying to the Rescue
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: Local pilots and nonprofit officials are taking their generosity to higher heights to help people in mountain municipalities that were ravaged by Hurricane Helene.
content:
Body
Local pilots and nonprofit officials are taking their generosity to higher heights to help people in mountain municipalities that were ravaged by Hurricane Helene.
On Thursday and Friday, planes packed with water, diapers, hand sanitizer, face masks and other necessities were flown to North Carolina, where many of the hardest-hit areas are isolated because flooding washed away many of the roads.
Florida Aviation Professionals, a flight school headquartered at the Palatka Municipal Airport, helped coordinate the local effort to assist people who lost most, if not all, of their possessions in the hurricane.
Daniel Rust, Florida Aviation Professionals' chief flight instructor, said he got the idea from Operation Airdrop, a Texas-based nonprofit that provides necessities to places affected by natural disasters. After doing more research, Rust learned the organization had resources in the areas that would assist Florida Aviation Professionals in delivering goods to people in need.
'So I started looking online and found out Operation Airdrop … has this ability to accept all this stuff with airplanes,' Rust said Thursday while unloading items in Greenville, North Carolina. 'The next thing you know, Epic-Cure sent us four pallets with (meals ready to eat). We have, like, thousands of dollars of baby formula, diapers, wipes. You name it; we've hauled it up here. We've even had the use of two large airplanes donated to us today to move stuff.'
Nearly 3,000 pounds of goods were flown to North Carolina on Thursday, said Rust, who planned to fly the same amount Friday. The planes from Palatka first landed in Concord, North Carolina, which had a surplus of donated items, Rust said.
The pilots were rerouted to Greenville, which was more in need, and he anticipated he'd be flying to Greenville or another city trying to recover.
'We know we're going to a separate city because Concord was so overwhelmed with supplies,' Rust said. 'We have a point of contact … who told us he would give the specific airport. Basically, we just told him what our planes were capable of doing and went from there.'
Rust said he's proud to take part in this humanitarian effort, but he acknowledged it hasn't been a one-man show.
He praised Epic-Cure, a nonprofit organization that provides food and other resources to food-insecure people in Palatka, St. Augustine and other Northeast Florida areas, for donating supplies and sharing Florida Aviation Professionals' Facebook post asking for assistance in this effort.
The group established drop-off locations in Palatka and St. Augustine where people can donate essential items to be given to people in need.
'After reading about the need this morning, we were able to deliver four pallets of rescued food and supplies to help families in crisis,' Epic-Cure posted Tuesday on Facebook. 'But this is just the beginning—our team is committed to continuing these efforts, collecting, rescuing and delivering more food in the coming days to ensure that no one goes hungry during this difficult time.'
Rust said he was grateful for the people who donated their planes to ship the goods because the aircraft his company uses to train pilots are small and would not have been able to hold as many items.
He said he is likely to look around for more people willing to donate the use of their planes to make sure the items that have been donated don't take up permanent residence in his hangar.
'We know we have the use of one of these airplanes for tomorrow, so we're trying to make the most of it,' Rust said Thursday. 'I want to make sure we can actually get this stuff up here in short order. I don't think it's doing any good if it sits in my hangar at the airport.'
Rust is thankful for people's generosity and is eager to keep the planes flying. He plans to 'keep shuttling supplies until we run out' and encourages people to donate to help victims of Helene.
Some of the goods may be donated to residents in the Florida Panhandle and other areas that also felt Helene's wrath, but local officials will need to find out which places are the most in need.
Rust believes this effort is bigger than any one person.
'I don't believe this was about us, though,' he said. 'Truthfully, I started out thinking this would be a fun thing to do. But seeing the response, we had over 18,000 people share our post yesterday. This is a move of God, I think.'
To donate items or aircraft to carry those items, call Florida Aviation Professionals at 904-315-7749.

title: Residents safe from Milton but flooding could worsen
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: Although Hurricane Milton didn't inflict the same severity on Putnam County as it did in other areas of the state, local officials are concerned about ongoing flooding that could continue to affect
content:
Although Hurricane Milton didn't inflict the same severity on Putnam County as it did in other areas of the state, local officials are concerned about ongoing flooding that could continue to affect areas in the days to come.
Putnam experienced flooding, downed trees and power lines as a result of Milton, which made landfall on Florida's West Coast on Wednesday night and barreled on a northeast path throughout the night and the following morning.
After the hurricane passed, the Putnam County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit visited people in the Sportsman Harbor area of Welaka, which experienced considerable flooding. Marine Unit deputies offered food and water to residents who stayed in their homes during the storm or returned home to find their houses partially flooded.
Although most people with whom deputies made contact declined the food and water, the sheriff's office wanted to make sure everyone in the area was safe, spokeswoman Allison Waters-Merritt said Friday.
'They basically were just trying to get to the people that had no other means to get out,' she said. 'If you don't have a lot, something is better than nothing.'
Waters-Merritt said Sportsman Harbor, which is adjacent to the St. Johns River, usually experiences flooding during tropical weather events. While some people in flood-prone areas of South Putnam sought shelter in Browning-Pearce Elementary School in San Mateo or Middleton-Burney Elementary School in Crescent City, others stayed put but took precautions to minimize damage, she said.
While surveying the area, she said, deputies noticed people had parked their vehicles in higher areas to prevent them from sustaining damage. Waters-Merritt said she and other sheriff's office employees were grateful people prepared for Hurricane Milton and sought shelter if they knew their homes were not the best place to be during the storm.
'We didn't have any rescues or anything,' Waters-Merritt said Friday. 'Our flood-prone areas, the people who did go to shelters, most of them yesterday were out by 11 o'clock in the morning. They wanted to go home. They wanted to assess their house. They wanted to see how things were.'
Milton has dissipated, but Waters-Merritt said there is still cause for flooding concerns. As stormwater that poured into the St. Johns River in Central Florida makes its way north toward the Atlantic Ocean, river levels in Putnam are expected to peak Tuesday.
Boaters are asked to not pilot their vessels in Sportsman Harbor, Dunns Creek or other areas experiencing or prone to flooding. If boaters are in those areas, they are being asked to slow down to minimize wake, which could exacerbate flooding.
'We know people are going to get on the water because they're curious,' Waters-Merritt said. 'Stay out of those areas. And if you do go through these areas, be considerate.'
Aside from flooding, Putnam's major concerns following Hurricane Milton were downed trees and power lines, which caused power outages throughout the county.
At one point, there were more than 20,000 properties without power, according to Putnam County Emergency Management data. At about 9 a.m. Friday, the agency reported 7,960 properties were without power.
Keeping in line with neighboring counties, the Putnam County Sheriff's Office issued a curfew that began at 8 p.m. Thursday and lasted until 6 a.m. Friday. The curfew was not reinstated for Friday evening because most of the dangers had been eliminated, Waters-Merritt said.
'Basically, the crews jumped on it and got ahead of schedule on restoring power,' she said. 'We still have lines down. They may not be live lines, but we do have a lot of … restoration work that has to be done. But safety-wise, we're in a much better position Friday, which is why they rescinded it.'
As people continue assessing damage, they are encouraged to apply for Federal Emergency Management Agency assistance. According to a FEMA news release issued before the hurricane made landfall, Putnam County is one of numerous Florida counties eligible for assistance with damage to or losses of uninsured or underinsured property.
People can apply by calling FEMA's helpline at 800-621-3362, visiting https://www.fema.gov/assistance/individual or using the FEMA mobile app.

title: Groups partner to bring more jobs to Putnam
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: The Putnam County Chamber of Commerce has partnered with a consulting group to increase the number of retail jobs in the area and stem the tide of Putnam residents leaving the county for work.
content:
Body
The Putnam County Chamber of Commerce has partnered with a consulting group to increase the number of retail jobs in the area and stem the tide of Putnam residents leaving the county for work.
The Chamber sought out Retail Strategies to maximize retail opportunities throughout Putnam County, according to Mark Litten, the Chamber's vice president of economic development. He said officials from Retail Strategies, a firm based in Birmingham, Alabama, spent time in Crescent City, Interlachen, Palatka and Welaka to get a better understanding of what types of businesses can be recruited to open in those municipalities.
Focusing on development in those areas should result in an economic windfall for all of Putnam County, he said.
'Retail Strategies, our partnership with them focuses on downtown development and retail development, and it touches into workforce development,' Litten said. 'And it's countywide versus just the city of Palatka. Obviously, the need's greater there with all the empty storefronts we have.
'Basically, it's to bring more retail and commercial operations to Putnam County that could be restaurants, clothing stores, you know, any type of retail that we lack right now.'
This partnership is part of Elevate Putnam, a five-year multi-million-dollar economic development campaign local officials launched this summer with the intention of attracting more businesses, improving housing and retaining workforce talent, among other goals.
Litten said the Chamber's board of directors approved the Retail Strategies partnership before Elevate Putnam was announced. Local business officials are eager to attract new establishments while nurturing Putnam County's existing businesses.
The partnership's success would be beneficial to the hundreds of Putnam residents who currently go elsewhere to work, Litten said.
According to a press release from the Chamber, more than 700 retail workers, 268 restaurant servers, 259 fast food workers, 207 cooks and 155 cashiers leave Putnam to work in other counties.
Litten said Putnam is a 'bedroom community' to cities like Jacksonville, St. Augustine and Daytona Beach, to and from which local residents commute for work. Housing in those areas might not be affordable for many retail workers, Litten said, and others simply prefer to live in Putnam.
'People like to live here, and they go elsewhere to work,' he said. 'And there's even that on the industrial side. … When I was doing my work for the strategic plan, 59% of people 18-65, which is our workforce, left the county to work every day. They live here, but they left here to work. There's more people leaving Putnam County to work every day in every industry sector than there are people coming here to work.'
Retail Strategies has wanted to work in Putnam County 'for some time now' because of the area's real estate, need for additional retail and restaurant businesses, and ample opportunity for growth, Clay Craft, the company's vice president of client services, said in the Chamber's press release.
He said the company will consult with its other partners to determine the best way to help Putnam County.
'We will work our network of retailers, developers and brokers in the region to attract new development to the county,' Craft said in the release. 'We're proud to be an extension of the Putnam County team and bring a proactive retail strategy to the area.'
By the end of the three-year partnership, Litten would like to see a diverse array of businesses that can accommodate more Putnam residents' skill sets. He said he'd like for there to be more businesses like HCA Florida Putnam Hospital, Seminole Electric and Georgia-Pacific that bring in workers from outside of Putnam.
If everything goes according to plan, he said, Putnam residents will rarely need to leave the county to even shop because of the boost in the number of retail, hospitality, tourism and restaurant opportunities.
'If we see that, then the partnership will be successful,' Litten said. 'And we retain the ones we already have, you know, all the restaurants and retail operations. We want you to be able to say, 'OK, I only go outside the county when there's some specialized item I need that we don't have a store that sells that here.''

title: City getting security, morale boost
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Palatka's interim city manager is focusing on improving employee safety, resident service and employee productivity as she spearheaded her fifth week in the role.
content:
Body
Palatka's interim city manager is focusing on improving employee safety, resident service and employee productivity as she spearheaded her fifth week in the role.
Marcia Carty, who is also the city's finance director, took over for former City Manager Troy Bell after the Palatka City Commission fired him in a 4-1 vote Sept. 12.
Since taking on the new duties, Carty has led initiatives to secure City Hall, 201 N. Second St., create more offices for employees and make residents feel more welcome.
'I do whatever needs to be done,' Carty said. 'There's no shame in my game.'
In recent years, numerous employees have worked in the bottom-floor lobby of City Hall, but they now have their own office spaces throughout the building.
The Grants Department has its own area, which it did not before, to manage 61 ongoing projects worth $68 million, Carty said. City Clerk Sunni Krantz also has her own office, something she did not have before Carty began renovating the building.
'Productivity has increased significantly, significantly,' Carty said Friday.
Carty said she began increasing security at City Hall to make it and the people who work and visit there less vulnerable to any unforeseen danger. The building has a new security system, rooms that were previously open to public view have been secured and commissioner protection efforts have increased, Carty said Friday during a tour of the building.
'I'm implementing all the security steps in phases now that the building is secure,' she said. 'And this is the first time ever.'
Residents can now meet one-on-one with commissioners in an office on the bottom floor of City Hall.
More departments have spread out to the City Hall Annex, 205 N. Second St., which once served as a post office.
Carty will come in on the weekends to clean and will complete work that needs to get done. She said she could not do her job effectively without 'Team Palatka,' which is how she referred to the city's employees.
'Oh, my goodness. They're doing so much phenomenal work,' Carty said. 'I mean, they are … responding to citizens like boom, boom, boom.'
Carty said she wants employees to address problems and come to her during weekly meetings with solutions. During Hurricanes Helene and Milton, all departments worked efficiently together despite the setbacks, she said.
'It's a very interactive, very positive involvement,' Carty said.
About six people waited in the Annex lobby to be interviewed for part-time labor positions that will begin Monday. Some people thought the city wouldn't be able to find the help in such a short time after advertising the jobs Wednesday, Carty said, but the city is proving naysayers wrong.
'Now, I prove my point,' she said. 'Efficiency, right, if you make people happy at work.'
The city has also been hiring new full-time employees, such as a project manager who was on-boarded two days ago to replace Marcia Ganoe, whose last day of work was July 23.
Carty said it is important for the city's employees to feel appreciated and for residents to be properly assisted when they visit City Hall.
Public Information Officer Peter Willott said he has seen city employees' moods have increased since Carty has been named interim city manager.
He attributed the positive turnaround to what he said was Carty's sincere desire to make the city a better place to work and live.
'There's remarkable improvement in the morale of the city,' he said. 'It's nice to work for someone who has the best interest of the city at her heart, at the soul of her job.'

title: Putnam shows up in force for early voting
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: More than 3,000 Putnam County residents got to the polls during the first two days of early voting.
content:
Body
More than 3,000 Putnam County residents got to the polls during the first two days of early voting.
Early voting began Monday and will continue from 8:30 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. until Nov. 2 at the following locations:
– Supervisor of Elections Office, 2509 Crill Ave., Suite 900, in Palatka.
– Interlachen Community Center, 135 S. County Road 315.
– South Putnam Government Complex, 115 N. Summit St. in Crescent City.
Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III said he saw people waiting for the doors to open at the Palatka polling location as early as 7:30 a.m. Monday.
'As far as I can tell, it's the best early voting day we've had,' he said Monday. 'Every location we had did unbelievable.'
By 5 p.m. Tuesday, 3,692 Putnam residents had voted early while 2,851 mail ballots had been accepted, bringing the turnout to 14.42%, according to the Elections Office.
By Tuesday evening, 613 people had voted at the Crescent City polling place, 1,010 residents voted in Interlachen and 2,069 people voted in Palatka, according to voteputnamflorida.gov.
'We've still got a long way to go,' Overturf said Monday, adding that the average turnout during a presidential-year general election is 72%.
San Mateo resident John Walter stopped by the Palatka location around noon Monday to make sure he cast his vote as early as possible.
He said he had planned for a while to vote early, knowing he might need surgery later this month. He said he's lived in Putnam for 71 years and tries to get to the voting booth every year.
'It seems like a good turnout,' Walter said. 'I think this year, I think more people are going to attempt to get out.'
Putnam residents can vote at any of the three early voting locations, but if they vote on Election Day, which is Nov. 5, they must vote at their designated polling location.
Election Day voting hours are from 7 a.m. – 7 p.m. Putnam residents can find their precinct at the Elections Office's website.
'I'm proud of the public,' Overturf said. 'I'm proud of everybody getting out.'

title: Memorial walls to appear in Palatka
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Palatka will play host to a series of memorials honoring the 58,300 service members who never returned from the Vietnam War and the 7,068 people who were lost in the War on Terror.
content:
Palatka will play host to a series of memorials honoring the 58,300 service members who never returned from the Vietnam War and the 7,068 people who were lost in the War on Terror.
The Vietnam and Global War on Terror Memorial Walls will be on display from 9 a.m. – 4 p.m. Saturday at American Legion Bert Hodge Post 45, 316 Osceola St. in Palatka. Admission is free for the public.
The walls belong to Patriot Guard Riders of Florida and have traveled across the state to let communities pay their respects to the fallen heroes. The Vietnam walls include 18 4-foot panels while the Global War on Terrorism includes six 4-inch panels.
Organizers will have a computer on hand Saturday to help the public find specific names.
Sandi Barrett, the Auxiliary Unit 45 children and youth chairwoman, said she is part of the Patriot Guard Riders.
'The memorial walls will allow the community to remember and honor the lives lost,' she said. 'It will be of special interest for family, friends and fellow soldiers.'
Those names will include fallen heroes from Putnam County.
'As a Patriot Guard Rider, I have seen the memorial walls at numerous other venues and thought it would be an honor to bring them to Putnam County,' she said. 'It allows the community, families of those who have family members' names on the wall and those who may have served with the heroes on the wall, to show their honor and respect.'
Barrett said due to the confidentiality of the families, those names on the walls' home locations are not shared.
Proceeds from Saturday's event will benefit the Gold Star Children in the Patriot Guard Riders room at the Gary Sinise Foundation's Snowball Express, which goes to Walt Disney World each year to allow the children of fallen heroes to enjoy themselves and bond with other children who have experienced a similar loss. Although the exhibit is free, donations will be accepted.
'As a volunteer at Snowball Express, I have had the opportunity to speak with many of the children and have learned there are numerous families from Florida,' Barrett said.
Breakfast will be available for purchase Saturday from 8–11 a.m. and lunch will be on sale from 11:15 a.m. – 3 p.m. For details, call 386-328-6976.
Other highlights include a silent auction, which will feature items such as a custom-made graphite fishing pole, tool sets, Armor All car cleaning kits, vintage glassware and a Kate Spade bag set, among other items.
The memorial walls will head next to Winter Gardens for an exhibit Nov. 2 and then go to St. Augustine from Nov. 10-11. Barrett is encouraging people to visit one of those exhibits if they can't attend Saturday.
'This will be an opportune time for everyone to come to the exhibit, especially since it is the first time it has been in the area,' she said. 'It's a chance for everyone to pay their respects and honor those who never returned home from battle.'

title: County officials provide clarity on hurricane debris cleanup
description: Putnam County Emergency Services officials are still receiving an influx of questions about the pickup of debris from the hurricanes that have affected the areas this season.
content:
Image
Body
Putnam County Emergency Services officials are still receiving an influx of questions about the pickup of debris from the hurricanes that have affected the areas this season.
Residents can still report and request pickup of debris at their homes or businesses as the cleanup from Hurricanes Debby, Helene and Milton continues.
Department officials provided the most asked questions they are receiving from residents and answers that may help clear up confusion among Putnam residents.
Q: What will be picked up?
A: Vegetative debris such as branches, logs, limbs, leafy material.
Q: What size do the logs and branches need to be?
A: Four feet or less.
Q: Will the trees that were pushed out of the road by fire and public works officials be picked up?
A: Yes
Q: Are private roads included in the pickup?
A: No, only county and state roads.
Q: In what part of the county is debris going to be picked up?
A: The entire county.
Q: Where do I need to put debris to be collected?
A: On the public right of way where it does not obstruct traffic. There should be a 3-foot space between the debris and anything else such as mailboxes, trees, power poles and hydrants.
Q: When did they start collecting hurricane debris?
A: Debris operations began Oct. 21, and they are working seven days a week.
Q: How long will debris pickup last?
A: Until there is a large drop of debris occurrence.
Q: How much has been picked up?
A: As of Monday, 1,185 cubic yards from 120 known locations.
Q: Will other items be collected?
A: No, only vegetative.
Q: How do I report debris?
A: Visit https://arcg.is/1aPKjH1.

title: Sheriff to keep fighting crime another 4 years
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The sheriff's race featured competitors who were no strangers to each other, and like in the last two sheriff's elections, the result was the same.
content:
Body
The sheriff's race featured competitors who were no strangers to each other, and like in the last two sheriff's elections, the result was the same.
Republican Sheriff Gator DeLoach won the sheriff's race after receiving 28,800 votes against no-party affiliation candidate Edison Edison, who received 6,105 votes, according to unofficial results from the Supervisor of Elections Office.
'I'm forever grateful to the voters of Putnam County who have entrusted me to serve as sheriff for another four years,' DeLoach said Tuesday. 'Law enforcement and service to our community is my passion.'
This is Edison's third time losing to DeLoach, with both men competing in the 2016 and 2020 elections.
DeLoach won his first term as sheriff in 2016, also winning against Jon Kinney, who filed to run for sheriff this year but later withdrew. In 2016, Kinney initially won by 18 votes, but Elections Office employees found additional ballots that pushed DeLoach past Kinney by 16 votes, the Daily News reported.
The 2024 general election had a record voter turnout with 80.45% percent of eligible voters making their voices heard, which made DeLoach proud.
'My sincere thanks to everyone who showed up and cast their vote in this monumental election,' he said. 'I'm so pleased to see the voter turnout we did for this election.'
All election results will be official Nov. 15, according to Elections Supervisor Charles Overturf III.
