title: Getting festive to help those in need
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Capturing the spirit of the season is what one group of volunteers is hoping to do while preparing the Beck Chevrolet GMC showroom in Palatka to house more than 85 trees and wreaths with the hopes
content:
Capturing the spirit of the season is what one group of volunteers is hoping to do while preparing the Beck Chevrolet GMC showroom in Palatka to house more than 85 trees and wreaths with the hopes of more to come.
The seventh annual Festival of Trees, a fundraiser for the Heart of Putnam, Palatka Christian Service Center, will benefit members of the community who are in crisis situations, according to Karen Clifford, a member of the festival's organization committee.
Area businesses, organizations and individuals can sponsor a 6-and-a-half-foot pre-lit green tree for $100 and a 4-foot pre-lit green tree for $50. There are also 24-inch pre-lit green wreaths available for a $50 sponsorship.
Sponsorship forms are available at HeartOfPutnam.com and at the dealership, 1601 Reid St. in Palatka. Trees and wreaths must be decorated by Saturday.
Sponsorship payment must be included in registration forms. In order to be listed in the printed event program, registration forms must be received by Saturday.
New this year, trees will have multi-function LED lights on them while wreaths will have battery-operated lights so they can be hung anywhere.
The public can purchase tickets for the drawings to win the trees and wreaths that are being decorated for the fundraiser. The cost is $20 per sheet of 25 tickets, $50 for three sheets or $100 for seven sheets.
Each decorated tree and wreath will have a box where tickets can be placed in hopes of that ticket-holder winning the selected item.
Tickets must be deposited in drawing boxes by 11 a.m. Dec. 7 to be eligible for the drawing. Ticket-holders should print their name and phone number on each ticket.
This year's entries have different themes, with trees and wreaths featuring hand-painted ornaments that feature the nation's 50 state birds, items from the movie Polar Express,' religious themes, Willy Wonka and other items.
Tickets will begin being drawn at 11:15 a.m. on Dec. 7. Santa and Mrs. Claus will be available starting at 9 a.m. the day of the drawing for photos.
Winners do not need to be present when ticket numbers are announced but will be contacted by phone.
If a winner cannot be reached by Dec. 8, a new winning ticket will be drawn Dec. 9.
'We have numerous first-time participants this year, which is exciting,' Clifford said. 'Last year, we had 77 participants, and we're hoping to surpass that total for this year's event.'
People who win more trees and wreaths than they want can donate them back to the fundraiser and a new winning ticket will be drawn or the winning item will be given to a family in need.
Winners must pick up their trees or wreaths from Dec. 7-23 during the dealership's regular business hours. The winning ticket stub and a photo ID are required to pick up trees and wreaths. Winners should consider bringing a sheet or blanket to wrap around trees for transporting, organizers advised.
The Festival of Trees is the primary annual fundraiser for the Palatka Christian Service Center. Money from the event goes to help people in need while spreading holiday cheer at the same time.
'Beck Chevrolet has been our gracious host for seven years, and their staff looks forward to sharing in the event each year,' Clifford said. 'This fundraiser is a way to bring together the community and people of all ages to share in something good.'
Event Co-chair Kim Daley agrees, saying this is her favorite time of the year.
'I believe we have had the biggest turnout of volunteers to help this year,' Daley said. 'The Festival of Trees has brought the community together in a beautiful way to kick off the season. I think it brings a sense of community, of hope and a shared love for the beauty of the season, all leading up to the most precious time of the season, the birth of our Lord and Savior.
Clifford is thankful for the wonderful group of volunteers who helped set up this year. Among the volunteers are the festival's organization committee members, their friends and family members, two students who needed the community service hours and two couples who heard the call for volunteers on Hope FM.
'It was wonderful to see so many helping hands and happy faces,' she said. 'Christmas is a special time of the year and it warms our hearts to share in the joy of the holiday season. Giving back is just a bonus.'

title: ‘Tis the Season to be Jolly
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The holiday spirit was showcased along St. Johns Avenue on Friday as thousands of spectators showed up to watch the Palatka Christmas Parade.
content:
Body
The holiday spirit was showcased along St. Johns Avenue on Friday as thousands of spectators showed up to watch the Palatka Christmas Parade.
Though the weather was chilly and rain made an appearance, people gathered along the parade route under blankets and draped in thick sweaters to see the century-long tradition. This year's Christmas season kickoff event included horses, marching bands, intricate floats and, as is tradition, candy for the eager children who gathered with their families.
One of the floats was manned by students and administrators of Hillcrest Academy in Palatka. They created a gingerbread candyland church for the Palatka parade this year, Principal Lisa Yaunk said.
'We come out every year and always support the Christmas parade,' she said, estimating that the academy staff and children have been part of the tradition for about nine years. 'The whole reason that we're here is because of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. This is his season, so we just really support everything about the Christmas season.'
Onlookers saw a festive ship, decked-out service repair trucks, a snow-covered karate demonstration, horses, vintage cars and a replica of the train from the 'Polar Express' movie.
Palatka Gas Authority constructed the detailed train, and Office Manager Ann Atkins said all employees contributed.
'The girls came up with an idea, and then we built it,' she said. 'So, all our service men built it; the girls in the office decorated it. We have 16 employees and I bet all 16 of them touched it. So, it's a creation of everybody.'
The parade ran along St. Johns Avenue from First Street to 11th Street. The parade has been going on since the early 1900s and has featured many parade marshals during its existence. This year, 83-year-old Evangelist Patricia Milton led the festivities, having been selected for her dedication to the community.
Other special guests included the 2024 Miss Teen Azalea Raylee McKinnon and Hastings' 2024 Miss Potato Queen.

title: Golden arches open in South Putnam
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: CRESCENT CITY – A new business popped up in the city Thursday, marking the sign of growth to come for the South Putnam County area.
content:
Body
CRESCENT CITY – A new business popped up in the city Thursday, marking the sign of growth to come for the South Putnam County area.
Crescent City's McDonald's, 896 N. Summit St., opened to a crowd of eager residents, employees and city leaders at 11 a.m.
It's the only McDonald's for almost 22 miles between Crescent City and East Palatka. It's also the only one between Crescent City and DeLand for about 29 miles.
Franchise owner Michael Potapow said the McDonald's company bought the property in 2012 to wait for the community to develop before adding the restaurant. When the company decided now was the right time, he said the business took just four months to build.
'Crescent City is a growing city,' he said Thursday. 'Obviously, it's been growing for several years, and it's time to come in and be part of the community.'The franchise owner said one person arrived at the business at 7 a.m. to be the first person in line for the opening. Even though the person found out the new McDonald's didn't open until 11 a.m., Potapow said the person didn't leave.
By 10:30 a.m., cars packed the new restaurant's parking lot, and people waited in the drive-thru until the fast-food place opened. On top of that, city commissioners turned out to cut the red ribbon for the opening and about 30 employees were ready to start their shift.
Potapow said the Crescent City location employs 65 people. It will eventually become a 24-hour McDonald's and breakfast starts at 5 a.m., although they were not serving breakfast yet Thursday.
Online hours for the business do list its hours of operation as 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., but Potapow said the location will become a 24-hour spot. Thursday was only the soft opening and the company will host a grand opening at a later date, he said.
'The community is very excited,' the franchise owner said. 'I know I've talked to the city and they're getting phone calls every hour asking if we've opened. We expect a banner weekend this weekend.'
Commissioner Cynthia Burton said she emailed a McDonald's public relations officer in 2020 because she knew the company owned the Crescent City property. She said she asked why no restaurant had been built yet because there is a great distance between Crescent City and the nearest McDonald's.
She said she thought Crescent City would be the perfect place to put a McDonald's. Now, seeing the idea come to fruition, and seeing the officer she spoke to attending the event, Burton said she was excited and impressed.
'I'm just so happy to see it,' the commissioner said. '... To me, this is going to be really good for our community. It really is. In a lot of different ways, too. It's not just about the burger.'

With 2025 mere hours away, there are secular and religious celebrations occurring today that should appeal to many in the area.
For the first time, there will be an event at the Palatka riverfront today that features something for all ages.
In keeping with tradition, churches throughout Putnam County will be hosting Watch Night services for congregations to usher in the new year.
Below are some of the events that are available to the public today.
Riverfront celebration
Blue Crab Productions will host the 2025 New Year's Celebration today at the St. Johns River Center, 102 N. First St. in Palatka.
The vendor market and boat rides will be available from 3–8 p.m. and there will be a Balloon Ball Drop for Kids at 6 p.m. A DJ will provide music from 3–8 p.m. at the amphitheater stage at the riverfront.
From 9 p.m. – 2 a.m., VIP Access Party ticket-holders will have rooftop access to the River Center, where there will be live music, hot hors d'oeuvres, drinks and a champagne toast. Passes include boat rides at designated launch times. VIP passes cost $150 per person or $250 per couple.
Performing at the VIP party will be The Hit Factory Band, a 10-piece musical group composed of some of the most electrifying top musicians, singers and performers, according to a news release from Blue Crab Productions. Some of the performers include R. Anthony, as seen on 'The Voice,' vocalists Sierra and Jaricha, and bandleader, trumpet player and emcee Andrew Garrison.
The drone light show will take place at midnight.
'We are super excited,' said Erin Hewes, director of events, programs and rentals for Blue Crab Productions. 'Guests will see some local references in the sky such as a blue crab and the Millennium Clock Tower courtesy of Open Sky Productions.'
Other highlights include food, fun for kids, a 360 photo booth and more. For details or to purchase VIP tickets, visit bluecrabproductionsllc.com or call 386-916-7867.
Church Celebrations
Mt. Tabor First Baptist Church will offer two New Year's Eve celebrations tonight.
The first will start at 6 p.m. at the Mt. Tabor South Campus, 608 Randolph St. in Crescent City, and the second starts at 10 p.m. at 4909 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka.
Highlights of the evening include praying out 2024, praying in 2025, worship songs and preaching. Pastor Christopher Harris will be the guest messenger at both services.
New Life Temple Fellowship, 161 W. Louis Broer Road in East Palatka, will host a Watch Night service from 7:30 p.m. – midnight.

The Palatka Daily News will undergo a slight change in its publication schedule this week as the nation lays to rest its longest-living president.
While the physical version of the newspaper will still be published today and Saturday, the newspaper that would normally come out on Thursday will be moved to Friday.
The U.S. Postal Service, which delivers the Palatka Daily News to subscribers, will be closed Thursday in observance of the state funeral of President Jimmy Carter in Washington, D.C.
Daily News reporters will continue to monitor news throughout the week to keep readers informed of the goings-on in their community. The regular publishing schedule is slated to resume next week.
Carter, who served as president from 1977 to 1981, passed away at age 100 on Dec. 29 at his home in Plains, Georgia. Carter lay in repose in the Carter Center in Atlanta from Jan. 4-7.
After his state funeral Thursday, his body will be flown back to Georgia for a private funeral and burial.

title: Group unlocks mystery during book club kickoff
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A mystery is afoot in Putnam County, and reading enthusiasts are encouraging local residents to step back into the 1930s to help solve it.
content:
Body
A mystery is afoot in Putnam County, and reading enthusiasts are encouraging local residents to step back into the 1930s to help solve it.
One Book One Putnam, a nonprofit that annually hosts events pertaining to a specific tome, had its kickoff event Thursday at the Palatka Golf Club. The event offered a look at Putnam County in the 1930s and a sneak peek of what's to come during the 2025 One Book season, which lasts until March.
This year's read is 'The Maltese Falcon' by Dashiell Hammett, a novel One Book, One Putnam committee member Lulu Gail Parish believes everyone will enjoy.
'We're excited, and hopefully, others are getting excited about reading and going back and reading one of the classic books from the past,' she said.
Published in 1930, 'The Maltese Falcon' centers around Detective Sam Spade, criminals, a beautiful woman and a missing statue, according to publishing group Penguin Random House. It was adapted into two movies, the first starring Bebe Daniels and Ricardo Cortez in 1931 and the second starring Humphrey Bogart and Mary Astor 10 years later.
People who attended Thursday's kickoff learned about film noir, the movie style that helped make the 1940 adaptation a classic Hollywood crime drama.
Putnam County Library System Archivist Mischa Johns gave attendees a taste of life in Putnam County in the late 1920s and 1930s.
She showed people relics, including registrar books from Putnam County during those decades and concert flyers for performances by Palatka resident C.S. Belton and his Society Syncopators.
In her presentation, Johns said Belton had a band that played nationwide and paved the way for musicians like Ella Fitzgerald and Duke Ellington to play in Palatka. Belton was called the 'Duke Ellington of the South.'
Johns said people told her they had not known of Belton despite there being a mural in his honor, 'Harlem Nights in Palatka,' on a building at the corner of St. Johns Avenue at North Eighth Street.
'He was such a big name, and (people I spoke with) were really interested to know that there was someone that was that famous that lived right here in Putnam County,' Johns said. 'His family is still a part of Putnam County.'
Although Florida is not mentioned in the book, Johns called the novel revolutionary for its time and encouraged everyone who likes to read to pick up a copy.
This year, the organization is adding more interactive activities. Not only are the traditional book discussions happening at every county library branch, but One Book will be hosting movie nights and a dance.
The finale will be in March, organizers said, but a date has yet to be announced.
Because 'The Maltese Falcon' is a detective novel, One Book members have invited readers to solve a mystery themselves.
There are 20 falcons placed around Putnam County and people must take a selfie with each falcon for a chance to win a prize. Three clues will be released each week.
One Book organizers said the person competing for the prize and the stop number must be visible in the pictures.
People can email their photos to onebookoneputnamfindthefalcon@gmail.com from Feb. 15-26. Entries will not be accepted before or after those dates.
The first three clues are as follows:
– 'Surrounded by books, including others by this year's author, all around the county.'
– 'You would not want to pay the tangible property tax if you found the original bird, but you could at all of these offices.'
– 'I can't help thinking that I saw it in the funny papers.'
'The Maltese Falcon' was never a required school reading, Johns said, but it's one she considers fantastic and great for anyone. It was revolutionary for its time because Hammett wrote the book authentically, adding relatable dialogue and characters, she said.
'Actually reading the book, it's a different experience,' Johns said. '... He is such a good author. I mean, I think even high school students would like this.'

title: Sacred tree inspires CC woman to author book
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Mindful meditation is important to Judi White, who last year released her first book, 'Bodhi Leaves: An Unfolding Journey of Depth Reflection.'
content:
Body
Mindful meditation is important to Judi White, who last year released her first book, 'Bodhi Leaves: An Unfolding Journey of Depth Reflection.'
The 80-year-old author, who has lived in Crescent City for more than 30 years, said she came up with the title for her book after taking a trip to India and hearing stories about the Bodhi trees near the sacred site of the original Buddha, where it has been said he was enlightened.
So, the South Putnam resident decided to bring home a tiny sampling from one of the favored trees from Sri Lanka, an island nation just southeast of India.
'The tree grew tall but with a freeze, I didn't know if it would survive,' she said. 'I wanted to save it.'
White said the tree, which is a member of the fig or mulberry family, has recovered, starting with a few branches that came up and then a trunk that has grown to around 12 feet tall.
According to White, each section in the book, which was released in August, is a reflection of her journal entries chosen from three blogs she published and daily journal entries with prompts for readers' reflections.
'It's an unfolding journey of depth (and) reflection,' she said. 'The book is a selection of stories, poetic prose, poems and prayers in four sections, plus an introduction to explain the evolution of the reflection process.'
The self-published book was printed through Sacred Path Publishing and is available on Amazon. The cost is $12.99 for a paper book, $9.88 for the e-book or $15 from the author, which includes tax and the cost of shipping.
White is a former exceptional student education teacher at E.H. Miller School and guidance counselor at Moseley Elementary School. In 2009, she retired from co-teaching at DeLand High School in Volusia County and founded Sophia Circle, a group counseling business.
'It has nourished my faith and enriched my understanding of love as kindness, compassion, joy and inclusion being the message of every religion, including my choice as a Christian,' she said about her book. 'The intention of publishing this book is to recommend journal writing as a way to remain resilient in stressful situations and trauma-causing experiences.'
Throughout her work-life experience, White said, she has found herself concerned about burnout for those – from teachers to community volunteers to caregivers – who serve others.
'Suffering from burnout myself, I slowly found mindful meditation and journal writing to be an effective way to renew and sustain resilience to be able to care with loving kindness and compassion,' she said. 'People's resilience in stressful situations and post-trauma has been my vocation in church and community renewal, teaching special education and guidance counseling and a group counseling business.'
Besides writing, White has a love of photography, especially nature, as well as cooking.
'Each week, I choose a new view of a sunrise or seasonal scene, write a poem, or choose another I find inspiring and post on Facebook,' she said.
White also has a goal of creating a food forest on her almost 1 acre of land in the center of town and planting trees and bushes to harvest.
'My son is doing most of the work,' she said, smiling.
Years ago, White said, she was a missionary elder and ruling elder in the United Presbyterian Church. She is a member of Christ Presbyterian Church in Crescent City, although her health and physical limitations have kept her from being active.
White is content with the meditation group she formed and meets at her home on Saturdays and a sunrise meditation at the lake.
'I enjoy teaching meditation and have a labyrinth on the northeast corner of my lawn open to all for walking meditation,' the mother and grandmother said. 'I dedicated 'Bodhi Leaves' to my seven grandchildren and a great-niece who shares her birthday with White and her grandfather.'
White hopes people who read her book will take away a curiosity about the value of meditation and journal writing as a daily practice.
'I am hoping and already finding that readers are reflecting with the prompts, reading the book slowly and being inspired to enjoy journal writing,' she said. 'Stress and trauma is an everyday occurrence for everyone these days and has been for a while worldwide.'
If the book can inspire readers to heal from the impact of this environment, White said, writing it will have fulfilled its purpose.
'I believe people need solitary spiritual tools to partner with their faith,' she said.
The release of the book was timely for White, who reached a momentous milestone: turning 80.
'It was one of my bucket list projects,' she said. 'My hope is that we be gentle with endings and patiently nurture the arrival of new growth. May our hearts touch the Bodhi's leaves.'

title: CC student 1 of 6 statewide fellowship winners
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: One South Putnam County student's four years of hard work in hopes of attending college paid off Monday as she was celebrated for winning an exclusive fellowship.
content:
Body
One South Putnam County student's four years of hard work in hopes of attending college paid off Monday as she was celebrated for winning an exclusive fellowship.
Take Stock in Children representatives announced Monday that the Asofsky Foundation chose Mithila 'Mia' Paul, a senior at Crescent City Junior-Senior High School and a Take Stock mentee, to win the Leaders 4 Life Fellowship.
Paul is one of only six students in Florida to be granted the opportunity, according to Take Stock, a program that provides high school students with mentorship, college coaching and a 60-hour credit scholarship.
As part of the fellowship, Paul will receive a MacBook Pro computer, leadership and professional development training, and $40,000 over four years to cover dormitory housing, meal plan, medical insurance and other expenses, according to Take Stock.
'My mom and dad, they could have chosen any state, any city, but, somehow, they ended up coming to small Crescent City,' Paul said through tears Monday. 'But I wouldn't have wanted my four years any other way, with any different friends, any different teachers.'
Paul's parents immigrated to America from Bangladesh to start a new life. In one of her application essays, Paul said that if her parents had not entered the U.S. Diversity Visa Program, she would not be who she is today.
She was one of 12 finalists announced in December, and Take Stock representatives said Monday's announcement was a surprise to Paul. She and her family will attend an all-expenses-paid trip to Tallahassee in March as part of the fellowship.
There, Paul will meet other fellowship winners, mentors and influential leaders, according to Take Stock.
On Monday, Paul's family, classmates, and Take Stock mentors as well as Putnam County School District employees congratulated her with a ceremony. Crescent City High Principal Tim Adams said he was proud of Paul and the hard work she put into obtaining the fellowship.
'It's a great model for others to learn from,' he said during the ceremony, directing his comments at Paul. 'Having the opportunity to work extremely hard the way you have for all these years, it's been a pleasure having you. Your commitment to us and our school and our community of being all in, you're second to none. You are the best.'
Paul has a passion for art and a desire to help others. She said she wants to pursue a career in occupational therapy while also helping people with her artistic skills.
Crescent City counselor Pamela Brown remembers meeting Paul and how the student had an entrepreneurial spirit, especially when it came to art.
'She's just an amazing young lady, and I love the way she cares about other people and her community,' Brown said. '... I look forward to seeing you bloom and blossom into the woman that you're going to become.'

title: City manager candidate interviews to begin Wednesday
description: Interviews not available online but residents can watch from City Hall The eight people hoping to be Palatka's new city manager will undergo interviews with local elected officials Wednesday and…
content:
Interviews not available online but residents can watch from City Hall
The eight people hoping to be Palatka's new city manager will undergo interviews with local elected officials Wednesday and Thursday.
Interviews will run from 9 a.m. – 1 p.m. both days, according to a notice the city sent the Daily News at 12:43 p.m. Tuesday, providing a notice of fewer than 24 hours.
City officials said the interviews, which will be conducted electronically, will not be streamed online, but the public is welcome to go to City Hall, 201 N. Second St., to watch the interviews as they occur. Each interview for the next city manager is scheduled to last 45 minutes.
Finance Director Marcia Carty, who is the interim city manager, has applied for the job and will be the first to interview at 9 a.m. Wednesday.
In a 4-1 vote during the Sept. 12 commission meeting, Carty was named the interim manager shortly after City Manager Troy Bell was fired.
Also interviewing Wednesday is Waycross, Georgia, resident Scott Moye who most recently served as the Ware County, Georgia, manager from 2016 to 2024, according to his resume.
Redmond Jones II, of Iowa City, Iowa, will be the third interviewee Wednesday. Jones was the deputy city manager for Iowa City from 2021-2024, his resume states.
The fourth candidate being interviewed Wednesday is Ricardo Mendez-Saldivia, a Miami resident whose most recent government experience has been working as the assistant city manager for West Palm Beach from 2020 to 2021, according to his resume.
On Thursday, the commission will interview four more candidates. The first contestant for the job is Michael Brillhart, who presently serves as the Crescent City's interim manager and the city's Community Development Area executive director.
Another interviewee is Patrick Comiskey, a Mount Dora resident who served as the Mount Dora city manager from 2021 to 2024.
Thomas Thomas, whose most recent job was serving as the Compton, California, city manager from March 2022 to July 2023, will be the third interviewee.
The final candidate being interviewed Thursday will be Washington state resident Blaine Oborn. He worked in Oak Hill, Washington, as the city administrator from August 2018 to February 2024.
After online interviews end Thursday, according to the city's interview agenda, commissioners will discuss which candidates they'd like to interview in person.

DEPARTMENT OF
ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION NOTICE OF DRAFT PERMIT
The Department of Environmental Protection gives notice of its preparation of a draft permit to the Seminole Electric Cooperative, Inc. (Seminole) for the Seminole Generating Station (SGS). This permit authorizes the permittee to operate wastewater treatment and effluent disposal facilities at the Seminole Generating Station.
The facility is an electric generating plant which includes the following Units:
SGS 2: SGS Unit 2 consists of a coal-fired steam electric generating unit with a total nameplate generating capacity of 735 megawatts (MW). The unit is equipped with a wet-limestone flue gas desulfurization (FGD) system, which produces commercial-grade gypsum. The unit is also equipped with selective catalytic reduction (SCR) systems to reduce nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from the plant. Wastewater consists of cooling tower blowdown (CTBD) from a natural draft cooling tower, low volume wastewater (LVW), on-site domestic wastewater, and FGD purge stream water.
Seminole Combined Cycle Facility (SCCF): SCCF is a 1,050 MW two-on-one, natural gas-fired, combined-cycle unit consisting of two combustion generators, two heat recovery steam generators, one steam turbine generator, and ancillary equipment. Wastewater from the SCCF consists of blowdown from a mechanical draft cooling tower, treated domestic wastewater and other LVW.
The treated wastewater streams from both facilities enter a surge tank and are then discharged via Outfall D-001 through a 900-foot submerged pipe with a multi-port diffuser to the St. Johns River, a Class III fresh water.
The facility consists of one Surface Water Discharge D-001: D-001 is an existing 7.46 MGD permitted discharge of combined plant wastewater to the St. Johns River, Class III Fresh Waters (WBID 2213L). The facility is subject to Section 316(a) of the Clean Water Act, operates as described above with intake structures subject to Section 316(b) of the Clean Water Act, and is subject to the Effluent Limitations Guidelines and Standards (ELGS) for the Steam Electric Power Generating Point Source Category (40 CFR Part 423).
The facility is located at 890 N Highway 17, Palatka, Florida 32177-8647 in Putnam County. The Department has assigned permit file number FL0036498-027-IW1S to the proposed project. The facility is also regulated under the Florida Electrical Power Plant Siting Act (License No. PA78-10). Stormwater associated with industrial activity is covered under a Multi-Sector Generic Permit (separate Permit No. FLR05B869).
The permit application file and supporting data are available for public inspection during normal business hours, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, except legal holidays, at the Department's Wastewater Management Program, 2600 Blair Stone Road, M.S. 3545, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-2400, at phone number (850)245-8589.
NOTICE OF RIGHTS
The Department intends to issue the permit unless as a result of public comment appropriate changes are made.
Written Comments or Request for Public Meeting
Any interested person may submit written comments on the Department's proposed permitting decision or may
submit a written request for a public meeting to Florida Department of Environmental Protection, Bob Martinez Center, Wastewater Management Program, 2600 Blair Stone Road, M.S. 3545, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-2400, Attention: Lauren Gottfreid, in accordance with Rule 62-620.555, F.A.C. The comments or request for a public meeting must contain the information set forth below and must be received in the Department's Wastewater Management Program.
The comments or request for a public meeting must contain the following information:
(a) The commenter's name, address, and telephone number; the applicant's name and address; the Department permit file number; and the county in which the project is proposed;

title: Palatka, Live Oak residents die in traffic collision
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Two adults died and a preteen was seriously injured in a Tuesday morning head-on crash near Carraway, authorities said.
content:
Body
Two adults died and a preteen was seriously injured in a Tuesday morning head-on crash near Carraway, authorities said.
By Tuesday afternoon, Florida Highway Patrol confirmed a 34-year-old Live Oak man and a 38-year-old Palatka woman died from injuries sustained in the crash, which took place around 7 a.m. A 12-year-old Palatka boy who was in the vehicle with the woman from Palatka was hospitalized with serious injuries, authorities said.
The first vehicle, a sedan driven by the man from Live Oak, had been traveling eastbound on S.R.100 east of Roberts Lane, according to FHP.
The second vehicle, a sedan driven by a 30-year-old Palatka man, had been traveling westbound on S.R. 100. The third vehicle, a sports utility vehicle carrying the Palatka woman and child, was traveling westbound behind the second vehicle, according to a report from FHP.
'The driver of (vehicle one) exited the eastbound lane and traveled into the westbound lane,' the agency reported. '(Vehicle one's) left side sideswiped (vehicle two's) left side.'
The front of the first sedan then struck the front of the SUV, according to the report, and the first car came to a stop in a position that obstructed traffic in the eastbound lane of S.R. 100 while facing northeast, according to FHP.
The second vehicle stopped in the grass of the north road shoulder tree line facing southeast, and the third car also stopped on the grass of the north shoulder but faced northwest, FHP wrote in its report.
The Palatka man driving the second vehicle received minor injuries, according to FHP.
The crash blocked both lanes of traffic on S.R. 100, according to a Facebook post from the Putnam County Sheriff's Office, which at about 9 a.m. expected the area to be blocked for at least five more hours.
'Traffic is being diverted to Springside Shortcut Road to Carraway Mail Route Road,' the sheriff's office wrote on Facebook. 'Avoid the area if at all possible as there is a large fire and law enforcement presence.'
Shortly after 1:30 p.m. Tuesday, officials from Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School, which is located near the crash site, wrote on Facebook to say traffic on S.R. 100 had resumed.

title: Fire, EMT training offered to high schoolers
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A partnership between two local government entities is giving Palatka Junior-Senior High School students firsthand experience that could fast-track them to a career in emergency services.
content:
A partnership between two local government entities is giving Palatka Junior-Senior High School students firsthand experience that could fast-track them to a career in emergency services.
The school is partnering with Putnam County Fire Rescue and the county's Emergency Services Department to offer more than 191 hours of training in a three-year fire and emergency medical services program, according to a newsletter from the county.
Students in the program will begin classes in 10th grade and complete the program at the end of 12th grade, according to the county.
Superintendent Rick Surrency said he is thankful to Emergency Services officials for partnering with the district's Career and Technical Education Department to offer the program.
The program joins welding, business management, allied health assisting and automotive maintenance, among others, as one of numerous programs being offered at the school, according to the district,
'These are jobs that are found in our community,' Surrency said in a text message about the EMS program. 'And we want to continue to fill those positions when they are available with our graduates.'
Gene Morgante, the Fire Rescue Department's health and safety specialist, and Jason Black, a firefighter and emergency medical technician in Putnam County, are teaching students how to work medical emergencies and treat trauma patients as well as instructing them on fire behavior, firefighting strategies and knowing how to safely operate fire equipment, according to the county.
'Our goal is to not only educate but also mentor and inspire students to see fire and EMS as a viable, long-term career,' Black said in a statement.
Once students turn 18 and graduate from the school program, they can participate in live fire training and complete the requirements to earn their Florida State Fire 1 certification and their Emergency Medical Responder certification, county officials said.
Students can dual-enroll at St. Johns River State College while in high school and work toward obtaining their EMT certification, according to the county. During dual enrollment, students will prepare for the National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians exam, which county officials said is critical to obtaining an EMT license.
There is already a student dual-enrolled in the program and serving as an apprentice with the Fire Rescue Department, according to the county.
'Several other students are actively working as apprentices with (Putnam County Fire Rescue), spending up to 10 hours per week observing and gaining firsthand experience on a rescue unit or fire engine,' county officials said in the newsletter. 'This real-world exposure provides valuable insight into the demands and rewards of a career in fire and emergency services.'
The program aims to mentor local youth and encourage them to pursue long-term and meaningful careers in the county, according to the county. Officials hope the program will strengthen the community's workforce with people dedicated to serving Putnam County.
'By giving them the training, certification opportunities and real-world experience, we're helping to build a workforce that will serve and protect our own community,' Black said.

title: Kids invited to splash into summer on Lake Stella
description: Putnam County kids are invited for some swimming, kayaking, fishing and other fun in the sun in Crescent City. The Putnam County Sheriff's Office is hosting its fourth annual Cops, Kids and Kayaks…
content:
Putnam County kids are invited for some swimming, kayaking, fishing and other fun in the sun in Crescent City. The Putnam County Sheriff's Office is hosting its fourth annual Cops, Kids and Kayaks from 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. Saturday on Lake Stella and Dexter Beach, 325 E. Grand Rondo. Allison Waters-Merritt, spokeswoman for the sheriff's office, said the event idea is not unique to the agency. The Crescent City Police Department came up with the idea for the event before it was dissolved and the sheriff's office took over law enforcement duties in the city in 2021, Waters-Merritt said. 'When we took over services in Crescent City, one of the things that we heard from the residents was they wanted to have that connection they had with their police department,' she said. 'Even though cops, kids and kayaks had gone away, I had always liked the premise of the event.' Waters-Merritt said Lake Stella and Dexter Beach are beautiful locations that are underused, which is why the sheriff's office chose to bring the event back there. A portion of Lake Stella will be sectioned off for kids to safely swim under the watch of a lifeguard, she said. Children can learn how to fish and kayak from professionals, like members of the Putnam Blueways and Trails and fishing instructor Lee Dayton. The last kayak launch will be at 2:45 p.m., and officials are urging people to show up early to sign up for a kayak trip. Kids can play on a water slide and in bounce houses, too. Waters-Merritt said each child must have a parent or guardian with them to participate. The event is free, but food is available for purchase. 'Everything is sort of geared toward kids to give them the availability to use the park in a safe manner,' she said. The sheriff's office will have its marine unit on the water and law enforcement trucks on land for the children to check out. Also slated to attend are emergency responders and elected officials, like Mayor Michele Myers, who has attended and been involved with the event for numerous years. The mayor said she's grateful to everyone who volunteers their time to make the event great for kids and their families. 'The weather Saturday will be perfect to paddle on our beautiful Lake Stella, swim, slide down the waterside, fish, enjoy good food and snacks and most especially meet the deputies and our city's first responders, which keep us all safe,' Myers said in a text message.

title: Historical marker unveiled at ‘Dear Old C.A.'
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: In front of an aged building left to crumble sits a brand new historical marker honoring a piece of Putnam County's Black history.
content:
Body
In front of an aged building left to crumble sits a brand new historical marker honoring a piece of Putnam County's Black history.
Central Academy alumni and preservation enthusiasts revealed the building's first historic marker Thursday morning to an eager crowd. It's been 26 years since the building, located on the corner of Washington and 13th streets, was placed on the National Register of Historic Places and 53 years since the school shut down.
Shirley Edwards, a Central Academy graduate and the daughter of one of the school's teachers, said milestones like adding a historical marker are part of the fight to preserve the school.
'It might be blighted, but we're here,' she said. 'And I welcome you to the fight, to the struggle and to join us in faith and hope.'
The original Central Academy building was built in 1892 to serve Palatka's Black residents in first through eighth grades. The school later expanded to serve students into 12th grade, according to the marker.
In 1925, the landmark became the first accredited Black high school in Florida. A fire destroyed the original building in 1936, and the structure standing today was erected during the 1937-1938 school year, the marker states.
When Putnam County schools were integrated in 1971, Central Academy closed, and the building eventually fell into disrepair.
Keynote speaker and Central Academy alumnus Andrew McRae, who enlisted in the Navy in 1973 and attended Bethune-Cookman College in 1981, said he remembers coming back to Palatka and watching Central Academy deteriorate over the years.
McRae said it didn't have to get to that point.
'I always considered this hallowed ground,' he said. 'I'm going to say, even though I consider it an honor to be here on this historical ground, I'm also appalled at the negligence of this building.'
He remembered standing in front of a statue of the school's Bulldog mascot before every home game and singing the school song, 'Dear Old C.A.' The statue is long gone.
McRae, who recalls seeing the building descend through a downward spiral over the years, said hardly anyone spoke up about saving the school when it first closed.
Efforts to restore the building rekindled in 1998 when historians and alumni made efforts to get the building placed on the National Register of Historic Places. Members of The Historic Central Academy Preservation and Community Development Corp. Inc., which is composed of young community members and Central alumni, are continuing those efforts.
However, McRae said he has heard people recommend letting the building go because it already served its purpose.
'Brothers and sisters, I have a problem,' he said. 'I say today that those of us who say, 'Central Academy Elementary is simply a relic of the past, wipe the slate clean, allow her to fade into Palatka's past,' these are (people who) either don't know or don't care or don't want to deal with the real reason why there was a need for Central Academy in the first place.'
The building, which has been reduced to a roofless structure with only four walls, is a reminder of segregation. America needs to own up to its past, not shy away from it, McRae said
'Nobody knows the real story of Central Academy Elementary, but we know it because we lived it,' he said. 'Until we come to grips with why we had to have it and what we are because (of it), we're never going to get to where we need.'

title: Veteran jumps into France to commemorate D-Day landing
author: Trisha Murphy
description: A local man had the honor and privilege of taking part in the 80th anniversary of World War II's D-Day this month when he parachuted into Carentan in the Normandy region of France.
content:
Body
A local man had the honor and privilege of taking part in the 80th anniversary of World War II's D-Day this month when he parachuted into Carentan in the Normandy region of France.
'All I could think about was what those guys 80 years ago endured on the jump,' Palatka resident Dylan Pacetti said. 'Flak, machine gun fire, planes being shot from the sky, and then having to jump out into the hell of war. It was extremely surreal to be able to step in their shoes, minus the live fire and dangers of the battlefield.'
D-Day was the first day of Operation Overlord, the Allied attack on German-occupied Western Europe that began on the beaches of Normandy, France, on June 6, 1944.
According to a news release from Dave Sirak, the public affairs officer for the Round Canopy Parachuting Team – USA, the parachuting team honored the Allied paratroopers of World War II by participating in four commemorative round canopy parachute jumps onto historic sites in Normandy, France, as part of the 80th anniversary of D-Day.
On June 2, Pacetti completed his first jump from a WWII C-47 aircraft, which was a cross-channel jump taking off in the United Kingdom and landing in France as the soldiers did in 1944.
Three days later, his second jump was into the Normandy commune of Azeville, an area where large guns blasted the beaches on Normandy, Sirak said.
'When Dylan landed on every jump, he was overwhelmed with emotion,' Sirak said. 'Retracing the steps of his veteran heroes was emotional as a combat veteran.'
'I couldn't help but think of the men and women who didn't make it off the field that day,' Pacetti said. 'In my mind, I kept thinking of them and how they never got to see the free world that they helped liberate from the Axis powers.'
Pacetti said he found himself trying to place himself in the moment some eight decades ago.
'I tried to feel what those guys might have felt, envisioned what they must have seen,' he said. 'It was a very emotional jump.'
The third jump on June 7 saw parachuters descend over Mont-Saint-Michel, France, a Catholic abbey on the coast that is more than 1,000 years old. The fourth and final jump was June 9 at the La Fiere Bridge. Pacetti didn't take part in the final jump.
Those troops involved in D-Day included women paratroopers who played a vital role before and after D-Day by jumping behind enemy lines, supporting and training the French resistance, and providing intelligence on German movements and troop strength.
'We had several women who jumped in France wearing dresses and lipstick under their jumpsuits as women did in 1944,' Sirak said.
Along with hundreds of jumpers from more than 10 countries, Round Canopy hosted a bipartisan delegation made up of 10 lawmakers from the U.S. House of Representatives who made a commemorative jump into Normandy over Mont-Saint-Michel on June 7. Two of the representatives were Republicans Mike Waltz and Cory Mills from Florida.
Sirak said the Round Canopy Parachuting Team – USA, a nonprofit organization headquartered at Skydive Palatka at Kay Larkin Field, safely performs round canopy, static line parachuting activities to commemorate paratroopers and veterans who fought to defeat despotism around the world.
'The purpose of RCPT-USA is to reinforce the worldwide memory of their priceless deeds of valor and the selfless sacrifices so many made to restore peace on earth,' he said. 'We bring awareness and educate the public about the sacrifices and heroism of Allied paratroopers from World War II onward.'
For information about the organization, visit rcptusa.org.
Pacetti, 32, joined the Army in July 2013 and was assigned to the 307th Engineer Battalion under the 20th Engineer Brigade and the 82nd Airborne Division. He was honorably discharged in 2014.
Pacetti said he was the only skydiver from Putnam County who participated in this year's event. He has performed 57 jumps at Skydive Palatka with the Round Canopy Parachute Team – USA.
He and his wife, Brianna, have a son, Weston, 5.
Pacetti said he and his wife arrived in Normandy, France, on May 31 and returned home on June 8.
'We went to Omaha and Utah Beach, where the invasion forces came ashore, and we also went to the (Normandy) American Cemetery,' he said. 'It was an extremely humbling experience to see all of the headstones of those brave men who never made it home.'
Pacetti believes it's more important than ever to keep that history alive and tell the stories of those brave soldiers so people never forget.
'This is something that I have gotten to share with my son, as he is passionate about aviation and history,' he said. 'I will talk about the 80th anniversary of D-Day until I leave this life.'

title: Wawa opens doors to hundreds of eager patrons
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The Palatka Junior-Senior High School Marching Band, an oversized goose and cheery employees greeted patrons Thursday as Wawa in Palatka first opened its doors.
content:
Body
The Palatka Junior-Senior High School Marching Band, an oversized goose and cheery employees greeted patrons Thursday as Wawa in Palatka first opened its doors.
Putnam County's first Wawa, 625 State Road 19, opened at 8 a.m. to a line of people that wrapped around the building waiting to grab a famous Wawa hoagie, get a free cup of coffee, meet Wawa's mascot Wally Goose or simply browse the souped-up gas station.
Palatka resident Valerie French, who arrived at 6 a.m., was the first person to enter the new Wawa, which is open 24/7. Employees gifted her with a special goodie bag packed with a cup, a T-shirt and other things she couldn't remember.
'(I came) to see what it's going to be like because I've never been inside a Wawa before,' French said. 'This is the first one. I like it. I really do. … I'll be back.'
Georgetown residents Linda and Ken Kienholz, who have been to several Wawa locations and wanted to be one of the first to shop at this one, got in line just after 7 a.m.
Linda Kienholz wore her 2015 Hoagiefest shirt to the opening to show her Wawa spirit. The pair traveled to New Jersey for the festival, which pays tribute to and offers special deals on Wawa hoagies throughout the summer.
Ken Keinholz said he was born and raised on Wawa coffee but also recommends its Italian and tuna hoagies.
'I tell you what, load it up and it's so good,' he said. 'I don't know where they get their tuna from, (but) it's so good.'
Karen Myers, the director of store operations, said the first Wawa Food Market store opened in 1964 in Folsom, Pennsylvania. Wawa is celebrating 60 years of serving communities this year, and in honor of the anniversary, the first 300 guests Thursday received commemorative shirts that read, 'In my Wawa era.'
Myers said Wawa aims to be not only a convenience store but part of the community.
'Our promise is simple; it's 'Fulfill lives every day,'' she said. 'And that sounds kind of, like, heavy for a convenience store, gas station kind of thing, right? But it's not because we really do know that we make a difference not only in our customers' lives every day when we brighten their lives but also in our associates' lives in many different ways.'
The new store brought 30 new jobs to the area, Myers said, and Wawa officials included local organizations, such as the marching band, the Palatka Police Department and the Palatka Fire Department, in the opening day festivities.
The two departments duked it out in a hoagie-making competition known as Hoagies For Heroes to see which team could make the most hoagies, for which Wawa is widely known, in three minutes.
Although the competition became a food fight between police and firefighting officials, they managed to get some sandwiches made. The police department won 33-30 and touted a trophy and Wally Goose stuffed animal.
In the spirit of friendly competition, Wawa gave both teams $1,000 to donate to the charity of their choice. The police department chose the Palatka's Police Athletic League, and the fire department chose the Palatka Christian Service Center.
'Way back in 1964, we opened based on people, not on profit,' Myers said. 'Many of you I can see shaking your head out there, nodding in agreement with me. That's a 'heck yeah.' This is a company that's based on people and customers, and we continue to do that 60 years later.'

title: Locals, visitors flock to Crescent City for early Fourth celebration
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: CRESCENT CITY – A large crowd gathered Saturday to watch fireworks explode across the sky in the first of numerous Independence Day celebrations that will take place in Putnam County.
content:
Body
CRESCENT CITY – A large crowd gathered Saturday to watch fireworks explode across the sky in the first of numerous Independence Day celebrations that will take place in Putnam County.
The 12th Red, White & Boom, hosted by the Crescent City Yacht Club, drew people from Crescent City and surrounding areas to visit the food, craft and other vendors along Central Avenue.
The event, which traditionally takes place the weekend before the Fourth of July, began at 5 p.m., but Yacht Club member Heather Harper said people were walking the street as early as noon while she and other club members were still setting up.
'We do this to give back to the community,' Harper said. 'We live here, and we want people to have a good time. People come here because this is the first one. It's a good show.'
Cheryl Dayton, another member of the yacht club, said she met people who came from Astor, which is about a 30-minute drive from there to Crescent City. One family came from Jacksonville to watch the fireworks, and another couple, Ben and Matilda Nolt, drove from Volusia County.
'We just heard from a neighbor that it's a super festive, fun thing to do in the area,' Matilda Nolt said. '(We're) kind of excited that there's fireworks.'
The couple dressed up in matching American flag outfits for the night. Matilda Nolt spray-painted her hair, got her face painted with stars and stripes, and donned red lipstick. Ben Nolt wore blue spray paint in his hair and Independence Day sparkles in his beard.
They always get dressed up for the holiday, Matilda Holt said.
'We call it his second birthday,' she said.
As the night came to a close, more people started packing Central Avenue, the Crescent Lake dock and the dock of nearby Three Bananas to watch the pyrotechnics.
'We like to watch people, and the people have been friendly,' Dayton said. 'And they've been excited, and the kids have been awesome. It's so cute.'
Upcoming Fourth of July events include the Community Affairs Department's celebrations from 5:30–9 p.m. at the St. Johns River Center, 102 N. First St. in Palatka. Activities will also take place at nearby Riverfront Park, 100 Memorial Parkway.
There will be live entertainment, games and a foam party for kids and fireworks to end the night. First Presbyterian Church, 123 S. Second St. in Palatka, will host a patriotic concert for the community at 6 p.m. Thursday.
Interlachen's Independence Day celebration will take place from 8 a.m. – 9 p.m. Thursday, starting with a kids' fishing tournament at Lake Lagonda.
Other highlights include a bike race at Dowda Field at 9 a.m., a veteran's ceremony at Jenkins Park with Rep. Mike Waltz, R-Florida, at 9:45 a.m., and a parade at 10 a.m. with state Rep. Bobby Payne, R-Palatka, serving as grand marshal.
There will be a plethora of other games and activities throughout the day before the 9 p.m. fireworks finale.
For the full schedule, click the Our Events tab at interlachen-fl.gov.

content:
The Putnam County Board of County Commissioners will meet in regular session on Tuesday, July 23, 2024 at 9:00 a.m. in the County Commissioner's Board Room located at 2509 Crill Avenue, Suite 100, Palatka.
In accordance with the Americans with Disabilities Act, any person needing a special accommodation to participate in this matter should contact (386) 329-0205 no later than three (3) days prior to the hearing or proceeding for which this notice has been given. Hearing impaired persons can access the forgoing telephone number by contacting the Florida Relay Service at 1-800-955-8770 (Voice) or 1-800-955-8771 (TDD).
BOARD OF COUNTY COMMISSIONERS
PUTNAM COUNTY, FLORIDA
Legal No. 00099793
07/13/24

Case No.: 54-2023-DR-1035
Division:
DOR obo BRENDA K. LANSING, Petitioner
and
LEE PRECIOUS JONES SR JOHN EARL LANGLEY JR, Respondents.
AMENDED NOTICE OF ACTION FOR
Petition to Determine Paternity and/or for Support and Other Relief
TO: JOHN EARL LANGLEY, JR.
59 E. 64th Street, Hialeah, Florida 33013-1044, 10000 nw 80TH CT #2440, Hialeah Gardens Florida 33016, 202 Dogwood Lane, Palatka, Florida 32177, 7279 W 24th Ave #243 Hialeah FL 33016.
YOU ARE NOTIFIED that an action for Paternity, Support and Other Relief has been filed against you and that you are required to serve a copy of your written defenses, if any, to it on Department of Revenue o/b/o Brenda K. Lansing, whose address s 4923 NW 43rd Street, Gainesville, Florida 32606, on or before May 31, 2024, and file the original with the clerk of the is Court at 410 Saint Johns Avenue, Palatka, Florida 32177, before service on Petitioner or immediately thereafter. If you fail to do so, a default may be entered against you for the relief demanded in the petition.
Copies of all court documents in this case, including orders, are available at the Clerk of the Circuit Court's office. You may review these documents upon request.
You must keep the Clerk of the Circuit Court's office notified of your current address. (You may file Designation of Current Mailing and E-Mail Address, Florida Supreme Court Approved Family Law Form 12.915.} Future papers in this lawsuit will be mailed or e-mailed to the addresses on record at the clerk's office.
Instructions for Florida Supreme Court Approved Family law Form 12 .913(a)(2), Notice of Action For Family Cases With Minor or Dependent Child(ren) (06/18)
WARNING: Rule 12.285, Florida Family Law Rules of Procedure, requires certain automatic disclosure of documents and information. Failure to comply can result in sanctions, including dismissal or striking of pleadings.
Dated: 5/21/24
Matt Reynolds
CLERK OF THE CIRCUIT COURT
(SEAL)
By: Katilyn Lee
Deputy Clerk

title: Column: Saying goodbye as press prints its final Daily News
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: 'How do I say goodbye to what we had? 'The good times that made us laugh 'Outweigh the bad.' – Boyz II Men
content:
Body
'How do I say goodbye to what we had?
'The good times that made us laugh
'Outweigh the bad.'
– Boyz II Men
Some people wonder what they'd learn if the walls of a particular place could talk. While the walls at the Palatka Daily News are unable to speak, a vital piece of our equipment has been telling tales since the 1980s.
Our printing press, a titanic piece of machinery that required major additions to our St. Johns Avenue headquarters to occur for us to house it, has been telling local, state, national and international stories to our readers for decades. Through the good times and the bad, the uplifting and the gut-wrenching, our printing press has taken so much work done by numerous people and packaged it into a relatively compact tangible item to help the residents of Putnam County and beyond stay informed of current events.
But much like the Oracle said in 'The Matrix Revolutions,' 'Everything that has a beginning has an end.'
Today's edition of the Palatka Daily News – Volume 139, No. 84 to be precise – is the last edition of the paper that will be printed in our building. Like many other newspapers around the country, the Daily News will be printed off-site. The change makes sense, given the nature of the journalism industry, advances in technology and difficulty in finding parts for a machine that was refurbished when it printed its first edition of the Daily News in 1986.
The logic is sound, but my sentimental nature has been dealt a massive blow. Actually, I'm surprised at how glum I have felt since learning the press would be shuttered. That well of emotions has only grown deeper as we've gotten closer to this day. I'm not going to pretend I know how the press works. I'm a believer in letting jobs be done by the people most qualified to do them. It's also wise to not tamper with a machine if it is too heavy, looks too complicated and, most importantly, is too expensive to fix.
The majority of my time spent in the pressroom involved me asking the press crew if they had all of the pages for the next day's edition. When I come to work every day, I walk directly to my desk or make a pit stop at the water cool, in both instances barely sparing a glimpse at that big hunk of metal. Knowing it was there, however, provided me comfort and a sense of stability that was apparently strong enough to make way for indifference. I guess you really don't know what you've got 'til it's gone.
This is a major shift, one that will be the genesis of many changes for the Daily News and her people. Our deadlines and scheduled printing schedule will change. Things will be hectic in this building for the first week – maybe even the first few weeks. Even more shocking still, I will have to abandon my night owl way of life to make sure the editorial side of the building meets its deadlines.
There is a more serious downside to losing the press. We will be losing the people who work in our pressroom and mailroom. These are great, talented people who have contributed more to this company than most people are aware. Just when I think I work late, reality slaps me in the face as I wave goodbye each night to our press and mail companions still hard at work.
On a personal note, I'm going to miss seeing those familiar faces most days of the week. There will be no passing conversations with Josh and Justin before and during the press process. Holly and I won't get to flap our gums about the goings on in the building or out in the community, and I won't get weekly updates about her grandson. The Christmas season won't be as merry because Petra won't be here to give me a chocolate-filled advent calendar.
Change is inevitable and often scary, but we must be prepared to meet it – whatever it may be. The employees of the Daily News will continue working our butts off covering a wide range of subject matter and events to ensure our readers are informed about their community. We won't cower and remain stagnant in the face of change; we will push forward.
So allow me this weekend to cope via sangria, 'Twisters' (plural) and sleep, my three biggest priorities today and Sunday. When I return to work Monday, it's business as usual, so to speak.
Thank you to our pressroom and mailroom crews. And to our press, thanks for the decades of service.
Alexa, resume Boyz II Men.

INVITATION TO BID
'BID FOR ROAD MILLING'
The Pomona Park Town Council requests sealed bids to fill potholes and low areas on Palm Ave with lime rock or millings and compact. Then, top with asphalt millings at a width of 12' (twelve feet) and a minimum depth of 3'' (three inches) and compact with a roller. The length of the road is approximately 350'. Road edges must be made true, with the addition of a 30' culvert under Cedar, and a 15' culvert under a driveway off Palm Ave. A swale constructed above the culvert on Cedar Street, to the upper culvert under the drive way on Palm Ave., then sod the constructed swale.
The bidder must provide proof of Worker's Compensation Insurance and General Liability Insurance and be licensed to work in Putnam County.
Bids must be written, signed, and sealed. Bids must be marked on the outside of the envelope: 'BID FOR ROAD MILLING.' An official seal will be placed by the Town Clerk's Office when received. Bids must be received by noon, August 8th, 2024, to be considered. LATE BIDS WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED. Bids can be hand-delivered to Town Hall at 1775 Hwy 17 South Pomona Park, FL, or mailed to Town Clerk, PO Box 518, Pomona Park, FL 32181. The Town Clerk will open bids at 1 pm August 8, 2024, open to the public. Bids will be presented at the next Town Council Meeting. The contract for this bid will be awarded to the lowest responsible and eligible bidder. The Town of Pomona Park reserves the right to reject any or all bids in the best interest of the Town.
For additional information, call the Public Works at 386-649-4902. If you would like more information, contact Bruce Wolfred, Public Works Superintendent. Additional information/site visit may be attained during working hours of 8 am-2 pm Monday through Friday with an appointment.

title: Backpacks, other school supplies to be given away
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Area groups are ready to help local residents kick start the new school year with backpack and school supply giveaways starting this weekend.
content:
Area groups are ready to help local residents kick start the new school year with backpack and school supply giveaways starting this weekend.
Lalita Thomas, the event coordinator of the Palatka Police Athletic League's Back to School Backpack, Food and Clothing Giveaway, and her group of volunteers are gearing up for Saturday's event from 11 a.m.–2 p.m. at Calvary Family Life Center, 1414 Bronson St. in Palatka.
'All the supplies are donated by organizations, or if we receive monetary donations, our organization purchases any of the items needed,' Thomas said.
She said she is pleased with the number of donations they have received, including the more than 900 backpacks in different colors and sizes donated from the businesses CertainTeed and Veritas Steel, Thomas said.
The giveaway is free for all children and will include free school supplies.
'The way the event works is that we ask organizations to host a table (and) provide one school supply and any other literature that would be beneficial to the community,' Thomas said.
She said she is happy to be a part of an event that turns out to be a big help to the community.
'I am overjoyed to be able not only to provide to the kids but to aid in assisting the parents' load on having to purchase the needed items for the youth,' she said.
Organizers are also planning to have community resources, social services league programs and education representatives on hand for those who attend.
Other people and groups are teaming up to host another event leading up to the start of school. Lakesha Session and her cousin, Marion Session, have been hosting Backpacks Full of Fun for 17 years.
'Since we first started, we have given out close to 10,000 backpacks,' Lakesha Session said.
Backpacks Full of Fun 2024 will be from 2–4 p.m. Aug. 10 at Jenkins Community Center, 1900 Napoleon St. in Palatka.
Creative Cuzinz and Run Your Race are partnering with the city of Palatka for the event, which will include a Fitness Fun Field Day from 1–6 p.m.
Highlights include free food, drinks, music and 'lots of family,' Lakesha Session said. 'This is open to everyone.'
The following is a list of area organizations offering back-to-school help for area students:
SATURDAY
– The Palatka Police Athletic League will have its annual Back to School Bash from 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. at Calvary Family Life Center, 1414 Bronson St. in Palatka.
The Back to School Backpack Giveaway is free for all children and will provide free school supplies for more than 500 children.
The event will also provide information on community resources, social services league programs and education.
Churches, businesses, nonprofits and other local groups are invited to join organizers in supporting this event by hosting a table and providing supplies and organizational information.
For details, contact event Coordinator Lalita Thomas at 386-546-0011 or Tobby Williams at 386-329-0115.
Donations of supplies are being accepted. Monetary donations can be mailed to the Palatka Police Athletic League, 110 N. 11th St., Palatka, FL 32177.
– Marilyn Baker and other volunteers are hosting the fourth annual Back to School Backpack Giveaway from 10 a.m. – noon while supplies last. The giveaway is for all students and will be at Williamson's Food Store parking lot, 840 N. State Road 21 in Melrose.
The giveaway will include 100 free backpacks filled with notebook paper, composition books, tablets, markers, erasers, colored pencils, crayons and other items. Students must be present and accompanied by an adult to receive free supplies.
There will also be free books given away, as well as hotdogs and drinks.
For details, call Baker at 352–214–0181.
TUESDAY
– Grace Fellowship, Church of the Heights and Hope FM are sponsoring their Edify Teacher Breakfast from 8:30–10:30 a.m. at Church of the Heights, 3111 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka.
Teachers are invited for a morning of food, fun, encouragement and free items as they prepare for the 2024–2025 school year.
Reservations are required in advance and can be done at bit.ly/pcsd-edify.
The first 275 teachers will receive a bag full of free supplies.
WEDNESDAY
– Ameris Bank's second annual Back to School event will be from 10 a.m. – 2 p.m. at the branch at 601 Reid St. in Palatka.
Donations are being accepted at that location and the branch at 100 N. State Road 19 in Palatka.
Each child present will receive supplies and a backpack while supplies last.
Aug. 10
– Faith Life Fellowship, 210 S. County Road 315 in Interlachen, will have its second annual Back 2 School Bash from 9 a.m.–1 p.m.
Highlights include the Rotary Mobile Dental Trailer, face painting, lunch, ice pops and a bounce house. E.W. Lawson & Sons Funeral Home will give out 100 backpacks.
Haircuts will be provided by Donna Revers from Twisted Sisters, Carlos Reyes from Redemption Cutz and Carmen Matos from Matos Salon/Barber Shop.
Wellness checks will be offered by Green Med Group.
– Backpacks Full of Fun 2024 will be from 2–4 p.m. at Jenkins Community Center, 1900 Napoleon St. in Palatka.
Creative Cuzinz and Run Your Race are partnering with the city of Palatka for the event.
Fitness Fun Field Day will be part of the event and take place from 1–6 p.m. Free food, drinks, music and lots of family fun will be available for everyone.
For details, call Marion Session at 386-336-5539, contact her on Facebook, or call Lakesha Session at 386-916-0809.
