title: Judge candidates cite experience among reasons to pick them
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible.
Three people are in the running to be elected to their first full term as a Putnam County judge in the Group 1 contest.
Judge Anne Marie Gennusa is fighting to stay in the position to which she was appointed, while challengers Constance Daniels and Alex Sharp are vying to unseat her.
The election could end on primary day if one of the candidates wins 50% of the vote and at least one additional vote. If not, the top two contestants will head to the general election.
Gennusa and Sharp answered questions posed by the Palatka Daily News about why they are qualified to be a Putnam County judge. Daniels did not respond to the Daily News by the deadline that was given to all candidates in the judge's race.
How will your background, legal or otherwise, shape how you carry out your duties as a judge?
Gennusa: I have 30 years of diverse legal experience including family, criminal, and juvenile delinquency. I have an extensive litigation background, including experience as an assistant state attorney, a criminal defense attorney, mediator, Guardian ad Litem, Teen Court Judge and Parenting Coordinator. I am admitted to practice law in Florida, New York, and the United States Supreme Court. I was an attorney for the National Police Defense Foundation, representing law enforcement officers accused of crimes. Together with my husband Bob, an army veteran and retired sergeant, we raised five children and have three grandchildren, with a fourth on the way.
Sharp: Growing up in Putnam, working and living here gives me a unique local experience of our community. Additionally, serving honorably in the military and later as a police officer gave me leadership skills, a strong work ethic, and a desire to help others. Later, I started and ran several successful small businesses, including a family-friendly restaurant. Finally, my legal experience as a former prosecutor and General Counsel with the Putnam County Sheriff's Office has allowed me to work closely with victims of crime, handle various legal issues, and understand a judge's role must always be fair and impartial.
What makes you qualified to be a judge in Putnam County?
Gennusa: Experience, transparency and community service. I am the only candidate with judicial experience. I have presided over 8,000 proceedings, hearings, and trials. I am assigned to criminal traffic, misdemeanor, juvenile delinquency, and truancy cases. I bring 30 years of legal experience to the position. I was appointed by the governor after a bi-partisan vetting process. Anyone is welcome to observe county court. I encourage the electorate to learn what a county judge does. I am also a member of the Woman's Pilot and Kiwanis clubs. Giving back to my community is important to me while serving in this position.
Sharp: I became an attorney in 2012. However, my 20 years of experience in our local court system as a law enforcement officer and prosecutor provide me with essential insight and knowledge. Having owned multiple successful small businesses here in Putnam, a family restaurant, numerous commercial properties, and a real estate office gives me a first-hand understanding of legal issues involving property disputes and managing staff. As a long-time resident, I also have personal knowledge of the problems we face as a community, and I believe all this, along with my diverse background, makes me your best choice for county judge.
What are some of your top priorities for serving on the bench if elected?
Gennusa: If I am fortunate to keep my position as county judge, I believe that maintaining efficiency due to the recent population growth, without sacrificing justice is critical. Searching for creative solutions for my increasing criminal and delinquency dockets including a specialized juvenile/adult domestic violence court, mental health court and a 'teen court' program. These initiatives would be a collaborative effort between court administration, the State Attorney, the Clerk of Court and our schools. I will continue to follow the law and ensure that anyone charged with a crime is brought before the court expeditiously. Justice delayed is justice denied.
Sharp: I believe those who work daily in the court system sometimes forget for many people, this is their first-ever courtroom appearance. People appearing in court can be nervous, scared, anxious, and angry. My primary role as a judge is to apply the law correctly. But I also understand the need to let the people who appear before me know the process. Communication to me is critical. My life experiences will allow me to communicate effectively while performing my judicial duties. As your best choice for local judge, I would never let my emotions influence or dictate my conduct in court.
What does being a county judge mean to you?
Gennusa: County court, or the 'people's court,' is usually the first interaction, whether criminal or civil, that a person has with the court. In addition to maintaining an efficient courtroom, judges are required to treat everyone fairly, follow the law, and not be influenced by race, gender, or community ties. I am thankful for the assistance of dedicated court clerks, my judicial assistant, the bailiffs, assistant state attorneys, and assistant public defenders that are always prepared. Their support is why I love being 'your' county judge. I will continue to serve Putnam County with fairness, experience, and transparency.
Sharp: For me, it is the culmination of a career dedicated to public service. Putnam County has been my family's home for approximately 50 years. I have always strived to make our community a better place to raise children, start a business, or live. A county judge's court is often described as the people's court. Because it is usually the first time anyone needs their court system. I believe despite any circumstances, the judge you appear before can determine whether that court experience is positive or negative. I would strive to make it a positive one as your local judge.

title: Candidates state plans for serving on school board
author: David Buckles
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible.
There are two Putnam County School Board races on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary.
Both races involve incumbents facing off against one challenger. Incumbent David Buckles will face off with Leon Edenfield for the District 2 school board race. Tim Houghtaling is challenging District 3 incumbent Sandra Gilyard.
Buckles, Edenfield, Gilyard and Houghtaling have answered questions asked by the Palatka Daily News ahead of the primary and their answers are below.
Q: Why do you believe yourself to be the best candidate for the position?
Buckles: I have the experience needed to serve our children and communities and understand the actions required to best meet their needs. The board exists to facilitate 'teaching and learning.' Policy and budget are the primary duties of board members. Serving three years as the chairman of the Florida School Labor Relations board provided me with insight needed to help our employees who directly impact the lives of our students. I have served our community in many roles (teacher, dean, assistant principal, principal, superintendent, etc…) and my community service, appointments, and recognition for educational improvement uniquely qualify my leadership ability.
Edenfield: My diverse professional experiences and successes far exceed my opponents. As an Educator, School Director, Preschool Administrator, Pastor, small business owner, retired A.F. Master (Sergeant), retired Administrator for the Department of Defense, and graduate of Liberty University, my whole life has been based around serving people. My professional managerial skills, knowledge, and responsible decision-making abilities from all levels, Federal to local, have established a proven record of success.
Gilyard: I feel I am the best candidate for this position because of my background/experience in the educational arena. I was a classroom teacher for 17 years, an assistant principal for 4 years, a principal for 13 years, and parent liaison for 2 years at the district level. I have served on the school board for 2 terms, acting as chairperson for 4 years.
In 2020, I became a certified board member through the Florida School Board Association. To achieve this distinction, I had to complete training sessions in curricular areas, school finance, policy governance, and personnel and bargaining issues.
Houghtaling: The incumbent is rightfully proud of her long career in education. Times and needs change. My undergrad and practical experience in industrial technology combined with over thirty years of enforcing State, City and Immigration laws with a healthy dose of HR tasks with employment arbitrations comprise tools most useful to the challenges of our District today - a proactive Board protective of our taxpayers now suffering from tax abuse. Truth is my standard, nothing else.
I am proud to report endorsements by the Putnam County Professional Firefighters Local 3529, the Greater Melrose Republican Liberty Caucus and the Republican Executive Committee.
Q: What three things would you improve or change about the school board?
Buckles: There's always room for improvement. More focus should be placed on making data-driven decisions to assess, identify and enhance learning outcomes for students. We also need to be more transparent and improve communication between the board, parents, students, teachers, administrators, etc. Board policies constantly need to be adjusted to better meet the needs of our students and teachers. Florida Law outlines the specific duties and responsibilities of a school board member. My experience having served as a superintendent and a board member enables me to understand how to build unity and provide support to benefit our students, employees, and county.
Edenfield: Improve school quality by addressing the issues of disrespect, classroom chaos, and campus violence our faculty, staff, and students are subjected to daily. As a school Director, I have various proven measures I initiated in my school, that instilled respect for authority, brought classroom chaos under control, and made violence a rare occurrence. Also, I learned by banning students from having their cell phones during academic hours made a positive change in classroom behavior, attention spans, academic participation, and increased test scores. I will introduce my plans and pathways to instill discipline back into our schools.
Gilyard: The first thing I would change would be our meeting times. I would set a time that would allow our teachers and staff to attend meetings without leaving their school sites early. This would truly be beneficial to the west and south ends of the county.
The second change would be the time allotted for the 'public to comment' on topics of concern. Public Comments would be more appropriately moved to the end of the board's business section.
Another change I recently addressed is currently being implemented. Our employees that retire are now being recognized at our board meetings.
Houghtaling: Change comes slowly to huge organizations, more so when it takes three votes to make change. A unified Board will direct change. A most pragmatic change will be creation of an Office of Inspector or Auditor General. They are charged with identifying 'best practices' then an in depth review of current practices followed by recommendations for improvement. The District will reap the benefits, moving out of the doldrums as reported by the Florida Department of Education! I look forward to learning how five part time School Board positions, without support staff, require $719,768.62 set aside for FY25-26.
Q: How do you feel about the way the general obligation bond was presented versus how it's being implemented?
Buckles: I briefed the board and Superintendent on my experience as a young administrator and how difficult the previous bond issue was in the early 1980s. It was extremely turbulent and resulted in numerous contentious school board meetings and the formation of a 'taxpayers league' to combat what was viewed as 'frivolous' expenditures, social media has exponentially exacerbated these similar concerns. However, the superintendent and a unanimous board voted to send it to the ballot to let the voters of Putnam County decide. The ballot language was compiled and approved by bond attorneys to legally comply with state requirements.
Edenfield: I feel it was presented to instill a need that wasn't as critical as portrayed. Since economic times reached hyperinflation, and building material costs doubled, we can now seemingly renovate buildings once deemed beyond repair. The plan proposed and passed, cannot go on as planned. Moving forward, if not handled cautiously and wisely, we will have immense debt to repay and still not have schools in needed locations to accommodate future population growth. The lack of fortitude, poor judgment, and reckless funding obligations only proves we are overdue for change on the Board.
Gilyard: The bond issue has become a controversial topic in our county. The need for safe and functional facilities to effectively educate our students is a concern. It is my earnest belief that we have handled the bond well based on the circumstances we have had to deal. The money needed to reconstruct schools in our original Revitalization Plan had to be submitted well before it appeared on the 2022 ballot. We did not foresee the unprecedented inflation that occurred due to the COVID19. The district adjusted the Revitalization Plan to meet the needs of students with monies that were available.
Houghtaling: In public presentations, Schools executives spoke of having contracted with a highly qualified and experienced firm to 'guide us through the process' of funding destruction and construction. I am perplexed how such a firm failed to issue warnings that project costs based on 2021 had no basis in fact. Traffic impact studies after destruction, while awaiting proper zoning for a planned 1,000 student elementary school on a two lane road needing stormwater ditches did not leave opportunity for second thought. A $300 million dream costing more than $700 million was no secret.
Q: How would you better fund different programs and services within the Putnam County School District?
Buckles: School finance is extremely complex! Like all Florida school districts, we regularly have state auditors in our finance office. Most funding is earmarked for specific use and very restrictive. Grant writing for federal funds gives us latitude to target specific instructional needs. Title 1 designation (due to our number of students living below the poverty level) allows our grant writers the ability to hone in on potential opportunities to increase funding targeting literacy and many other instructional areas. Utilizing federal funds, our wonderful food service department worked hard to feed our eligible students throughout Putnam County all summer long.
Edenfield: I interpret the phrase 'better fund' to mean 'more wisely.' I would utilize the expertise of our Program/Service Managers as key advisors. As front-line managers, their input is paramount for reviewing and recommending areas of possible reductions, adjustments, and reallocations of funds, to streamline spending without compromising services or efficiency. I will focus on the issues causing students to leave public schools for the School Choice Program. When students leave public schools and enroll in nonpublic schools, their state funding leaves with them. The district immediately loses those operational funds. We must stop the exodus and loss of funds.
Gilyard: A program area in our system that I feel could benefit most from additional funding would be the mental health services offered. School mental health services are generally funded through various federal and state funds, and Medicaid. When these fund are divided between the 4,202 state schools getting a portion of 'the pie,' there isn't much left to work with. I would like to see the different agencies in our county working together, coordinating their efforts and resources. I would also like to see generated grants written specifically addressing mental health in our school district and county.
Houghtaling: My first focus will be on maintenance and construction operations. Public presentations were that no current school building was environmentally safe for students, that roof and HVAC issues plague old buildings. Upon awareness of a lack of money, some buildings were deemed habitable and salvageable. Other buildings, now without students, continue to be used and maintained. One or more of these 'stories' is a fib(s).

title: Districts 1 and 3 board contenders lay out plans for office, if elected
author: News Staff
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Image
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible. Other than that, no other editing was done to candidates' answers.
Four candidates are fighting to fill two Putnam County Board of Commissioners seats for which the current occupants are not seeking reelection.
Competing for the District 1 seat are Republicans J.R. Newbold III and Jeovanny Palencia, while Josh Alexander and Les Sims are contending for the District 3 position. The primary will be Aug. 20, but early voting has already started.
Most candidates have answered questions asked by the Palatka Daily News ahead of the primary and their answers are below. The Daily News contacted Jeovanny Palencia numerous times using the contact information on the Supervisor of Elections website but did not receive a response by the Aug. 2 deadline given to all candidates.
Q: Why do you believe yourself to be the best candidate for this position?
Newbold: I believe the 34 years of experience I've gained from managing a successful agricultural business and my 30 years of dedication to numerous community service organizations makes me the best candidate to represent District 1.
Alexander: I've dedicated my entire life to family and the citizens of Putnam County. Honesty, integrity and principled leadership have guided me throughout every chapter of my life and I'm excited to leverage those values while serving as your next District 3 County Commissioner.
Sims: My involvement on over 5 local boards has taught me how to maneuver through tough situations and has prepared me to serve at the highest levels.
Q: What are your top three priorities, if elected?
Newbold: A) Developing well designed Growth Management Strategy that embraces growth while preserving our rural look, feel, and lifestyle. B) Focus on bringing business / jobs to Putnam County. C) Looking at issues through a 'quality of life lens.' Making improvements with many 'smaller issues' that truly improve the quality of life of our residents can make a huge improvement to the look, feel and pride in our community. (Parks & Rec, Library System, Building and Zoning, Codes Enforcement, Animal Services, Historic preservation, etc.)
Alexander: Sensible growth without compromising our character. Growth is here and we must make some difficult decisions now to ensure we're the ones deciding what we want our community to look and feel like in the future. We can solidify our tax base without compromising our quality of life. Unwavering support of our first responders, educators and working-class. Our community has an attainable housing gap with those who protect our safety, save lives and educate our youth. My passion for ensuring Putnam County's best and brightest have more opportunities to shine than ever in our hometown is second to none.
Sims: 1) Growth management. Start with a heavy involvement in amending the current land development code. 2) Creating sustainable infrastructure. 3) Lowering taxes.
Q: Where do you believe the Putnam County Board of Commissioners needs to improve?
Newbold: Strategic thought and a focus on relationships with State and Federal counterparts. We need to strengthen the relationships with our partners in Tallahassee and Washington DC. The infrastructure improvements and services necessary to effectively cope with the expected growth in our community will require extensive help from our State and Federal partners. Strategic Planning will be a must. Boards / Commissions can get mired down looking 'backwards' at past performance and lean towards micromanagement. We must focus on effective planning for the future.
Alexander: Strategic planning and supporting staff. When county commissioners are involved in day-to-day operations not only are they not focused on the long-term success of our community, they are also paralyzing the wonderful, hard working employees who have a passion for Putnam no differently than you and I. We must ensure decision rights are delegated to the appropriate levels in the organization and that typically means the subject matter experts. I will ensure they're empowered to do exactly that and are incentivized for the additional value they create along the way.
Sims: 1) The commission needs improve on communicating their actions to the public. 2) Create a program where they community can watch & interact with the commission meetings while at work or home. Other Counties have live interaction programs to allow counties to address commissions without attending meetings.
Q: What's the best way to accommodate growth in Putnam County while also retaining the rural Florida environment this county loves?
Newbold: Updates to our Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code will be crucial in this effort. Keeping dense residential growth in the proper places while encouraging our rural look and feel throughout the county. We should leverage and upsell our abundance of waterways and woodlands, promoting outdoor based activities and businesses; camping, cycling, boating of all kinds, hunting, ecotourism, etc.
Alexander: The rural charm of Putnam County is what brought my grandparents, Jim and Kitty Holt, to Putnam County in the 1950's. We must first understand and value who we are if we intend to protect the character of our community as we grow. My greatest childhood memories were made rowing down the Oklawaha River.
Ensuring our future generations have the same opportunities, and more, can be accomplished while facilitating high quality growth that improves our tax base while lightening the heavy load being placed on the Putnam County natives. These two qualities are NOT mutually exclusive.
Sims: Amend the land development code to protect our current citizens' property rights while also designating amendments for future growth in both residential and commercial/industrial markets. Attracting commercial/industrial tax base's we will lessen the burden to our citizens.
Q: Budget season is here. What is the most important change to the budget you believe needs to be made?
Newbold: Our county budget is a complex fiscal tool. We as commissioners must have a thorough understanding of its component parts and how it's crafted. Much of the budget is fixed and discretionary funds are limited. Better education for commissioners will enable us to make the best use of limited funds.
Alexander: Simply put – ensuring we're constantly working to accomplish more with less. Our budgets are not keeping up with inflation over the last three years. I take great pride in my ability to stretch a dollar as far as anyone as that's how my family has gotten by my entire life. Oftentimes simply a fresh set of eyes brings a valuable, new perspective. I bring that to the commission and will not be more of the same when I serve District Three.
Sims: The biggest change in my opinion is investing and revising for efficiency. With the current labor market, we need to look to subcontract every service we possibly can to private industry.
Q: Commissioners are the face of Putnam County but it's often commissioners' employees that do the heavy lifting behind the scenes. Where do you stand on how much the county should be paying employees?
Newbold: Human Capital is an area we must pay close attention to. If we are to keep the best talent, we should be meeting the market salary wise. The county has made progress in this area of late, we must continue the focus on developing and retaining a first-class workforce.
Alexander: Some of the best in their businesses work for Putnam County and those folks deserve to be competitively compensated for the value they create. They make it happen and deserve all the credit. Commissioners looking to get their pictures in the paper are not serving selflessly. I've always been told I have a great face for radio, anyway, so I know I'm best served as resource behind the scenes in that regard.
Sims: Our staff should be compensated according to skill level and seniority similar to private industry. The commission should strive to create programs that reward efficiency which will save the citizens tax dollars.

title: Palatka High, school district mourning death of student
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A Palatka Junior-Senior High School student-athlete died during the night, but details surrounding his death have not been made public.
content:
Body
A Palatka Junior-Senior High School student-athlete died during the night, but details surrounding his death have not been made public.
The student, whose name had not been released by 1 p.m., died at home, authorities confirmed Tuesday morning. His age and grade are also not being released, according to the school district.
'The Palatka Junior-Senior High School community and Putnam County School District are deeply saddened by the recent passing of a student,' Superintendent Rick Surrency said in the press release.
The district did not confirm if the student was on a Palatka High athletic team. However, community members have commented on or shared a Daily News Facebook post about the child's death and said he was a member of the Palatka High football team.
Sheriff Gator DeLoach also referred to the student as a teammate.
"There are not words to express the sorrow we feel for the family, friends, classmates, staff of Palatka Junior-Senior High and teammates of the student who died unexpectedly this morning,' DeLoach said in a Facebook post Tuesday afternoon. 'As parents our hearts break for his parents. As the agency charged with the safety of our schools, our concern is now turned to the well-being of this student's family and the students, faculty and staff of PJSHS.'
Although details surrounding the child's death haven't been made public as of 1 p.m. Tuesday, community members said via Facebook that the student who passed away had been experiencing chest pains following football practice Monday afternoon.
District officials confirmed the student's passing in a press release Tuesday morning and said they are offering grief counseling to students and staff.
Ashley McCool, the district's director of community relations, said school personnel and other district officials are working with the Palatka Police Department, which is responsible for investigating the case, to inquire if the student was having health issues at school leading up to his passing.
'We extend our heartfelt condolences to the family and friends affected by this tragedy,' Surrency stated. 'As they cope with this profound loss, we respectfully ask for privacy and understanding for the family during this difficult time.
McCool said all events and activities districtwide are canceled today.

title: River center playing host to Reggae Night
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Peace, love and unity are the messages DJ Fast Eddie hopes to bring to Palatka during Reggae Night at the St. Johns River Center rooftop in Palatka.
content:
Peace, love and unity are the messages DJ Fast Eddie hopes to bring to Palatka during Reggae Night at the St. Johns River Center rooftop in Palatka.
The event will be from 6–9 p.m. Friday for ages 21 and older at the center, 102 N. First St. According to organizers, the event will give area residents a chance to jam to the rhythm of the Caribbean.
'We hope everyone will join us for a night of island music, good vibes, delicious food and drinks, Caribbean-style finger foods and food trucks,' said Jessica Cruz, a Palatka Community Affairs Department employee.
Tickets are $25. For details, call Cruz at 386-213-0948 or Courtney James at 386-916-5916.
Fast Eddie is Jacksonville resident Ed Kinney, who organizers say will delight event-goers with signature funky beats and a toe-tapping mix of music.
'I want to share my joy and passion for music while pouring my heart and soul into curating a dynamic and soulful blend of tracks that are sure to get your feet moving and lift spirits with a tapestry of soulful, funky sounds that will immerse guests in the groove,' he said.
According to Cruz, Kinney was voted 'Best of Jax Djs' in Jacksonville Magazine.
'We hope to create two themed social events each month,' she said. 'We want to get the community out and engaging with family, friends and neighbors.'
According to a news release, Fast Eddie, a one-man show, has been playing in festivals throughout Florida and Georgia.
'I'm looking forward to coming to Palatka,' he said. 'I believe reggae music is uplifting, has an iconic rhythm and can convey messages from the heart. It is going to be a blast pumping out the beats.'
Cruz agrees.
'Reggae music has a profound impact on global music culture and we are hoping for that positive impact locally,' she said. 'From its roots in the 1960s to its current status as a global phenomenon, reggae has been a powerful force for social change and cultural expression. It's powerful, and the vibes are always amazing.'

title: Former educator, superintendent to remain on school board
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A Putnam County School Board member surged to victory in Tuesday's primary and is looking ahead to another four years on the governmental body.
content:
A Putnam County School Board member surged to victory in Tuesday's primary and is looking ahead to another four years on the governmental body.
District 2 incumbent David Buckles received 8,923 votes (67.83%) to beat challenger Leon Edenfield, who landed 4,231 votes (32.17%) Tuesday in the primary, according to unofficial results from the Supervisor of Elections Office.
With the primary secured, Buckles said he wants to continue the work the school board and Putnam County School District are doing to provide kids with new opportunities. One thing he touched on was keeping the momentum going in building new schools in the district.
'We've got to continue this buildings project to try to get the buildings underway and the kids in them as soon as possible to meet the newer safety requirements of the state of Florida and to give them more appropriate facilities,' he said.
The primary data will be made official Aug. 27, according to Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III.
The Putnam County Canvassing Board will meet at 4:30 p.m. Thursday to review the nine provisional ballots the Elections Office reported in this year's primary.
Voters whose ballots are in question have until 5 p.m. Thursday to provide proof of identification to the Elections Office.
Buckles spent Tuesday celebrating his win at Corky Bell's in East Palatka alongside Superintendent Rick Surrency, who won his primary contest and will face a write-in candidate during the Nov. 5 general election.
Buckles has served as a teacher, assistant principal, principal and superintendent before being appointed to the school board in 2013 and winning his first school board election in 2014.
Working in education runs in the family, Buckles said. He said his mother was a teacher, his two sisters became teachers and he has two granddaughters who are in college to be teachers.
'We've got to do the best we can to keep our kids safe, figure out ways to better serve their educational needs and to realize that we're here because it's about teaching and learning,' Buckles said. 'Everything else that we do has to focus on that, whether it's keeping them safe, providing facilities or feeding them lunch.'

title: Veteran employee victorious in tax collector's race
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: A woman with 12 years of experience at the Putnam County Tax Collector's Office was chosen in Tuesday's primary to lead the agency.
content:
A woman with 12 years of experience at the Putnam County Tax Collector's Office was chosen in Tuesday's primary to lead the agency.
The unofficial results show Brenda Bridges to have won the tax collector's race with 6,803 (52.54%) votes, beating Brittany Goodson, who won 3,355 (25.91%) votes, and Sydney Myers, who received 2,789 (21.54%) votes.
Bridges, who was hired at the Tax Collector's Office in 2012 and became the deputy tax collector within two years of being hired, chalked up her victory to people wanting the office to continue operating as it is now. She mentioned her partnership with outgoing Tax Collector Linda Myers and how customers can expect the same level of service the two have been providing.
'I think the biggest thing is people want consistency,' Bridges said. 'I'm happy that that's what the voters are looking at. I am pleased to carry on this legacy.'
Another factor Bridges believes pushed her past the finish line was her experience as a private business owner. People who show up to the Tax Collector's Office want it to run smoothly, said Bridges, who believes her customer service skills from running a business and working for the county will ensure continued efficiency.
Bridges credited Linda Myers with appointing her to be the deputy tax collector and teaching her the tools to do the job. Although Linda Myers doesn't step down until January, Bridges said it will be bittersweet to see her go.
Linda Myers, who previously served as a county commissioner and has been the tax collector since January 2013, has more than earned her retirement from public life and all the rest and relaxation that comes with it, Bridges said.
'Having worked with her so long … she has served Putnam County well,' Bridges said. 'This is a long-deserved different chapter for her.'
Other candidates in Tuesday's primary must compete in runoff competitions in the Nov. 5 general election but not Bridges.
Because only Republicans qualified to run for tax collector, Tuesday's contest was a universal primary and Bridges is the presumptive winner. The results will be made official Aug. 27, Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III said Tuesday night.
Bridges and other constitutional officers will be sworn in to office in January. In the months leading up to taking office, Bridges said she wants to assure Putnam residents and her co-workers that the agency is still an 'office of public trust.'
'The immediate thing is making sure the public and the staff know it's business as normal,' Bridges said.

title: 2-year-old found dead in Satsuma waterway
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The search for a missing child ended Tuesday after two hours when his body was discovered in a canal near his home, authorities said.
content:
The search for a missing child ended Tuesday after two hours when his body was discovered in a canal near his home, authorities said.
Gabriel Paguio, 2, was located around 5:30 p.m. Tuesday after going missing from his Clearwater Road home shortly after 3 p.m., Putnam County Sheriff's Office spokeswoman Allison Waters-Merritt said.
She said he would have turned 3 on Dec. 8.
Paguio is believed to have had special needs, Waters-Merritt said. His family had been looking into getting an official diagnosis but had not yet received it, she said.
Paguio's family had been searching for the child for about 20 minutes before they called 911 around 3:30 p.m., the spokeswoman said.
The sheriff's office's marine unit, K-9s and dive team were dispatched to search for the child.
'At this time, we ask for you to say a prayer for the family,' Sheriff Gator DeLoach said Tuesday in a Facebook statement. 'No family should undergo the tragedy of losing their child, and we ask for comfort from our community to support them as they navigate the difficult journey ahead.'
Authorities are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the boy's death.
Paguio is the second child with special needs to be found dead in a body of water this year. Mason Newstead, 4, was found under a dock near his Front Street home in Welaka in March and was determined to have accidentally drowned, the Daily News reported.
Newstead was nonverbal and diagnosed as having autism. While sheriff's office deputies are trained to work with people who are nonverbal or have been diagnosed with mental illnesses, caregivers can go a step further and complete a scent kit.
People will receive a boxed kit that includes gloves, a glass jar, gauze, tamper-proof tape, an identification label, instructions to secure the scent and a computer flash drive.
The sheriff's office's K-9 unit is trained to use the scent kit to track the person associated with the smell. The kit can retain a person's scent for 10 years, the Daily News reported in 2021.
To request a scent kit, call the sheriff's office's victim's assistance program at 386-329-1282.

title: Satsuma community gathers to grieve child
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: SATSUMA – Neighbors and friends held candles and sang earlier this week to honor a local child whose body was found earlier this week near his Clearwater Road home.
content:
Body
SATSUMA – Neighbors and friends held candles and sang earlier this week to honor a local child whose body was found earlier this week near his Clearwater Road home.
A thunderstorm held off just long enough for residents to partake in a vigil for Gabriel Paguio, 2, who went missing from his home Tuesday.
Putnam County Sheriff's Office deputies found the child dead in a canal near his residence after searching for two hours.
Paguio's grandmother, Samantha Corson, said she and her family had only lived in the area for a few years, but she received help from everyone around her when Paguio went missing.
'When I tell you that everybody from Dollar General back was out in full force yesterday while we were searching, that was not a lie,' Corson said Wednesday evening. 'The streets were flooded with people.'
Paugio's family had searched for him for 20 minutes with no luck before calling authorities around 3:30 p.m. Tuesday, sheriff's office spokeswoman Allison Waters-Merritt said.
The sheriff's office's marine unit, K-9 deputies and dive team took to the canal behind the Paguio family's home to look for the child, who would have turned 3 on Dec. 8, before finding his body.
The people who organized the vigil didn't know the family but wanted to lift up the family in prayer.
'I just appreciate everything you all have done,' Corson told the crowd of about 30 people. 'People I didn't even know reached out that I would now call friends.'
Corson said deputies found him in the water directly behind her home.
'A lot of this was the devil,' Corson said about her grandson's death. 'He's going to target (children) because they're new and they're fresh. And Gabriel did not deserve this.'
After praying aloud to help the family grieve, the crowd began singing 'Amazing Grace' and comforted the family.
Welaka Councilwoman Kathy Washington attended the vigil to support Paguio's mother, who recently started leading the women's Bible study three weeks ago at Dunns Creek Community Church.
'I feel like there's a place and time that God has us all together beforehand,' Washington said.
Paguio is the second child to be found dead this year in Putnam County in a body of water. Washington said Paguio's death stirred up memories of Mason Newstead, 4, who went missing from his Welaka home March 21 and was found dead nearby in the St. Johns River that same day.
Newstead had been diagnosed with autism, and although Paguio hadn't been diagnosed with any ailment, authorities said he had special needs.
'I was shocked, just shocked and, you know, hurt,' Washington said. 'My heart goes out to (Paguio's mother) and the family because you know we just lost someone in Welaka.'

title: Q.I. Roberts mourning beloved science teacher
author: Carter Mudgett
description: Colleagues and former students are looking back fondly on a longtime high school science teacher who died earlier this month.
content:
Colleagues and former students are looking back fondly on a longtime high school science teacher who died earlier this month.
Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School teacher Richard Brown died Aug. 15 after a year-long battle with colon cancer, according to his sister, Martha Brown.
The oldest of five children, he had a life-long love of teaching, his sister said.
'We used to joke because when he was at least 5 or 6, he could frequently be found reading the Encyclopedia Britannica,' Martha Brown said.
Ric Brown stayed in contact with all his siblings, she said, and loved traveling and all forms of music. As a kid and even into adulthood, Ric Brown sang in choirs, played piano and played French horn as a freshman at Auburn University.
At Q.I. Roberts, he was the science department chair and taught marine science and environmental science, Principal Joe Theobold said. He'd been teaching at the high school for nine years.
'As a person, he was cut from a different mold,' said Theobold, calling Ric Brown an old-style, 'no-nonsense' teacher who had high expectations for everybody around him, including students, teachers and friends.
Ric Brown was a 'legend' at Q.I. Roberts, the principal said.
Kendal Asbury took his science classes during her sophomore and junior years at the high school in the 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 academic years. Now a junior studying journalism at the University of Central Florida, Asbury described Ric Brown as especially dedicated to the craft of teaching.
'You could tell he wanted you to succeed,' she said.
Asbury told the Daily News she knew other students who took his courses and swapped their fields of study to match because they enjoyed their time with him so much.
That was a sentiment echoed by Theobold, who said Ric Brown was a sought-after teacher.
Ric Brown had planned on teaching an extension course this academic year for seniors who had taken one of his classes last year as juniors because they enjoyed it so much, Theobold explained.
Beyond teaching, Ric Brown was the adviser for Q.I. Roberts' Interact Club, of which Asbury was a member for several years when she attended the school.
Working closely with the Rotary Club of Palatka Sunrise, Interact students have the opportunity to volunteer and host events to give back to the community that has nurtured them.
Theobold said a quarter of Q.I. Roberts students are in Interact Club, an achievement he credited to the late teacher.
Before Ric Brown passed away, his sister said, his siblings were wondering how to best honor his memory. Since he wanted to be cremated and there wouldn't be a headstone for anyone to visit, they settled on something that would give back to the community.
'We thought, 'What could we do to honor his memory?'' Martha Brown said. 'It was funny (because) we all came up with the same idea at the same time.'
The longtime science teacher's legacy will live on in the form of the Ric Brown Science Scholarship, the Putnam County School District announced last week.
The scholarship will go toward supporting up to two Q.I. Roberts students per year who will be pursuing studies in a science-related field, Martha Brown explained.
As Ric Brown battled cancer, one could find him secretly talking to medical students about their aspirations in the field and his cancer, she said.
'He was all about the kids and helping kids get on in life,' Martha Brown said. 'Especially those who didn't have the means to.'
She told the Daily News she hopes the scholarship will be self-funded 'for years to come.'
It was Ric Brown's passion that made him so well-liked at Q.I. Roberts for the nine years he taught there, Asbury said.
'He was very driven about conveying what he was teaching,' she said. 'He wasn't just a teacher, but a friend to all of us.'

The Putnam County Board of County Commissioners is requesting sealed bids from General and Building Contractors for the renovations, remodel, and addition of SMA Healthcare located at 330 Kay Larkin Drive, Palatka, Florida 32177.
Base Bid:
The Scope of Work for Building 2 will reconfigure two of the five bathrooms into storage rooms while the remaining bathrooms will receive ADA updates. In five of the patient's rooms, closet doors will be removed, and new shelving will be installed. The majority of the building will receive modernized LVT flooring and vinyl base. The kitchen will be upgraded with new base cabinets and countertops. In the dispensary office, lockable cabinets will be added along with a passthrough door for dispensing medication. At the nurse's station, an existing window and door will be removed. Both front and back porches will be updated. Gypsum wallboard will be provided on the front screened porch, and the back porch will be reroofed and receive upgrades of new flooring, drywall/insulation, painting, and baseboards.
New fencing for the back portion of the campus is also integrated into the scope of work. The top two priorities of this proposal include repairs of the fire sprinkler system, south building (half has previously been repaired), and replacement of the outdated and inefficient 5 HVAC units with 5-ton units, south building.

title: Editorial: It's about time
description: 'You don't need a smug 'I told you so' from me. And smug it would be because tell you so I most certainly did.' – Mallory Archer
content:
'You don't need a smug 'I told you so' from me. And smug it would be because tell you so I most certainly did.'
There are certain occurrences we all know are bound to happen. The sun will rise in the east and set in the west. It will be humid in Florida after it rains. Every new year begins Jan 1.
Another event that seemed destined to occur was the firing of Palatka City Manager Troy Bell, which happened as Thursday's Palatka City Commission meeting neared midnight. The only thing mildly surprising about his firing is that it finally happened after repeated flagrant behavior during his short time in the position.
Despite a seemingly bottomless well of news stories detailing Bell's short, sometimes contentious stints as city manager – sometimes interim, sometimes in the full-time position – city commissioners selected Bell to lead the city. Bell, who had made it to the final three in the city manager search a year earlier, was chosen in late January using an easy-to-fudge point system rather than having commissioners motion, second the motion and vote on that motion.
Since his contract, some of the negotiations for which were conducted at a public meeting, was approved in February, Bell's minuscule tenure as city manager has been a display of fecal proportions.
In February, Bell had the GPS monitor in his city-owned vehicle removed without getting permission from the mayor and four city commissioners, all of whom are his bosses. Fast forward to late June and the week of July 4, Bell took it upon himself to take off six days to go home to Michigan without commissioners' approval, coming not long after elected leaders had admonished him for taking off so much time in such a short time. Seemingly intoxicated on power, he rebuked City Attorney Jane West for speaking while at her assigned seat, like she had done since she started working for the city, instead of standing behind the lectern.
Throughout this time, Palatka lost its planning and public works directors, project managers and other employees. One of the biggest blows was last month's resignation of Jonathan Griffith, the 14-year employee who had most recently served as the assistant city manager with a stint as interim city manager until Bell was hired. Whether publicly stated or confidentially told to Daily News staff, some of these resignations were because of the hostile work environment Bell allegedly fostered in City Hall.
Bell's firing comes near the end of a week when the public and commissioners learned he'd approved a $50,000 check be made out to RQ Music LLC to organize next year's Blue Crab Festival. He approved the action Aug. 30 despite West and Finance Director Marcia Carty, who has been named the new interim city manager, advising him against doing so because the city manager is allowed to spend no more than $25,000 on a single item without the approval of the city commission.
Whether to cover his tracks or just to remain spiteful to a media organization to which he refused to speak directly, he disregarded Florida law by not fulfilling public records requests the Daily News made to obtain a copy of the check and copies of emails regarding the check.
A finger must be pointed at the Palatka City Commission – three members of which refused to answer our questions in February about why they chose a man with such a sketchy past – for taking so long to see what many people, even the most near-sighted among us, saw before Bell got the job. Their refusal to fire Bell when it was clear he had no regard for anyone else's opinion or authority was shameful. All of them, not just one or two, should have had confidential conversations with city employees to hear how miserable their working conditions had become.
When one of your employees bursts into tears of joy in full view of the public shortly after her superior is fired, that should be an indicator something had been – to borrow from Billy Shakespeare – rotten in the state of Denmark.
As we move forward, we hope the city will regain stable footing. The city manager search should be transparent, and the vote to approve the next pick should be done by a majority-rules vote. The city needs stability in its leadership, so why not provide it?
We just hope qualified candidates won't be scared off when they read up on our city government and learn about the seven-month mess that was inflicted on us.

title: Authorities on alert after 2 men injured in shooting
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Two men sustained trauma-related injuries during a shooting Monday in Palatka.
content:
Image
Body
Two men sustained trauma-related injuries during a shooting Monday in Palatka.
The shooting occurred around 12:45 p.m. along Reid Street between 19th Street and Moseley Avenue, said Matt Newcomb, the assistant chief of the Palatka Police Department.
'One was shot in the upper torso, and one was shot in either the head or the neck,' Newcomb said at 1:36 p.m. 'We're not sure.'
Traffic is being diverted for people heading west from 19th Street onto Reid Street. The police department and Putnam County Sheriff's Office have set up caution tape between 19th and Moseley.
Newcomb said someone drove one of the victims to HCA Florida Putnam Hospital in Palatka, and rescue personnel took the other victim to the hospital.
There were reports of the hospital being on lockdown, but hospital officials had not verified that claim by the time of this reporting.
Both victims are being transported to trauma centers outside of Putnam County, he said.
'We'll do a press release as soon as we can get everything under control,' Newcomb said.
Editor Brandon Oliver contributed to this story.

title: Preparing for the worst
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Local government leaders urged residents Tuesday to take heed of Hurricane Milton as they prepared for the storm to strike.
content:
Body
Local government leaders urged residents Tuesday to take heed of Hurricane Milton as they prepared for the storm to strike.
County Commissioners declared a state of emergency, and officials advised residents who live in flood-prone areas to evacuate out of caution. Hurricane Milton dropped briefly to a Category 4 storm today but reached Category 5 again by 5 p.m.
People need to take Milton seriously, Deputy County Administrator J.R. Grimes advised Monday when the Putnam County Board of Commissioners called a special meeting to declare the state of emergency.
'We do want to make sure people understand we do have to prepare for a worst-case scenario,' Grimes said. 'And the worst case scenario on this one is 10 to 15 inches of rain during the storm.'
Officials from the county's Emergency Operations Center in Palatka advised people who lived in evacuation Zone A, which is near Possum Bluff in Satsuma, and Zone F, which consists of areas along the St. Johns River in Welaka, to leave Monday.
Evacuations were not mandatory, but County Commissioner Terry Turner said people who know their homes are prone to flooding should get out while they can.
'I'm gonna just say it,' he said Monday. 'If you live in Dunns Creek, if you live in Sportsman's Harbor, if you live at Federal Point, get the hell out. I mean, it's going to get bad. The river's going to back up. It's already rising.'
Putnam schools closed today and were set to stay closed through Thursday. A decision had not been made about whether to reopen schools Friday.
St. Johns River State College will be closed through Friday.
The Putnam County Sheriff's Office's administrative offices closed at 3 p.m. today and will remain closed through Thursday. The Putnam County Courthouse will be closed Wednesday and Thursday.
Administrative offices in Crescent City are slated to remain closed at least through Thursday. Palatka administrative offices will stay closed until Monday.
Interlachen's administrative offices will close Wednesday and Thursday.
The town of Welaka will close its offices at 3 p.m. and all day Thursday.
However, the county and all municipalities will still have law enforcement, emergency operations, public works, water, gas and sewer operations ongoing.
The following schools will be opening as shelters at 6 p.m. today:
– Ochwilla Elementary School, a pet-friendly facility, 299 N. State Road 21 in Hawthorne.
– Kelley Smith Elementary School, a shelter for people with special needs, 141 Kelly Smith School Road in Palatka.
– Robert H. Jenkins Jr. Elementary School, 251 S. State Road 315 in Interlachen.
– Middleton-Burney Elementary School, 1020 Huntington Road in Crescent City.
– Browning-Pearce Elementary School, 100 Bear Blvd. in San Mateo.
'If you feel like you're in an unpredictable structure, please utilize our shelters,' Grimes said Monday. 'Please let us take care of you. We'd rather take care of you pre-storm than what we would after the storm or during.'
People who need transportation to the Kelley Smith shelter should call Stacie Branam from the Florida Department of Health in Putnam County at 386-937-3563 until 6 p.m. today. After 6 p.m., call the Emergency Operations Center at 386-329-1904.
Grimes said that by Tuesday morning, call center operators had 10 people registered to stay at the Kelley Smith shelter, but none of them needed transportation.
Officials urged people to do whatever they needed by Tuesday night to prepare for the hurricane. An update from the Emergency Operations Center at 2 p.m. today stated residents can expect the storm to begin overnight.
Welaka, especially the area of Sportsman's Harbor, is known to flood during many rain storms and hurricanes.
The town is offering temporary storage at Jefferson Smith Park, which is located at the corner of County Road 308B and Palmetto Street, for residents who plan to evacuate, Mayor Jamie Watts said in a Facebook post Tuesday.
'The situation is critical, and the town of Welaka is under direct threat from these hazardous conditions,' Watts said Tuesday in a Facebook post. 'The danger posed by storm surge flooding is severe and could cut off emergency services, trap residents in flooded areas, and result in catastrophic damage.'
Since Sunday, people have been taking advantage of sandbag sites to secure their homes. The following sandbag sites are open:
– 145 W. Washington St. in Hawthorne.
– 51 Sportsmans Drive in Welaka.
– 223 Putnam County Blvd. in East Palatka.
– 341 Paradise Circle in San Mateo.
– Jonas Road in Crescent City.
– 5226 Silver Lake Drive in Palatka.
– 107 Johns Road in Palatka.
– 114 S. 11th St. in Palatka.
– 100 Drayton Island Road in Georgetown.
– 126 Boat Ramp Road in Palatka.
– 300 Tremont St. in Interlachen.
The sites are self-serve, and people need to bring shovels, according to county officials.
WastePro will not be picking up trash for county customers on Wednesday, according to emergency management, and the county landfills will be closed that day.
Palatka sanitation employees will collect yard debris from curbsides until noon Wednesday, according to a city news release. Residential garbage collection will be suspended Thursday.
If the weather is clear, residential garbage collection in Palatka will resume Friday, with Thursday customers getting serviced that day and Friday customers having their trash picked up Saturday.
People who have any questions about the storm or how to prepare can call 386-329-1904.

title: Fall-themed events planned throughout area
description: Palatka Daily News As autumn continues, events will be taking place across the county and in neighboring areas.
content:
Body
As autumn continues, events will be taking place across the county and in neighboring areas.
Some events are Halloween festivities, while others are seasonal events that are not associated with the holiday.
Below is a listing of events planned throughout the area:
– Melrose Makes, a nonprofit organization, is organizing its Kids Halloween Costume Drive and is looking for new, gently used and pre-washed costumes in all sizes.
Costumes will be handed out for free from 3–5 p.m. Oct. 26 at Melrose Bay Park, 25500 Devonia St. The deadline to receive donated costumes is Oct. 24. For details, call Mandi at 407-621-1804.
– American Legion Post 293, 145 S. County Road 315 in Interlachen, has its pumpkin patch open to the community. Hours are from 11:30 a.m. – 7:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday, 11:30 a.m. – 8 p.m. Friday, 9 a.m. – 8 p.m. Saturday, noon – 7 p.m. Sunday and 9 a.m. – 8 p.m. Halloween.
Pumpkin patch events include Halloween movie night from 6–8 p.m. Friday, campfire/ghost stories from 6–8 p.m. Oct. 25, and haunted house and Trunk or Treat from 5:30–8 p.m. Halloween.
For details, email info@post293fl.org or call 386–684–0339.
– Trinity Global Methodist Church, 1400 Husson Ave. in Palatka, will have its 25th annual pumpkin patch through Oct. 31. Hours are from 9 a.m. – 7 p.m. Mondays through Saturdays and noon – 7 p.m. Sundays. Field trips are welcome. Storytime with Farmer Bob and Mrs. Pumpkin will be from 6:30–7 p.m. Oct. 23. The patch is available for families to take their fall photos with no purchase necessary. For details on scheduling a tour, call the church office at 386-325-5272.
– The 11th annual Fall Festival and Maze Dayz will be Fridays through Sundays through Nov. 3 at Cowart Ranch & Farms, 8185 W. U.S. 100 in Bunnell. Hours are from 5–10 p.m. Fridays, 10 a.m. – 9 p.m. Saturdays and 11 a.m. – 7 p.m. Sundays. Admission is $15 for ages 3 and older and free for kids 2 and younger. The event is hosted by Flagler Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram.
OCT. 25
–Berndt Ends BBQ will have a pumpkin painting event from 5–7:30 p.m. at 125 State Road 20 in Palatka. The pumpkins cost $5 each. Reservations for pumpkins can be made by calling 386-385-3164.
OCT. 26
– The Fall Wine Stroll in Palatka will be from 5–8:30 p.m. with check-in at the corner of Sixth Street and St. Johns Avenue from 5–630 p.m. Guests are invited to wear their favorite Halloween costume and taste a variety of wines, appetizers and hors d'oeuvres. Proceeds will benefit Revitalize Historic Palatka. Tickets cost $30 and are available at eventbrite.com under Palatka Fall Wine Stroll.
– Pak's Karate, 187 Carter Road in Palatka, will offer Trunk or Treat from 5–8 p.m. A food truck will be available for families to purchase meals. To make reservations to attend, call 386-546-1456. For information, visit palatkasbesttrunkortreat.com.
– Francis Baptist Church, 155 County Road 309-C in Palatka, will have its Fall Fest from 5–7 p.m. with inflatables, games, trunk or treat, food, hay rides, a pumpkin patch and more features. Everyone is invited.
– The Mad Monster Halloween Market will be from noon – 7 p.m. at the Putnam County Fairgrounds, 117 Yelvington Road in East Palatka. The market will include creepy crafts and eerie artists under the pavilion.
– Ravine Gardens State Park Spooktacular will be from 6–9 p.m. at 1600 Twigg St. in Palatka. Highlights include food trucks, trick-or-treating, a haunted walk, games and more. Tickets cost $5 per person, cash only. For details, call 386-329-3721.
OCT. 27
– St. James Independent Methodist Church, 400 Reid St. in Palatka, will host its fall festival from noon – 3 p.m. Highlights include games, food and a bounce house. Admission is free.
OCT. 29
– The Palatka Center for Rehabilitation and Healing, 110 Kay Larkin Drive, will host its Trunk or Treat Extravaganza from 4–6 p.m. Highlights include a car decorating contest, popcorn, drinks and prizes. Admission and parking are free.
OCT. 31
– Bethel Church, 119 N. County Road 315 in Interlachen, will host its 20th annual JoyFest from 5:30–8:30 p.m. Highlights include games, hayrides, candy, snow cones, popcorn, music, laser tag and more. This family-friendly event will include concessions at a minimal charge. No dogs or scary masks allowed.
– Beck's Halloween Trunk or Treat will be from 5–7 p.m. at 1601 Reid St. in Palatka.
– Boo on the Avenue will be from 3–5:30 p.m. along St. Johns Avenue. The event is for kids in costume from ages 1-12. Downtown businesses will hand out candy to trick-or-treaters. Children must be accompanied by an adult. The event is sponsored by Develop Palatka Inc. and Downtown Palatka Experiences.
NOV. 2
– The town of Interlachen's second annual Fall Festival will be from 10 a.m. – 3 p.m. at 311 Atlantic Ave. Vendors are invited to participate for $10; food trucks can participate for $20. Highlights include pet adoptions, food, sack races, a bike race, pumpkin bowling and decorating, and more. People can acquire vendor applications by visiting Interlachen-fl.gov/our-events/ or calling 386-684-3811.
– Interlachen's Fall Festival will include a pie contest. Entries should be delivered to the Town Council chambers, 311 Atlantic Ave., by 11:15 a.m. the day of the event. Judging will begin at 11:45 a.m. For details, call Joni Conner at 954-812-8735.
The first-place winner will receive $50, second will win $25 and third will get $15.

title: Commissioner, challenger compete for open seat
author: News Staff
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, answers that went over the limit were cut to be as close to 100 words as possible.
A South Putnam County official is embarking on a quest to serve a second term on the Crescent City Commission but has to fight off an opponent to do so.
Commissioner Cynthia Burton and challenger Christopher Coleman are competing for the Group 4 seat, despite Burton currently occupying the Group 3 seat. Coleman, who had previously been entered in the Group 3 race for the 2024 election cycle, filed to run for the Group 4 seat after Burton announced her candidacy in that race.
The Daily News emailed the same questionnaire to Burton and Coleman. Below, they state why they would be the best people to occupy the Group 4 commission seat:
Why did you decide to run for a seat on the Crescent City Commission?
Burton: I always watched my local government work and appreciated the dedication, hard work and time that was devoted to building communities. I wanted to be a part of that and after moving to Florida 23 years ago, and choosing Crescent City for retirement in 2017, I was given an opportunity to serve my community in that capacity. Having had the chance to advocate different ideas and causes to facilitate the revitalization, infrastructure and community improvements to enhance livability here in Crescent City, I feel I have made a difference and hope to continue the progress as Commissioner, Group 4.
Coleman: I am running for Crescent City Commissioner Group 4 because I love the people of Crescent City and I want to be their voice. I believe Crescent City citizens deserve a fair and honest government that puts them and their needs above special interests. As the next city commissioner, I will work with the city commission and residents to uphold Crescent City's values and affect positive change that reflects our cherished rural way of life.
What government experience do you have that would make you an ideal choice for the Crescent City Commission?
Burton: I have successfully served as Commissioner Group 3 for the past four years. We have brought Crescent City's future to the present by creating Main Street, Downtown Partnership, focused on CRA for revitalization, used ARPA funds to help obtain over 6 million dollars in grants to update our infrastructure and provided professional law enforcement at a substantial savings. The commission was able to cut our millage rate for the first time in 12 years. On a personal note, I continue to learn the State legislative process by taking classes offered through the League of Cities.
Coleman: I am not a politician. I am someone that has served our country proudly through my military background and I have served on the Crescent City Code Enforcement board since 2017. I look forward to working with the new city commission from day one to ensure stability within our city government and to make sure residents inside and outside Crescent City's city limits are heard and respected. As your next city commissioner, I will always stand for the pledge and prayer.
What do you believe the city commission's main priorities should be and why?
Burton: Priorities are to hire a city manager that will follow our current vision, ensure the work our water and sewer projects are completed and continue with infrastructure upgrades. Our city has only just started to bloom! With a new elementary school being built in the city and the high school being updated, new young families are expected in our area to take advantage of the updated technology and equipment a new school provides. The city must be ready for growth and must be managed effectively to maintain our history while progressing into the future.
Coleman: Citizens' safety, transparency and responsible growth. Crescent City has the highest property taxes in Putnam. We can achieve responsible growth by actually cutting back on taxes, not just rolling back the millage rate in an election year and then falsely claiming that taxes are lowered when they aren't. I believe we need to reduce our city utilities bill, as residents are being overcharged for the services provided without transparency. I believe we need to make it a priority to preserve our historic buildings and enhance citizens' safety by bringing back community policing.
Crescent City has seen its share of conflict, especially within the past few years. What would you do to bring stability to the city so it can function efficiently?
Burton: Stability is in the experience citizens elect to office, having leaders with well thought out decisions, consistent behavior and moderate temperament. The current commission has these qualities. We have worked very well the last four years to bring stability back into our government with efficiency of operation, transparency and citizen input. Everyone should respect the knowledge, experience and commitment it takes to be part of the commission. One can easily see the city's progress, in spite of the conflict being generated by people that enjoy disruption, using disinformation, badgering and defaming our officials to create division of some citizens.
Coleman: We can only achieve stability if we have respect and trust. Respect needs to be earned from our citizens, not demanded. We can earn that respect back by actually listening to our citizens, rather than doing the opposite of what the majority of residents have asked. We can gain trust by allowing citizens the ability to speak uninterrupted, without threatening to remove them from City Hall. Stability will come when we have financial transparency. I will work with the new commission from Day 1 to complete a full forensic audit of Crescent City's last four years to protect our citizens.

title: Superintendent clenches another 4 years in office
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The leader of the Putnam County School District, who won his reelection bid in a landslide, is looking forward to continuing his momentum as he looks toward a third term.
content:
Body
The leader of the Putnam County School District, who won his reelection bid in a landslide, is looking forward to continuing his momentum as he looks toward a third term.
Superintendent Rick Surrency beat write-in candidate Pat Wilson, winning 30,589 votes compared to her 1,546 votes, unofficial Elections Office results show.
'I want to continue moving the district forward,' Surrency said Tuesday. 'I think it's extremely important that we have continuity.'
He said the school district is making many changes, and while progress doesn't happen overnight, it will continue.
'We have a lot of things that are improving student achievement, and I want to continue improving that for the next four years,' Surrency said.
Not only is the district working to enhance student performance, but district officials remain diligent in working to upgrade Putnam schools, he said.
Surrency, who was first elected in 2016, won the August primary with 5,393 votes against challenger Paul Adamczyk, who serves as the District 5 member of the Board of County Commissioners. Adamczyk received 4,497 votes in August.
While Surrency celebrated in August alongside a crowd of people at Corky Bell's in East Palatka, he opted for a quiet night at home Tuesday as he waited for election results.
In August, incumbent David Buckles won his bid for reelection to the Putnam County School Board. Buckles received 8,923 votes in August to beat challenger Leon Edenfield, who earned 4,231 votes.
Board member Sandra Gilyard also won in August and, like Buckles, did not have to compete in the general election. She received 8,513 votes to beat Tim Houghtaling, who received 4,550 votes.
Putnam County had an 80.45% voter turnout in the general election. All results will be finalized Nov. 15, according to Elections Supervisor Charles Overturf III.

title: Tight judge's race ends in Gennusa victory
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: The incumbent in the circuit judge contest squeaked out a win Tuesday night in a nail-biter that ended with a margin of less than 1% between the two competitors.
content:
The incumbent in the circuit judge contest squeaked out a win Tuesday night in a nail-biter that ended with a margin of less than 1% between the two competitors.
Unofficial results show 7th Circuit Judge Anne Marie Gennusa walking away with 16,187 votes (50.35%) while attorney Alex Sharp earned 15,961 votes (49.65%), according to the Supervisor of Elections Office.
Had the margin between the two been less than half of a percent, a recount would have been required. After the results had been tallied, Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III said it was unlikely the 69 provisional ballots, which will be counted at Friday's Canvassing Board meeting, would be enough to necessitate a recount.
Gennusa, whom Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed to the bench in April 2023, said she was thrilled to serve a full six-year term as a judge.
'I really appreciate the people and the voters of Putnam County,' she said. 'I'm really grateful that God has given me another six years to serve.'
Gennusa's victory comes as she is embroiled in a different battle with the state Judicial Qualifications Committee, which released a notice last month accusing her of improper behavior in her capacity as a judge.
On Tuesday, however, Gennusa was more focused on her win and the term ahead of her. She attributed her victory to the friends she made while practicing law in Putnam County.
'They've all showed out (for me),' Gennusa said of her supporters.
Admitting defeat, Sharp expressed his gratitude to his wife, other family members and everyone else who supported him in his bid to be a circuit judge.
Despite the loss, Sharp said, he plans to continue his service to his community.
'I think the people of Putnam County made their decision,' he said. 'I respect that 100%. And I will continue to give back to my town and community the same way I did before – just won't be as a judge.'
Sharp commended Gennusa for her victory and had pleasant words for her and what is to come.
'I want to congratulate Judge Gennusa,' Sharp said. 'I wish her the best of luck going forward.'
Elections results are slated to be officials Nov. 15.
