title: Leading the Christmas celebrations
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Evangelist Patricia Milton has had her heart, soul and hands in her church's ministry for decades, and it's something the 83-year-old Palatka resident is proud to proclaim.
content:
Evangelist Patricia Milton has had her heart, soul and hands in her church's ministry for decades, and it's something the 83-year-old Palatka resident is proud to proclaim.
'I loved doing that work,' she said. 'I loved it.'
Because of her faithful work in the ministry and after working more than 28 years at City Hall in the Water Department, Milton is being recognized as the 113th Downtown Palatka Christmas Parade grand marshal.
This year's parade will begin at 7 p.m. Nov. 29 and proceed down St. Johns Avenue from Second Street to 11th Street.
Area clubs, organizations and businesses are invited to partake in the parade, which is sponsored by Develop Palatka Inc., Downtown Palatka Experiences and Visit Palatka.
Registration forms are available on Facebook under the event name or at Deputy's Attic, 623 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka. The theme is Christmas.
For details, call Sam Deputy, parade coordinator, at 386-983-4897.
According to Milton, her church and ministry work has always been an important part of her life.
She taught Sunday school for 45 years and worked in the church ministry at Calvary Missionary Baptist Church in Palatka since she was 30. She also was part of a prison ministry that dated back to 1992 when she would make regular trips to the Putnam County Jail when it stood on the Palatka riverfront and Walt Pellicer was the sheriff.
Milton and a friend started a street ministry, where they stood on North 19th Street in Palatka and shared the good news. The two would make trips twice a week to provide the prison ministry.
Milton relies on Bible scripture to keep her motivated, especially Matthew 25:35-36, which are words by which she tries to live: 'For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you invited me in, I needed clothes and you clothed me, I was sick and you looked after me, I was in prison and you came to visit me.'
Born and raised in Palatka, Milton is the oldest of five children and still lives on Madison Street in the area where she was raised.
Milton recalls feeling happy each time she participated in the jail ministry.
'It made me happy, helping those in need,' said the mother of four and grandmother of 11. 'My life was fulfilled when I did it.'
Having a minister's heart, Milton recalls God speaking to her when she saw a girl on the corner of 11th Street in Palatka one day.
'She couldn't walk and the Lord spoke to me and told me to go take that girl a meal,' she said. 'Come to find out, she had not had any food all day. She was very thankful.'
Milton recalls taking leftover food from funerals to hand out to those she came across on the streets of Palatka.
'I used to cook soup and carry it around to people,' she said.
Milton can't participate in her ministry work today like she once did, including being a caregiver to some local women. Despite that, Milton believes her work in different ministries has been well worth it.
'I don't do a whole lot of things now,' she said. 'Since I retired in January 2004, I started reading a lot, and I cook when I feel like it and take food to others.
'Because I worked at City Hall all those years, I came to know a lot of people. Sometimes I see people who I met and ministered to in jail, mostly women.'
Milton recalls one Mother's Day when she was at Corky Bell's in East Palatka when a woman who saw her came to where she was sitting and told her she had been drug-free for 15 years. Another woman saw her at Winn-Dixie and told her she had been clean for 20 years.
'My life has been complete and full by doing the things that I've done,' she said.
Milton said Palatka is the only town where she has lived, but she has made many trips across Putnam County ministering in 30 different churches.
'I've traveled to conventions in other towns many times spending my own money and vacation time doing it,' she said. 'I was so thankful for my mother and grandmother for the times they came to my home to care for my children so I could go.'
Milton said she has spent her life serving God, something that has made her extremely happy. She is also appreciative of being named this year's Palatka Christmas Parade grand marshal and hopes her life's testament will encourage others.
'Jesus is the real reason for the season,' she said. 'His birth, he came into the world to save people from their sins. That's reason enough to celebrate Christmas. What else is there? No one else can save us. We all need him.'
Deputy said he is looking forward to this year's parade and seeing the community come together in a holiday spirit to celebrate the season with family and friends.
'Everyone is invited to come forth and participate or to gather as family and friends and experience the season,' he said.

title: PDN offering cash to decoration contest winners
description: Putnam County residents who decorate their homes for the holidays this season will have the chance to win a total of $300.
content:
Body
Putnam County residents who decorate their homes for the holidays this season will have the chance to win a total of $300.
The Palatka Daily News is hosting its inaugural holiday decorations contest, where the paper's readers will decide the winner.
To compete in the contest, people must email up to two high-quality, in-focus pictures of their outdoor Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa decorations to boliver@palatkadailynews.com. All participants must also submit their first and last name, phone number and municipality of residence.
Three winners will be chosen, with first place receiving $150, second place winning $100 and third place getting $50. Each winner will also receive a plaque.
'Putnam County is no stranger to festive holiday decorations, so we decided to highlight that in the newspaper and offer a prize we knew everyone would love,' Editor Brandon D. Oliver said. 'In addition to those coveted plaques, we decided to offer a bit of cash, as well.'
Contestants have until 5 p.m. Dec. 9 to submit up to two pictures of their outdoor holiday decorations. Daily News employees will choose the 10 best pictures – no more than one per contestant – and publish those in the print edition, at palatkadailynews.com and on the Palatka Daily News' Facebook page on Dec. 11.
To have a better of making the top 10, submitted photos should be of high enough quality to be resized and reproduced.
After the top 10 photos are published, the outcome of the contest will be in the hands of the Daily News' readers. People can vote for their favorite photo via a poll on the Daily News' website or by giving a thumbs up or heart reaction on their favorite photo on Facebook.
Contest winners will be announced Dec. 24, and Daily News employees will reach out to the lucky three afterward.

title: Putnam County to spread Christmas cheer Saturday
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: People can Jingle Bell Rock their way around Putnam County as events are happening throughout the day to get the community in the holiday spirit.
content:
Body
People can Jingle Bell Rock their way around Putnam County as events are happening throughout the day to get the community in the holiday spirit.
In keeping with tradition, Crescent City and areas in West Putnam will host a variety of Christmas events the first Saturday of December. Meanwhile, a Palatka neighborhood will have music acts performed on different porches.
Below are some of the events that will be available to the public Saturday.
South Putnam
The festivities begin at 8 a.m. at the General Federation of Women's Clubs Woman's Club of Crescent City, 604 N. Summit St., where families can have breakfast with Santa Claus until 11 a.m. The cost is $6 per person, according to the club's Facebook page.
At 9 a.m., First Presbyterian Church of Crescent City's Warner Fellowship Hall, 301 Cypress Ave., will host the annual Silver Tea & Christmas Bazaar. People can shop for Christmas gifts among the handmade crafts on sale, snack on baked goods and tea, or participate in the Christmas carol sing-along at 1 p.m.
From noon – 6 p.m., the Crescent City Downtown Partnership will host a holiday market at Eva Lyon Park, 100 S. Summit St.
Attendees will have access to vendors, cuisine from local food trucks and more, according to the organization's Facebook page. A holiday parade will start at 1 p.m. along Main Street, and karaoke will be from 1:30–4:30 p.m. in the park gazebo.
Santa and Mrs. Claus will make appearances throughout the day starting at 2 p.m. There will be games and crafts for kids during the market, which is a precursor to Light Up Crescent City, a tree-lighting ceremony in the park.
The ceremony begins at 5 p.m. with performances by the Shwarb Family Band and St. Augustine Dance Conservatory. Free cookies and hot chocolate will be available at 5 p.m.
'It's a great day to visit Crescent City and get in the holiday spirit,' partnership officials said on Facebook.
Palatka
Palatka Porchfest will fill downtown streets with music Saturday starting 11 a.m.
There is no cost to go from house to house in the South Historic District to listen to local musicians serenade onlookers from different porches. People can start at Grand Gables Inn, 603 Emmett St., and work their way around the neighborhood.
Musicians include country music band The Sound, St. Augustine singer Shayla Nelson and Ancient City Jazz Coalition's Burn Unit, according to Porchfest's website.
A full schedule can be found at palatkaporchfest.com/schedule.
West Putnam
The Florahome Park and Heritage Association is getting ready for an afternoon of Christmas caroling. The festive event will begin at 4 p.m. Saturday at Palmetto Hall, 102 S. Magnolia Ave.
Refreshments will be provided to celebrate the holiday. Even Santa Claus plans to make an appearance.
'Opening historic Palmetto Hall for the Christmas season gives the community a nice chance to get together for caroling, a visit with Santa and to share food and fellowship,' association President Meri-lin Piantanida said. 'Together, we will light our community Christmas tree and usher in the beautiful holiday season.'
Also at 4 p.m., the town of Interlachen's 28th Christmas celebration, themed 'Christmas of Olde,' will start.
People can peruse the Christmas Village near Town Hall, 311 Atlantic Ave., or grab cookies, hot cocoa and apple cider. County Commission Larry Harvey, who is organizing the town's Christmas parade later that evening, said organizers plan to have 3,000 cookies for attendees.
Children can play miniature golf, make crafts and write letters to Santa Claus while they wait for Kris Kringle to make a special appearance after the parade.
The Interlachen First Baptist Church choir will perform at 4:30 p.m. at the Caboose downtown. At 5:45 p.m., people who want to dust off their old Christmas sweaters or pink rabbit pajamas can compete in the Ugly Christmas Outfit Contest at the Caboose.
The Christmas Parade will start at 6:05 p.m. and make its way through downtown. Santa will be taking Christmas gift requests following the parade at 6:30 p.m.
Harvey said people who want to enter a float in the parade can stop by Town Hall for an application or download one from interlachen-fl.gov/our-events.
A community prayer will close out the event at 6:45 p.m., and all local pastors are invited to attend.
'We look forward to a good time this weekend,' Harvey said Monday. 'It'll be fun to kick off the holiday season.'

title: Charitable event to lead to increased boat traffic
description: Boaters are being asked to exercise caution this weekend as a more-than-usual number of vessels are expected to be in local waterways to spread holiday cheer.
content:
Body
Boaters are being asked to exercise caution this weekend as a more-than-usual number of vessels are expected to be in local waterways to spread holiday cheer.
Toys Tour, an annual event where boaters from Florida and numerous other states deliver holiday gifts to be given to local children, will take place Friday and Saturday in different areas of South Putnam County.
Boaters are expected to be in Dunns Creek from about 10:30 a.m. – 3 p.m. Friday, according to Allison Waters-Merritt, a spokeswoman for the Putnam County Sheriff's Office, which will be collecting the toys and distributing them to participating organizations.
Toys Tour boaters will be on the St. Johns River throughout Saturday afternoon in Crescent City and nearby locations.
Waters-Merritt said the sheriff's office is more concerned with boating traffic Friday since Dunns Creek is a narrower body of water than the St. Johns River, but she encouraged people to be cautious both days.
Toys Tour is meant to provide gifts for children in state care, in crisis and who are victims of crimes.
The toys will not be given to families this weekend, Waters-Merritt said. The organizations that will eventually receive the toys will distribute them to people who qualify.
More information about the program can be found at thetoystour.com.

title: New park official a familiar face
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Once upon a Christmas in Palatka, there was a new park service specialist at Ravine Gardens State Park who had lots of fun plans for the community starting this holiday season.
content:
Once upon a Christmas in Palatka, there was a new park service specialist at Ravine Gardens State Park who had lots of fun plans for the community starting this holiday season.
A well-known artist in her own right, Sally Jan Smith has been busy making plans for everything from a Marketplace In The Gardens and a Ranger Read-Along that will feature Christmas stories and poems.
It's all happening in December, said Smith, who is excited to welcome people to the festivities at the park, 1600 Twigg St. in Palatka.
'I want to put a more familiar face of the park back into the community through wonderful events and programs,' she said.
And with that comes Smith's drive to increase membership of the Friends of Ravine Gardens community support group.
'I am also working hard to attract new volunteers,' she said. 'My plan for the immediate future is to raise money through our fundraisers to restore the historic rose garden with antique roses and to begin restoration of the rock work that was built in the 1930s.'
Smith has been a painter for 30 years and is currently illustrating her first children's book. She also was the art teacher at Children's Reading Center in Palatka for a decade.
'I created and held summer art programs for the children of Putnam County while having a thriving after-school art program with the support of Geri Melosh, the founder of the Children's Reading Center,' she said.
Smith believes the park adds historic value to the community as well as opportunities and activities area residents may not know exist.
'The park is on the National Register of Historic Places and has two historic buildings, which are very special,' Smith said. 'There are formal gardens with beautiful rock work, as well as the ravine, which is a very unique geologic feature in the state.'
Besides that, Smith said, the park offers history talks from knowledgeable rangers on programs about bats, owls, snakes and more.
'There is so much diversity in plant and animal life right here in our own backyard,' she said. 'Sometimes, you might see baby alligators, otters, foxes, bobcats, a black bear and many bird species. This lovely, fascinating place should not be missed.'
The park will host Marketplace in the Gardens from 10 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Dec. 14, which will include more than 50 vendors, live music, a visit from Santa from 1–4 p.m., kids' crafts and more. There will also be a gingerbread competition, for which contestants should bring their gingerbread houses already complete.
Entertainment will be provided by Shane Johns Project, Tommy Clay, Lori Gill and the Putnam County Community Band.
For details, call Smith at 386-329-3721 or email sallyjan.smith@floridadep.gov.
The Ranger Read-Along, which will feature Christmas stories and poems, will start at 10 a.m. Dec. 21 inside the Garden Club of Palatka's log cabin clubhouse, which is at the park. Highlights will include holiday refreshments provided by the Friends of Ravine Gardens and caroling around the piano, courtesy of Smith's husband, Tommy Clay, the music director at First Presbyterian Church of Palatka.
'We are going to have hot chocolate and lemonade, a Christmas tree cake and assorted homemade cookies and Rudolph sandwiches,' Smith said.
Children's book author Pamela Reader will read to guests a book that is special to Smith.
'The book is the 'Giant Book of Christmas,' a Golden book that was mine since childhood,' she said. 'My mother always read us a story on Christmas Eve out of the book before bedtime.'
Park admission is $5 for two to eight people in a vehicle, $4 for an individual in a vehicle, and $2 for pedestrians and bicyclists. Annual passes, which give access to all Florida state parks, are available for $60 per person plus tax annually or $120 per family plus tax.
Smith said the park has a lot to offer and is open daily throughout the year, weather permitting.
Smith said the 59-acre Ravine Gardens State Park, which is open daily throughout the year, is a hidden gem and probably one of the greatest tourist attractions in Palatka. The park was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1999 and has two historic buildings.
The park will offer other Ranger Read-Alongs on Jan. 18 featuring 'Babar,' Feb. 15 with 'Peter Rabbit & The Tale of Tom Kitten,' March 8 with 'Make Way for the Ducklings,' April 26 with 'Peter Pan' and May 10 with 'Charlotte's Web.'
Smith is excited about seeing families come to the park this holiday season and in 2025.
'We want to get to know the visitors and be available to them to make their park experience wonderful,' she said.

Body
Traffic officials are asking motorists along U.S. 17 near the south end of Putnam County to be cautious as a nearby wildfire is reducing visibility.
Around noon, Florida Highway Patrol officials reported a wildfire near 602 Hickory Nut Trail at noon Friday. Drivers were warned to be careful when driving along U.S. 17 in the area of the wildfire.
'Visibility may deteriorate quickly due to smoke/fog-type conditions, especially during the night and early morning hours,' FHP officials said Friday in a press release.
Drivers should reduce their speed and use low-beam headlights while driving near Hickory Nut Trail. Low-beam headlights will help drivers adapt to the smoky areas, according to FHP.
The agency said its officials were placing smoke signs along U.S. 17 to alert drivers to the hazy conditions.

title: Kelley Smith the site of upcoming primary school
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: If things go according to plan, the vast majority of kindergarten through second grade students enrolled in traditional public school in Palatka will be attending one school by the 2027-2028 academ
content:
If things go according to plan, the vast majority of kindergarten through second grade students enrolled in traditional public school in Palatka will be attending one school by the 2027-2028 academic year.
On Tuesday, Putnam County School District officials announced Kelley Smith Elementary School, 141 Kelly Smith School Road, will become Palatka Primary School by that academic year but will no longer cater to grades three through six.
James. A Long Elementary School, 1400 Old Jacksonville Road, and William D. Moseley Elementary, 1100 Husson Ave., the city's only other general public elementary schools, will close at the start of the 2027-2028 school year, Superintendent Rick Surrency said.
The Children's Reading Center Charter School, 7901 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka, will continue to accommodate students from kindergarten through sixth grade, while Mellon Learning Center, 301 Mellon Road in Palatka, will continue to cater to preschool students and students with developmental differences.
Students in third through sixth grade will start attending Palatka Intermediate School, 156 Horseman Club Road, during the 2026-2027 school year, district officials said. The intermediate school will open at the site of the former E.H. Miller School.
Construction on the intermediate school began last year, and district officials said construction at the Kelley Smith property will begin in July or August and take place during the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 academic years.
Surrency acknowledged the primary and intermediate schools are only 1.6 miles away from each other. He and Thomas Bolling, the district's associate superintendent for support services, said one reason the district and Public Schools Advisory Committee, which is made up of district, county and city officials, chose the sites is because they are both on the same side of town.
'It's conveniently located (next) to the (the) intermediate school,' Bolling said. 'So, if parents have younger kids at the primary school … they could drop those kids off and then go over to the intermediate school.'
The idea of closing James A. Long and Moseley sparked concern at a past meeting of the Bond Oversight Committee, which is made up of Putnam residents to oversee the district's use of a general obligation bond to build new and renovate existing elementary schools.
​​In the 2022 general election, 54.8% of Putnam voters approved the district using a $300 million general obligation bond to fund the construction of six new elementary schools throughout the county. As part of the referendum, Putnam voters will pay back the bond over 30 years via an additional property tax.
James A. Long will be the second school to close on the north side of Palatka, with all of the district's middle schools, including Jenkins Middle School, 1100 N. 19th St., having closed at the end of the 2020-2021 school year.
However, district officials said, with the way school zoning in Palatka is configured, not every student who lives on the north side attends James A. Long.
'There's a number of, especially on the north side, there's a number of students who are already transported to Kelley Smith, you know, like at the James. A. Long apartments and some of those,' Surrency said. ' It's not like those students are not familiar with that area.'
Another reason officials chose Kelley Smith is because the district needed to keep the sixth-grade wing of the school. The wing will be remodeled but will continue to serve as the county's hurricane shelter for people with special needs, Bolling said.
The Florida Department of Education required the wing to be kept intact because it is newer than other parts of the school.
By the end of construction at Kelly Smith, all parts of the school, except for the sixth-grade wing, which is at the southernmost part of the facility, will be razed and rebuilt, Bolling said.
Finances were also a factor in choosing the locations of the primary and intermediate schools, district officials said. James A. Long and Moseley would each cost at least $4 million more to reconstruct than Kelley Smith, Surrency and Bolling said. However, when asked Tuesday, Surrency and Bolling would not release the exact cost – or even an estimate – for the near-total reconstruction of Kelley Smith.
'I don't necessarily want to put that out right now because it's not exact pricing,' Bolling said. 'It's just a rough estimate. … We've got to get plans, and we have to get construction firms to – well, we have to choose a construction firm, and they have to come back with a price.'
The district plans to post its request for architects to submit their qualifications for the project within the next week, Bolling said.
Kelley Smith students will not have to change schools during the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 academic years. Students will need to transfer from Kelley Smith to James A. Long during the 2026-2027 school year, Bolling said.
The district bought an extra 5.5 acres of land south of the school to add to Palatka Primary, officials said.
'The biggest reason that we bought that piece of property was to be able to have more room on that campus and pull traffic off of the road because Kelley Smith traffic is a bit – well, it's not the best right now,' Bolling said. 'We want to make sure we pull that traffic onto the actual campus itself to get it out of the neighborhoods and off the highway.'
While Surrency understands the district might receive backlash because of these decisions, he said the district has had to make many difficult decisions since the plans for revitalization were introduced four years ago.
'That bond thing was a very tough one because – we've said this many times – this bond election happened when the economy tanked, right?' Surrency said. 'We almost backed out, but we stood behind it. All of this is taking place because of that.'
When all of the school construction is complete, which includes reconstruction of most junior-senior high schools being paid for with state funds, Putnam residents will benefit from the outcome, district officials said.
Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School does not require renovations because it is the county's newest school, according to the district.
Passionate Palatka Junior-Senior High School Panthers might also be happy to know the primary and intermediate Palatka schools will adopt blue and gold school colors and the panther mascot, officials said.
'I think to see … construction taking place and actually having some plans of our students actually moving into the building is very gratifying,' Surrency said. 'It's great to see a plan come to fruition.'

title: Early voting opens to choose congressional nominees
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Putnam County is starting early voting Saturday for a special primary to choose the person who will represent Florida's 6th Congressional District.
content:
Putnam County is starting early voting Saturday for a special primary to choose the person who will represent Florida's 6th Congressional District.
Polls will be open from 8:30 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. through Jan. 25. for Putnam residents to choose their parties' nominees, who will compete to succeed U.S. Rep. Mike Waltz.
During early voting, registered Democrats and Republicans can vote at any of the following locations:
– The Supervisor of Elections Office, 2509 Crill Ave., Suite 900, in Palatka.
– The Interlachen Community Center, 135 S. County Road 315.
– South Putnam Government Complex, 115 N. Summit St. in Crescent City.
Polling locations on primary day, which will be Jan. 28, will be open from 7 a.m. – 7 p.m., and people must vote in the polling place listed for their residence.
The special primary and April 1 election were required after Waltz resigned Nov. 25 amid President-elect Donald Trump selecting him to be the national security adviser.
'Both major parties will have the opportunity to pick who they want to represent them in the general election,' Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III said.
The 6th Congressional District comprises all or parts of Putnam, Flagler, Lake, Marion, St. Johns and Volusia counties.
As part of the primary being closed, only registered Republicans can vote for Republican candidates, and the same goes for registered Democrats and corresponding candidates. Republicans on the primary ballot are Aaron Baker, Randy Fine and Ehsan Joarder, while Democrats up for election are Ges Selmont and Joshua Weil.
Democrat Purvi Bangdiwala withdrew from the race earlier this month, according to the Supervisor of Elections' Office.
All eligible voters can vote in the April special election, which will feature the Republican and Democratic primary winners, as well as Libertarian, no party affiliation and write-in candidates.
Overturf said he hopes voters show up in droves for the primary, especially after having such a large showing for the presidential election in November. However, the state average turnout for a special primary election is about 10%, he added.
'We just experienced the biggest turnout we've ever had at 80.5%,' Overturf said. 'We'll be lucky to even hit 20%.'
As of 1 p.m. Friday, only 100 people, or 0.26% of eligible voters, had their mail ballots reach the Elections Office.
For other election information, including primary day voting locations, visit voteputnamflorida.gov.

title: Shelter reopens as cold expected to grip Putnam
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A Palatka cold weather shelter is again opening its door tonight as temperatures this week are predicted to drop to near or below freezing this week.
content:
A Palatka cold weather shelter is again opening its door tonight as temperatures this week are predicted to drop to near or below freezing this week.
The Putnam County Caring Coalition, a nonprofit organization formed to provide shelter for homeless people, is hosting the shelter at First Presbyterian Church's Westminster Hall, 126 S. Second St. in Palatka, today through Saturday morning. The shelter will be open from 7 p.m. – 7 a.m. beginning today.
Georgia Mitchell, the executive director of the Caring Coalition, said the area is expecting to see record-low weather. The Weather Channel forecasters predicted freezing rain and temperatures as low as 37 degrees Wednesday night.
'In this type of weather, it makes it difficult for unhoused people to stay warm, safe and dry,' Mitchell said.
She said the shelter can accommodate up to 30 people but cannot accept pets at this time. People who may be experiencing power outages and are without heat at their residences are also welcome to shelter at Westminster Hall.
'We know that during this type of weather, things you don't expect to happen happen,' Mitchell said.
She suggested people who want to stay at the shelter bring an emergency bag filled with any medicine they might need, battery packs, phones, electronic chargers and snacks if people have dietary restrictions.
While the shelter will open today when the weather is predicted to get as low as 32 degrees, The Weather Channel predicted temperatures to continue to drop as the week goes on.
The agency predicted the thermometer to dip to 21 degrees Thursday night and 29 degrees Friday night.
People can access the shelter throughout the night, but a shelter attendant will lock the doors at night for shelter inhabitants' safety. People can still get inside to warm up at any time of the night if they knock on the hall's windows or doors, Mitchell said.
'We want to make it as easy as possible to keep people comfortable,' Mitchell said.
Shelter volunteers will provide coffee, tea and snacks while providing access to hot showers. Earlier this month, Mitchell said the coalition could not provide full meals at Westminster Hall, but the Caring Coalition partners with Bread of Life, volunteers for which serve meals at 320 N. Fifth St. in Palatka on Mondays through Fridays from 11:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.
If people want to help the cold weather shelter, the coalition is searching for people who would like to volunteer in two- to four-hour shifts.
The coalition could also use blankets, sleeping bags, coffee and tea supplies, and shelf-stable food, Mitchell said.
People who want to volunteer can call Mitchell at 609-865-6706. Donations can be made at the First Presbyterian Church office, 123 S. Second St.

title: Author sharing book sale money with group
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Author Bob Lee has written plenty about his community, and this weekend, he will be giving back to a group in that same community.
content:
Author Bob Lee has written plenty about his community, and this weekend, he will be giving back to a group in that same community.
Lee, a retired Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission lieutenant who spent 30 years with the agency, will be the presenter at the Putnam County Historical Society meeting at 11 a.m. Saturday at the Bronson-Mulholland House, 100 Madison St. in Palatka. The public is invited to the meeting, where light refreshments will be served.
While at the meeting, he will be selling his latest book, 'Bones in Water,' and plans to give back to the organization hosting the meeting.
'Mr. Lee is generously planning to share proceeds from the books sold at this program with the Putnam County Historical Society,' historical society President Nicole Grace said. 'We will be using these funds to purchase archival materials to preserve recent donations to the society, including a collection relating to Hubbard Hart's steamboats and historical materials related to the community of Edgar and the Edgar family.'
Lee's newest book is a murder thriller set on the St. Johns River and nearby locales in Northeast Florida. Lee will be on site until 1 p.m. Saturday for the book sale and signing.
During Lee's career, he was part of numerous complex wildlife investigations and caught hundreds of poachers in the act. The officers he worked with and the people he met on the job formed the foundation for his first two nonfiction works, 'Backcountry Lawman' and 'Bad Guys, Bullets, and Boat Chases.' These two books, along with his new release, will be available for purchase for $20 each. Payment can be made by cash, check or credit card, but cash is preferred.

title: Churches hosting events to celebrate Black history
author: Trisha Murphy
description: As part of Black History Month, two local churches are coming together today to celebrate Absalom Jones, who was the founder of the first Black Episcopal Church in 1794 in Philadelphia.
content:
Body
As part of Black History Month, two local churches are coming together today to celebrate Absalom Jones, who was the founder of the first Black Episcopal Church in 1794 in Philadelphia.
St. Mary's Episcopal Church is partnering with St. Mark's Episcopal Church for the public service that will start at 4 p.m. at St. Mary's, 809 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka.
Following the service at 5 p.m. there will be a free community dinner at St. Mark's Parish Hall, 310 N. Second St. in Palatka, where neighbors and friends connect, according to the Rev. Jon Davis, rector at St. Mark's and St. Mary's.
Among some of Jones' other accomplishments was his ordination in 1802 as the first Black person to be ordained as a priest in the Episcopal Church of the United States.
Davis said the close friendship between the congregations of St. Mary's and St. Mark's began in 1882 when the land at 809 Lemon St., now St. Johns Avenue, was donated by George Burt, a parishioner at St. Mark's.
'That's when the Carpenter Gothic structure was established and constructed with funding from the congregation at St. Mark's,' he said.
Both churches are loaded with history and historical figures, including St. Mary's first minister, John Purcell, a 50-year-old Black man who in 1882 began having Episcopal worship services in the parlor of his residence at 616 Lemon St. in the Newtown community, where the majority of Palatka's Black population lived at the time.
'Within two years, his congregation outgrew his home,' Davis said.
According to Davis, Purcell and his two sons whom he had taught carpentry, hand-built today's board-and-batten church for his congregation.
'In 1883, Purcell became the first Black delegate to the annual Diocese of Florida meeting,' Davis said.
Other Black historians who will be recognized at the service include the Rev. Edward H. Butler, the chancel of St. Mary's, who was ordained as the first Black Episcopal or Catholic priest ordained in Florida.
Butler, his wife and another teacher were also known to be the instructors of 27 students beginning in the 1890s at St. Mary's Day School. That number was seven more than were enrolled at the time at St. Mark's Academy, Palatka's parochial school.
John Alexander, the senior warden at St. Mary's, has been the curator of the church and steward of its property for more than 30 years. St. Mary's weekly services and active life were discontinued due to the COVID pandemic, and there have been no regular services since.
St. Mary's is Florida's oldest Episcopal church used by Black congregants and one of the state's oldest Black wooden churches of any denomination.
Davis believes today is the beginning of a larger conversation to define how the sacred and historical space of St. Mary's could be used on an ongoing basis to serve the community as a gathering place and a vibrant life to bless people once again.
'It's a treasure in our historic Palatka neighborhood,' he said. 'St. Mary's deserves recognition on state and national historic listings, a destination on the Florida Department of State's Black History Trail and a future to return in service to the community.'
Information was provided by Dianne Taylor of St. Mark's Episcopal Church in Palatka.

title: Azalea Festival in bloom this weekend
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Everything's coming up azaleas this weekend when the annual Florida Azalea Festival comes to Palatka for its 76th year.
content:
Body
Everything's coming up azaleas this weekend when the annual Florida Azalea Festival comes to Palatka for its 76th year.
Festivities will kick off Saturday at 9 a.m. and continue until 5 p.m. The celebration of the flowering shrub will continue Sunday from 10 a.m. – 5 p.m.
According to Kathy Griffin, the festival chairwoman for the second year, it's going to be bigger and better than before.
'We've got up to 75 vendors between the merchants, the sponsors and participating vendors,' she said. 'Guests can expect to find arts and crafts and food vendors, shop in the downtown businesses or have lunch at one of our restaurants. Azalea plants will also be available for purchase for those looking for a special souvenir.'
Sponsored by Revitalize Historic Palatka, the two-day festival is being held in conjunction with the Bassmaster Elite Series, which the Putnam County Chamber of Commerce is hosting at the Palatka riverfront. Other major sponsors of the festival include iHeart Realty and Visit Palatka.
Griffin said the Bassmaster tournament has helped generate interest for the downtown festivities by combining their tournament with the festival.
'We are piggybacking off each other,' she said. 'The Chamber has helped with this and has been great to work with.'
According to Griffin, St. Johns Avenue will be closed from the riverfront to Seventh Street and visitors with children will not want to miss the kiddie carnival at Ameris Bank in the 600 block of St. Johns Avenue.
'We've got face painters, rock painting, cotton candy, an ice cream truck, lemonade and more – everything to keep kids happy and entertained,' she said.
The festival will also run along the banks of the St. Johns River. One of two entertainment stages will be located at the Palatka City Dock, while the other will be at the Putnam County Courthouse.
For those eager to take their four-legged friends with them for all the downtown festivities, don't fret. However, pets must be kept on leashes.
'Pets aren't just allowed, they're encouraged,' Griffin said. 'Pets in costume are a traditional part of the Azalea Festival.'
According to palatkaazaleafest.com, the festival is one of the longest-running celebrations in Florida. Griffin hopes people will attend to continue the tradition of celebrating the azalea.
'This two-day outdoor festival will include lots of vendors selling their wares and, of course, azaleas,' Griffin said. 'We hope those who come out will shop our downtown businesses, restaurants and food vendors.'
The winners of the 2025 Miss Azalea Scholarship Pageant will be at the festival to meet festival-goers.
Griffin said the family-friendly festival will offer diverse activities for an enjoyable day out.
'Our expectations are to have an exceptionally good outcome at this year's Florida Azalea Festival,' she said. 'My committee and I are staying positive about the turnout for the festival and expecting the weather to be great.'
For details about the Florida Azalea Festival, call 386-328-7502.

title: Arc clients honored for resilience, leadership
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The dedication and hard work of four local residents were celebrated Thursday during an award ceremony highlighting their accomplishments.
content:
Body
The dedication and hard work of four local residents were celebrated Thursday during an award ceremony highlighting their accomplishments.
Hundreds of people from near and far lauded Arc of Putnam County consumers during the 27th Eddie Mooney Awards ceremony at the Roy E. Campbell Civic Center at Ravine Gardens State Park.
Thursday's event was more than just a dinner and awards ceremony, Arc CEO Denis Sousa said.
'It's a celebration of community,' he said. 'It's about recognizing the bright supporters and dedicated team members who lift us up, push us forward and inspire us every day.'
Since 1974, the Arc has served people who have intellectual and developmental disabilities by providing them with programs, living environments and work experience.
Justin Hafner took home the evening's grand prize, the Eddie Mooney Award. Sousa said Hafner started attending the Arc programs before he graduated from the former E.H. Miller School in Palatka. Since then, Sousa said, Hafner has been an integral part of the Arc.
'He is someone who shows up every day with a smile on his face, eager to help, eager to make a difference,' Sousa said. '... He does it all without hesitation. His willingness to help is unmatched. And all you have to do is ask and he will be there.'
Hafner is an advocate for his peers and cares about the well-being of everyone around him, Sousa said.
'It is rare to come across someone who touches the lives of everyone he meets in a profoundly positive way,' Sousa said. 'He has a remarkable ability to improve our lives simply just by being here.'
The award ceremony was started in honor of Eddie Mooney, who experienced many challenges but was committed to his friends, family and goals, according to Arc.
On Oct. 24, 1998, months after his death in January of that year, the first dinner took place in his honor to recognize people who have intellectual and developmental disabilities but show just as much courage and resilience as Mooney, according to the Arc.
While presenting another award that evening, Terry Massey, the Arc's manager of human resources and compliance, remarked how he saw many of Mooney's qualities in its recipient.
Ola Mae Session won the Employment Excellence Award for her unwavering leadership, courage and success, Massey said. Session lives independently, has worked at Pizza Hut since 2017, is a beloved friend and family member, and continues to focus on personal growth, according to Massey.
The Peter Prater Self-Advocacy Award was given to Arc client Marilyn Lancaster, who has demonstrated resilience by overcoming challenges in foster care, learning to speak up for herself and gaining more confidence, said Patti Dame, the Arc's manager of administrative services. Lancaster also obtained a job at St. Johns River State College.
'Tonight, we celebrate not only Marilyn's achievements but the person she has become – a confident, empowered young woman who is no longer afraid to speak up (and) laugh,' Dame said. 'And she also enjoys life to the fullest.'
Latasha Obry took home the Community Contributions Award for her willingness to help and desire to be involved with as much as possible. Like Hafner, Obry loves making the Arc's bArc Bites, which are dog biscuits Arc clients make using grain from Azalea City Brewing Co.
While the award-winning Arc consumers were the main focus of Thursday's event, the ceremony also recognized the volunteers and advocates who make it possible for the Arc to operate. Dame and Teresa Jones, who works in the administrative office, won Unsung Hero awards for the work they do behind the scenes to organize events such as Thursday's ceremony.
Convenience store Wawa also won the Lucille Flint Volunteerism Award for the numerous donations it has made to the Arc despite the store being open in Palatka for less than a year, Sousa said.
Wawa has donated 14,000 pounds of food valued at $27,000 to the Arc and supports Arc day programs, residential housing and consumer care, Sousa said.
'We are proud to recognize an organization that embraced our community with open hearts since opening their doors last year,' Sousa said.

title: Panthers say goodbye to Palatka High grads
description: People packed the Palatka Junior-Senior High School football field to standing-room-only Friday night to see seniors end one era of their lives. Cheers, balloons and signs rose up from Bennett-Cooper…
content:
People packed the Palatka Junior-Senior High School football field to standing-room-only Friday night to see seniors end one era of their lives.
Cheers, balloons and signs rose up from Bennett-Cooper Field at Veterans Memorial Stadium to celebrate the Palatka High Class of 2024. Officials lit up the scoreboard to honor the final quarter in these students' game called high school.
Class president Amaris Mack gave her honor to God for getting her to the graduation stage, and gratitude to everyone's families, teachers, advisors and mentors. She said it is because of their sacrifices that each graduate accomplished all they had.
'I also have to recognize the strongest woman in my life, my mother Kenya,' Mack said. 'My mother has instilled in me the importance of education and learning since I was able to read. I can't say I would be the person I am today without her.'
She also touched on a tragedy that happened to her family in 2021. Mack said she learned a lot from her brother's sudden death.
'Time is precious,' she said. 'You never know when it is your last time seeing someone or being with someone. It is very hard to understand how fast time goes by until you're at the end. … I implore you all today to take advantage of the time we have spent here at Palatka Junior-Senior High School, and never forget the memories and lessons we have learned here.'
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News. The Palatka Junior-Senior High School football/soccer field scoreboard pays tribute to those who graduated from the school Friday night. Principal Cathy Oyster said Palatka High was built on traditions that each class continues to make their own.
Some graduates already received associate degrees from St. Johns River State College in May, others received industry certifications allowing them to seek specialized jobs straight out of high school and a few graduates were in line to go to the military.
'The greatest accomplishment carries no cord or sash,' Oyster said. 'It comes with the great satisfaction of knowing you persevered through challenges, obstacles and unexpected outcomes.'
She said everyone experienced adversity in their lives. On the cusp of a new start, Oyster said the graduates should look at their own accomplishments but acknowledge all the strengths the class of 2024 found together.
'You modeled empathy. You modeled compassion and inclusivity – so much of what this world is missing right now,' Oyster said. 'You showed understanding over judgment, acceptance over rejection and empathy over indifference. Never underestimate the power you have on changing lives.'

title: Candidate enters race to retain mayoral position
description: Pomona Park's mayor has launched his campaign to continue leading the South Putnam County municipality. According to the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office, Joseph Svingala turned in his…
content:
Pomona Park's mayor has launched his campaign to continue leading the South Putnam County municipality. According to the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office, Joseph Svingala turned in his candidacy paperwork Friday. He will face off against challenger Anthony Cuevas in the nonpartisan race. Svingala became the mayor in 2018 and won elections in 2020 and 2022 to retain his mayoral position, which comes with two-year terms. If Svingala and Cuevas are the only candidates in Pomona Park's mayoral race by noon Aug. 9, the end of the qualifying period, they will compete in the Nov. 5 general election. For more election information, call the Elections Office at 386-329-0224 or visit soe.putnam-fl.com.

title: Libraries offering children's summer programs
description: School's out for the summer, but that doesn't mean there's no place for children to learn while also having a fun time during the break. The Putnam County Library System is hosting a kickoff event…
content:
School's out for the summer, but that doesn't mean there's no place for children to learn while also having a fun time during the break.
The Putnam County Library System is hosting a kickoff event Saturday from 10 a.m. – 1 p.m. in the library headquarters, 601 College Road in Palatka.
Interactive music group Just Add Rhythm will start the summer adventures off at 10:30 a.m.
Mischa Johns, who oversees archives and special collections for the library system, said the group is from Tampa and travels to events to play music with kids.
'They are a percussion group that comes in and makes a big circle,' Johns said. 'And they give out tambourines and drums and sticks … and everybody gets together, and they're all drumming and partying when they play music together.'
For science-minded kids, a science-geared art class will take place at 11:45 a.m. Saturday that combines art with science, technology, engineering and mathematics.
'I don't know what (the instructor is) doing,' Johns said. 'It's a surprise to me.'
Children and their parents can show up early Saturday when the library opens at 9 a.m. to register for the numerous activities taking place this summer. Kids can pick up a reading log, which challenges them to read as many books as they can over the summer for a chance to win prizes and celebrate at a special party Aug. 17.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – Mischa Johns, who oversees archives and special collections for the Putnam County Library System, shows off the mural she digitally drew for this summer's Adventure Begins At Your Library activities. Library branches in Interlachen, Melrose, Crescent City, Bostwick and Palatka are offering programs Monday through Saturday until Aug. 3. There will be no classes July 4.
'We are planning for 300 (children from) 0 to 5 and 300 (children from) 6 to 11,' Johns said. 'That's our plan, and we can add to it if we need to.'
It took library employees about three months to turn the Palatka library into a jungle and other landscapes to resemble different continents and countries. Johns digitally drew some of the scenes and had them printed onto the walls.
Youth and Family Coordinator Brooke Conway decorated some of the ceilings with stuffed wild animals hanging on paper branches to resemble the African savanna.
'(I'm) just excited to … show the kids to learn about the different countries and continents we have,' Conway said. 'I hope they like it.'
Kids will learn about Africa's savannas, Australia's outback, Brazil's rainforests, Canada's tundras, Egypt's deserts, Greenland's glaciers, Ireland's dales and Vietnam's jungles.
The libraries will have storytimes, movie nights, crafting programs, coloring nights and family board game nights.
'It's a family thing,' Johns said. 'Everybody has fun together. We craft together and everything. It's going to be a lot of fun. It's eight full weeks of stuff.'
Activities for young adults, like Kingdom Builders, are also available. Johns said she will host Kingdom Builders workshops at different libraries for children to build their own fantasy world and work their way up to writing about their world during National Novel Writing Month in November.
For information on the library's summer events, visit youseemore.com/putnam/calendar.asp, the Putnam County Public Library System Facebook page or one of the county's library branches.

title: 3rd superintendent contestant enters race
description: The race for superintendent of schools got more crowded after a write-in candidate filed her intent to run for office. Pat Wilson turned in her candidacy paperwork May 28, according to the Supervisor…
content:
The race for superintendent of schools got more crowded after a write-in candidate filed her intent to run for office. Pat Wilson turned in her candidacy paperwork May 28, according to the Supervisor of Elections Office. Her competitors in the superintendent contest are incumbent Rick Surrency, who was first elected in 2016 and won his reelection bid four years later, and challenger Paul Adamczyk, a sitting county commissioner who was elected in 2020. Although her Republican opponents will compete in the Aug. 20 primary, Wilson will not because of her write-in status. She will be on the Nov. 5 general election ballot where voters will have to write in Wilson's name if they intend for her to be the new superintendent. Because she is a write-in candidate, Wilson will not run under any political party. For more election information, call the Elections Office at 386-329-0224 or visit soe.putnam-fl.com.

title: Putnam Celebrates Juneteenth
description: A local group hosted its first riverfront Juneteenth celebration Wednesday to share the history behind the holiday while celebrating local young people who excelled in school. African American Arts…
content:
A local group hosted its first riverfront Juneteenth celebration Wednesday to share the history behind the holiday while celebrating local young people who excelled in school.
African American Arts Council of Putnam County members hosted Jubilee on the St. Johns River to commemorate the federal holiday that celebrates the anniversary of June 19th, 1865, which was the day the last enslaved Americans in Galveston, Texas, were notified they were free.
'It was two-and-a-half years later that they found out because we know Abraham Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation on Jan. 1, 1863,' council Vice President Pamela Brown said. 'So, we celebrate Juneteenth and the freedoms that we have in this country that so many Texans didn't know that they had (until) June 19, 1865.'
A museum dedicated to Juneteenth will be opening soon in Fort Worth, Texas, and Brown hopes to visit. According to the National Juneteenth Museum's website, the facility is scheduled to open in 2026.
Texas was the first state to declare Juneteenth a state holiday in 1980, according to the museum. President Joe Biden signed the Juneteenth National Independence Day Act into law in 2021, declaring Juneteenth a federal holiday.
Putnam County language arts teacher Erica Robinson made sure to attend Palatka's Juneteenth celebration, but she wished more people had shown up.
'They can come out and learn from this,' she said.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – African American Arts Council of Putnam County vice president Pamela Brown, left, explains the history of Juneteenth on Wednesday alongside Lalita Thomas, right, who organized the Jubilee on the St. Johns River Festival. Palatka's celebration included music, food trucks, bounce houses for kids, line dancing, speakers and a scholarship presentation to four recent graduates from Putnam County schools.
Each graduate received $250 from the arts council for their hard work and outstanding academic performance. Palatka Junior-Senior High School graduate Chloe Dasher, a student-athlete who finished school with an associate degree from St. Johns River State College and a 4.4 high school GPA, will attend Spelman College in Georgia.
Palatka High Class President Amaris Mack, another student-athlete, finished high school with a 4.2 GPA and plans to attend Florida A&M University in Tallahassee.
Palatka High graduate Ymira Passmore also received a scholarship. She graduated with a 4.3 GPA, and plans to attend the University of Central Florida in Orlando.
The final recipient was Trenton Williams, who graduated from Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School with a 4.3 GPA but played sports at Palatka High. He plans to attend the University of North Florida in Jacksonville.
Despite the awards and jubilation, the Juneteenth observance wasn't as well attended as other events at the riverfront. Robinson said she wishes everyone had shown up to learn about the culture and history behind Juneteenth because it isn't taught in schools.
She hopes the event will grow as more people learn about the holiday and decide to observe it. While this is the first year of the riverfront Juneteenth event, organizers said they plan to keep the jubilee going every year on June 19.
'This is so important because today really is about the suffering, the contributions and just the struggles of our ancestors from 1865,' Robinson said. 'As an educator, just two years ago, I learned about Juneteenth and that's sad.'

title: Officials launch plan to Elevate Putnam
description: Local business and community leaders unveiled an ambitious plan Thursday to take Putnam County's economic development and talent retention efforts to the next level. Community stakeholders gathered at…
content:
Local business and community leaders unveiled an ambitious plan Thursday to take Putnam County's economic development and talent retention efforts to the next level.
Community stakeholders gathered at the Roy G. Campbell Civic Center at Ravine Gardens State Park in Palatka to hear about Elevate Putnam, the five-year, multi-million-dollar initiative its leaders say will increase local residents' quality of life.
With a feasibility study and other groundwork initiated by the Putnam County Chamber of Commerce and Putnam County Economic Development Council, Elevate was started to attract a wide range of businesses while supporting existing businesses, boost wages, increase consumer expenditure in the county and keep Putnam residents from having to travel elsewhere for opportunities. BRANDON D. OLIVER/Palatka Daily News – Community stakeholders show off how much money had been collected for Elevate Putnam by Thursday.
Mark Litten, the Chamber's vice president of economic development, said the council conducted its feasibility study in the fall of 2023 and originally settled on a fundraising goal of $2 million. However, he said, council members soon realized they should shoot for more startup funding.
'As we progressed forward – the beginning of this year – we realized that to fully support our vision, we needed to aim higher,' Litten said. 'And we had early success in the capital campaign, and we increased the goal to $3 million.'
The goals for Elevate Putnam include creating 750 near primary jobs and more than 220 indirect support jobs, securing $500 million in new capital investment, generating more than $65 million in new annual earnings and adding $36 million in new local annual consumer expenditures.
The group's ambitious fundraising goals proved to be attainable, as 10 local leaders – each holding a piece of paper displaying either a digit, comma or dollar sign – stood in front of the room to show $3,033,750 had been raised.
Businessman and Putnam native Benjie Bates, one of Elevate Putnam's co-chairs, said the county is on the precipice of greatness, but the campaign needs the community's support to succeed.
A graduate of Palatka High School, Bates said Elevate is meant to improve retail, tourism, workforce development, education, agriculture and other sectors in the area. The campaign's success could be the catalyst that brings home many Putnam residents who left the county because of a lack of opportunities.
'The excitement and energy that I feel for this event stems from a profound belief that our community is on the verge of greatness,' Bates said. 'We're about to take a giant step forward, and with that comes unparalleled opportunity.
'We don't want future generations to feel that they need to leave for better opportunities. Instead, I want to send a beacon of hope and opportunity signaling far and wide that this community is a place where dreams can be realized.' BRANDON D. OLIVER/Palatka Daily News – Mark Litten, the vice president of economic development for the Putnam County Chamber of Commerce, talks about the feasibility study and other work that was done in the early stages of Elevate Putnam.
Charlie Douglas – who, like Bates, is a Palatka High alumnus and local business leader – shares the desire to keep Putnam's talented and knowledgeable residents in the county.
Many students will leave for college, he said, but he wants to see them return once they've finished school. There are also career technical and entrepreneurial options in Putnam County, he said, and one of the goals for Elevate is to increase the number and quality of those options.
'For me, it's about keeping our best and brightest here in Palatka,' he said. 'If we are going to succeed as a community, I believe that we must bring more industry, more jobs, to Putnam County.
'We have to swing for the fences. We're going to have strike-outs, but when we connect, it's going to be something big. It's going to be bold. It's going to be impactful for our generation and many generations to come.'
With all of the development happening in surrounding counties, Putnam should not miss out, said Kelley Smith, a former county commissioner and state legislator. Smith, who was the keynote speaker at Thursday's event, said St. Johns County is developing faster than its infrastructure can handle, and Clay County is undergoing its own projects.
'It's our job … to get out there and make sure that we do things like try to keep that small-town atmosphere but yet encourage the growth,' he said. '(Elevate) is going to involve a lot of people here, and it's going to evolve us into a community that we can all be proud of. … The potential is certainly here.'
After it was announced more than $3 million had been raised for Elevate, Bates announced a new stretch goal of $3.5 million. He and Douglas acknowledged the numerous businesses and individuals who had already invested in Elevate Putnam and stressed the importance of additional community buy-in.
Douglas said Thursday there were 60 more days left in Elevate's fundraising efforts. He wants to recruit more donors to invest in Elevate, which he said is an investment in Putnam County.
'Together, it's worth it, not just as a charitable contribution,' Douglas said. 'This is truly a business investment, that the jobs that will come to Putnam County, the industry that will locate here, will directly impact all of the businesses represented here as part of the Chamber. Together, we're going to see tremendous success. Thank you all for supporting Putnam County.'

title: PDN's publishing altered due to post office closure
author: News Staff
description: Palatka Daily News There will be changes to this week's publication schedule of the Palatka Daily News because of the Fourth of July.
content:
Body
There will be changes to this week's publication schedule of the Palatka Daily News because of the Fourth of July.
Instead of publishing an edition Thursday, the paper will be distributed Friday. The schedule change was necessary because the U.S. Postal Service, which delivers the newspapers, will be closed Thursday in observance of Independence Day.
Friday, which is normally not a publication day, was chosen as a makeup day for the delivery.
Daily News employees will still be working hard Thursday to provide stories about July Fourth as well as other news, sports and other goings-on in Putnam County.
Anyone with questions about the change can call the Daily News at 386-312-5200.

title: Drone camp steers Putnam teens toward future careers
author: Carter Mudgett
description: Drones have grown in popularity in recent years, as they offer a new dimension to the photography and videography worlds.
content:
Drones have grown in popularity in recent years, as they offer a new dimension to the photography and videography worlds. Their introduction also opens new doors for potential money-making ventures with the right training.
A camp offered by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension Putnam County aims to do just that: helping teens understand and fly drones.
While many of his Putnam County high school classmates were relishing the first half of their summer break last month, Liam Sayler instead spent his time memorizing Federal Aviation Administration regulations and the basics of aerodynamics.
All that work paid off when Sayler passed an FAA exam, certifying him to fly a drone. He's one of eight Florida 4-H members who attended the drone camp last month, according to a press release from UF/IFAS.
'This is a job skill,' Joseph Strickland, one of the camp's instructors, a certified drone pilot and a UF/IFAS employee, said in a statement. 'These students can go out today with a drone license and start working — and for really good money, too. We've had students who, after school, would fly a drone and make hundreds of dollars in an afternoon.'
Some participants planned to capitalize on their new skills by applying them toward aerial photography jobs in the real estate, construction and agriculture sectors.
One of the teens saw the certificate as a stepping stone to securing a pilot's license, and another wanted to use drone photography as a firefighter, according to the press release.
'I am so proud of these students,' said Wendy Mussoline, director of UF/IFAS Extension Putnam County. 'They dedicated a week of their summer to commit to an intensive academic drone training program and obtained their licenses. I believe this experience can truly enhance their future career endeavors.'
Instructors also tapped a young entrepreneur, Lance Dollar, a 2024 graduate of Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School in Florahome, to share his insights with the students.
The recent graduate launched a business using drones to take photographs and videos of agricultural operations, sporting events and property advertised for sale, according to the release.
With Dollar's drone, campers practiced takeoffs, landings and other maneuvers. In a mock exercise, they took aerial photos of the extension office building as if marketing the property for sale and photographed two Putnam County Fairgrounds buildings as if conducting roof inspections.
The camp was sponsored by the Putnam County Soil and Water Conservation District, which put forward $5,500 so students paid only $25 for services valued at $450, according to the press release. That included the weeklong course and a trip to Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Daytona Beach, where campers took the exam.
The date of the next drone camp has yet to be released but the organization's director hopes additional funding will make it so more young people can learn how to fly drones and potentially apply those skills to their future careers.
A report from Drone Industry Insights, the leading drone market research and analytics brand, forecasts the global drone market size to reach $54.6 billion by 2030, with photography and filming applications among the top three usages.
There are over 782,000 drones registered in the U.S., of which 383,302 are registered for commercial use, according to FAA figures updated in May.
The only skills separating the drone curriculum taught to students last month from the one taught to future airplane pilots are fuel management and night flight, Strickland said in the press release.

title: Editorial: There are (at least) two sides to every story
description: We all know what happens when we assume something, and it's usually not good.
content:
We all know what happens when we assume something, and it's usually not good. There is an old saying that goes 'no matter how flat the pancake, there is always another side.' In today's paper we printed a story about the closing of the Palatka Press Plant, which is separate from the Palatka Daily News. Some people reading the story may have made the wrong assumption that we are closing the newspaper or that our new owner made the decision to no longer print the paper here. Those people have assumed wrong on both counts.
It was an end of era with the newspaper being printed here. We wanted to memorialize the moment that our presses cranked out the final paper and so we did. The article was not meant to imply that our new owner, Charlie Douglas, had something to do with it. In fact, the decision to close the press plant was made by the previous owners long before Douglas purchased the newspaper. Douglas' desire to preserve the Palatka Daily News and continue to be an integral part of our community was the driving force behind his purchase. Douglas has a vision for the newspaper that will lead us into the future so we can continue to grow and be here for many years to come. We are excited to be a part of the many things he is doing to make our community a place to enjoy and be proud of.
In newspapers all over the country, presses are being closed mainly because they are old, outdated and increasingly impossible to maintain. Our press is over 40 years old with replacement parts no longer available to repair or people with the knowledge to repair them. It is just the nature of the business.
While closing the press plant is sad for our employees, we will still print at a consolidated location with the press capacity and equipment that will bring you a better, cleaner newspaper with more color pages and pictures.
Our future at The Palatka Daily News is bright and we are looking forward to serving you, our readers, for generations to come.
When you flip that pancake over, you might just see another side.

title: Stop the Presses
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: Today marks the end of an era as this edition of the Palatka Daily News is the last one to be printed on the paper's press.
content:
Body
Today marks the end of an era as this edition of the Palatka Daily News is the last one to be printed on the paper's press.
All future editions of the Daily News will be printed in Callahan, one of the changes the newspaper is undergoing following its sale to Blue Crab Publishing LLC, which is owned by Putnam County native and attorney Charlie Douglas. The sale was finalized June 30.
The press, which first went into operation in Palatka in September 1986, ran for the final time Friday evening into the early hours of this morning to print today's edition.
With the printing change, however, comes personnel changes in the form of pressroom and mailroom employees no longer working at the Daily News.
Daily News Publisher Jennifer Moates said the change in printing locations is following the trend of other industry publications that have abandoned printing in-house. Following industry standards doesn't make saying goodbye to employees any easier, she said.
'Newspaper publishing has gone through many changes over the years and like any other business, we must adapt,' Moates said. 'I am sad to see our press plant close after being a mainstay in our community for many years and it means some of our employees will no longer be here. We are a family and it is never easy to lose family members.'
The Daily News received the refurbished press when it underwent a massive addition to the paper's headquarters, 1825 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka, in 1986 and continued printing the paper until 1996. A few weeks after Community Newspapers Inc. purchased the Daily News from the New York Times Co. in September 2000, printing on-site resumed and continued until today's edition.
More recently, the Palatka press printed not only the Daily News but also the Lake City Reporter, the News-Leader of Fernandina Beach and the Nassau County Record of Callahan.
During the break in on-site printing, the Daily News was printed in Ocala and Gainesville.
Press Plant Manager Keith William has been at the Daily News for both spates of in-house printing.
After the press was moth-balled in the 1990s, Williams spent time working in the Florida Keys. He was called back to Palatka when printing resumed in 2000.
'It was kind of nice (to get brought back) because the hurricanes weren't my favorite thing in the Keys,' Williams said Friday before turning on the press for the final time.
Williams said the press closure is tough for many people, but given the nature of the business, it wasn't surprising to learn the paper would be printed elsewhere. He sang the praises of all of the pressroom and mailroom employees with whom he has worked over the years, noting how they worked hard during late hours.
While Williams knows the situation for the mailroom and pressroom isn't ideal, he has faith they all will find other opportunities.
'It's kind of sad, but, you know, every time a door shuts, another one opens,' he said. 'The paper will be around, just (printed) somewhere else.'
Moates echoed those sentiments, saying the Daily News will continue its coverage of local governments, sports, lifestyles, education and other topics that are important to its readers.
This is a new period for the Daily News, she said, but the paper will continue to stay steeped in the community.
'As we look to the future, we will continue to cover local issues with the same determination we always have,' Moates said. 'The printed edition of the newspaper is still important and we will continue to bring it to our readers. It will just be printed at a different location.'

title: Voters hear from candidates as primary approaches
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: It was standing room only Thursday evening during a political forum that involved 17 candidates pleading their cases in person, one hopeful addressing the crowd via letter and an incumbent being ba
content:
Body
It was standing room only Thursday evening during a political forum that involved 17 candidates pleading their cases in person, one hopeful addressing the crowd via letter and an incumbent being barred from participating.
In keeping with tradition, the General Federation of Women's Clubs Woman's Club of Palatka, 600 S. 13th St., hosted its candidate forum in the lead-up to the Aug. 20 primary.
Candidates of numerous contests that will be on the ballot in August – and some candidates whose names won't appear until the Nov. 5 general election – introduced themselves before participating in a question-and-answer session.
Woman's Club member and event Chairwoman Diane Wolfe said political forums are vital to the democratic process. People should be informed before going to the polls, she said, and candidate forums are a great way for voters to know more about the people up for election.
'The Woman's Club is an important part in the community,' said Wolfe, who served as the forum moderator. 'And we need to allow the opportunity for the candidates to come to speak and the residents of Putnam County to have the opportunity to come listen and to meet our candidates one on one.'
The following candidates participated in Thursday's event:
– Brenda Bridges, Brittany Goodson and Sydney Myers, candidates for tax collector.
– Paul Adamczyk and Rick Surrency, candidates for superintendent of schools.
– Josh Alexander and Les Sims, candidates for Board of County Commissioners, District 3.
– Buddy Goddard, Walton Pellicer and Tim Williams, candidates for Board of County Commissioners, District 5.
– Constance Daniels, Anne Marie Gennusa and Alex Sharp, candidate for county judge, Group 1.
– Leon Edenfield, a candidate for Putnam County School Board, District 2.
– Tim Houghtaling, a candidate for Putnam County School Board, District 3.
– Annie Henderson Davis and Allegra Kitchens, candidates for Palatka City Commission, Group 1.
– Elizabeth van Rensburg, a candidate for Palatka City Commission, Group 3.
Sandra Gilyard, who's seeking reelection to her District 3 school board seat, was out of town but had a letter read in her absence.
School board District 2 incumbent David Buckles was in attendance and got on stage to participate. However, Wolfe informed him he could not partake in the forum because he did not RSVP by the Woman's Club's deadline.
After the event, Wolfe told the Palatka Daily News she prohibited Buckles from speaking out of fairness. Another political candidate had reached out to her after the RSVP deadline, she said, and was informed he could not participate because of that.
Wolfe said she emailed all candidates at the email addresses listed on the Supervisor of Elections Office website. There are other candidates who did not attend the forum.
The Woman's Club plans to have a forum Oct. 8, less than a month before the general election, and Wolfe is advising candidates to check their emails.
'I'm hoping that they will reach out to me,' she said. 'But I will start sending them emails again after the (primary), giving them plenty of notice of what we can do.'
Although some candidates were absent, there were plenty of voters on hand to hear from the people trying to get their support.
Retired educator Jennifer Cox wanted to hear from all of the political hopefuls, especially the school-related candidates.
The county has 'phenomenal teachers,' but not all of them are placed in areas where they would be most effective, Cox said. She'd like to see more 'information gathering' so the Putnam County School District employees are performing in roles best suited to their skill sets.
Superintendent and school board races are important to everyone, not just people who have children in public schools, she said.
'It's super important because as they later discussed (in the forum), our tax base is dependent upon attracting business,' Cox said. 'In order to attract business, we have to have a good education system.'
After the forum concluded, Wolfe said she hoped voters received the information they sought before it began.
Having forums before the primary is as important as the club's general election forum because many contests will be decided before summer is over, she said.
'How many of our elections that were here tonight are being decided in the primary?' Wolfe asked. 'And sometimes, the primary is the only election that they have to do, so that's why I feel primary elections are vitally important to the community.'
The entire candidate forum can be viewed on the Palatka Daily News' Facebook page.
