title: Pellicer one step closer to regaining board seat
author: Carter Mudgett
description: A former county commissioner narrowly won Tuesday's primary contest for the District 5 seat on the Putnam County Board of Commissioners.
content:
Body
A former county commissioner narrowly won Tuesday's primary contest for the District 5 seat on the Putnam County Board of Commissioners.
Voters chose Walton Pellicer, who earned 3,585 (36.79%) votes, to be the Republican nominee, according to unofficial results from the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office.
Pellicer ran against Buddy Goddard and Tim Williams, who got 3,403 (34.92%) votes and 2,757 (28.29%) votes, respectively, according to the unofficial results.
'It's not as large a victory (as) I'd like, if it holds, but a victory's a victory,' Pellicer said minutes before the last three precincts' votes were displayed.
He credited his primary victory to the 500 voters who switched parties to vote in the Republican primary.
But the race isn't done yet for Pellicer. He'll go head to head with write-in hopeful Tim Grose during the Nov. 5 general election.
If Pellicer wins that vote as well, he'll take the District 5 seat from Commissioner Paul Adamczyk, who unsuccessfully competed in the superintendent's race in this primary.
Pellicer told the Daily News he's excited to 'serve people of all (political) parties in Putnam County, not just Republicans.'
The job isn't entirely new to Pellicer. He was first elected to the District 5 position in 2012 but lost his reelection bid four years later to Goddard.
About 31% of Putnam County voters participated in the primary, casting a total of 13,987 ballots, according to the Supervisor of Elections Office website.

title: Fall semester begins as college looks toward future
author: Carter Mudgett
description: St. Johns River State College students returned to the Palatka campus for the first day of the fall semester Monday morning.
content:
Body
St. Johns River State College students returned to the Palatka campus for the first day of the fall semester Monday morning.
College faculty and staff welcomed many back at the Viking Center where students could play table tennis, make crafts and get ready before class.
The rhythmic sound of workers striking nails and banging hammers could be heard from across campus where future student housing was under construction.
Monday was also SJR State President Joe Pickens' 16th first day of the fall semester, which he likened to spring training in baseball.
'Everybody's optimistic and happy and enthusiastic and looking forward to the semester,' he explained. 'The campus is coming alive.'
That's not the only thing 'coming alive' at the Palatka campus.
As students get back into the swing of things on campus, college leaders are looking forward to a few multi-million-dollar construction and renovation projects on the horizon.
The projects are efforts to broaden how SJR State is meeting the needs of the local community. But even as college leaders expand their horizons, Pickens emphasized his desire to never lose sight of the college's core identity.
'We want to always be thought of as the community's college,' he said.
Rising enrollment
Over the past two years, enrollment at the college has increased nearly 20%, according to Pickens. It's a big win, he said, because it's part of a nationwide journey to bounce back after enrollment took a hit during the COVID-19 pandemic.
For the Palatka campus, which is smaller than its counterparts in St. Augustine and Orange Park, growth is really coming, in part, from the Florida School of the Arts. It enrolled 120 students this fall compared to 89 during the spring semester earlier this year, according to SJR State data.
College leaders are also looking to add five more bachelor's degree programs to their repertoire, the first new ones in a decade, according to Pickens.
Those degrees would be a Bachelor of Science in digital art and media, performance design and production, biological sciences, exceptional student education, and social and human services, according to the college.
The Bachelor of Science in exceptional student education could be approved at the upcoming state Board of Education meeting Sept. 25 at the St. Augustine campus, Pickens said.
More than 80% of SJR State students are seeking their two-year transfer degree, Pickens said. So the idea isn't to pivot completely away from its community college roots.
Instead, once bachelor's degrees are added and construction is completed, the next step is to stop and take a lay of the land.
'As we go forward, I don't expect ever for the percentage of students that are taking that traditional community college track of an (associate) degree to go below 80%,' said Pickens. 'It will always be our bread and butter.'

title: Playwright to bring Hamer story to Crescent City
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Mzuri Moyo Aimbaye has gone beyond being sick and tired of being sick and tired and will express it when she brings the Fannie Lou Hamer story to Crescent City in a one-woman play next week.
content:
Body
Mzuri Moyo Aimbaye has gone beyond being sick and tired of being sick and tired and will express it when she brings the Fannie Lou Hamer story to Crescent City in a one-woman play next week.
The production, which will take place at 2 p.m. Sept. 14 at the Miller Middle School auditorium, 101 S. Prospect Road in Crescent City, is part of the national tour commemorating women of civil rights and social justice.
Light refreshments will be served at the Crescent City event.
According to Aimbaye, who lives in Orlando with her husband, 400 years of slavery and inhuman treatment will cause one to go beyond being sick and tired.
'You become even sick and tired of that,' she said. 'It's the feeling of nowhere to go.'
The play was written and will be performed by Aimbaye under the direction of Byron C. Saunders. The play's theme is 'Triumph. No Matter What, I Must Press On.'
Tickets cost $20 for adults and are free for children 12 and younger. For details, call organizer Angel Duke at 678-906-9770 or email thedukegroup4@aol.com.
Aimbaye won Best Solo Performances at the 2002 AUDELCO VIV (Black Tony) Award ceremony. She had four sold-out performances at the National Black Theater Festival in 2017 and was named Best Actor, Play & Producer at the Black Theater Festival in 2015. She has also performed other one-woman productions.
Aimbaye said she started writing this play in the late 1990s when she saw video of Fannie Lou Hamer on a talk show recounting her story of how she was beaten for registering to vote.
'Voter suppression is at its highest with people being discouraged from voting through intimidation and threats and also through gerrymandering and redistricting. But it's the same voter suppression that Mrs. Hamer experienced,' said Aimbaye, who is also a singer.
Aimbaye said Hamer had lots of accomplishments in her lifetime, including being an American voting and women's rights activist, community organizer and a leader in the civil rights movement.
Hamer was the vice-chair of the Freedom Democratic Party, which she represented at the 1964 Democratic National Convention. She was also a co-founder of the National Women's Political Caucus, an organization created to recruit, train and support women of all races who wish to seek election to government office.
She ran for Congress several times but was unsuccessful in her attempts. She died March 14, 1977, at the age of 59.
Duke, the president and founder of the A. Philip Randolph Gallery & the Duke Group Production, organized the event along with local women and groups, as well as officials from the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, a specialized agency of the United Nations with the aim of promoting world peace and security through international cooperation in education, arts, sciences and culture.
Duke said the one-woman show is going to be riveting, and she appreciates locals showing their support in an effort to bring women together.
'This is something for women to appreciate and show their support by participating, regardless of their political affiliation,' she said.
For details on the Fannie Lou Hamer story, visit fannielouhamerstory.com or email info@thefannielouhamerstory.com.
Aimbaye said she played the character of Lucy of Sankofa in a film and later was inspired to channel the indomitable spirit of Hamer in a continuation of telling the story and plight of her people from Africa to America.'
Other highlights of the Sept. 14 event will be live Gospel music featuring the group Day 3 and live African drummers.
Duke hopes the public will show their support by attending.
'You really don't want to miss this one,' she said. 'I don't believe this will ever happen again in Putnam County.'
As history has it, Duke said, Hamer, Victoria Jackson Gray and Annie Robinson Devine were the first black women allowed on the floor at the Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in August 1964.
By invitation of Congressman Bennie Thompson, Aimbaye appeared at this year's 2024 Democratic National Convention in full costume and character as Hamer for the 60th anniversary commemorating her Aug. 22, 1964, testimony that became a tipping point to the passage of the Voters Rights Act of 1965.
Aimbaye is excited about her first visit to Crescent City, which has its own notable Black history.
'I am looking forward to coming to the birthplace of A. Philip Randolph,' she said. 'He is also given an honorable mention in the play because of the role he played providing Black men jobs and also created the first Negro union.'
Aimbaye said Hamer is hailed as a prophetess of civil rights and social justice to promote dignity and freedom for all Americans.
'We hope to raise awareness for people to understand that others have died and suffered for the right to vote and that everyone should vote because they have a civil duty to do so,' she said.

title: Putnam native returns home as hospital CEO
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The new leader of HCA Florida Putnam Hospital has come full circle as he works to improve the facility in which he was born 39 years ago.
content:
Body
The new leader of HCA Florida Putnam Hospital has come full circle as he works to improve the facility in which he was born 39 years ago.
Landon Smith, who started his new job as CEO of the Palatka hospital Sept. 3, said he has hit the ground running regarding his plans for the hospital.
Smith said he and his team at HCA Putnam want the hospital a place everyone wants to go, whether as a patient in search of help or an employee seeking a career.
'We want to be the place that patients choose,' he said Thursday. 'So, when someone is in need of our services … they just think about us and they come straight to us. … We want to be the best employer.'
While he is the leader of the hospital's operations, Smith said it takes more than just him to make the facility function.
'This is a team, without a doubt,' he said. 'We have a robust team of people, you know. I'm not a clinician. I don't see patients, but there's also no one person in our building that can provide everything a patient needs.'
He said he views himself as the coach of a team of the hospital's employees, vendors and the community, all of whom are needed to take great care of the patients.
The Putnam community has been welcoming Smith home as he settles into his new role. He said he's received hand-written notes from residents and hospital employees wore T-shirts with his face on them for his first day on the job.
'I've heard a lot of positive things,' he said. 'I've had people reach out and say they've had great experiences with the hospital. I would say, you know, the biggest thing is we just have opportunities to really build and develop programs and … to increase the service offerings at the hospital today.'
Smith returns to Putnam County with 12 years of experience working in health care administration, he said. His first job at 14 was delivering home health equipment, he said.
Benji Bates, the chairman of the hospital's board of trustees, said the board is excited to welcome Smith. In a statement Friday, Bates said he's confident there are great things to come with Smith at the helm.
"Landon and I share a unique connection – we were both born at this very hospital,' Bates said in the statement. 'It's rare to have a CEO with such deep ties to the community, and I believe it makes a real difference. Our patients aren't just numbers or statistics. They're our friends, family, and co-workers.
'Having someone like Landon, who turned down other opportunities to be here because he's passionate about this community, is something we should all be grateful for. This isn't just another step in his career, it's where he wants to make a real impact.'
Smith wanted a career in the health care business because he was intrigued, especially because his dad worked at the Putnam hospital in the 1980s. He said his father worked his way up from being an accountant to the chief financial officer.
Smith lived in Putnam County for three years before his family moved to Georgia, but he remembers visiting other family members in East Palatka for Christmas break, spring break and the summer. He said his mom was a teacher whose entire family is made up of East Palatka natives.
'I've been in and out of Palatka my entire life,' Smith said. '... (My mom) grew up right over there, you know, where the Ace Hardware is.'
While he's been back in Palatka for only two weeks, he's already looking ahead to the goals he wants to accomplish. He said he has plenty of ideas he's mulling over, but he needs time to vet them before announcing any grand plans.
'This place is very meaningful for the community,' Smith said. 'We certainly recognize that, understand that, you know, and want to just really continue to add value for the community.'

title: Officials warn Milton could bring ‘worst-case scenario'
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Local government officials are closing offices and schools and recommending people living in flood-prone areas to evacuate as Hurricane Milton continues its charge toward Florida.
content:
Body
Local government officials are closing offices and schools and recommending people living in flood-prone areas to evacuate as Hurricane Milton continues its charge toward Florida.
The hurricane escalated to a Category 5 Monday, and officials in Putnam County aren't taking it lightly. The Board of County Commissioners declared a state of emergency Monday morning during a special meeting.
Sandbag stations opened throughout the county Sunday, emergency shelters are slated to open at 6 p.m. Tuesday, and the Putnam County School District canceled classes and closed its offices from Tuesday through Thursday.
People need to take this storm seriously, Deputy County Administrator J.R. Grimes advised during Monday's special meeting. He believed it could be a long time before the county fully recovers from Milton, which might not pass over the state quickly.
'We do want to make sure people understand we do have to prepare for a worst-case scenario,' Grimes said. 'And the worst case scenario on this one is 10 to 15 inches of rain during the storm.'
While evacuations weren't mandated Monday, county officials recommended residents in areas prone to flooding consider finding a safer place to stay.
'If you feel like you're in an unpredictable structure, please utilize our shelters,' Grimes said. 'Please let us take care of you. We'd rather take care of you pre-storm than what we would after the storm or during.'
The following schools will be opening as shelters:
– Ochwilla Elementary School, a pet-friendly facility, 299 N. State Road 21 in Hawthorne.
– Kelley Smith Elementary School, a shelter for people with special needs, 141 Kelly Smith School Road in Palatka.
– Robert H. Jenkins Jr. Elementary School, 251 S. State Road 315 in Interlachen.
– Middleton-Burney Elementary School, 1020 Huntington Road in Crescent City.
– Browning-Pearce Elementary School, 100 Bear Blvd. in San Mateo.
People who need transportation or who have family members who need transportation to the Kelley Smith shelter should call the Emergency Operations Center at 386-329-1904 as soon as possible to make accommodations, Grimes said Monday.
County Commissioner Terry Turner reiterated the need for people who know their homes are prone to flooding to get out as soon as possible.
'I'm gonna just say it,' Turner said. 'If you live in Dunns Creek, if you live in Sportsman's Harbor, if you live at Federal Point, get the hell out. I mean, it's gonna get bad. The river's gonna back up. It's already rising.'
If people plan to stay, self-service sandbag stations opened Sunday. People who visit those stations should bring their own shovels, but the bags will be provided for free.
Sandbag stations are at the following locations:
– 145 West Washington St. in Hawthorne.
– 51 Sportsmans Drive in Welaka.
– 223 Putnam County Blvd. in East Palatka.
– 341 Paradise Circle in San Mateo.
– Jonas Road in Crescent City.
– 5226 Silver Lake Drive in Palatka.
– 107 Johns Road in Palatka.
– 114 S. 11th St. in Palatka.
– 100 Drayton Island Road in Georgetown.
– 126 Boat Ramp Road in Palatka.
School district officials canceled after-school activities and athletics Tuesday through Thursday and had originally canceled school Wednesday and Thursday. On Monday evening, however, district officials announced via social media classes would be canceled Tuesday.
The district had not made a decision Monday about school and activities for Friday.
St. Johns River State College activities and classes, including online classes, are canceled Wednesday through Friday, according to an SJR State Facebook post.
WastePro will not be picking up trash for county customers on Wednesday, according to emergency management, and the county landfills will be closed that day. Residential garbage service for the city of Palatka is expected to continue Tuesday but not occur Wednesday and Thursday, according to a news release from the city.
'If conditions allow, regular residential collection will resume on Friday,' city officials said in the release. 'Commercial collection is expected to continue if conditions allow.'
The county's trash collection operations will depend on the impact Milton has on the area, emergency management officials said in their social media post.
Even when the storm ends, Grimes said, people should stay off the roads to give emergency personnel and utility workers time to clean up debris.
The city of Palatka's business offices will close at 3 p.m. Tuesday and are expected to reopen Monday, according to the city. The administrative offices of the city's police and fire departments will follow the same schedule.
'While city offices may be closed, the city police, firefighters, public works, and city water, gas, and sewer services will operate continuously during this storm to serve and protect residents,' Palatka officials said in the press release.
Welaka Town Hall will be open Tuesday, but Mayor Jamie Watts said Monday that he was unsure about being open for the rest of the week.
Interlachen government offices will close Wednesday and Thursday, but whether they will be closed Friday had yet to be determined Monday, officials said.
The Putnam County Courthouse will be closed Wednesday and Thursday, according to a Facebook post by the 7th Judicial Circuit of the State Attorney's Office.
The Putnam County Sheriff's Office's administrative offices will close at 3 p.m. Tuesday and remain closed Wednesday and Thursday, according to the agency's Facebook post.
Despite the fatigue people might be feeling from the tropical weather events the county has experienced over the past few years, Putnam residents need to take Milton seriously and prepare as best as they can, Turner said.
'I know that we've had multiple ones of these in the last few years, and so we're all getting a little burnt out,' he said. 'I got a feeling this is not going to be one of them we want to turn our back on.'

title: Riverfront to play host to folk festival
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Area residents are in for a treat with a day of music and relaxation this weekend after days of storm-watching living through Hurricane Milton this week.
content:
Body
Area residents are in for a treat with a day of music and relaxation this weekend after days of storm-watching living through Hurricane Milton this week.
With the storm having come and gone, the third annual North Florida Folk Network Folk Festival will take place from 11 a.m. – 5 p.m. Saturday at the Palatka riverfront pavilion, 100 Memorial Parkway in Palatka, and will feature headliner Bear and Robert, an award-winning singer-songwriter duo from Jacksonville, as well as performers from the North Florida Folk Network roster.
The event is free for the public to attend.
Cindy Bear and Franc Robert, who make up Bear and Robert, perform catchy melodies, toe-tapping rhythms and soulful lyrics that touch people's hearts in many ways and leave them wanting more, according to bearandrobert.com.
The group placed in sixth place in the Top 10 in the 2024 Will McLean Best New Florida Song Contest. Their latest CD, 'Travels With Bear & Robert,' was released in March.
Saturday's event is hosted by Putnam County's Acoustic Circle.
In an effort to encourage children to tap into their musical side, there will be a Musical Instrument Petting Zoo, where they can touch and play instruments.
Volunteers are needed to interact with children at the Instrument Petting Zoo. Some instruments have been donated but more of different types are needed. For details, message Billy Ennis at 386-538-9852 or email billyennis1950@gmail.com.
For details on event sponsorship or vendor space, visit www.nffolk.com.
'Our festival promises a full day of fun and free family-friendly entertainment, showcasing some of North Florida's most talented folk, Americana, blues and country musicians,' said Ennis, the organizer of the event. 'Festival-goers can look forward to a stellar lineup of artists.'
Other highlights of the festival include vendors selling arts and crafts, food trucks and more.
Participants should bring lawn chairs. Pets are welcome but must be leashed.
The Folk Network is a nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving, promoting and celebrating the rich tradition of folk music in North Florida.
Through events, performances and educational programs, the organization fosters a vibrant folk music community in the region, according to a news release.

title: Q.I. among 15 state schools to get national honor
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Putnam County School District officials are celebrating after one of its learning institutions was among a handful of schools throughout the nation to be recognized for its academic excellence.
content:
Putnam County School District officials are celebrating after one of its learning institutions was among a handful of schools throughout the nation to be recognized for its academic excellence.
U.S. Department of Education officials in September deemed Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School a National Blue Ribbon School – a designation awarded to just 15 other Florida schools and 356 schools in 46 states, according to the federal agency.
Q.I. Roberts Principal Joe Theobold said he and other school officials found out the Florida Department of Education nominated Q.I. Roberts for its performance in the 2022-2023 academic year.
'I think it's representative of what we aspire to as a school and what our expectations are of ourselves,' Thebold said Wednesday.
Other Florida schools to receive the designation include Stanton College Preparatory in Jacksonville, West Shore Junior-Senior High School in Melbourne and Coronado Beach Elementary School in New Smyrna Beach, according to the Blue Ribbon's website. Of all the public schools selected nationwide, just 18% were high schools.
The National Blue Ribbon program began in 1982 to spotlight the country's best-performing schools, the program's website states.
In a Blue Ribbon press release, U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona said the selected schools can serve as an inspiration for students at other schools to aspire to brighter futures.
'The National Blue Ribbon Schools Award is a testament to the exceptional achievements of students and educators at each of these schools,' he said in the press release. 'The 2024 National Blue Ribbon Schools are raising the bar for our nation's students, serving as models for effective teaching and intentional collaboration in their schools and communities.'
The program designated Q.I. an exemplary high-performing school, an achievement made possible thanks to the school's teachers, Theobold said.
Superintendent Rick Surrency, Theobold and Q.I. English teacher Matthew Bergen will attend the National Blue Ribbon School awards ceremony in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 7 and 8.
Theobold said he was allowed to bring along one teacher and chose Bergen, who was instrumental in improving students' grades on state tests in the English section during the 2022-2023 school year.
That school year, Thebold said, 95% of Q.I. students passed the state tests, putting the school in the top 10 statewide for test scores.
'It was one of the highest scores in the state,' he said. '(Bergen) did a lot of great work. Everybody's done a lot of great work that led to that, but certainly, he was hugely responsible, especially in that year specifically.'
During Tuesday's Putnam County School Board meeting, Chairwoman Sandra Gilyard commended Q.I. students and employees for their accomplishments. It is great to see Putnam County represented at the national level, she said.
Despite whatever challenge Q.I. faces, she said, its people remain resilient.
'It's not the size of the dog in the fight,' Gilyard said. 'You're doing great things – the leadership team and the administration. … They're getting tested and hit over and over again, but they rise to the challenge.'

title: Judge hopefuls lay out cases for election
author: News Staff
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, answers that went over the limit were cut to be as close to 100 words as possible.
Palatka Daily News
An incumbent and a local attorney are in a runoff to be elected to their first full term as a Putnam County judge in the Group 1 seat.
Judge Anne Marie Gennusa is fighting to stay in the position to which she was appointed, while challenger Alex Sharp is vying to unseat her. Gennusa and Sharp received the most votes in the Aug. 20 primary race that also featured Constance Daniels.
Gennusa and Sharp answered questions from the Palatka Daily News about why they are the most qualified to be a Putnam County judge.
How will your background, legal or otherwise, shape how you carry out your duties as a judge?
Gennusa: I have 30 years of diverse legal experience including family, criminal, and juvenile delinquency. I have an extensive litigation background, including experience as an assistant state attorney, a criminal defense attorney, mediator, Guardian ad Litem, Teen Court Judge and Parenting Coordinator. I am admitted to practice law in Florida, New York, and the United States Supreme Court. I was an attorney for the National Police Defense Foundation, representing law enforcement officers accused of crimes. Together with my husband Bob, an army veteran and retired sergeant, we raised five children and have three grandchildren, with a fourth on the way.
Sharp: Growing up in Putnam, working and living here gives me a unique local experience of our community. Additionally, serving honorably in the military and later as a police officer gave me leadership skills, a strong work ethic, and a desire to help others. Later, I started and ran several successful small businesses, including a family-friendly restaurant. Finally, my legal experience as a former prosecutor and General Counsel with the Putnam County Sheriff's Office has allowed me to work closely with victims of crime, handle various legal issues, and understand a judge's role must always be fair and impartial.
What makes you qualified to be a judge in Putnam County?
Gennusa: Experience, transparency and community service. I am the only candidate with judicial experience. I have presided over 8,000 proceedings, hearings, and trials. I am assigned to criminal traffic, misdemeanor, juvenile delinquency, and truancy cases. I bring 30 years of legal experience to the position. I was appointed by the governor after a bi-partisan vetting process. Anyone is welcome to observe county court. I encourage the electorate to learn what a county judge does. I am also a member of the Woman's Pilot and Kiwanis clubs. Giving back to my community is important to me while serving in this position.
Sharp: I became an attorney in 2012. However, my 20 years of experience in our local court system as a law enforcement officer and prosecutor provide me with essential insight and knowledge. Having owned multiple successful small businesses here in Putnam, a family restaurant, numerous commercial properties, and a real estate office gives me a first-hand understanding of legal issues involving property disputes and managing staff. As a long-time resident, I also have personal knowledge of the problems we face as a community, and I believe all this, along with my diverse background, makes me your best choice for county judge.
What are some of your top priorities for serving on the bench if elected?
Gennusa: If I am fortunate to keep my position as county judge, I believe that maintaining efficiency due to the recent population growth, without sacrificing justice is critical. Searching for creative solutions for my increasing criminal and delinquency dockets including a specialized juvenile/adult domestic violence court, mental health court and a 'teen court' program. These initiatives would be a collaborative effort between court administration, the State Attorney, the Clerk of Court and our schools. I will continue to follow the law and ensure that anyone charged with a crime is brought before the court expeditiously. Justice delayed is justice denied.
Sharp: I believe those who work daily in the court system sometimes forget for many people, this is their first-ever courtroom appearance. People appearing in court can be nervous, scared, anxious, and angry. My primary role as a judge is to apply the law correctly. But I also understand the need to let the people who appear before me know the process. Communication to me is critical. My life experiences will allow me to communicate effectively while performing my judicial duties. As your best choice for local judge, I would never let my emotions influence or dictate my conduct in court.
What does being a county judge mean to you?
Gennusa: County court, or the 'people's court,' is usually the first interaction, whether criminal or civil, that a person has with the court. In addition to maintaining an efficient courtroom, judges are required to treat everyone fairly, follow the law, and not be influenced by race, gender, or community ties. I am thankful for the assistance of dedicated court clerks, my judicial assistant, the bailiffs, assistant state attorneys, and assistant public defenders that are always prepared. Their support is why I love being 'your' county judge. I will continue to serve Putnam County with fairness, experience, and transparency.
Sharp: For me, it is the culmination of a career dedicated to public service. Putnam County has been my family's home for approximately 50 years. I have always strived to make our community a better place to raise children, start a business, or live. A county judge's court is often described as the people's court. Because it is usually the first time anyone needs their court system. I believe despite any circumstances, the judge you appear before can determine whether that court experience is positive or negative. I would strive to make it a positive one as your local judge.

title: Prep football preview: Raiders set for battle with 'Cats
author: Corey Davis

title: Commission lists why why should be elected
author: News Staff
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, answers that went over the limit were cut to be as close to 100 words as possible.
The District 1 seat of the Putnam County Board of Commissioners is up for grabs in the general election.
Vying to replace Commissioner Bill Pickens, who decided not to run for reelection, are Republican J.R. Newbold III and write-in candidate Douglas Hays.
The Palatka Daily News asked local candidates whose names are on the ballot why they should be the person Putnam voters should elect.
Below, Newbold states why he will be an ideal county commissioner:
Why do you believe yourself to be the best candidate for this position?
Newbold: I believe the 34 years of experience I've gained from managing a successful agricultural business and my 30 years of dedication to numerous community service organizations makes me the best candidate to represent District 1.
What are your top three priorities, if elected?
Newbold: A) Developing well designed Growth Management Strategy that embraces growth while preserving our rural look, feel, and lifestyle. B) Focus on bringing business / jobs to Putnam County. C) Looking at issues through a 'quality of life lens.' Making improvements with many 'smaller issues' that truly improve the quality of life of our residents can make a huge improvement to the look, feel and pride in our community. (Parks & Rec, Library System, Building and Zoning, Codes Enforcement, Animal Services, Historic preservation, etc.)
Where do you believe the Putnam County Board of Commissioners needs to improve?
Newbold: Strategic thought and a focus on relationships with State and Federal counterparts. We need to strengthen the relationships with our partners in Tallahassee and Washington DC. The infrastructure improvements and services necessary to effectively cope with the expected growth in our community will require extensive help from our State and Federal partners. Strategic Planning will be a must. Boards / Commissions can get mired down looking 'backwards' at past performance and lean towards micromanagement. We must focus on effective planning for the future.
What's the best way to accommodate growth in Putnam County while also retaining the rural Florida environment this county loves?
Newbold: Updates to our Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code will be crucial in this effort. Keeping dense residential growth in the proper places while encouraging our rural look and feel throughout the county. We should leverage and upsell our abundance of waterways and woodlands, promoting outdoor based activities and businesses; camping, cycling, boating of all kinds, hunting, ecotourism, etc.
What is the most important change to the budget you believe needs to be made?
Newbold: Our county budget is a complex fiscal tool. We as commissioners must have a thorough understanding of its component parts and how it's crafted. Much of the budget is fixed and discretionary funds are limited. Better education for commissioners will enable us to make the best use of limited funds.
Commissioners are the face of Putnam County but it's often commissioners' employees that do the heavy lifting behind the scenes. Where do you stand on how much the county should be paying employees?
Newbold: Human Capital is an area we must pay close attention to. If we are to keep the best talent, we should be meeting the market salary wise. The county has made progress in this area of late, we must continue the focus on developing and retaining a first-class workforce.

title: Commission hopefuls state why they deserve votes
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, answers that went over the limit were cut to be as close to 100 words as possible.
Two candidates are running to fill a Crescent City Commission seat up for grabs.
Jamaad C. Batts Sr. and Linda Moore are competing for the Group 3 seat, which Commissioner Cynthia Burton, who chose to run for the Group 4 seat, currently occupies.
The Group 3 race is open to only voters who live within the city limits of Crescent City.
The Palatka Daily News emailed both candidates questions to learn why they think they should be elected to the commission. Among other reasons, Batts and Moore said they want to be a voice for residents and work to improve the community.
Below are the candidates' responses in their own words:
Why did you decide to run for a seat on the Crescent City Commission?
Batts: My main motivation for running for commissioner is to make a positive impact on our community. I want to be a voice for the citizens and address the important issues that directly affect our daily lives. Additionally, I want to advocate for the needs and concerns of the next generation, ensuring a better future for our community.
Moore: I am running for Crescent City commissioner because I want to make a difference in our community. I have lived in Crescent City all my life, and as a resident, homeowner, parent and grandparent, I want our city to stay a great place to raise a family. I have the experience in leadership, community service and simply working with the people in our city that is necessary to be an effective city commission member. I plan to work hard and make sure everyone has a voice that is heard.
What government experience do you have that would make you an ideal choice for the Crescent City Commission?
Batts: My extensive experience in the government sector has given me a unique perspective on the needs of the community. As a successful businessman, I am equipped with the skills and knowledge to efficiently manage and allocate resources to serve the best interests of the community. I am committed to using my experience and expertise to serve and benefit the community as a whole.
Moore: I currently have no experience in government, and this is my first time running for office. But I think I am the ideal choice because I have integrity and a good moral compass that is needed for the position. I will make sure to articulate my positions well while being open-minded about the positions of others. I am also open to working constructively and collaboratively with everyone to find the best results for our community.
What do you believe the city commission's main priorities should be and why?
Batts: Financial transparency, city financial audit and lowering taxes.
Moore: I think that the city commission's main priorities should be doing what is best for our city. As a city commissioner, you should make sure to keep yourself informed on what the community thinks. I think researching, studying, and discussing issues with the people is key to knowing if you are making the right decisions.
Crescent City has seen its share of conflict, especially within the past few years. What would you do to bring stability to the city so it can function efficiently?
Batts: As the next commissioner, I will bring fairness and a strong focus on advocating for the citizens. I believe in creating a transparent and inclusive government that works for the people. My goal is to ensure that all voices are heard and represented and that everyone has equal opportunities to thrive in our community. Together, we can build a better future for all.
Moore: I believe that negativity does nothing to actually help the community with the policies and ordinances that will work best for us all. When you are in the public eye, your words and actions always matter and will affect the city. To bring stability, we need to get more people in the community involved in citizen advisory committees. Most people don't know what they are, so they don't volunteer to join, and we need to change that. Giving a voice to more people around the city is a good way to better understand the interests of the city.

title: Incumbent, newcomer win in Palatka commission races
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: There will soon be new blood on the Palatka City Commission, but one incumbent's victory ensured there wouldn't be a complete shake-up.
content:
There will soon be new blood on the Palatka City Commission, but one incumbent's victory ensured there wouldn't be a complete shake-up.
Commissioner Will Jones, who was first elected to the Group 3 seat in 2020, won his reelection bid by claiming 1,960 votes (56.11%) against the 1,533 votes (43.89%) Elizabeth van Rensburg earned, according to unofficial results from the Supervisor of Elections Office.
Meanwhile, the Group 1 contest ended with newcomer Annie Henderson Davis winning 2,243 votes (65.62%) against former Commissioner Allegra Kitchens' 1,175 votes (34.38%).
Davis and Kitchens were competing to take over for Commission Tammie McCaskill who had filed to run for reelection but eventually withdrew from consideration.
Jones and Davis will be sworn in to office in January. Calls to both winners were not returned Thursday evening.
The election results are expected to be official Nov. 15.

title: Bluegrass tunes to fill the air at boys ranch
author: Trisha Murphy
description: It will be a big reunion of sorts when the Palatka Fall Bluegrass Festival takes place at Rodeheaver Boys Ranch this week.
content:
It will be a big reunion of sorts when the Palatka Fall Bluegrass Festival takes place at Rodeheaver Boys Ranch this week.
The event, which begins Thursday and continues until Saturday evening at 380 Boys Ranch Road just south of Palatka, will include numerous popular bluegrass acts, many of which have previously performed in Palatka. Many of the audience members have also frequented the fall and spring versions of the Palatka festival and have wmade friends with other bluegrass enthusiasts.
'The atmosphere of the festival is upbeat and friendly,' said David Poupard, the executive director of Rodeheaver Boys Ranch. 'Everyone is relaxed and glad to be here. Some people have been coming for years and use this as a time to meet up with friends and family. Sometimes, it is friends they have made through coming to the ranch for the festivals.'
The ranch has hosted the festival, which takes place in February and November, for 22 years. An estimated 1,000 to 1,200 people are expected to attend each day of the upcoming festival.
'Bluegrass is fun and entertaining to watch and wholesome family fun,' Poupard said.
The festival will also pay a special tribute to military veterans and will include a classic car show Saturday starting at 10 a.m.
According to Poupard, the festival promoter, Evans Media Source and the ranch hold veterans in very high esteem.
'Time will be set aside at the very beginning of the festival to recognize the sacrifice of our veterans, many of whom are in attendance,' he said. 'The typical bluegrass crowd is very patriotic and this recognition is always a special time.'
One of the featured performers includes a crowd-pleaser who has performed at the ranch for years.
'Rhonda Vincent & The Rage is our most popular artist,' Poupard said. 'However, there are several crowd favorites like the Malpass Brothers, East Nash Grass and Williamson Branch, and everyone loves our emcee Sherry Boyd.'
Vincent, who has been dubbed the Queen of Bluegrass, won the Grammy Award for Best Bluegrass Album in 2017. In 2020, she was inducted as a member of the Grand Ole Opry.
She has appeared on recordings with Dolly Parton, Alan Jackson, Tanya Tucker, Joe Diffie, Faith Hill and others.
Rhonda Vincent & The Rage is scheduled to perform at 3 and 8:30 p.m. Saturday, the latter of which will be the festival finale.
The cost to attend is $55 for a daily ticket, $110 for a three-day general ticket and $125 for a three-day VIP pass. Three-day tickets for ages 12–16 are $50 and $20 for a one-day youth pass.
Guests should bring their own lawn chairs. Coolers are welcome but must fit under the participant's chair.
Lodging will be available in the ranch's RV Park and includes water and power hook-ups.
Burgers, pulled pork sandwiches, fries and soup will be available at the festival's concession stand open from 10 a.m. – 8 p.m. daily. Guests can also have a choice of a home-cooked meal of a main dish, two sides, bread, salad bar, drink and dessert for $18 plus tax in the ranch's dining hall each day from 4:30–6 p.m. For details about lodging or food, call the ranch at 386–328–1281.
For other details about the festival, contact Evans Media Source at 386–385–3500 or EvansMediaSource.com.
Some of the festival's other entertainers include The Gibson Brothers, The Malpass Brothers, East Nash Grass, Southern Legacy, Williamson Branch and Justin Mason & Blue Night. There will be a special performance by The Cox Family, a Grammy award-winning bluegrass group.
New this year is the Bluegrass Gospel Hour hosted by Sandy Back Porch at 7 p.m. today and an open mic time starting at 8 p.m. There is a charge for the service today but officials did not say Tuesday what the charge would be.
'We would love to see some local artists come out,' Poupard said.
Poupard said he loves bluegrass music and invites all of Putnam County and the surrounding areas to visit the ranch for the festival.
'It's a great way to support the work of the ranch and have great fun,' he said. 'We also like how the festival allows us to be part of the Palatka community.'

title: County commissioners, school officials sworn in
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Left hand on the Bible and right hand in the air, six elected officials took their oaths of office Tuesday as they prepared to begin their four-year terms.
content:
Body
Left hand on the Bible and right hand in the air, six elected officials took their oaths of office Tuesday as they prepared to begin their four-year terms.
Family and friends packed the Putnam County Government Complex to see their loved ones step into public life or enter another term in the position in which they were already serving.
Judges Joe Boatwright and Elizabeth 'Libby' Morris swore in District 1 County Commissioner J.R. Newbold III, District 3 County Commissioner Josh Alexander and returning District 5 Commissioner Walton Pellicer II, Putnam County School Board members David Buckles and Sandra Gilyard, and Superintendent Rick Surrency.
Elections Supervisor Charles Overturf III said this year's general election had by far the best turnout he's seen, with 80.5% of eligible voters casting ballots. He said that number is at least 8 percentage points higher than the last presidential election.
'That's the way it ought to be every election,' Overturf said. 'We ought to be in that 75% range all the time, but, unfortunately, I have a pile of people say, 'Charles, I'll see you in four years.' And we really don't see them until the next presidential (election).'
Overturf believes 40 candidates ran for office in Putnam County this year, which is another accomplishment, he said.
'Each one of you should be proud for what you did – one, for just putting your name out to the public,' he said. 'But you understand now that a lot of times, the public doesn't realize how much time and effort and money and stress that there is running a campaign. And when it's successful, it's OK. When it's not, you just have to do the best you can to live through it.'
This is not the first rodeo for Buckles, Gilyard and Surrency, all of whom were reelected to their respective positions. Each said they were happy to help make the Putnam County School District a better place for the area's children and their families.
'My heart belongs to Putnam County, but, most especially, my heart belongs to the children of this great school district,' Gilyard said. '... It takes all of us, and even if it does not go our way, we have purposed in our heart that for the sake of our children, we will still hold our heads up and push forward with whatever was chosen.'
Newbold and Alexander are newcomers to the Board of County Commissioners. Newbold replaced former Commissioner Bill Pickens, who served for eight years.
The District 1 commissioner said he plans to use the support he's received to launch into a successful four-year term on the board.
'I thank the citizens of Putnam County who trusted me with this task ahead,' Newbold said. 'I'm excited. I'm encouraged. I've gotten a lot of support, and I'm going to do my very best to fulfill that.'
Alexander replaced former Commissioner Terry Turner, who served for a bit more than seven years, having been appointed to the position in 2017.
Alexander said he is looking forward to serving Putnam residents, to whom he must always be accountable.
'The way I look at this, I'm a public servant,' Alexander said. 'You guys are my boss. All I'm here to do is make this a better place and enact the policies and procedures that you guys request from me.'
Pellicer isn't a stranger to the board, though. He was first elected to the District 5 seat in 2012 but lost his reelection bid four years later to former Commissioner Buddy Goddard.
This time, Pellicer replaces former Commissioner Paul Adamczyk, who defeated Pellicer and Goddard in 2020. While Pickens and Turner opted out of seeking reelection to public office, Adamczyk ran in the superintendent's race but lost in the Aug. 20 primary.
Pellicer said he knows his late father is looking down on him with pride at this accomplishment.
'I'm glad to be back,' he said. 'There's a lot of challenges facing our county coming up, and I look forward to meeting those head-on and driving our county in a positive direction that we can all be proud of.'

title: Radio station continues turkey day tradition
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Running and walking enthusiasts can trot along downtown Palatka on the morning of Thanksgiving before taking part in their holiday feasts later in the day.
content:
Body
Running and walking enthusiasts can trot along downtown Palatka on the morning of Thanksgiving before taking part in their holiday feasts later in the day.
WHIF 91.3 Hope FM is inviting people to Riverfront Park, 100 Memorial Parkway in Palatka, on Thursday for the Trot For HOPE. The 2-mile walk/run for older children and adults will start at 9:15 a.m., but the Tiny Tot Turkey Trot Kids Fun Run for children 10 and younger will begin at 9 a.m.
The children's event will take place along the riverfront, while the 2-mile walk/run will span downtown Palatka.
Hope FM General Manager Robin Robinson said this will be the radio station's 11th time hosting the race. When the event first began, there were only 150 people who attended.
'As it turns out, Thanksgiving is the largest day for races ever,' she said Monday. '... It's just kind of grown from there
Now, Robinson said, more than 800 people have registered for the Thanksgiving Day festivities, including volunteers.
The cost to sign up before race day is $20 for adults and $10 for kids. Online registration at runsignup.com/Race/FL/Palatka/TrotForHOPE ends today.
People can also register Wednesday at the Hope FM, 3419 St Johns Ave.
Participants are welcome to sign up at 8 a.m. the day of the event, but the 2-mile race registration cost will be $25, Robinson said. The kids' race will still be $10, she added.
All funds raised will benefit the nonprofit Christian radio station.
Although the event has hundreds of people already signed up, Robinson is hoping for more participants Thursday.
'We're hoping we can get 1,000,' she said. 'Most people come just for the fun and for the ministry.'
The first five men to finish in the adult race and the first five women will receive a $25 gift card to Hog Wild Country Cafe, 888 County Road 310 in Interlachen, Robinson said. The first five children to cross the Tiny Tot finish line will get a $10 gift card to the Hoot Owl Farm House ice cream shop, 1821 Reid St. in Palatka, she added.
Robinson said some runners have come from nearby areas like St. Augustine and Jacksonville to participate. She's heard from one family who plans to travel from a different state to trot in honor of their family member who loved to run and was from Putnam County.
'It's just fun,' she said.

title: Young actor eager to shine in ‘Mermaid'
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Get ready to sail the high seas with a young, dashing prince of a seaside kingdom when 'Disney The Little Mermaid Jr.' comes to Palatka.
content:
Body
Get ready to sail the high seas with a young, dashing prince of a seaside kingdom when 'Disney The Little Mermaid Jr.' comes to Palatka.
The show will be performed by the Palatka Junior-Senior High School Musical Theatre Department students under the direction of Jim Pignato.
Showtimes are at 7:30 p.m. Dec. 5–7 with a matinee at 2:30 p.m. Dec. 8 at the Jim Pignato Theater on the campus of the Charles Overturf Jr. District Center, 1100 S. 18th St. in Palatka.
The tickets are $15 in advance at Ralph's House of Flowers, 605 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka, or $20 at the door by cash or check only. All seats are reserved.
Pignato said the show is an adaptation of an 1837 Danish fairy tale written by Hans Christian Anderson. It was a dark and sad story until it was 'Disneyfied,' becoming an animated film in 1989 and later a Broadway show in 2008, Pignato said.
''The Little Mermaid Jr.' is a shortened version of the Broadway show,' he said. 'We like to choose junior versions because instead of the more-than-two-hour Broadway version, they are reduced to about 75 minutes with no intermission.'
According to Disney Theatrical Licensing, show-goers will see the beautiful young mermaid Ariel, who longs to leave her ocean home to live in the world above. But first, she'll have to defy her father, King Triton, make a deal with the evil sea witch, Ursula, and convince Prince Eric she's the girl with the enchanting voice.
Senior Lucas Bergen plays the part of Prince Eric, who has a strong desire for adventure.
'He's very playful, which is why he is not fond of having to be a prince,' said Lucas, 17, who lives in Palatka.
Lucas has been a member of the musical theater program since he was a freshman. His first show was 'Hello Dolly' in the spring of 2022. Some of his favorite shows he has performed in include 'Aladdin,' 'Titanic,' 'The Christmas Carol' and 'The Drowsy Chaperone.'
Lucas finds a certain freedom while acting and being on stage.
'It's all types of acting coming together,' he said. 'You can be subtle or dramatic, quiet or loud. You can play every type of emotion and because of the nature of the stage, you have to actually be what you are trying to portray.'
He plans to go to a university after graduation and said he will 'hopefully' major in kinesiology or health sciences.
'But I won't rule out pursuing a theater degree in college just yet,' he said, smiling.
Lucas said having camaraderie with the show director and his fellow cast members is truly what makes the theater enjoyable to him.
'We are such a family,' he said. 'We spend so much time together learning together. It's difficult to separate yourself from everyone else.'
Lucas admits he still gets very nervous at the beginning of every show, but he pushes past the nerves, even when mishaps occur.
'Usually, there is a specific number or song within the show that I get really anxious about performing,' he said. 'An embarrassing moment for me was in 'The Christmas Carol' during my duet when I had to get on one knee and propose. When I knelt down, the entire inseam of my pants ripped open and I had to stay on stage like that for two more songs.'
Being on stage is a lot of fun, he said, and he hopes that's evident to audience members when they watch the upcoming performances.
'I hope, specifically for the younger audience, they find a love for theater, partly because this is the first show I remember seeing at the Jim Pignato Theater,' he said.
Pignato has loved working with Lucas and will hate to see him leave the theater group when he graduates.
'He is very talented, dependable and hardworking,' the director said.
Pignato said his crew first performed this show in 2013.
'It is expensive to put on a professional-caliber show like we try to produce,' he said. 'The theater program is not a school-budgeted item. All our money comes from ticket sales and donations. We truly appreciate all our donors and the folks in the audiences who support us.'

title: Student ready for spotlight ‘Under the Sea'
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Tasked with tagging along with a headstrong fictional teenager, Peter Fisk has realized 'the seaweed is always greener in somebody else's lake.'
content:
Body
Tasked with tagging along with a headstrong fictional teenager, Peter Fisk has realized 'the seaweed is always greener in somebody else's lake.'
Fisk, 17, will play the role of Sebastian in the Palatka Junior-Senior High School Musical Theater Department's production of 'Disney's The Little Mermaid Jr.' this weekend in Palatka.
'Sebastian is a caring, passionate, stressed-out crab,' Fisk said. 'I love that I have to know my character so well that I can walk, talk and think like him. I also love the energy of a live audience.'
Showtimes are at 7:30 p.m. today through Saturday with a matinee at 2:30 p.m. Sunday at the Jim Pignato Theater at the C.L. Overturf Jr. District Center, 1100 S. 18th St. in Palatka.
The tickets are $15 in advance at Ralph's House of Flowers, 605 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka, or $20 at the door by cash or check only. All seats are reserved.
The show is based on an 1837 Danish fairy tale written by Hans Christian Anderson, according to Jim Pignato, the high school theater department's director. Pignato's musical theater group first performed the show in 2013.
'The Broadway version follows the original animated film but with added songs,' he said. 'The only real noticeable difference is that the climactic final scenes are changed to be less dark and scary for children.'
Fisk is looking forward to being immersed in his character, a meticulous and anxious red Jamaican crab who is a loyal servant to King Triton and a musical composer in the underwater kingdom of Atlantica. He is also in charge of watching over Ariel, the king's youngest daughter, and keeping her safe while leading some of the most memorable songs in the show.
A Hastings resident, Fisk has been part of the high school theater group for four years, and this will be his seventh show. Some of the other shows Fisk has been part of include 'Aladdin,' 'Titanic the Musical,' 'A Christmas Carol' and 'The Drowsy Chaperone.'
Pignato said Fisk, who plans to pursue musical theater in college, has been a staple of the theater department since he entered high school.
'He is talented, dependable and hard-working,' he said. 'He has had several leading roles in shows.'
Peter, whose first show was 'Elf' during his freshman year, said he gets nervous right before every show.
'Nothing too embarrassing, although once I accidentally pushed over a large set piece during a performance,' he said, smiling.
Pignato said the fall show was chosen in an effort to offer matinees to local schools as field trips.
'There are limited options now for school groups to go now, partially because of the expense but also because of a shortage of buses,' he said. 'We also want to expose young children to live theater. The great majority of our cast members tell us that their first experience with live theater was at one of the PHS shows. We often hear that students leave our shows saying, 'I want to do that when I get in high school.''
Fisk is looking forward to this production and hopes the audience has a good time.
'I hope that for an hour and a half, everyone forgets everything else and becomes fully immersed in the show,' he said. 'I hope everyone will come and support us by seeing the show.'
Pignato said half of his cast of 31 students are rookies but are working hard to learn the ropes.
'I don't think most of them knew it was so much work to put on a musical,' he said. 'Now they know.'
Pignato acknowledges it takes a huge crew of helpers to make these shows work.
'I won't name anyone here for fear I will leave someone out,' he said. 'Everyone is a volunteer, and I hope they all know how much they are appreciated.'
Looking back over his tenure with the musical theater department, Fisk loves the people with whom he has gotten to work.
'I met my closest friends through theater,' he said. 'Taking a part as a character in a play allows me to examine the world from someone else's perspective. It lets me practice empathy in a way that many don't get to experience.'

title: Suspected Mullen accomplice granted bond
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A judge granted a hefty bond to a Satsuma woman officials said is connected to the murder of a man whose body was found buried in Hastings.
content:
Body
A judge granted a hefty bond to a Satsuma woman officials said is connected to the murder of a man whose body was found buried in Hastings.
Although she is still incarcerated in the Putnam County Jail, Tina Marie Lee-Ellis, 56, was handed a $540,000 bond during a hearing Monday, according to the Putnam County Clerk of Court. Lee-Ellis is in jail for alleged involvement in the death of Chad Mullen, who was reported missing in September.
Having been arrested last month, Lee-Ellis is charged with accessory to first-degree murder after the fact, tampering with evidence, and failing to report the death of a person with the intent to conceal the death or alter evidence or circumstances around the person's death, according to hearing minutes.
Lee-Ellis must obtain 10% of the bond amount, or $54,000, to be released from the jail.
Conditions of her bond state she must be monitored electronically if released and she is to have no contact with Mullen's family, court documents state. She will return to court Jan. 9 for a pretrial hearing.
On Nov. 7, Lee-Ellis surrendered to the Putnam County Sheriff's Office after being wanted in connection to the death of Mullen, whose body was found Oct. 28 buried at 852 Federal Point Road in Hastings, less than a half-mile from the Putnam-St. Johns boundary.
Mullen's girlfriend, Caylen Deller, 30, was arrested Nov. 8 and charged with first-degree murder with a firearm, tampering with physical evidence and failure to report Mullen's death. Records show she has been denied bond and is set to return to court Jan. 9.
The indictment against Deller alleges she fatally shot Mullen Sept. 9 or 10 and that the act was premeditated. Deller is also accused of tampering with evidence between Sept. 9-12.
Mullen's phone last pinged Sept. 10 near Deller's business, Stormy's Stables, 465 San Mateo Road, his family said in September.
'Caylen Suvanna Deller, knowing that a criminal trial, proceeding, or investigation by a duly constituted prosecuting authority or law enforcement agency was pending or about to be instituted related to a capital felony, did alter, destroy, conceal, or remove the body of Chad Patrick Mullen and/or ropes, ratchet straps, a net, cinder block, grappling hook and/or other items with the purpose to impair its verity or availability in such proceeding or investigation,' Deller's indictment states.
During their investigation, sheriff's office officials searched Lee-Ellis' residence, 131 Pine St. in Satsuma, on Oct. 1 and found numerous items that gave cause for concern, authorities said last month.
'During the search, firearms, ammunition and methamphetamine was located,' Putnam officials stated in a press release in November.
Lee-Ellis was arrested Oct. 21 and released on $25,000 bond a day later before later being arrested in connection to Mullen's murder.
Sheriff's office spokeswoman Allison Waters-Merritt confirmed Lee-Ellis was still in jail Wednesday.

title: Public asked to help libraries fulfill angel's wishes
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Angels are among Putnam County residents and can be seen adorning trees in all five of the area's libraries.
content:
Angels are among Putnam County residents and can be seen adorning trees in all five of the area's libraries.
They aren't just any trees or angels, though. The Angel Book Tree project has Christmas trees that have paper angels with names of children, their ages and the kind of book on their wish lists.
The children who will receive the books are currently staying at the Lee Conlee House domestic violence shelter with their mothers or a safe place with a family member.
'We know there are a lot of national and statewide toy drives, but the Lee Conlee House is a local organization that can always use help, especially around the holiday season,' said Mischa Johns, who oversees special collections with the Putnam County Library System. 'We wanted to make sure that the generosity of Putnam County was shared directly with Putnam County residents in need.'
The library system has sponsored Angel Book Tree for at least 10 years, and area residents are invited to take part this year by picking an 'angel or two or three,' Johns said.
'We need books in good condition, and gently used books will be accepted,' she said. 'We still have plenty of ornaments that need to be selected.'
The deadline to drop off new, unwrapped books to any of the five libraries is 6 p.m. Wednesday. People who choose an angel ornament but cannot fulfill the book wish are asked to return it to the library as soon as possible so it can be put back on a tree.
The participating libraries are the Palatka library, 601 College Road; Bostwick library, 125 Tillman St. in Palatka; Interlachen library, 133 County Road 315; Crescent City library, 610 N. Summit St.; and Melrose library, 306 Wynwood Ave. For details, call Johns at 386-329-0126.
Lori Slaven, the executive director of the Lee Conlee House, said the shelter currently has eight children and moms living there with about 25 people staying in safe homes.
'We're extremely appreciative to receive these books,' she said. 'It's unfortunate when families have to leave their homes and come into shelter. Often, they don't bring anything with them. So to have something they can call their own is so special to them.'
According to Johns, the Lee Conlee House hosts a toy drive every year and area residents show out with their generosity.
'We are glad that they are able to have lots of fun toys, but also want them to have the experience of owning and enjoying books about the things they love,' she said. 'We hope that it will foster a love of reading when they are able to own books of their own.'
Johns is happy to have the library be part of the Angel Book Tree project.
'Our library-loving residents have always been kind and generous for years,' she said. 'And we want to thank them for helping out Putnam County kids in need have a special holiday season filled with joy and reading.'

title: Palatka man arrested after police find stabbing victim
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Authorities said it didn't take long to find the person accused of stabbing a man they found bleeding on a Palatka porch.
content:
Authorities said it didn't take long to find the person accused of stabbing a man they found bleeding on a Palatka porch.
Palatka resident Tavarous Quenard Wright, 32, was arrested Thursday and charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, according to a Facebook post by the Palatka Police Department.
Officers responded to 116 Belmont Drive on Thursday in reference to someone being stabbed, officials wrote without specifying the time of day.
Upon arrival, officers found a 39-year-old Palatka man lying on the front porch and bleeding from several stab wounds, according to the social media post. Officers gave the victim medical aid until emergency medical technicians arrived on scene, the department reported. Authorities said the victim told the officers Wright was the person who stabbed him.
Despite where the victim was found, the police reported the primary crime scene was at 114 Belmont Drive.
'Officers formed a perimeter and with the help of the Putnam County Sheriff's Office and were able to quickly apprehend Wright,' police personnel said in the press release.
Police detectives took over the investigation and concluded Wright was the person who stabbed the victim, according to the release.
'(The victim), who was transported to a local trauma center, is in stable condition and expected to make a full recovery,' the police said in the statement, which was posted shortly before 3 p.m. today.
People who have any information about the stabbing are asked to call Detective David Lazo at 386-329-0115.
Wright is being held in the Putnam County Jail without bond, according to the police. Jail records, however, show he has been given the benefit of a $100,000 bond but is still in custody.

title: Former cheerleaders return to ROAR in Jax
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Five women with ties to Putnam County had a unique opportunity to step back in time to experience the power of the ROAR.
content:
Body
Five women with ties to Putnam County had a unique opportunity to step back in time to experience the power of the ROAR.
The former Jacksonville Jaguar cheerleaders – La'Farrah Davis, Jaime Williams Hampton, LaShan Simmons, Jade Skidmore Altman and Julie Hunsicker Purinton – were invited to EverBank Stadium on Dec. 15 to give a special combined performance with current cheerleaders. The performance took place during the Jags' game against the New York Jets and was part of the commemoration of the Jacksonville franchise's 30 season.
Davis performed with the ROAR from 2010 to 2015 and was named Rookie of the Year in 2010 and the cheer group captain in 2015.
'The best memory I had as a member of the ROAR of the Jaguars was auditioning three times before making the team the fourth year of auditioning,' said Davis who cheered for Palatka High School before graduating in 2001. 'When I was awarded Rookie of the Year, it was truly my time and my year.'
Davis, 42, said she was told more than 150 cheerleaders came from near and far to take part in the reunion.
'It was an absolutely phenomenal weekend to reminisce on those glory days of sharing my gifts and talents, serving as an ambassador of the Jaguars organization and dancing alongside other phenomenal women,' said Davis, who lives in Jacksonville with her 17-month-old son, Carter L. Wilson.
Davis, who also danced and cheered on the collegiate level, is employed full time with the city of Jacksonville's utility company, JEA. She is also the coordinator of the Palatka Juneteenth community cultural event and president of Heart & Soul Youth Fine Arts Club, which she started with a goal of empowering, inspiring and motivating children through the arts.
Although the Jacksonville team lost 32-25 to the Jets, spirits remained high for the Putnam County ladies who returned to their stomping ground to visit family, friends and fellow ROAR alumnae during the celebration.
Hampton, who cheered with the ROAR in 2000 and 2001, was excited to make the trip from her home in Waynesville, North Carolina, where she lives with her husband, Bernie, and three children, Elijah, Ethan and Elise.
'It was a nostalgic moment, stepping onto the field to perform another pregame dance,' she said. 'It has been five years since the 25th reunion in which we also danced the pregame performance.'
Hampton said the past ROAR members had only three days to learn the fast-paced choreography, with heavier-than-normal pompoms no less.
'Don't they know we are getting older and need as light of a pompom as possible,' she joked. 'The next reunion, I'm requesting more than a week to learn choreography since we will be five years older.'
Hampton is a full-time hygienist for Great Smiles Pediatric, is active in her church and her children's extracurricular activities, and loves mountain bike riding and going to the gym regularly.
Hampton is looking forward to the next alumnae ROAR reunion.
'What an adrenaline rush and such a blast to be back with 20 of the girls I specifically cheered with, along with my Palatka girls,' she said.
Altman, who graduated from Palatka High School in 2001, said she was moved by the outpouring of support from her family and friends outside of the ROAR.
'Many people reached out and said they were willing to travel to see me dance again in person and got to the game early to make sure they saw me,' she said. 'It made the weekend very memorable.'
Altman also enjoyed meeting up with old friends she met while cheering with the ROAR in 2007 and 2008.
'Many of them, I still hang out with today,' she said.
Altman, 41, lives in St. Augustine with her husband, Jesse Daniel Altman, and three kids, twin daughters, Laiken and Maxwell, 6, and son, Zev, 2.
'My best memory is meeting amazing women whom I am still in touch with today,' she said. 'Being a Jaguar cheerleader allowed me to meet some amazing people.'
Simmons, who graduated from Palatka High School in 1994, has been employed with Duval County Public School for more than 13 years as the internal accounts/finance supervisor. She cheered with the ROAR from 2000 to 2001 and the Atlanta Falcons in 2003.
Simmons said there was never a dull moment during the ROAR reunion.
'How can it be when you get hundreds of beautiful, talented, educated and successful ladies together that are enjoying life, including the crew from Palatka?' she said. 'Performing with the ROAR, I made a lot of friendships with beautiful women that shared the same goal and passion as myself.'
Simmons, who is a member of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, said that in addition to performing in the pregame show, the reunion involved the former ROAR members attending a black-tie formal.
'We represented Palatka in the NFL,' said the mother of two boys, A'darius and Kenoy, who lives in Jacksonville. 'We are all former Palatka High School cheerleaders, college graduates, moms and successful women in our field of work.'
Simmons, 48, said it was exciting to await the arrival of fellow teammates at the reunion so they could share stories, family pictures and life experiences.
'Being a part of the ROAR introduced me to women I may have never met otherwise,' she said. 'Cheering with the ROAR provided the opportunity to travel abroad as well. The routine we performed was challenging, but us older ladies made it through the performance.'
Purinton, 49, lives in Jonesboro, Arkansas, with her husband, Jeff, who is the athletics director at Arkansas State University, and their two daughters, Jillian and Jose. She graduated in 1993 from Palatka High School and was a pioneer of sorts for Palatka cheerleaders hoping to join the ROAR.
'I was the first woman from Palatka to make the team,' said Purinton, who was part of the ROAR from 1997 to 1999 and served as captain from 1998 to 1999. 'I loved being a part of the Roar Palatka sisterhood.'
Although her days are no longer spent practicing for and performing at Jaguar games, Purinton still finds ways to stay occupied.
'I stay busy being a stay-at-home mom, part-time fitness instructor, and attending tons of sporting events for my daughters and Arkansas State University,' she said.

title: Groups offer warm refuge from frigid temperatures
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Volunteers are opening the doors of a Palatka church tonight and Wednesday night to house people who need a place to stay as temperatures plummet.
content:
Body
Volunteers are opening the doors of a Palatka church tonight and Wednesday night to house people who need a place to stay as temperatures plummet.
The Putnam County Caring Coalition, a nonprofit organization formed to provide shelter for homeless people, is hosting the Temporary Overnight Safe Space program at First Presbyterian Church's Westminster Hall, 126 S. Second St. in Palatka. The shelter first opened Monday evening and will reopen from 7 p.m. – 7 a.m. today and Wednesday.
Georgia Mitchell, the executive director of the Caring Coalition, said the church offered the space for the organization to use. Thanks to volunteers and donations, the group can give people a warm place to stay as temperatures are predicted to be in the low 30s for most of the week.
'We just want our folks to know that at 2 o'clock in the morning, they're safe,' Mitchell said. 'Their stuff is safe. … There's someone awake and watching over them and their items. It's very important when you're unhoused.'
Each night, the center stays open for the first two hours for people to grab a snack, water or a cup of coffee before the doors are locked and the lights are dimmed as people prepare to sleep.
On Monday, some people parked their bikes outside Westminster Hall and prepared to sleep on cots or in sleeping bags inside. They watched 'Walker, Texas Ranger' or talked with some of the attendants.
One man said he had just come inside after discovering his bike pump and clothes had been stolen. Another man said he was down on his luck after experiencing a back injury, which is why he had taken refuge at the shelter.
While First Presbyterian has opened its facility as a cold weather shelter during the past few winters, Mitchell said the coalition first started running an emergency weather shelter there in October.
She estimated about 10 people used the facility each night it is open.
'We're seeing that steadily trend upward,' Mitchell said. 'We started out with five, and then we went to eight. And then really weather-adverse, whether it's cold or raining, that'll pop up and be a little larger.'
Sue Hege, who has been volunteering at the shelter for three weeks, said there have been many people putting in the effort to provide resources for people who are homeless. The coalition is receiving a lot of support, Hege and Mitchell said.
'I'm just giddy over this,' Hege said.
The Safe Space program is not fully complete so volunteers are unable to provide full meals yet, but they share whatever donations they receive. Mitchell said the organization partners with Bread of Life, which offers meals at 320 N. Fifth St. in Palatka on Mondays through Fridays from 11:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.
People can also use showers at Westminster Hall twice a week if there are enough volunteers, Mitchell said. The coalition has a volunteer there to connect homeless people with resources that may be able to help them get back on their feet, she added.
'For us, it's more than just giving people a warm place to stay or a cool place to stay,' Mitchell said, referencing the hot weather shelter they operate in the summer. 'It's about giving them dignity and a ramp up if they want to do something different with their life.'
People can donate to the coalition by dropping items off at the church office, 123 S. Second St., or they can call Mitchell at 609-865-6706.
