Palatka Housing Authority
Accepting Applications
for the Assisted Housing Program
(Housing Choice Voucher / Section 8)
The Palatka Housing Authority (PHA) will be accepting Pre-applications for the Assisted Housing Program (Housing Choice Voucher/Section 8) starting Wednesday, January 15, 2025 until Thursday, February 27, 2025.
Pre-application eligibility is based on family income ONLY. Housing Choice Vouchers will be issued based on availability, local preferences, time and date of application, and eligibility screening, including background and landlord checks.
TO APPLY
In order to be placed on the waiting list, you must complete a pre-application that can be obtained from the lobby of the PHA. The pre-application can be mailed to Palatka Housing Authority, P.O. Box 1277, Palatka, FL 32178-1277(must be post-marked no later than 02/27/25); or placed in the drop box at the PHA located at 400 North 15th Street, Palatka, FL 32177 (no later than 02/27/25). You may also visit the PHA website at www.palatkaha.org to download a pre-application. Applicants that require a reasonable accommodation can contact the PHA at (386) 329-0132 or submit a written request.
To qualify, annual gross household income cannot exceed:
FAMILY SIZE - MAXIMUM GROSS
INCOME
1 Person - $22,850
2 Persons - $26,100
3 Persons - $29,350
4 Persons - $32,600
5 Persons - $35,250
6 Persons - $37,850
7 Persons - $40,450
8 Persons - $43,050
All applicants will be screened for eligibility. The PHA gives local preferences to military veterans; families whose head of household or spouse is elderly or near-elderly; families that include a person who is the head of household or spouse that has a disability; families that have been displaced through no fault of their own due to a federally-declared natural disaster; victims of domestic violence; victims of a pandemic; and families that are homeless.
If you have any questions, please contact the PHA Monday thru Thursday at (386) 329-0132, between the hours of 8:00 a.m. and 6:30 p.m.

title: Race to raise money for women's resources
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Organizers of a 5K run are inviting people to get their sneakers ready to raise money for a local resource center and celebrate the life of a teen who would have supported this mission.
content:
Organizers of a 5K run are inviting people to get their sneakers ready to raise money for a local resource center and celebrate the life of a teen who would have supported this mission.
The sixth annual Life Distance, 5K and Fun Run starts at 4 p.m. Jan. 25 at Coventry Oaks Farm, 104 Springside Cutoff Road in Palatka. Participants will be helping raise money for A Women's Resource Center, 219 N. Palm Ave. in Palatka.
The organization is funded through community donations and aids women and families during unplanned pregnancies, 5K organizer Kraig McLane said.
'(It) serves all of Putnam County and beyond,' he said. 'All the things they do (include) counseling parents, men and women, and providing for their families. … That's the real focus of the events, hence the name the 'Life 5K.''
The race categories will be a 6.8-mile run, a 1-mile run and the traditional 5K. Each includes a barbecue chicken dinner, but people are also welcome to sign up to eat the meal without breaking a sweat.
Sign-ups start at $15 for the meal only and can reach $65 if people register on race day to run and grab a meal. Registrations can be done at runsignup.com/Race/Info/FL/Palatka/LifeRun in advance or at Coventry Oaks on Jan. 25 starting at 2 p.m.
While the event has been going on for six years, this will be the second year the races are honoring former Palatka Junior-Senior High School student Baylee Holbrook. Holbrook died at 16 in September 2023 after being struck by lightning during a hunting trip with her father.
Now, her parents continue to honor her legacy with the Baylee Holbrook Foundation. Her mother, Casey Holbrook, said they are not raising money for the foundation because they, too, want to give back to the resource center.
'We actually wanted to donate everything back because we believe in this because I was a teen mom,' Casey Holbrook said.
She got pregnant with her first daughter at 18 and with Baylee Holbrook six months after her first daughter was born. Casey Holbrook said she was 19 when Baylee Holbrook was born.
'So just for me, being a teen mom and looking at the impact that my teen girls had on their community through their faith, this is so important to us,' Casey Holbrook said. 'This is why this ministry and what they do there, it's a big deal.'
Casey Holbrook said her late daughter loved children and was constantly babysitting or helping kids at their church, Trinity Baptist Church of Palatka. Baylee Holbrook would have wanted to pour her heart into a ministry like A Women's Resource Center, her mother said.
Not everyone who becomes pregnant has the resources or support to carry a child, but Casey Holbrook believes that no child is unwanted.
As Christians, she said, people should not only say they are pro-life but also stand up to help families who might have nowhere else to go.
'I think it's very important that, for mothers especially, to know that they've got a town that'll stand behind them,' she said. 'And they've got resources, and they've got things – if they choose to parent or choose adoption – to not just be so scared.'

title: Frigid weather prompts 1-day school closure
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Putnam County School District announced its schools and other buildings will close Wednesday as the county could face treacherous conditions brought on by cold weather.
content:
Body
Putnam County School District announced its schools and other buildings will close Wednesday as the county could face treacherous conditions brought on by cold weather.
A freeze warning for Putnam County is in effect through 10 a.m. Wednesday, according to The Weather Channel. The agency cautioned drivers to look out for slippery road conditions, especially this morning, and prepare for cold wind chills.
Superintendent Rick Surrency said all students and district employees will have the day off so no one tries to drive to or from any district facility.
'Out of an abundance of caution due to the icy roads and hazardous driving conditions we want our students and employees to remain home off the road for their safety,' Surrency said in a text message.
Individual schools should let families know if after-school activities for today are canceled, according to a district press release.
Students and employees are expected to return to the district Thursday, Surrency said. Despite district facilities reopening Thursday, Surrency advised parents to make sure their children are prepared for the frosty temperatures that are expected throughout the week.
'Please ensure students are dressed warmly for bus rides and outdoor activities,' district officials said in a press release.
The Putnam County Parks and Recreation Department announced today via Facebook that all recreational events had been canceled for the evening.
The Weather Channel predicted rain to start around 5 p.m. today and last through Wednesday morning.
'Appropriate action should be taken to ensure tender vegetation and outdoor pets have adequate protection from the cold temperatures,' Weather Channel officials said in an alert today. 'Young children, the elderly and the homeless are especially vulnerable to the cold. Take measures to protect them.'
Some parts of the Panhandle received snow this afternoon, but no snow has been forecasted to fall in Putnam County.
Still, one local organization is preparing to keep vulnerable people warm as temperatures plummet.
The Putnam County Caring Coalition is opening a cold-weather shelter at First Presbyterian Church's Westminster Hall, 126 S. Second St. in Palatka, at 7 p.m. today. Executive Director Georgia Mitchell said the shelter will be open from 7 p.m. – 7 a.m. daily through Saturday morning.
The shelter can house up to 30 people, she estimated as she echoed The Weather Channel's warning about protecting the young, elderly and homeless.
'In this type of weather, it makes it difficult for unhoused people to stay warm, safe and dry,' Mitchell said.
She said people who lose heat in their homes this week are also welcome to take shelter at Westminster Hall, where hot drinks, snacks and hot showers will be provided.
'We want to make it as easy as possible to keep people comfortable,' Mitchell said.
For more information about the shelter, call Mitchell at 609-865-6706.

title: From Heartache to Triumph
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: The crowd gathered this week at the former school bus depot next to the historic Central Academy had much to celebrate.
content:
Body
The crowd gathered this week at the former school bus depot next to the historic Central Academy had much to celebrate.
Epic-Cure, a nonprofit food distribution center that less than a year ago was forced to find a new Putnam County base of operations, had a ribbon-cutting ceremony Thursday to celebrate moving into its new location and forming additional partnerships.
Having started in St. Augustine and setting up shop in Palatka in May 2020, Epic-Cure donates food to other food banks for them to give to members of the community. The nonprofit also has people visit its facility by appointment only to collect food as if they were shopping in a grocery store.
Epic-Cure Co-founder Sunny Mulford, who is also the organization's executive director, said opening the new distribution center at 1207 Washington St. has removed a tremendous weight from her and other volunteers' shoulders.
She was informed in August the group would need to vacate its previous building, 389 U.S. 17 in Palatka, by Dec. 1, so Epic-Cure officials began scrambling to find a new location and raise $100,000 to cover moving costs.
'And the first building that we had selected, that one kind of fell apart,' Mulford said. 'So, really, we didn't even get this place until November. And we had only six weeks to get it ready for us to be in here.
'The timeline and the financial crisis that we went through, I mean, it was very, very stressful. We weren't sure we were going to survive.'
She said there had been talks of completely shuttering its Palatka setup and operating solely out of St. Augustine. But given how much hard work Epic-Cure's volunteers had been putting in – as well as the great need for the service in Putnam County – the only solution was to work harder to ensure the nonprofit found a new Palatka location, Mulford said.
Ken Mulford, who co-founded Epic-Cure with his wife, was excited to begin operating in a new building. He was especially thankful for Historic Central Academy Preservation CDC Inc., the group that owns the Epic-Cure property that sits next to the former school.
Despite its troubles last year, Ken Mulford said, Epic-Cure had doubled the amount of food it collected and distributed per month from 500,000 pounds to 1 million pounds. He hopes this new beginning will lead to Epic-Cure supplying even more food to the community.
'We have gone through a hell of a 15-month period, and we have come out with this wonderful place with all these wonderful people with their broad shoulders and their big hearts,' Ken Mulford said. 'We could not be more happy, nor could we be more proud. … And we're only going to get bigger now because of all this, because of all of our partnerships, because of all the people who contributed.'
Shirley Edwards, the president of Historic Central Academy Preservation, said she anticipates great things coming from the partnership between the two groups.
While Epic-Cure continues its mission of providing food to the community, Edwards said, Historic Central Academy Preservation will carry on its efforts to return the school to its former glory.
'So they're literally feeding the community,' Edwards said of Epic-Cure. 'And we're on a task to feed our community by continuing our project here with restoring and rebuilding Central Academy.'
Thursday's ceremony wasn't without tears, albeit tears of joy. Epic-Cure board member and volunteer Wendy Caudill presented her sister, Sunny Mulford, with flowers as she congratulated her and the rest of Epic-Cure's volunteers for their tenacity and strong desire to serve.
Breaking her promise to not cry, Caudill said her sister's big heart and desire to carry on with the group's Palatka efforts reflect the hope Epic-Cure officials leaned on during their tumultuous second half of 2024.
Now in a new building, Epic-Cure will continue to lead with love as volunteers and community partners work to feed people in need, she said.
'As you may know, the heart and soul of this charity has always been about bringing people together, ensuring that no one goes hungry,' Caudill said. 'But beyond the practical surface of this building, it is a symbol of dedication, the love and the care this entire community has poured out.'

The intent to issue and application file are available for public inspection during normal business hours, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, except legal holidays, at the Department's Northeast District Office, 8800 Baymeadows Way West, Suite 100, Jacksonville, Florida 32256-7577, at phone number (904)256-1700.
NOTICE OF RIGHTS
The Department will issue the permit unless a petition for an administrative hearing is timely filed under Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S., before the deadline for filing a petition. On the filing of a timely and sufficient petition, this action will not be final and effective until further order of the Department. Because the administrative hearing process is designed to formulate final agency action, the hearing process may result in a modification of the agency action or even denial of the application.
Petition for Administrative Hearing
A person whose substantial interests are affected by the Department's action may petition for an administrative proceeding (hearing) under Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S. Pursuant to Rules 28-106.201 and 28-106.301, F.A.C., a petition for an administrative hearing must contain the following information:
(a) The name and address of each agency affected and each agency's file or identification number, if known;
(b) The name, address, any e-mail address, any facsimile number, and telephone number of the petitioner, if the petitioner is not represented by an attorney or a qualified representative; the name, address, and telephone number of the petitioner's representative, if any, which shall be the address for service purposes during the course of the proceeding; and an explanation of how the petitioner's substantial interests will be affected by the agency determination;
(c) A statement of when and how the petitioner received notice of the Department's agency decision;
(d) A statement of all disputed issues of material fact. If there are none, the petition must so indicate;
(e) A concise statement of the ultimate facts alleged, including the specific facts that the petitioner contends warrant reversal or modification of the agency's proposed action;
(f) A statement of the specific rules or statutes the petitioner contends require reversal or modification of the agency's proposed action, including an explanation of how the alleged facts relate to the specific rules or statutes; and
(g) A statement of the relief sought by the petitioner, stating precisely the action that the petitioner wishes the agency to take with respect to the agency's proposed action.
The petition must be filed (received by the Clerk) in the Office of General Counsel of the Department at 3900 Commonwealth Boulevard, Mail Station 35, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-3000, or via electronic correspondence at Agency_Clerk@FloridaDEP.gov. Also, a copy of the petition shall be mailed to the applicant at the address indicated above at the time of filing.
Time Period for Filing a Petition
Petitions filed by any persons other than the applicant, and other than those entitled to written notice under Section 120.60(3), F.S., must be filed within 14 days of publication of the notice or within 14 days of receipt of the written notice, whichever occurs first. The failure to file a petition within the appropriate time period shall constitute a waiver of that person's right to request an administrative determination (hearing) under Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S., or to intervene in this proceeding and participate as a party to it. Any subsequent intervention (in a proceeding initiated by another party) will be only at the discretion of the presiding officer upon the filing of a motion in compliance with Rule 28-106.205, F.A.C.
Extension of Time
Under Rule 62-110.106(4), F.A.C., a person whose substantial interests are affected by the Department's action may also request an extension of time to file a petition for an administrative hearing. The Department may, for good cause shown, grant the request for an extension of time. Requests for extension of time must be filed with the Office of General Counsel of the Department at 3900 Commonwealth Boulevard, Mail Station 35, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-3000, or via electronic correspondence at Agency_Clerk@FloridaDEP.gov, before the deadline for filing a petition for an administrative hearing. A timely request for extension of time shall toll the running of the time period for filing a petition until the request is acted upon.
Mediation
Mediation is not available in this proceeding.

title: Church celebrating historic marker with day of events
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Members of the Peniel Baptist Church in Palatka will celebrate their heritage Saturday when the Florida Division of Historical Resources will honor the church with an official marker designating th
content:
Body
Members of the Peniel Baptist Church in Palatka will celebrate their heritage Saturday when the Florida Division of Historical Resources will honor the church with an official marker designating the old chapel built in 1870 as a historic site.
The late Billy Graham is known to have preached at the old chapel, which stands across the street from 5227 Silver Lake Drive in Palatka, where Peniel currently has its church services.
According to the Rev. Bob Bogart, the interim pastor at Peniel, a young Billy Graham was baptized in 1938 by Peniel's pastor at the time, the Rev. Cecil Underwood, in Silver Lake at the Edward Day property.
In January 1939, Graham was ordained to the Gospel ministry by Underwood, who is buried in the church's cemetery.
'Peniel Baptist Church is mentioned in Billy Graham's autobiography, 'Just As I Am,'' he said. 'He describes his ordination in the book (as), 'The little white frame church, about four windows long; it was hot and I was nervous.''
Special guests at Saturday's Heritage Day celebration will include local dignitaries, as well as representatives from the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, Samaritan's Purse representative Jason Kimak and Division of Historical Resources employee Jeremy Heiker.
The event will be from 10 a.m.–2 p.m. and will have an opening prayer by Bogart. Other guests will include Graham's grandsons, William Franklin 'Wil' Graham IV and Roy Graham.
According to Bogart, the celebration is open to everyone.
'This day has also morphed into an unofficial Old Fashion Day, where, if desired, people can attend in a late 19th century period style,' he said.
Peniel member Kaye Tucker got the ball rolling for the historic site designation by applying to the state in early 2023. On Sept. 14, 2023, the church was notified the marker had been approved, and in July 2024, it was installed.
'It is really an honor that Peniel Baptist Church has this heritage of Billy Graham's worldwide ministry, which was started right here,' she said.
That ministry included Samaritan's Purse's Operation Christmas Child, which provides gifts for children in need around the world.
Celeste Bass, Peniel's director of missions, said Operation Christmas Child is not just about gifts. It's also about sharing the gospel with families.
'The church is so honored to be a part of this, even if it's in a small way,' she said. 'This is making an impact on lives around the world.'
Other highlights of Saturday's event will be tours of the old chapel, music and plenty of food.
'We are thrilled to commemorate these memorable events,' Bogart said. 'We hope everyone will come be a part of making this a memorable day for them and their family. Why not come dressed in old-fashioned style? It could be fun. Come on out.'

title: Alumni look back fondly on historic college
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Targie Fisher remembers looking out the window on the bus she rode every day to high school and dreaming about a better future.
content:
Body
Targie Fisher remembers looking out the window on the bus she rode every day to high school and dreaming about a better future.
Now 80, the Johnson Crossroads area resident, whose married name is Targie Rhim, remembers how tough times were when she grew up on a farm helping her parents.
'My motivation was not to live as my parents,' she said.
That hard work was the driving force for Rhim to register for classes at Collier-Blocker Junior College in Palatka following graduation in 1962 from Central Academy, where she was named valedictorian.
As a way to observe Black History Month, six alumni of Collier-Blocker Junior College and other guests met Feb. 18 at St. Johns River State College in Palatka to share memories and recall the students and faculty who had a lasting impact and helped shape the school.
The meeting took place at the exhibit wall dedicated in 2012 to the Black college.
Collier-Blocker Junior College, named for educators Nathan W. Collier and Sara Blocker, was established in 1960 and was one of 12 Black junior colleges in the state.
The college began offering classes at what is now Greater Shiloh Missionary Baptist Church, 1000 N. 19th St. in Palatka. There were 59 students enrolled during the first year and 105 at the college's peak. Collier-Blocker eventually merged with St. Johns River Junior College in 1965.
The following people attended the February meeting at SJR State:
Sammie L. Tomblin
Making the trip from Casselberry was Sammie L. Tomblin, 82, who was 18 when he started attending Collier-Blocker, where he eventually became the student body president.
Tomblin graduated from the local Black college in 1962 with his associate degree before transferring to Florida Memorial College to complete his Bachelor of Science in science and elementary education in 1964.
According to Tomblin, what stuck out to him about Collier-Blocker was that some of the students were much older than the rest.
'They were there to further their education,' he said. 'We had students in the initial group from Clay, St. Johns and Putnam counties.'
Tomblin didn't stop his education process after receiving his bachelor's degree. He later went on to earn a master's degree in education in 1973 and a PhD in higher education from Florida State University.
Tomblin says he is proud to be a member of the Collier-Blocker alumni, which includes educators, administrators, business managers, leaders, professors, social workers, military veterans and more.
'I was so happy that someone decided we needed to get together,' he said. 'It's an honor to have attended Collier-Blocker. It's something I will carry with me to my grave.'
Vivian McRae
Another Collier-Blocker alumna at the meeting was Palatka resident Vivian McRae, who attended the Palatka college for a year before transferring to Florida A&M University in Tallahassee.
A 1963 Central Academy graduate, McRae, now 78, attended Collier-Blocker when the school was adjacent to her high school.
'I enjoyed the small classes and still being able to see classmates,' she said.
McRae also attended Bethune-Cookman College – currently known as Bethune-Cookman University – where in 1984 she earned a degree in management.
Cleo S. Higgins
Sean C. Higgins, 62, of Daytona Beach, was at the alumni meet-up and brought newspaper clippings and other documents about the Black college his mother, Cleo S. Higgins, who was dean at the college, had saved.
She was the first Black instructor at then-St. Johns River Junior College in 1965 and was voted Teacher of the Year the same year.
According to Higgins, his mother and father, Dr. William H. Higgins Jr., were activists and helped the Department of Education with integrating the Putnam County School District.
Donald DeBose
Donald DeBose, 78, of Interlachen didn't have to travel far to meet with her college classmates.
In 1964, he attended one semester at Collier-Blocker before joining the U.S. Air Force, serving three years and nine months on active duty and two years and three months on inactive duty.
Annie B. Jackson
Now 86, Annie B. Jackson has fond memories of attending Collier-Blocker.
'The two things I liked best was that it was easily accessible and I could walk to school, and it was affordable,' she said.
Jackson graduated from Central Academy in 1955 and was a student at Collier-Blocker from 1962 to 1963 before transferring to Florida Memorial College in St. Augustine, where she received her Bachelor of Arts in elementary education. She later earned her master's and doctorate degrees.
Targie Rhim
Targie Rhim attended Collier-Blocker from 1962 to 1964 and received her associate degree. She would later receive a Bachelor of Science in mathematics from Florida A&M University.
Her first teaching position was at Central Academy, where she taught math from 1966 to 1968.
Levetta Pierce Parker
Levetta Pierce Parker, 78, of Palatka, was a 1963 graduate of Central Academy. She enrolled at Collier-Blocker in 1964 and stayed for two years before taking classes at St. Johns River Junior College.
In 1969, she graduated from Florida A&M University with a degree in sociology and social welfare.
She went on to receive a degree in social work, a career that spanned 40 years.
Parker said she has fond memories of her college experience at Collier-Blocker.
'It was my first adventure of being exposed to different types of culture,' she said.
'I enjoyed college because even though I was at home, I got a taste of what it was like to be out on my own. I learned a lot from my family, but Collier-Blocker was like an extended part of my family.'

CALL FOR BIDS
The Putnam County Board of County Commissioners is requesting sealed bids from qualified contractors for South Putnam Drainage Improvements. The work includes furnishing all material and labor to expand the drainage improvements related to the South Putnam Drainage Ditch project. Following is a description and map of the proposed improvements:
1. Provide approximately 135 lf of 15' wide (2,025 sf) rubble riprap ditch lining along the east side of CR309 from 20' south of the cross culvert, north to the intersecting ditch from the east. Use lining detail (Typical Section 1) included in the design plans, adjusting the bottom width to match existing ditch.
2. Extend approximately 1,000 sf of ditch lining along west side of CR309 from the cross culvert, approximately 30' to the north. Use lining detail (Typical Section 1) included in the design plans, adjusting the bottom width to match existing ditch.
3. Provide approximately 1500 sf rubble riprap ditch lining within the ditch intersection at the south end of the cross culvert under St Johns Fishing Lodge Rd. Extend lining approximately 20' from end of culvert down the north-south ditch. Use lining detail (Typical Section 1) included in the design plans, adjusting the bottom width to match existing ditch.
4. Shave down east shoulder of CR309 and remove material to 3' below edge of pavement from Alabama St north to the cross culvert. Remove vegetation and regrade ditch from Alabama St to the cross culvert (approximately 450 lf). Provide 6% slope 5' from EOP and 4:1 max slope to bottom of ditch. Install 6' of Argentine bahia sod along edge of pavement. Seed and mulch all other slopes with Argentine bahia.
5. Replace 60 lf, 18' CMP under Alabama St with 24' RCP. Install two straight headwalls per FDOT Index 430-030 and repair approximately 500 sf of asphalt road per Asphalt Patch Detail.
6. Replace 60 lf, 36' CMP under Tennessee Ave St with 36' RCP. Install two straight headwalls per FDOT Index 430-030 and repair approximately 900 sf of asphalt road per Asphalt Patch Detail.
7. Replace 60 lf, 36' CMP under Maryland Ave with 36' RCP. Install two straight headwalls per FDOT Index 430-030 and repair limerock road.
8. Clean and regrade ditch from Park Ave north to the cross culvert at St Johns Fishing Lodge Road, approximately 1,000 lf. Ditch bottom should provide continuous slope between pipe inverts. Any inverted driveways shall be removed and the ditch slope reestablished.
The CONTRACTOR shall be responsible to ensure that all installations that are completed shall be equal to or exceed the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) specifications as outlined in the latest edition of the Standard Specifications for Road and Bridge Construction and the latest addition of the FDOT Roadway Design Standards.

title: Well-rounded Beyond the Classroom
description: New Palatka High clubs, sports enhance students' school experience A student's high school career can involve more than just hitting the books, and school officials have worked to offer a wide array…
content:
New Palatka High clubs, sports enhance students' school experience A student's high school career can involve more than just hitting the books, and school officials have worked to offer a wide array of activities to appeal to all of their students. The number of extracurricular activities Palatka Junior-Senior High School offers its students continues to grow, to include a pickleball club and a drone team. Assistant Principal Cindy Bellamy said the school tries to offer as many opportunities as possible – and not just in academics – to students. 'These are well-rounded kids,' she said. 'They aren't just smart. They aren't just talented. They aren't just athletic. They're a little bit of everything.' This school year, Palatka High added extracurricular activities like a competitive dance team and competitive cheerleading, administrators said. Photo submitted by Cathy Oyster – Palatka Junior-Senior High School Drone team members Mason Blevins and Evan Williamson hoist a trophy after winning a tournament in the club's inaugural year. The school now has an Esports team, too. The Palatka High drone team won the Putnam County Schools Drone Races Championship this year, the team's inaugural year. Students might be interested in theater, sports, band, JROTC or more, and Palatka High has it, Assistant Principal Joy Eubanks said. Principal Cathy Oyster said the school has the only Putnam County Junior Bassmasters Club fishing team in the area. Two students took home first-place awards in February during the Florida BASS Nation fishing tournament. School officials also started a travel club and a pickleball club and are working to rebuild the Palatka High band and chorus programs to their former glory. 'I feel like we offer such a variety here that they can find something that they're really interested in, and we really encourage them to find the area that you're interested in,' Eubanks said. Photo submitted by Cathy Oyster – The Palatka Junior-Senior High School competitive dance team wins trophies and medals during one of their competitions. School sports have expanded to prepare junior high students for Florida High School Athletic Association-designated sports. Assistant Principal Lamar Purifoy said the seventh and eighth grade football team became part of the Suwannee Middle School Association, where the players will get to compete for a championship at the end of the football season. Eubanks said the school added numerous other junior-level sports for the seventh and eighth-graders since the high schoolers merged with the younger students three years ago. The older students are role models for the younger athletes, which has helped curb bad behavior, she added. The younger athletes feel like they're training to perform on varsity, Eubanks said. Even if junior high students don't play sports, Oyster said, they still attend games and cheer on their fellow classmates. 'They want to be a part of something larger,' she said. 'So, the school spirit has grown tremendously as well.' Photo submitted by Cathy Oyster – Palatka High pickleball club members take a break from their game to pose for a picture.

title: Official's loyalty points benefit kids in need
description: Three years of a community leader shopping at an Interlachen grocery store helped feed Putnam County children this week. County Commissioner Larry Harvey bought 2,200 packets of tuna fish from…
content:
Three years of a community leader shopping at an Interlachen grocery store helped feed Putnam County children this week.
County Commissioner Larry Harvey bought 2,200 packets of tuna fish from Hitchcock's Market in Interlachen and donated them to Feed the Need of Putnam County on Monday. He purchased the tuna using 25,000 loyalty points he accumulated by shopping at Hitchcock's.
'I didn't want to use them for personal gain,' Harvey said of the points.
The commissioner set his sights on helping Feed the Need, 110 N. State Road 19 in Palatka, and bought all the tuna packets he could.
Feed the Need Executive Director Denise Bramlitt said the organization needs nonperishable products like tuna to put in backpacks full of food that are sent home with food-insecure children every weekend. The purpose is to ensure children will have food to eat on the weekends when they can't count on breakfast and lunch being served at school, she said.
'I was like, ‘Wow, I didn't even know you could do that, to purchase stuff,'' Bramlitt said. 'I knew you could buy certain stuff, but I had no idea (about this much food).'
Harvey said he worked with the Interlachen store manager, Brandy Degeyter, to make the donation possible. The tuna packets were originally on sale at two packets for $1, but Degeyter marked the cost down to 25 cents per packet because Harvey bought all 11 cases of the store's tuna.
'It's an incredible thing for him to do,' Degeyter said.
She said she always sees Harvey shopping for cookouts and community events. After a while, his points finally accumulated, Degeyter noted.
She said he's been trying to find a way to use his loyalty points for something other than himself.
'He does a lot for a lot of people,' Degeyter said. 'When he comes here, sometimes there's customers that need groceries and stuff. And he'll come in and he'll buy their groceries. That's what he does.'
Anyone who has signed up for Hitchcock's loyalty program can follow Harvey's lead. Degeyter said all people need to do to register is provide an email address and phone number.
Every dollar someone spends earns them a point, and for every 500 points, people get $10 off an order, she said.
Hitchcock's corporate office sends out different deals, including ones where buying an item earns the purchaser double points, Degeyter added.
This month, Feed the Need is asking for breakfast bars, and anyone can donate to the Palatka location, which is also the Bramlitt's Plumbing & Electric warehouse. People can donate money by mailing checks to Bramlitt's Plumbing & Electric, P.O. Box 132, Palatka, FL 32178.
If people learn how a Hitchcock's card can be used to help people in need, Harvey said, they might be inspired to use their points to buy items to donate.
'I don't know if people think the way I do, but maybe a little encouragement might help people, you know,' Harvey said. 'It's just an idea.'

title: Tea Time for Mother's Day
description: Moms feel the love during classroom party Everyone was in a festive mood Friday when a Palatka school celebrated Mother's Day early with students having tea with their mothers and mother figures.…
content:
Moms feel the love during classroom party Everyone was in a festive mood Friday when a Palatka school celebrated Mother's Day early with students having tea with their mothers and mother figures. Celebrations took place in a prekindergarten class and in one of the classes at the One in a Mellon daycare at the school. Sawyer Barnes, 4, made her mom a Mother's Day card. 'Our class is beautiful,' Sawyer said. 'My mom gives me toys and helps me take care of my animals. I love her all day.' Five-year-old Harper Dunn said she loves having her mom put her to bed at night. 'She reads me a book and tells me goodnight before she leaves,' Harper said. When Harper was asked what she does with her mom, she answered, 'I help her plant her garden. She loves me and takes me places.' TRISHA MURPHY/Palatka Daily News – TeKeira Williams has her picture taken with her children, Kella, 4, and De'Kota Williams, 5, during the Mother's Day tea. One of the moms at the pre-k tea was Katie Harris, where her son, Kieran Helms, 5, is a student. 'My mom gives me candy and cookies and lets me have McDonald's for lunch,' Kieran said, giving a thumbs up. 'She's my friend.' Harris said the Mother's Day Tea with her son was a wonderful experience. 'I love getting the opportunity to share moments like this with him at his school,' she said. 'Meeting his classmates and getting to see all of his hard work displayed was so fun. I love that his school and his teachers are always working towards creating a safe and loving space to learn and make memories. It's just amazing to see.' Aiden Pacetti, 4, was happy to see his mom and little sister, Arlo, 3, arrive at the tea at his pre-k class. 'She gives me a hug and kiss,' Aiden said. 'I love her 4,' which his mom thinks came from him being 4. The pre-k tea also had another special guest, Dakota Williams' great-grandmother, Georgia Florence, who came from Hollister, his mom, TeKeira Williams, and his little sister, Kella, 4. TRISHA MURPHY/Palatka Daily News – Kieran Helms, 5, shows his mom, Katie Harris, what he made her for Mother's Day in his pre-k class at the Mellon Learning Center in Palatka on Friday. 'There needs to be more events like this, you know, where the parents and grandparents can get an idea on what goes on and things of that nature,' Florence said. 'Everyone in that room is like a family. It was just so cozy.' Frankya Clark sat at the tea watching as her 5-year-old son, Asher Harris, talked about the things he likes best about his mom. 'She always helps me with my homework, letters and numbers,' he said. 'I love my mother 5. She plays on the playground with me and watches Spiderman with me. She also buys pizza for us to eat.' When asked what the best gift he could give his mom is, Asher said, 'A teapot.' Joannie Millan, the director of One in a Mellon Learning Center daycare, said these kinds of events are important for children. 'It makes children happy to bring in parents into their place they learn every day,' she said. TRISHA MURPHY/Palatka Daily News – Mothers hold their children at One in a Mellon Learning Center daycare during a Mother's Day tea Friday.

title: Veterans, residents remember comrades' sacrifices
description: People young and old braved the heat Monday in their most patriotic attire to commemorate members of the Armed Forces who died while serving the United States of America. Memorial Day events in…
content:
People young and old braved the heat Monday in their most patriotic attire to commemorate members of the Armed Forces who died while serving the United States of America.
Memorial Day events in Palatka began with a parade down St. Johns Avenue from 11th Street to Riverfront Park, 100 Memorial Parkway.
People scattered along the sidewalks in front of the Putnam County Courthouse and local businesses before 10 a.m. to get good spots to view the parade.
One person who attended the parade Monday morning was Palatka resident and Air Force veteran Chuck Foster, who brought his father-in-law, Howard Burks, to help pay tribute to fallen service members. Foster served for 24 years, spending part of that time as an Air Force recruiter in Palatka in the early 2000s.
'One of the guys I worked with, one of the guys I recruited, actually, got killed in action,' Foster said.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – A firefighter from the Palatka Fire Department hands children red fire hats during the Memorial Day parade in Palatka on Monday. He said he tries to attend every event honoring veterans and had planned to visit Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 3349 and American Legion Bert Hodge Post 45, both in Palatka, later that day.
'I decided to bring my father-in-law out,' Foster said. 'We went to breakfast and turned around and came over and decided we'd enjoy the day.'
Veterans from both posts showed their patriotism in the parade and during the ceremony that occurred afterward at Riverfront Park.
Legion Post Commander Lester Sheppard said Memorial Day is the one time of the year people can gather together and focus on what soldiers who lost their lives while serving gave to the citizens of this nation.
'It's not about picnics. It's not about parades. It's not about parties and things like that,' he said about the reason Memorial Day is observed. 'This is the day that we should take deep stock in our heart and think about what they gave up for us.'
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – Memorial Day parade grand marshal Dr. Roy Hinman II, a retired Army colonel who served for nearly 40 years, asks veterans at the remembrance ceremony to stand to be recognized. This year's parade grand marshal and ceremony keynote speaker was Dr. Roy Hinman II, a retired Army colonel who served for nearly 40 years. Hinman owns and operates Island Doctors, which has numerous Putnam County locations.
Hinman paid tribute to every branch of the military and reminded people why they gathered for Memorial Day.
'Today is about remembrance,' he said. 'It remembers those that have fallen and give their all for our country.'
Although fallen soldiers may not be around to experience Memorial Day, he said, the people in the audience who served can keep their fallen comrades' memories alive.
Veterans who lost friends while serving know it could have just as easily been them, which is why veterans have such a strong appreciation for their brothers' and sisters' sacrifices, Hinman said.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – Memorial Day parade grand marshal Dr. Roy Hinman II rides on a special parade float Monday in Palatka. 'As we go forth and enjoy this wonderful holiday, which we should because it's a time to rejoice those and thank those … over their sacrifice,' he said.
Sheppard likes to reflect on the words 'some gave all, but all gave some' when he thinks about Memorial Day. He said he prays no one forgets to remember the fallen.
'They're not here today to enjoy any of this,' he said. 'They're not here to enjoy the beautiful sights and the flags. They're just not here.
'We just thank them for their service. We thank them for what they gave and just pray now for the families of them. We just pray that they are comforted somewhat because of what they gave us.'
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – The Memorial Day parade in Palatka travels down the 400 block of St. Johns Avenue as the crowd watches Monday morning.

title: Groups hosting auction to support Welcome Center
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Develop Palatka Inc. and Downtown Palatka Experiences will host the Silent Auction, a Welcome Center Fundraiser with an open reception, from 3–5 p.m.
content:
Body
Develop Palatka Inc. and Downtown Palatka Experiences will host the Silent Auction, a Welcome Center Fundraiser with an open reception, from 3–5 p.m. Saturday at the Palatka Welcome Center, 900 St. Johns Ave.
'We've got big items, home goods, usable items, gift certificates and more,' said Wendy Beeson, chairwoman of the event and secretary for both sponsor groups.
Part of that 'more' list includes Beeson's original pen-and-ink drawing of 419 Mulholland Park in the city's North Historic District, a stained glass swag lamp, vases and a book that was donated by Dunns Creek author G.A. 'Jerry' Teske titled '100 Plus! Stories of Unique People & Special Events in Putnam County, Florida.'
In the beginning of the book Teske wrote, 'The people you will meet and events you will read about will take you from one end of Putnam County to the other and provide you with some insight to many of the remarkable people who reside in our community.'
In '100 plus!' is a section titled 'Big League Baseball in Palatka,' where Teske wrote about Babe Ruth having his own stint at the Azalea Bowl coaching in 1940 and 1941.
'If you read these stories for the first time, I'm sure many will bring a smile to your face or trigger a pleasant memory or even give the readers a few laughs,' Teske said.
Silent bidding in the auction is available from 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. through Friday and 3–5 p.m. Saturday before the reception begins with refreshments and drawings. The public is invited.
Anyone interested in donating an auction item can do so by taking items to the center or Gem City Cottage, 218 St. Johns Ave., between 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. through Friday. For details, call 386-328-0909 or 386-530-1549.
Winners for the silent auction will be called July 30, and payment and pickup will be available from July 30 to Aug. 2.
Beeson said the Welcome Center has been an advocate for small businesses in Putnam County and the surrounding area for many years.
'It gives tourists and new residents a place to go to see local businesses and restaurants and services in Putnam County by gathering their business cards at the center,' she said. 'Businesses are free to put their cards and rack cards in the welcome center.'
Besides that, Beeson said it's also the only place in town to view the original renderings of the murals in the city.
'Visitors can buy prints of the murals at the Welcome Center,' she said. 'Our focus at the center is to bring awareness to the many talented people and businesses in our county.'
Anyone interested in joining Develop Palatka Inc. can get an application at the center or at Gem City College.
Beeson said other fundraisers have taken place to raise support for the Welcome Center.
'We have done the Gem City Market on Reid Street in Palatka seven times where we raise money through vendor fees,' she said. 'We have also had art and craft shows inside the center and the Comic Book Show.'
Beeson said the center is run by four volunteers and a manager.
'Each lady serves one day a week from 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. but we could always use more volunteers.'
For details on volunteering, contact Linda Brent at 904-612-7326.

NOTICE OF APPLICATION
FOR TAX DEED
NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that KEREN IRA LLC the holder of the following certificate has filed said certificate for a tax deed to be issued thereon. The certificate number and year of issuance, the description of the property, and the names in which it was assessed are as follows:
Certificate Number 0000048
Year of Issuance 2017
Description of Property:
INTERLACHEN LAKES ESTATES, UNIT 15 MB4 P186 BLK 11 LOT 17
PARCEL NUMBER 17-10-24-4074-0110-0170
Name in which assessed NOURELDIN RONALDO + LUIS G CORRAL.
All of said property being in the County of Putnam, State of Florida.
Unless such certificate or certificates shall be redeemed according to law the property described in such certificate or certificates will be sold to the highest bidder ONLINE at http://putnam.realtaxdeed.com on the 14th day of August, 2024, at 10:00 A.M.
Dated this 21st day of June, 2024
MATT REYNOLDS
CLERK OF CIRCUIT COURT
AND COMPTROLLER
PUTNAM COUNTY, FLORIDA
By: /s/ Debbie Wilkinson
Deputy Clerk
You can find more information online at http://apps.putnam-fl.com/coc/taxdeeds/list

title: District welcomes new teachers at training event
author: Carter Mudgett
description: Whether new to the profession or new to the area, dozens of teachers are participating this week in training officials said will increase their chances of success in the classroom.
content:
Whether new to the profession or new to the area, dozens of teachers are participating this week in training officials said will increase their chances of success in the classroom.
The first day of school will be Aug. 12 and Putnam County School District leaders are already getting a headstart on helping new teachers get acquainted in the Novice Teacher Institute.
More than 35 new teachers attended Tuesday, the first of three days of training to help teachers learn more about the district, its staff and its systems before school begins in fewer than two weeks.
Some who attended Tuesday said they were completely new to teaching, while others were simply new to Putnam County. One such person in the latter category was Angela Klaverkamp, who moved from Virginia to Florida after teaching for 11 years.
'It has been an amazing experience. I already feel like part of the family,' Klaverkamp said, praising district officials for how personable and accepting they'd been, even before the event.
'The main thing is, every year, our goal is that they understand that they are supported, that we invest in them and that we really appreciate that they went into teaching and that they have chosen us to come and teach at our school district,' said Kristin Carroll, a district administrator who helped organize the event.
'We want them to be able to make those connections, where they feel like they're at home, not just within our school district, but within our community.'
For the first time, the district also brought in a motivational speaker to help open the Novice Teacher Institute.
Daryl Williams, an assistant principal in North Carolina and a creator on TikTok with more than 60,000, spoke about making the learning experience engaging and developing a relationship with students.
The new teachers who attended the event Tuesday came from all over the country and even internationally. One person told the group they came from the Dominican Republic and another from Jamaica.
District organizers emphasized how the in-person event was more than just a way to disseminate information. It is a chance for new teachers to get to know each other.
'So it's not just a sit-and-get. It's an interact-and-learn,' Carroll said. 'And (they) leave here with some quality items ready to take to their classrooms and put them in place. They are able to learn from each other. They are able to just get an overview of our district because every district is different.'
Superintendent Rick Surrency, who attended the event Tuesday, emphasized school culture and ensured teachers, new and experienced, they have a support system.
'I can remember my first year of teaching,' he said. 'Every Sunday night, I was freaked out because I had to go the next morning and try to teach and try to figure out what I was gonna teach because I had no support. I just got thrown to the wolves. I was a high school teacher.'
Making sure the district is guiding its teachers is something he takes personally, he said. As a result, he said, students are supported.
Surrency told a story of how he recently chatted with one of the students he taught years ago. That student had told him, 'Your class got really boring.'
Without guidance from his district at the time, Surrency said he taught history, took notes on the overhead projector and lectured during class.
'I thought I was doing a good job. I thought I was teaching,' he said. 'And really, all I was doing was just standing up there just talking and they weren't really learning.'
That moment taught him a lot, he said, and emphasized the need to make sure students are engaged with their teacher so they learn.
'I just want to welcome you, and more than anything else, I just want to thank you for being part of the Putnam County School District,' Surrency told the group of new teachers. 'Just know that I'm your No. 1 fan.'

title: No severe damage reported as Debby douses Putnam
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Putnam County officials expect the stormy weather from Hurricane Debby to continue subsiding as the day continues.
content:
Body
Putnam County officials expect the stormy weather from Hurricane Debby to continue subsiding as the day continues.
The hurricane has decreased to a tropical storm, according to a 1:30 p.m. update from the county's Emergency Management Department. County officials said their biggest concerns are water on the roads, downed trees and powerlines, and power outages.
Steffen Turnipseed, the chief of emergency operations and preparedness, said the most damage reported had been trees knocked down.
'We're gonna keep getting rain the rest of the day and probably through tomorrow and the rest of the week,' he said. 'It's gonna die down, and the impacts will lessen.'
Turnipseed reported 1.8 inches of rain in some parts of Putnam County but as much as 4 inches of rain near the Rodman Reservoir.
At 4 p.m., Florida Power & Light reported 1,830 Putnam customers without power, and Clay Electric Cooperative reported 1,947 of its customers in the area were without power.
FPL users can report power outages at fpl.com while Clay customers can do so using the MyClayElectric app or by calling 888-434-9844.
Crescent City Mayor Michele Myers said the city experienced minor damage, including fallen trees and branches. She said city staff have been working to clean up debris throughout the day.
'Our area was blessed with only small, manageable impacts,' Myers said in a text message. 'Our thoughts and prayers go out to those communities harshly impacted by the wrath of Debby.'
People who see downed trees or powerlines can report them to the county's non-emergency phone number, 386-329-0800.
In Interlachen, Town Clerk Joni Payne said she did not receive any reports of damages. Town Hall is set to reopen at 8 a.m. Tuesday.
'Our water utilities have remained in service during the storm,' Payne said in a text message. 'We have had a few trees down, our public works department has worked diligently at keeping the roads open.'
Palatka Public Works Department officials suspended residential garbage pickup today. According to a city press release, Monday's garbage collection will move to Tuesday, and Tuesday's collection will take place Wednesday.
The city will not be collecting yard debris this week, but officials asked residents to pile any yard debris next to the curb of their homes once the storm ends.
'There will be no change in commercial collection,' the press release stated.
The county's trash pickup will continue to run as usual since there was no change in Monday's schedule, according to the Emergency Management Department.
The county could still see some scattered showers and thunderstorms during the rest of this week, according to weather.com, and Putnam was still under a tornado watch by 4 p.m.
'(A) tornado threat is still out there so we are still watching that for now,' Turnipseed said.

title: District 5 hopefuls tout private, public experience as primary nears
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible. Other than that, no other editing was done to candidates' answers.
The District 5 seat on the Putnam County Board of Commissioners is up for grabs, and three candidates – two of them former occupants of that seat – are vying to claim that spot.
Republicans Buddy Goddard, Walton Pellicer and Tim Williams will face each other in the Aug. 20 primary. While Williams has never been a member of the Board of County Commissioners, Pellicer was elected to the District 5 seat in 2012 but lost his reelection bid four years later to Goddard.
All three candidates have answered questions asked by the Palatka Daily News ahead of the primary. Listed below, candidates, in their own words, will explain why they're the best choice for the position.
Q: Why do you believe yourself to be the best candidate for this position?
Goddard: Passion to serve. County Commissioner (2016-2020) – Vice Chairman and Chairman. Advanced County Commissioner status. Northeast Florida Regional Council – 2nd Vice President and Finance Committee. Transportation Disadvantaged Board Chairman. Small County Coalition member (advocating in Tallahassee and Washington, D. C.). 35+ years of business and management experience in the private, public, and government sectors. Currently serve on BOCC Waterways and Trails Committee.
Pellicer: I have been a lifelong resident of Putnam County and have served as Commissioner of District 5 from 2012-2016. This has given me experience in all areas of the Putnam County Government. I am eager to hit the ground running and I know who to talk to, not only here in Putnam County but also in Tallahassee to get things done.
Williams: Owning and operating a small business allows me to understand how budgets are set, how revenue is generated, and how expenditures are made. Looking at past commissions and the way expenditures and budgets have been handled, I believe I am in the unique position of being able to offer changes that would benefit the public by allowing more input into the budgeting process, and knowing where our monies are spent year over year. Understanding the budget process from the county is imperative and my opponents who are both previous commissioners either chose not to understand the process or ignored it.
Q: What are your top three priorities, if elected?
Goddard: Full-time commissioner not just showing up at scheduled meetings. Maintaining a full-time schedule to stay engaged and to advocate for Putnam County. Funding law enforcement and first responders to entice employees to stay in Putnam County as continued growth will need reassessed allocations to still provide sufficient critical public services. Most of the Putnam County growth will be in areas that infrastructure is currently in place. We need to focus on managing the controlled growth while still keeping our ruralness.
Pellicer: First, I would like to work with our chamber of commerce to bring clean industry jobs to Putnam County. I will reach out to our municipalities to help create a stronger working environment. Thereby expanding our taxable base, and lightening the tax burden of homeowners across our County. In addition, I wish to expand the fresh and gray water system in East Palatka. Which will relieve the septic systems along the river to protect one of Putnam County's greatest resources. To conclude, building and zoning is a department that has several issues that need to be addressed.
Williams: Reviewing and offering changes to the board with regards to the comprehensive plan and including more citizens input on what the next 15 years for Putnam County looks like with regards to growth, industry, housing, and workforce development. At the last review of the comprehensive plan in 2020, the citizens made it clear Putnam County wanted to maintain its rural and agrarian nature. I think this needs to be spelled out in such a way that we understand what kind of growth the citizens want, where it will happen, and do it on a percentage basis based on projected trends.
Q: Where do you believe the Putnam County Board of Commissioners needs to improve?
Goddard: My general philosophy about the role of government is to keep it in the hands of the people. With that being said, I would like to implement publicized workshops for upcoming BOCC meetings that would be recorded for the public to see at their leisure or that they could attend in person.
Pellicer: I believe the board of commissioners needs to be more available to all residents of Putnam County. This is why I vow to be the commissioner 'who calls you back.'
Williams: Developing a sense of trust with the community. With all that is going on locally money spent with no increases in services, people I talk to are concerned about government overspending. As a true physical conservative, I think we need to learn how to operate more efficiently, spending less money and collecting less dollars in taxes so we can help move our community forward. This year was a perfect opportunity for the board to reduce the military since it had so much new revenue coming in. Instead it shows how to spend all of it.
Q: What's the best way to accommodate growth in Putnam County while also retaining the rural Florida environment this county loves?
Goddard: Update the county's strategic plan as well as enhance the infrastructure in currently zoned areas that will be necessary to accommodate new development. This will allow us to maintain our ruralness and to better prepare for the inevitable growth that is coming.
Pellicer: I will accommodate growth by aspiring to regulating the density of homes being built in our area. It is my hope to maintain our rural Florida life that we call home.
Williams: The last time the County commission took a look at the comprehensive plan. The data that was used was so old, It showed that Putnam County would experience a 3% net growth over a 10-year period of time. It looks like we will experience that much growth over the next 2 years. If we were to take a step backwards and reduce the density that would allow us to have some growth but not too much at one time and would allow us to be able to provide the necessary services as the growth came and not be overwhelmed.
Q: Budget season is here. What is the most important change to the budget you believe needs to be made?
Goddard: After a percentage of the funds are allocated to the constitutional officers, the remaining dollars need to be discussed in an advertised budget workshop. The BOCC has mandatory budget meetings to determine the millage rate but collaboration is needed to decide upon the appropriation of the remaining funds. Hopefully this would also encourage public participation in the budget process. Then, budget versus actuals is monitored to make sure that the taxpayers money is being spent wisely.
Pellicer: Our budget fluctuates year by year. This needs to be reviewed on a department base level. This will give us more flexibility to redirect funds in areas that will benefit Putnam County as a whole.
Williams: I believe the commission needs to take a look at each and every department individually. Looking at the goals and objectives of each department and then budgeting accordingly in order to meet the current demand and if possible adjust for the future as well. At the same time we should be looking at what the citizens would like their community to be like and how it should operate. It looks like an overwhelming majority of the revenue for the county will be spent by the sheriff's department. Increasing the population in Putnam County will only cost the local citizens.
Q: Commissioners are the face of Putnam County but it's often commissioners' employees that do the heavy lifting behind the scenes. Where do you stand on how much the county should be paying employees?
Goddard: I believe that we should pay salaries competitive to surrounding counties as well as I also believe in promoting from within before looking outside of the county if applicable or possible.
Pellicer: By increasing our tax base this will allow us to increase all of our employees pay across the board. On an individual basis it can be decided on years of service and skill level. Besides pay, we can seek other avenues that we can possibly provide our workers with a more rewarding work environment.
Williams: I think there has to be a balanced plan that affords each employee a livable wage, but also takes into consideration the median average income in Putnam County. Because of the $15 hour minimum wage, the wage scale was compressed. Senior employees in some cases are making as much or less than new employees. The commission will need to make adjustments to reward those who have been with the county for long periods of time. Looking at the current administration, it is very top heavy with administrative positions that are highly compensated in some cases between two and four times.

title: Teachers rejoice at school supply giveaway
author: Carter Mudgett
description: The C.L. Overturf Jr.
content:
Body
The C.L. Overturf Jr. Gymnasium was full of school supplies and gratitude Friday afternoon as teachers filled up on free notebooks, sticky notes, pens, classroom decor, cleaning supplies and other classroom items.
The Education Foundation of Putnam County hosted the event, which was free for Putnam County teachers, from noon – 5 p.m. today and will continue from 9 a.m. – 1 p.m. Saturday.
There was around $15,000 worth of supplies numerous local businesses donated for the event, said organizers, citing a desire to have a back-to-school event for teachers to coincide with the numerous events that have been happening for students and parents.
'You see throughout the county, there's tons of giveaways for students, right?,' asked Les Sims, the Education Foundation chairman. 'We're doing really (well) with that, but not a lot's done for the teachers.'
Teachers have to show their Putnam County School District ID, take a brown bag and fill it with whatever they want at no cost. Supplies lined the bleachers and filled tables set up in the middle of the gymnasium.
'That way, the teachers don't have to spend their own hard-earned money,' Sims said Thursday as volunteers began setting out the donated supplies. 'That was our biggest problem — they're already doing a job that's underpaid. They're not appreciated like they should be. So if we can help relieve some of that (stress), that's our focus.'
It's the second year the Education Foundation has helped organize the school supply 'store' for teachers. Last year, the group partnered with the Palatka Coffee Co. but soon realized the space they used last year wasn't big enough, Sims said.
The Overturf gymnasium could become the permanent home for what foundation leaders said will be an annual event.
Teachers arrived in droves before the doors officially opened at noon Friday. Some of them have been teaching in Putnam County for years. For others, it was their first time at the event and teaching in Putnam County.
'It's amazing,' said Jessica Shifrin, a first-time Putnam County School District teacher who will be working at Palatka Junior-Senior High School. 'I will take every supply anybody will give me so I don't have to buy it myself.'
On top of the free supplies, organizers had Staples gift cards for every first-time teacher in the district who attended the event.
Joe Rush, a member of the foundation's board of directors, donated $200 for each elementary school teacher for supplies, which totaled $64,000, Sims said. As of Friday afternoon, event organizers were determining if they would give the money directly to those teachers via gift cards or give the money to the schools, which would allocate the funds to their teachers.
As teachers shopped along the bleachers Friday, 'thank you' and 'this is amazing' were heard repeatedly. Part of that gratitude stems from the event minimizing the amount of money teachers would have to pay out of their own pockets to stock their classrooms, said Lisa Hawkins, a speech language pathologist assistant.
'As a speech teacher in particular, we don't get any funds for classroom supplies,' she said. 'So, this is huge, because anything like (supplies) usually comes out of our pocket or out of the general pool within the (Exceptional Student Education) department.'
The event is a joint project between HCA Putnam, the Rotary Club of Palatka and Beck Automotive Group. Some of the event's sponsors included HCA Florida Putnam Hospital, Staples, Rotary International and Seminole Electric Cooperative.
'This year is just great, everybody's so happy,' said Joyce Oliver, an Education Foundation board member. 'All the teachers, their eyes are just big, you know, looking at all the stuff that they can have.'

title: Senate contenders list why they should be elected
author: David Shoar
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible.
A member of the Legislature and a former sheriff are two of the candidates trying to be the Republican nominee for the District 7 state Senate seat.
Trying to emerge victorious in the Florida primary are Gerry James, state Rep. Tom Leek and former St. Johns County Sheriff David Shoar. With early and mail voting already occurring, the three Republicans hope to be the winner Tuesday.
Leek and Shoar completed the questionnaire the Palatka Daily News sent all primary candidates for the House and Senate. James did not reply by the deadline given to all of the Senate candidates.
Below, Leek and Shoar explain why they're the best candidate for the job, what they plan to accomplish and how they will get it done. Other than editing for clarity, the answers are in the candidates' own words.
What inspired you to run for a seat in Florida's Senate?
Leek: As a member of the state Senate, I would like to continue serving the people of Northeast Florida by establishing Florida as the most law enforcement-friendly state in the union, and by working on many of the recent conservative advances in school choice, economic development and important social issues that strengthen the family. My experience as a state House member these last eight years in leadership positions has given me the unique opportunity to build upon these historic achievements and best represent the people of Senate District 7.
Shoar: At eighteen years of age, I raised my right hand and after taking the oath, served the next forty-one years in public service, forty years of law enforcement in St. Johns as Chief of Police and Sheriff and twenty-four years of service in the U.S. Army retiring as a Major. I decided after much thought to stand for election to the Florida Senate when it became clear to me there was not a pro-Trump conservative in the race who would fight for our community, not the special interests in Tallahassee.
What makes you the best candidate to step into this role?
Leek: As a conservative member of the Florida House, I have served as a committee chairman and on the leadership team of the last three Speakers in the Florida House. I served with House Speaker Paul Renner as Chairman of the House Appropriations Committee and previously chaired the Public Ethics and Integrity Committee, the Pandemics and Public Emergencies Committee and the Redistricting Committee. This experience allows me to effectively and immediately serve the constituents of Senate District 7 on day one and continue my valued partnership with State Rep. Bobby Payne.
Shoar: I am proudly endorsed by President Trump. I am a lifelong conservative Republican and will always fight for our values. I have a record of protecting this community over my 40+ year law enforcement career. I believe we could use more common sense in Tallahassee and get back to the basics of limited government and returning as much power and authority back to local government as possible. I have a long history of telling folks what I thought they needed to hear, not what they wanted to hear regardless of the possible repercussions.
There seems to always be development occurring in counties surrounding Putnam County. How will you help Putnam County bolster its infrastructure to be ready to accommodate whatever development and growth that may occur?
Leek: I share the position of my friend and colleague, State Rep. Bobby Payne, that addressing infrastructure needs in Putnam County is critical if we are to remain competitive in the region, addressing bridges and roads for transportation needs, as well as expanding broadband and connectivity services. There should also be a balanced approach between sensible development and our environmental needs so the district may preserve its uniqueness. These are decisions that should be made at the local level.
Shoar: We need to have smart growth to protect our quality of life and work to ensure funding is available for the necessary infrastructure. The growth of the neighboring counties adds pressure to Putnam County and I believe and many do that Putnam County is going to experience strong growth now and in the future. I think working with our locals and not just writing one-size-fits-all edicts from Tallahassee regarding growth and development and forcing them on local government would be a great start.
How do you plan to work with your colleagues on the other side of the aisle to accomplish great things for Florida residents, especially in Putnam County?
Leek: As a trusted member of House leadership, I have worked on many of the conservative advances of the past few years in school choice, economic development and important social issues that strengthen the family. In working with colleagues on the other side of the aisle, there are many things that unite us rather than divide us, and together we have reached consensus on many issues that make Florida and (Senate)District 7 the best place to live, work, play and raise a family.
Shoar: I have always been part of team throughout my career and led many of them. If we all focus on the health, safety and welfare of our constituents instead on so much of the nonsense and noise out there, we can get a lot done. A great issue to collaborate on might be the state of our Mental Health system in Florida. I worked with stakeholders of all parties as Sheriff and know how to work with and listen to people whose views differ from my own. While I believe in collaboration, I will not compromise my conservative values.
How will you ensure Florida is fiscally responsible while also providing resources and programs to make this state the best in the nation?
Leek: A challenge we face in Northeast Florida is in providing a strong economy, as it relates to families making ends meet and allowing businesses to thrive in recruiting and retaining a talented workforce. As chair of the House Appropriations Committee, overseeing negotiations between the House and Senate for a $117 billion budget in the nation's third largest state, my motto is 'start with zero, justify the rest' in every allocation. These are our dollars, not the government's. We need to be prudent in spending and ever mindful in returning funds to the people of Florida with a balanced budget approach.
Shoar: One of the best ways to start is to carefully assess the current programs, are they programs that are effective and more importantly, are they programs that government should not even be involved in? Most citizens do not know that 'earmarks' exist in state government but they do they are just called something else; this needs careful analysis as well. Fortunately, we are required to maintain a balanced budget in Florida. I will prioritize our key needs – public safety, education, and infrastructure, root out waste, and also cut taxes for our families.
Much attention has been paid to diversity, equity and inclusion programs and resources. What are your opinions on those items, especially as it relates to the millions of people who benefitted from them?
Leek: I believe in merit-based systems over DEI-driven policies, focusing on diversity and inclusion can often undermine meritocracy and result in hiring and admissions policies that are not based solely on qualifications and merit. DEI initiatives promote a divisive and ideological agenda that emphasizes identity politics and creates a discriminatory environment. I agree with Governor (Ron)DeSantis that DEI programs in schools and universities often lead to indoctrination – not proper education. DEI initiatives are an example of government overreach. As a conservative, I oppose any attempt to impose specific values on individuals that infringes on personal freedoms and liberties.
