title: Community gathers at vigil to grieve student's passing
author: Carter Mudgett
description: By Carter Mudgett and Sarah Cavacini
content:
Body
Panther pride extended far beyond Palatka Junior-Senior High School on Tuesday as the community united around a family grieving the sudden death of their 15-year-old son.
Hundreds gathered in the school's gymnasium that evening to remember sophomore Robert 'RJ' Gillon III, who died in the early morning hours of Tuesday. His family, his friends and community members grieved his loss but also uplifted his loved ones with prayers and songs.
Gillon, who played football with the Palatka High Panthers, passed away of natural causes, according to a Facebook statement from the Palatka Police Department.
Authorities initially responded to the Gillon home early Tuesday morning for a suspected cardiac arrest but found the sophomore had already died, according to the police.
'There's no human answers,' said the Rev. Karl Flagg, pastor of Mt. Tabor First Baptist Church of Palatka. 'Even with the best investigators, there are no human answers. We are all struggling, and we're going to struggle through this together. But we're not going to struggle with our own strength. We're going to go through this by the grace of God.'
During the prayer vigil, Gillon's mother, Dedra Dean McCormick, wore her son's blue football jersey, emblazoned with the No. 8 in gold. His family was escorted into the vigil by Sheriff Gator DeLoach, some of whose deputies are resource deputies in Putnam schools, and other community members.
The late sophomore had been excited about the upcoming football season and had shared a strong bond with his teammates, his family said in a statement. The Panthers' season is now dedicated to him, players told the media.
Head football coach Patrick Turner praised Gillon's character, saying the student-athlete never complained. All Gillon said was, 'Yes, sir,' Turner reflected Tuesday night.
'What we wouldn't give to see Robert … work out one more time, to run one more sprint,' Turner said. 'He is truly one of the best students I have ever had the opportunity to coach.'
Gillon was more than an athlete. He was a beloved family member and friend to many.
Numerous Putnam County School District officials attended the vigil, including Superintendent Rick Surrency, school board member David Buckles and board Chairwoman Sandra Gilyard.
'God, we give thanks … for you gave us 15 years. But if we count it the way that you count it, for you said that a day is like a thousand years,' Gilyard said. 'And so God help us, most especially mom and dad and brothers and sisters and grandpa, to hold onto their memories – the last of the good times, the sad times, whatever it might be.'
Gillon's is the second death of a Palatka High student in the last year.
Baylee Holbrook died in September 2023 after being struck by lightning while hunting with her father. Her parents and pastor attended the vigil Tuesday to support the Gillon family.
The faith community had a strong showing, with numerous pastors there to support the Gillon family.
'No one here, that you can see, is equipped with anything to explain why we are here,' Flagg said. '... Take the time and grieve. Take the time and accept a reality that none of us could have ever imagined.'
In a statement Tuesday, the Gillon family described Robert Gillon as a teenager who had a deep love of God and cherished his relationship with Jesus.
'RJ's love for his church and his community was evident in everything he did,' his family said in the statement. 'He was a well-mannered and respectable young man, and his presence will be deeply missed by all who knew him.'

title: School board member cinches win in primary
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The current Putnam County School Board chairwoman will serve another four years on the board after Tuesday's primary results returned in her favor.
content:
Body
The current Putnam County School Board chairwoman will serve another four years on the board after Tuesday's primary results returned in her favor.
District 3 board member Sandra Gilyard won 8,513 (65.17%) votes to beat Tim Houghtaling, who received 4,550 (34.83%) votes, according to unofficial results from the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office.
'I saw all of those who voted for my opponent,' Gilyard said. 'I'm not upset with them. What I want to do is to know how do we get those people back on board to see that we are doing what we feel is in the best interest of our children in the district.'
Gilyard does not have to face a write-in candidate as other hopefuls do in November, which means she is set to continue her job on the board.
Because Gilyard and Houghtaling were the only two people who competed in the nonpartisan school board race, no runoff in the Nov. 5 general election is necessary.
Gilyard, who was first elected to the board in 2016 and won her reelection bid four years later, said she plans to continue the work the board and Putnam County School District have planned, like making sure the new schools in the district are constructed according to plan.
'We're going to make sure that these schools are built, that we are fiscally responsible,' she said. 'We're going to make sure, absolutely sure, that we cross every T and dot every I and do everything within our power to take good care of the monies that are entrusted to us, especially with building these new facilities.'
The primary results will be made official Aug. 27, Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III said Tuesday evening.
The Putnam County Canvassing Board will meet at 4:30 p.m. Thursday to review the nine provisional ballots reported in the primary.
Voters whose ballots are under review have until 5 p.m. Thursday to provide proof of identification to the Elections Office.

title: St. Johns Avenue completion pushed to March
author: Carter Mudgett
description: The completion date of the effort to reconstruct a portion of St. Johns Avenue in Palatka has been pushed back and at least one business owner is frustrated.
content:
Body
The completion date of the effort to reconstruct a portion of St. Johns Avenue in Palatka has been pushed back and at least one business owner is frustrated.
This section of road from South 19th Street to the railroad tracks near the Palatka Fire Department, was originally slated to be completed by Jan. 28, 2025.
As of Tuesday, workers were under a 55-day delay due to 'unforeseen utility lines' that weren't on the city's plans and had to be shut off, according to J.T. Stout, the executive director of Putnam County Public Works. The project has a new finish date of March 28, 2025, he said.
Resurfacing St. Johns Avenue from Palm Avenue to Fourth Street is a joint project between the county and city of Palatka.
Earlier this year, the county finished the portion from Palm Avenue to just near 19th Street, while the city completed the portion from just west of the railroad tracks to Fourth Street.
The Palatka Gas Authority was working on the utility lines, and Stout anticipates that work will be done Monday so road work can continue.
Stout said the county has talked to businesses impacted by the continued construction, but at least one business owner told the Daily News she hasn't heard anything.
Toni Scroggins of St. Johns Auto Body, 1609 St. Johns Ave., said she hasn't heard any updates on when construction will be done.
Before the work began earlier this year, Scroggin said the city told her there would be a sign put up to tell people her business was still open.
In addition to a tall detour sign being erected at the 16th Street intersection, there is a smaller campaign sign-sized green sign alerting motorists the auto shop and other nearby businesses are open.
'By numbers, we have lost 23% of our business,' Scroggins said, referencing customers who have told her they didn't think the shop was open.
When the Daily News asked Scroggins if she knew the road's completion date had been pushed back to March 2025, she said no.
Scroggins, who owns St. Johns Auto Body with her husband, Kent Scroggins, said she had called the city numerous times to ask for more communication and a proper sign for customers, to no avail.
'We pay our bills, we pay a lot of taxes and we contribute to Palatka and have for 46 years,' she said. 'And we're being treated like this? Twenty-three percent is a lot to swallow.'

title: West Putnam Knight celebrated for service to community
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Faith, hope and charity is an accurate description of a West Putnam County man known to put his heart and soul into helping others in his community.
content:
Faith, hope and charity is an accurate description of a West Putnam County man known to put his heart and soul into helping others in his community.
Colonel O. 'Bud' Surratt, who will turn 85 in September, was recently recognized as the 2023-2024 Knight of the Year by the Knights of Columbus, St. John's Mission Council 8917 in Interlachen.
Jim Dandeneau, the Grand Knight for the Knights of Columbus in Interlachen, nominated Surratt for the award and presented it to him.
'I have personally known Bud for over 19 years,' Dandeneau said. 'During this time, I have observed his dedication to serving the community. He has been a great inspiration to me.'
Surratt said he is honored to receive the Knight of the Year award.
'I do what Knights do normally,' he said. 'Knights are all about charity and helping each other out. It's nice to be able to call other members and get help. They always do what they can.'
Surratt joined the Navy in 1957 when he was 17 and later took part in two tours with the Marine Corps during the Vietnam War. He retired as a lieutenant commander in April 1980.
According to Dandeneau, the Knights of Columbus was founded March 29, 1882, in New Haven, Connecticut, by Father Michael J. McGivney and a group of men in the basement of St. Mary's Church.
'The Knights were formed to render financial aid to members and their families,' Dandeneau said.
According to kofc.org, the organization provides mutual aid and other assistance to people who are sick, disabled or otherwise in need.
'The Knights of Columbus was founded on the principles of charity, unity, fraternity and patriotism,' said Surratt, who joined the Interlachen group in 2000 and serves as a fourth-degree Knight, the highest degree with the group. 'These principles serve as the foundation of our core values.'
Surratt is active with St. Vincent de Paul Society in Interlachen, where he serves as its president. That organization maintains a thrift store and food bank, and it provides financial assistance and vouchers for furniture, clothes and food to those in need.
He also serves as the building site manager for a Putnam Habitat for Humanity home being built in the area and coordinates payments through the Knights organization made to Seminarians, who are studying for the priesthood. He also serves on several church councils.
'He is very active in helping many people in our community,' Dandeneau said. 'Bud represents the very best in our community. Based on his involvement with so many things to help others, he was the most outstanding candidate for our council.'
Knights of Columbus has more than 14,000 councils in many countries around the world, including nearby areas like Interlachen, Palatka, Crescent City, Keystone Heights and Starke.
The groups host fundraisers for local charities such as The Arc, Special Olympics, A Women's Resource Center, Lee Conlee House and the local parish through fundraiser dinners.
'Through our insurance programs, many hundreds of families are protected in the event of the loss of a member,' Dandeneau said.
Surratt believes it's important for everybody to help people in their communities but admits help is sometimes hard to find.
'I believe if you are able to do something or help someone, you should,' he said. 'People need to help better their communities and do whatever is needed. To sum it up, I'm proud to be able to do what I can to help.'

title: The Final Cut
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Editor's note: Charlie Douglas is the owner of Blue Crab Publishing LLC, which owns the Palatka Daily News.
content:
Body
Editor's note: Charlie Douglas is the owner of Blue Crab Publishing LLC, which owns the Palatka Daily News.
It's 5 o'clock somewhere, and for Albert and Donna Rogero of San Mateo, 5 p.m. couldn't have come soon enough Friday when their salon, Albert's & Donna's, closed after 54 years of operation.
'People have been so nice to us over the years,' said Donna Rogero. 'It's time for us to live out our lives and enjoy our family.'
The Rogeros, who are Putnam County natives, were married May 5, 1970, when Albert was 26 and Donna 23. That same day, Albert Rogero was honorably discharged from the Coast Guard after serving four years, with his last tour of duty in Vietnam.
Living in Jacksonville and trying to decide on a career, Albert Rogero applied for the GI Bill and went to school for nine months to become a licensed barber. He received his associate degree from St. Johns River Community College in 1982.
'I thought about being a barber during high school,' he said. 'I knew I needed to make a living doing something.'
After receiving his license, Albert Rogero spent 18 months as an apprentice at Trotman's Barber Shop, 310 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka, where his wife was the receptionist and manager. In 1974, the Rogeros purchased the shop and renamed it Albert's Style and Barber Shop.
'Albert was the first barber-blow dry hairstylist to practice in Putnam County,' said Donna Rogero. 'Long hair for men was the trend, but many women chose to patronize our shop for an additional 11 years.'
In 1982, Donna Rogero joined her husband at the salon as a cosmetologist, and the shop's name changed to Albert's & Donna's. It was also relocated to 466 S. U.S. 17 in San Mateo.
'We set up a room adjoining Albert's for a cosmetologist who could not meet her overhead,' Donna Rogero said. 'I interviewed several cosmetologists and finally decided to do it myself. … I took the first all-written exam offered by the state and passed.'
For 40 years, Donna Rogero worked with her husband at the salon in an adjoining room providing women's haircuts and chemical services.
Reminiscing, the Rogeros recalled a regular haircut costing $2.50 in 1974 but today costs $18, while styles were $7 then and $27 today.
The couple worked a full five days a week until the last two years when they most recently were open from 9 a.m. – 5 p.m. Thursdays and Fridays by appointment.
They have two children, Walter Albert Rogero Jr. and Tara Herrington, seven grandchildren and one great-grandchild on the way.
With a history of 54 years in the community and 42 at the San Mateo location, Albert Rogero, 80, recalls several of his clients coming to him as children for first their haircuts and as boys in high school. He and other area barbers volunteered their time and services to the boys living at Rodeheaver Boys Ranch just south of Palatka.
'We have solved many problems of the world and prayed over them, as well,' Donna Rogero said of the time spent at their business. 'Now we are looking forward to spending time with family and gardening, fishing and hunting.'
Longtime client former Putnam County Sheriff Taylor Douglas said Albert Rogero has been his family's barber for three generations.
'My son, Charlie, and his son, Graham, got their first haircuts from Albert,' he said. 'I can't remember when Albert was not my barber.'
Despite the stigma that accompanies salons and people sharing personal stories, Douglas said he and Albert did not gossip when he came into the shop.
'We only repeated what we had heard,' he said, smiling. 'We did have a lot of conversations about hunting and fishing.'
Besides that, Douglas knows firsthand the Rogeros have another specialty besides hair.
'They make the best guava jelly ever,' he said. 'Albert was more than just my barber, he is a valued friend. I wish him the best in the years ahead.'
What the Rogeros will remember most about their time at their shop is their customers and the friendships made.
'We will love and miss them,' the couple said. 'But now we want to enjoy the rest of our lives together as long as our Savior permits.'
Jackie Feagin of East Palatka considers the Rogeros family, but that's because they are. She and Albert Rogero are distant cousins.
Feagin said she was honored to be Donna Rogero's last appointment Friday at a place she had been going to for 26 years.
'I loved going to Donna to have my hair done,' she said. 'Donna is such a wonderful friend.'
Feagin finds the closing of the Rogeros shop to be bittersweet.
'I am so happy they are going into their retirement years, but sad for me because I'm going to miss the lady that always did such a good job on my hair.'
Longtime friend Lucius Noyes has fond memories of Albert Rogero, who he has known since they were boys growing up in San Mateo.
'We grew up together playing basketball and baseball,' he said. 'He's been cutting my hair for 52 years after I got out of college.'
Albert Rogero calls his friend the mayor of San Mateo because of his notoriety for spending 37 years working as a pharmacist at Eckerd Drugs in Palatka, where many locals would get their prescriptions filled.
'The Rogeros are fine upstanding people with great families and came from great families,' said Noyes, 76. 'They're straight-arrow people. The kind of people you would like to live next door to.'
While Noyes is sad to see them close shop, he wishes them the best.
'I'm happy for them, but now, I have to find another barber,' he said.

title: Editorial: Making threats against schools no laughing matter
description: We all know about the listeria outbreak at the Jarratt, Virginia, Boar's Head factory that health officials said led to the death of nine people and the hospitalization of 57 others as of Sept.
content:
We all know about the listeria outbreak at the Jarratt, Virginia, Boar's Head factory that health officials said led to the death of nine people and the hospitalization of 57 others as of Sept. 13.
Although no one in Putnam County has died from a different, more recent scare, we can't help but wonder: Has someone drugged the Capri-Sun? Are the children's Crocs affecting their judgment?
We need answers because the number of students who have been arrested this week in connection with suspected violent threats toward schools or specific classmates is astronomical. As of Friday, six children have been arrested, but even one child put in handcuffs because because of alleged school shooting or stabbing threats is too much.
On Monday, a 13-year-old Palatka Junior-Senior High School boy was arrested for allegedly sending two classmates messages saying he would kill them. An 11-year-old Putnam Academy of Arts and Sciences boy was taken into custody later that day after a parent was said to have looked at her son's group chat and saw the suspect making gun threats. Both students included pictures of guns with their threats, according to the Putnam County Sheriff's Office, but both insisted they were merely joking.
After a quiet Tuesday, a 14-year-old Interlachen Junior-Senior High School student was arrested Wednesday after authorities said he used one of the school's computers to write 'I have a gun' in Spanish. He was said to have tried to blame the threat on a Spanish-speaking student.
Thursday was the busiest day, with sheriff's office deputies confiscating a 'cleaver-style, fixed-blade kitchen knife' from an 11-year-old Browning-Pearce Elementary School student authorities said intended to use it on another student for talking to her boyfriend. Later that day, two students at Mellon Learning Center in Palatka were arrested for making false reports about bringing their guns to school.
Exasperated sighs could be heard in our newsroom every time this week when we refreshed Facebook to see another sheriff's office post about children being arrested on suspicion of making threats. Not only are we tired of being stuck in journalist deja vu but these occurrences are much more damaging than these and other students probably realize.
Aside from being a massive distraction to students trying to learn, these 'joke' threats are likely to have lasting damage. All of the students who were arrested this week were placed in handcuffs, were taken to the Putnam County Jail, were charged with felonies, and had their names and mugshots posted online as a deterrent to other students. All but the Browning-Pearce student were taken to the state Department of Juvenile Justice facility in Daytona Beach.
The offenses they are accused of committing will follow them for the rest of their lives. Because they are minors, their cases won't be available to the public. However, a simple Google search of their names, even years in the future, might bring up the sheriff's office posts about them.
Posting child suspects' names and mugshots is extreme, but we are hard-pressed for what else can be done to dissuade students – or anyone else for that matter – from making these threats. Sheriff Gator DeLoach, Superintendent Rick Surrency and their respective staff have been reiterating how severe the consequences can be, but children, who might lack strong long-term vision, continue to be accused of threatening schools.
The memory of the Sept. 4 fatal Apalachee High School shooting in Georgia, which resulted in four people dying and nine others being wounded, is still fresh in people's minds. It's all but guaranteed local law enforcement and school officials won't treat any school threat as a joke.
It past time students realize this is no joking matter.

PUBLIC NOTICE OF INTENT
TO ISSUE AIR PERMIT
Florida Department of Environmental Protection Division of Air Resource Management, Permit Review Section
Draft Air Permit No. 1070005-114-AC
Georgia-Pacific Palatka LLC, Palatka Mill Putnam County, Florida
Applicant: The applicant for this project is Georgia-Pacific Palatka LLC. The applicant's authorized representative and mailing address is: Joseph Webster, VP Operations, Georgia-Pacific Palatka LLC, Palatka Mill, County Road No. 216, Palatka, Florida 32178.
Facility Location: Georgia-Pacific Palatka LLC operates the existing Palatka Mill, which is in Putnam County at 215 County Road 216 in Palatka, Florida.
Project: The Palatka Mill is an existing Kraft paper and pulp mill consisting of the following major activities: chip handling, pulping, bleaching, chemical recovery, utilities, paper machines, converting, and turpentine and tall oil production.
The purpose of this project is to install two former exhaust systems, one for each of the paper machines, Nos. 4 and 5 Tissue Paper Machine to eliminate the process mist that is emitted by paper machines forming sections to reduce corrosion damage to the paper machine building structure and to improve the machine room environment for operators. Emission increases from the project will result in the following emission increases: 4.3 tons/year (TPY) for carbon monoxide; 4.25 TPY of particulate matter (PM); 2.20 TPY for PM with a mean diameter of 10 microns or less (PM10); 1.48 TPY of PM2.5; and all other pollutant emission increases were minimal, less than 1 TPY. Therefore, the project did not trigger preconstruction review for the Prevention of Significant Deterioration of Air Quality per Rule 62-212.400 of the Florida Administrative Code (F.A.C.).
Permitting Authority: Applications for air construction permits are subject to review in accordance with the provisions of Chapter 403, Florida Statutes (F.S.) and Chapters 62-4, 62-210 and 62-212, F.A.C. The proposed project is not exempt from air permitting requirements and an air permit is required to perform the proposed work. The Permitting Authority responsible for making a permit determination for this project is the Permit Review Section in the Department of Environmental Protection's Division of Air Resource Management. The Permitting Authority's physical address is: 2600 Blair Stone Road, Tallahassee, Florida. The Permitting Authority's mailing address is: 2600 Blair Stone Road, MS #5505, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-2400. The Permitting Authority's phone number is 850-717-9000.
Project File: A complete project file is available for public inspection during the normal business hours of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday (except legal holidays), at the address indicated above for the Permitting Authority. The complete project file includes the Draft Permit, the Technical Evaluation and Preliminary Determination, the application and information submitted by the applicant (exclusive of confidential records under Section 403.111, F.S.). Interested persons may contact the Permitting Authority's project engineer for additional information at the address and phone number listed above. In addition, electronic copies of these documents are available on the following web site by entering the draft permit number:
https://fldep.dep.state.fl.us/air/emission/apds/default.asp.
Notice of Intent to Issue Air Permit: The Permitting Authority gives notice of its intent to issue an air construction permit to the applicant for the project described above. The applicant has provided reasonable assurance that operation of proposed equipment will not adversely impact air quality and that the project will comply with all applicable provisions of Chapters 62-4, 62-204, 62-210, 62-212, 62-296 and 62-297, F.A.C. The Permitting Authority will issue a Final Permit in accordance with the conditions of the proposed Draft Permit unless a timely petition for an administrative hearing is filed under Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S. or unless public comment received in accordance with this notice results in a different decision or a significant change of terms or conditions.
Comments: The Permitting Authority will accept written comments concerning the proposed Draft Permit for a period of 14 days from the date of publication of the Public Notice. Written comments must be received by the Permitting Authority by close of business (5:00 p.m.) on or before the end of this 14-day period to the above address and electronically to David Read at David.Read@FloridaDEP.gov. If written comments received result in a significant change to the Draft Permit, the Permitting Authority shall revise the Draft Permit and require, if applicable, another Public Notice. All comments filed will be made available for public inspection.
Petitions: A person whose substantial interests are affected by the proposed permitting decision may petition for an administrative hearing in accordance with Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S. Petitions filed by any persons other than those entitled to written notice under Section 120.60(3), F.S., must be filed within 14 days of publication of the Public Notice or receipt of a written notice, whichever occurs first. Under Section 120.60(3), F.S., however, any person who asked the Permitting Authority for notice of agency action may file a petition within 14 days of receipt of that notice, regardless of the date of publication. A petitioner shall mail a copy of the petition to the applicant at the address indicated above, at the time of filing. A petition for administrative hearing must contain the information set forth below and must be filed (received) with the Agency Clerk in the Office of General Counsel, 3900 Commonwealth Boulevard, MS 35, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-3000, Agency_Clerk@dep.state.fl.us, before the deadline. The failure of any person to file a petition within the appropriate time period shall constitute a waiver of that person's right to request an administrative determination (hearing) under Sections 120.569 and 120.57, F.S., or to intervene in this proceeding and participate as a party to it. Any subsequent intervention (in a proceeding initiated by another party) will be only at the approval of the presiding officer upon the filing of a motion in compliance with Rule 28-106.205, F.A.C.
A petition that disputes the material facts on which the Permitting Authority's action is based must contain the following information: (a) The name and address of each agency affected and each agency's file or identification number, if known; (b) The name, address, any email address, telephone number and any facsimile number of the petitioner; the name, address any email address, telephone number, and any facsimile number of the petitioner's representative, if any, which shall be the address for service purposes during the course of the proceeding; and an explanation of how the petitioner's substantial interests will be affected by the agency determination; (c) A statement of when and how each petitioner received notice of the agency action or proposed decision; (d) A statement of all disputed issues of material fact. If there are none, the petition must so state; (e) A concise statement of the ultimate facts alleged, including the specific facts the petitioner contends warrant reversal or modification of the agency's proposed action; (f) A statement of the specific rules or statutes the petitioner contends require reversal or modification of the agency's proposed action including an explanation of how the alleged facts relate to the specific rules or statutes; and, (g) A statement of the relief sought by the petitioner, stating precisely the action the petitioner wishes the agency to take with respect to the agency's proposed action. A petition that does not dispute the material facts upon which the Permitting Authority's action is based shall state that no such facts are in dispute and otherwise shall contain the same information as set forth above, as required by Rule 28-106.301, F.A.C.
Because the administrative hearing process is designed to formulate final agency action, the filing of a petition means that the Permitting Authority's final action may be different from the position taken by it in this Public Notice of Intent to Issue Air Permit. Persons whose substantial interests will be affected by any such final decision of the Permitting Authority on the application have the right to petition to become a party to the proceeding, in accordance with the requirements set forth above.
Extension of Time: Under Rule 62-110.106(4), F.A.C., a person whose substantial interests are affected by the Department's action may also request an extension of time to file a petition for an administrative hearing. The Department may, for good cause shown, grant the request for an extension of time. Requests for extension of time must be filed with the Office of General Counsel of the Department at 3900 Commonwealth Boulevard, Mail Station 35, Tallahassee, Florida 32399-3000, or via electronic correspondence at Agency_Clerk@dep.state.fl.us, before the deadline for filing a petition for an administrative hearing. A timely request for extension of time shall toll the running of the time period for filing a petition until the request is acted upon.
Mediation: Mediation is not available in this proceeding.

title: Shelters open to house residents as storm rages on
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Even though Putnam County students are off until Monday, Putnam County School District employees haven't gone anywhere.
content:
Body
Even though Putnam County students are off until Monday, Putnam County School District employees haven't gone anywhere. Instead, many of them are preparing to staff local shelters during Hurricane Milton.
Five schools opened at 6 p.m. Tuesday to serve as shelters for residents to take refuge from the incoming hurricane.
The following schools are open to residents:
– Ochwilla Elementary School, a pet-friendly facility, 299 N. State Road 21 in Hawthorne.
– Kelley Smith Elementary School, a shelter for people with special needs, 141 Kelly Smith School Road in Palatka.
– Robert H. Jenkins Jr. Elementary School, 251 S. State Road 315 in Interlachen.
– Browning-Pearce Elementary School, 100 Bear Blvd. in San Mateo.
– Middleton-Burney Elementary School, 1020 Huntington Road in Crescent City.
Browning-Pearce Principal Yolanda Brady said she and other school employees spent hours leading up to the shelter's opening cleaning the cafeteria, where most people stay when the school acts as a shelter, and other areas of the school.
'Residents can kind of set up where they need to be,' she said.
Brady has worked at the school during other storms, most recently Hurricane Helene, but she is expecting a bigger crowd for Hurricane Milton.
'With Helene, we had very few people,' she said Tuesday. 'With this storm being that it's coming in a little stronger and there's expected (to be) more water, we're definitely expecting more folks to come on in.'
Brady did not know Tuesday afternoon when shelters throughout the county would close. She said closures would depend on the weather.
Schools closed to students Tuesday, and since then, district employees have been working to clean out classrooms and other spaces to take in residents, district officials said in an email. Q.I. Roberts Junior-Senior High School can also be used as a shelter, but county and district officials have not opened the facility in anticipation of Milton.
Browning-Pearce can take 2,255 residents, Jenkins can house 2,000, Middleton-Burney can take 805, Ochwilla can accommodate 325 and Kelley-Smith can shelter 240 residents, according to the district.
State guidelines called for the schools to be constructed to withstand hurricane-force winds and be equipped with generators if the power goes out.
Brady said she and other administrators usually work 12-hour shifts at the shelter, and the district's food service staff will serve three meals per day to residents staying at the shelter.
District officials confirmed the same happens at every school serving as a shelter. Maintenance and custodial employees are also there to keep the facility operational during the storm, district officials said Tuesday in an email.
'We appreciate the work of our school and district administrators to go above and beyond their regular duties to manage our Putnam County shelters,' Superintendent Rick Surrency said in an emailed statement. 'Many of our support staff have been at schools today preparing the shelters with supplies and equipment that may be needed.'
Law enforcement officers are stationed at each shelter, and American Red Cross volunteers can stay at the shelters to help if needed, according to the district.
'The Putnam County School District is committed to working with other agencies to help provide safety for our community members during a dangerous weather event,' Surrency said.
District officials said Florida Department of Health employees will assist at the Kelley Smith shelter, which serves primarily people with special needs.
People who qualify to use the Kelley Smith shelter must register ahead of time before going to the facility, Deputy County Administrator J.R. Grimes said Tuesday.
Residents staying in shelters should bring bedding, any necessary medications, personal identification, hygiene items, extra clothing and any entertainment they might want, district officials said. People should also shower before they stay at any of the shelters because the facilities do not offer bathing opportunities, according to district officials.
Anyone who stays at a shelter must register when they show up, and children must be supervised by a parent or guardian at all times, according to the district.
People who have questions about the storm or want to stay in the Kelley Smith shelter can call the Putnam County Emergency Operations Center call line at 386-329-1904.

title: Putnam spared from Hurricane Milton's wrath
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Putnam County residents experienced power outages, downed trees and flooding Thursday, but emergency officials said the damage from Hurricane Milton could have been much worse.
content:
Body
Putnam County residents experienced power outages, downed trees and flooding Thursday, but emergency officials said the damage from Hurricane Milton could have been much worse.
Milton peaked as a Category 5 hurricane but made landfall as a Category 3 around 8:30 p.m. Wednesday in Siesta Key, according to The Weather Channel. The greatest damage occurred in Tampa, Fort Myers and other areas on Florida's West Coast, according to weather.com
However, Putnam residents were delighted they experienced much less severe damage.
Crescent City residents Jennifer Boegler and William Brock spent Thursday afternoon cleaning tree branches and moss out of their front yard.
'I thought it was going to be worse,' Brock said.
Despite the debris, large gusts of wind that had been predicted never attacked their Crescent City home.
Brock said he lived in Daytona Beach for 30 years before moving to Crescent City a few months ago and has seen his share of hurricanes. Boegler said she has lived in the South Putnam city for longer but still had concerns leading up to Milton making landfall.
'I was really worried because it was built in (1977), so I was worried about it,' Boegler said of the home. 'But it did fine. We didn't have any issues.'
She and Brock, her fiancé, lost branches on one of the cedar trees on their property and lost power overnight. By noon Thursday, she said, their power had not returned.
At 7 a.m. Thursday, Putnam County Emergency Management officials reported more than 20,000 Putnam properties were without power. But by 3 p.m. that day, Florida Power & Light's outage map showed 5,750 Putnam customers without power.
At 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Clay Electric showed 6,501 of its Putnam customers had been affected, but the company's outage map did not list how many of those customers' power had been restored.
Statewide, 1,037,413 FPL customers were experiencing power outages at 3 p.m. Thursday, according to the utility company's outage map.
In a press release Thursday, FPL President and CEO Armando Pimentel said the company restored more than 730,000 customers' power outages across Florida within hours of Milton making landfall.
'Our team is working around the clock and will continue to do so until we get every customer's lights back on,' Pimentel said in the statement. 'We have assembled and strategically positioned a restoration workforce of 17,000 men and women from 41 states to restore power as quickly as possible.'
High-risk flood areas like Sportsmans Harbor in Welaka and along Dunns Creek experienced rising waters, county and town officials said.
In a press release, Danelle Rich, an emergency management specialist for the county, said the St. Johns River was at a moderate flood stage by 2 p.m. Thursday. She said the flooding is projected to be a long-term event, with peak flood levels happening Oct. 15.
'People are advised to be aware of the road conditions and be vigilant,' she said in her 2 p.m. update Thursday. 'Do not drive through flooded areas.'
There were downed power lines across Putnam, especially in Crescent City. The downed cables are part of the reason why the Putnam County Sheriff's Office announced a curfew set for 8 p.m. Thursday through 6 a.m. Friday.
Agency spokeswoman Allison Waters-Merritt said the curfew was initiated to keep people safe from the numerous downed cables that are hard to see at night and trees that will continue to fall.
'The reasons that we are putting this curfew in place aren't to prevent anybody from going to work,' she said Thursday in a Facebook video. 'In fact, you are allowed to go to work. You are allowed to get medication. You are allowed to get food. But the idea is to minimize the amount of travel, especially in our communities that do not have power right now because they will not have power, most likely, by tonight.'
While some places reopened Thursday, numerous agencies will remain closed Friday. The Putnam County Governmental Complex, Putnam County Courthouse, Tax Collector's Office, public K-12 schools, St. Johns River State College and city of Palatka offices will remain closed, according to local officials.
School district students will not return to school until Wednesday because Monday is Columbus Day and Tuesday is a teacher planning day, according to district officials. The college is also closed Monday for the holiday but will reopen Tuesday.
County trash pickup will resume Friday.
Residents whose trash is usually collected Wednesday will have theirs collected Friday, emergency officials said. People who have their garbage picked up Thursday and Friday will have their trash collected Saturday, according to emergency management.
Recycling and yard waste pickup are suspended until Monday, but all county landfills will remain open until 7 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
Garbage pickup in the city of Palatka will also resume Friday when Thursday customers will have their trash collected, according to a news release from the city. Palatka residents whose trash is usually collected Friday will have pickup Saturday.
People who have questions about debris pickup can call the county's Emergency Operations Center at 386-329-1904.

title: Former Palatka official eager for reelection
author: Allegra Kitchens
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates whose names are on the ballot for the Nov. 5 general election. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, answers that went over the limit were cut to be as close to 100 words as possible.
A former commissioner is one of two challengers for a seat on the Palatka City Commission during this election cycle.
Having served on the governmental body for nine years, former Commission Allegra Kitchens wants to use her experience and zeal to make Palatka a better place. To do that, she will have to defeat Annie Handerson Davis, a commission candidate for the first time.
The same questionnaire was sent to Davis and Kitchens, but only Kitchens responded by the deadline.
Below, in her own words, are the answers to explain why Kitchens believes she is the best person to occupy the Group 1 seat on the commission:
Why did you decide to run for a seat on the Palatka City Commission?
Kitchens: I've watched the city commission: become less responsive to the basic needs of their citizens, waste taxpayer money on special funds for themselves, have special events aimed at non-city residents, hire outside firms to do things they could do themselves or have done in house. I've seen a commission that can't or won't follow Roberts Rules of Order, who can't stay on the agenda topics causing meetings to last sometimes six hours with no resolution. The city needs help if it is to survive, and I can bring that help.
What do you believe the Palatka City Commission's main priorities should be and why?
Kitchens: The first priority is to hire a city manager who can do the job required of him or her by city code, which is to present a balanced budget to the commission and make sure the city's departments all run smoothly. The commission should assure future and ongoing road, sewer and water projects are finished as quickly as possible. Their priority should be current residents' needs today instead of trying to force involuntary annexation on county citizens. The city should extend water and sewer to non-city residents, but at a higher cost without requiring them to annex into the city.
There has been high employee turnover, especially this year. How would you help keep the city stable in terms of employment and the services workers can offer?
Kitchens: I will make sure the next city manager is fully vetted and investigated. I personally will investigate him or her and report my findings to the rest of the commission during a public meeting. I will not insult or talk down to city staff in public meetings or in private. If I have a problem with a staff member, just like when I was previously on the commission for nine years, I'd talk to that employee in private to work out a solution. I'd treat the staff with respect and equality, not like underlings to be reamed out in public.
What are things the Palatka City Commission is currently doing that you would like to continue? What would you like to see changed?
Kitchens: I'd continue the sports programs, the road, water and sewer improvements, and continue to give support to our police and fire departments. I'd like to see the $5,000 special event funds for each commissioner done away with, and the proposed $50,000 dollars per commissioner for special projects stopped. I'd like to see the commission focus on bringing industry and business in, not on affordable housing. Housing never brings in enough taxes to pay for the one-time cost for city services let alone the ongoing cost for those services. More housing automatically follows industry/ business, not vice versa.
What makes you the ideal candidate for the job?
Kitchens: I represent what the average Palatka citizens of all races want. That is stability at City Hall, a commissioner that concentrates on the needs of the current residents instead of planning to care for the needs of future citizens, and a commissioner who doesn't play politics with citizens' lives or their tax money. I will bring experience and common sense to the commission.

title: Rams to compete in statewide Raider contest
author: Trisha Murphy
description: The JROTC Team from Interlachen Junior-Senior High School has earned the honor of competing in the North Central Florida Raider Competition on Saturday in Brooksville.
content:
Body
The JROTC Team from Interlachen Junior-Senior High School has earned the honor of competing in the North Central Florida Raider Competition on Saturday in Brooksville.
The state competition will be the first for the West Putnam school since 2006.
Interlachen's JROTC program consists of 18 members, 14 of whom will be competing at the state level Saturday.
The four not competing will provide logistical support to the team as well as early reconnaissance of the event lanes.
'We have a male-mixed team of nine males and five females available for the competition,' said Lt. Col. Korey Brown, the senior Army instructor of the JROTC program at Interlachen High. 'The male-mixed team will compete with six males and four females at each event.'
The competition will include a 5K run, a 100-meter tire flip, the Raider Fitness Challenge, which is a ¾-mile obstacle course, a 1-mile cross-country rescue, which is a simulation of evacuating a casualty over various types of terrain, and other challenges.
The local team is one of 76 across the state that earned a spot to compete after placing in the state qualifier.
The group took three first-place wins, one each in the 5K Run, Raider Fitness Challenge and tire flip. Interlachen cadets took second place in cross-country rescue and third in a one-rope bridge challenge.
'I could not be more proud of this team,' said Brown, who is in her fourth year coaching the Interlachen team. 'Over the last four years, we have progressed from the worst team in the area in the first year to gaining individual Raider event wins in the second year and placing overall in the third year and now representing all of North Central Florida this year.'
Brown said the competition will be separated into three male, male-mixed and female categories. The 76 teams in the competition will also be the winners of their regional Raiders state competitions.
Brown is excited to see her group compete this weekend.
'They have been working very hard three to five days a week,' she said. 'They have had to overcome many physical and mental challenges during training and the season, including maintaining a 2.5 academic grade point average to remain on the team.
Training for the Raider season started in July when cadets traveled to Gainesville for obstacle training, made several trips to Memorial Bridge in Palatka for hill training, went to Ravine Gardens State Park in Palatka for trail and distance running, and kept it local in downtown Interlachen for distance running.
Brown said the Interlachen team is made up of a select group of JROTC cadets and represents the best of the program.
'We are very proud to not only represent North Central Florida, Putnam County and the town of Interlachen, but our school as well,' Brown said. 'The JROTC Raider State Competition is the super bowl of competitions for us.'

title: Authors to converge at inaugural book festival
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Local authors and book promoters are coming together to share their love of reading and writing with the community as the Putnam County Writers Association hosts the Putnam County Book Festival.
content:
Local authors and book promoters are coming together to share their love of reading and writing with the community as the Putnam County Writers Association hosts the Putnam County Book Festival.
Presented by Blue Crab Productions, the two-day event will be from 5:30–7:30 p.m. today at the St. Johns River Center, 102 N. First St. in Palatka. Tonight's event is open to authors only and will include workshops for writers by Marjory Lyons and Anthony Dixon. The registration fee is $10 and can be paid at putnambookfestival.square.site/.
The second part of the festival will be from 530–7:30 p.m. Thursday and is free to everyone. Participating artists will have their books and other merchandise available for sale on Thursday at the River Center.
For details, email putnamwritersassociation@aol.com or call 410–670–1481.
'Thursday's event is a chance for the community to come and discover new authors, support local talent and encourage continual literacy in our Putnam County community,' said Cowan Amaye-Obu, the interim director of the Putnam County Writers Association.
Some of the participating writers include Amaye-Obu, who recently published the second edition of 'The Dancing Mastodon Magazine'; Rae Hill who wrote the novel 'The Dark Mysteries of Castile Free Shy'; and Bill Shuey, who is a member of the Western Writers' Association, who writes Western and mystery novels. Also available will be books written for the Baby Brain Builders program.
Hill said she is excited to be a part of this year's book festival.
'This event is so important to our local and budding authors,' the Fruitland author said. 'It provides a great opportunity to be seen and for us to learn from one another.'
According to Amaye-Obu, the Putnam County Writers Association's mission is to organize local authors and to facilitate the marketing and sales of quality content across Putnam County.
'The association will work with local businesses, libraries, bookstores and schools to encourage literacy and reading in our community,' he said. 'We will offer publishing services for authors and literary programs for readers to encourage continual literacy into the next generation.'
Amaye-Obu is looking forward to a good turnout for the two-day inaugural book festival.
'This event will give guests a chance to cultivate a love for reading and writing in our community,' he said.

title: Elfs eager to give out toys to families in need
author: Trisha Murphy
description: The hall at one local church is looking a lot like Toyland these days as it is providing a temporary home for donated toys that will be handed out to area families.
content:
Body
The hall at one local church is looking a lot like Toyland these days as it is providing a temporary home for donated toys that will be handed out to area families.
Sponsored by the Junior Woman's Club of Palatka, the Putnam County Elfs for Kids toy giveaway is in its 40th year.
Toys will be handed out from 8 a.m. – noon and 1 – 4 p.m. Dec. 14 at Trinity Global Methodist Church, 1400 Husson Ave. in Palatka. Signs will direct attendees to a room behind the church, adjacent to Cecille Avenue, where the toys will be given away.
Children should not be present for the pickup. Walk-ups for assistance will be accepted if toys are available.
'It is always a good feeling knowing the toys will make a child have a merry Christmas and help their parents stretch their funds a little further,' said Vicki Hare, one of the club members making sure it happens. 'The cost of living has gone so high that it takes a lot of money to cover the necessities. Raising children is expensive.'
Applications are available for families to receive toys for children ages 1-10 and can be picked up at the Palatka Police Department, 110 N. 11th St.; the WIC office and the Florida Department of Health in Putnam County, 2801 Kennedy St. in Palatka; AZA Health in Palatka, Interlachen and Crescent City; local pediatrician offices; and some day care centers.
The application deadline is Dec. 6.
Hare said the group provided 1,000 children with toys last year and she is expecting to help the same number or more this year.
'We are one of the original recipients of the Frank V. Oliver Foundation (Fund) and we get a large donation each year,' Hare said. 'We add the donations from the public to that to provide the toys.'
The club currently is in debt $14,000 for the ordered toys, but it has some of the money.
Monetary donations for Putnam County Elfs for Kids can be mailed to P.O. Box 1723, Palatka, FL 32178.
Those who would like to make a toy donation can do so by dropping off new, unwrapped toys with a value of $10 or more to Masters Funeral Home, Dollar General on Reid Street, Dollar General on Crill Avenue, Dollar General in East Palatka and Dollar General at Peniel. No gun toys will be accepted.
Volunteers are needed to help with the toy distribution in areas like signing in, general organization, distributing gifts and packing up any leftover items at the end of the day.
'We need volunteers to help with a little bit of everything,' said Christi Bellamy, a club member.
Bellamy feels blessed when she hears families say to her, 'This is exactly what my child wanted,' and, 'Thank you,' she said.
The club is appreciative of Trinity Global Methodist Church, which stepped up after hearing Elfs for Kids organizers needed a place to store and distribute toys.
'Every year, we need a place, and to have them speak up and allow us to use their building makes us grateful,' club member Jackie King said.
Hare said the Junior Woman's Club is small and its members rely on the public's assistance to provide the needed toys each year. She and other volunteers have already started looking for a place for next year's distribution.
'We are always searching, especially for gifts for girls and boys ages 7-10,' Hare said. 'We always need balls and games and encourage things that promote activity inside and outside.'
Hare is thankful for Putnam County residents and the support they give every year to Elfs for Kids.
'There are other groups popping up doing toys (for) older children,' she said. 'My wish is that groups would work together, not duplicating to one age group but making it possible to extend the gifts to older children. We can only do up to age 10, but another group could work with us and extend the age to 15, instead of each group beginning at 1.'
Hare admits toys are not cheap, no matter the age group, and older children tend to want electronics, which are out of the club's price range.
'By helping with the gifts for the younger children, we hope the parents can provide for the older ones,' she said. 'When we started, $5 bought a nice toy. Now, the same type of toy runs $10 to $15 so it takes more money to buy them. We buy a large bit from a toy distributor.'
Hare is looking forward to the distribution because children expect toys for the holidays.
'It gives everyone a good feeling knowing that the children will have toys for Christmas,' she said.
Gift-giving always has a way of making the giver feel good, whether giving to their church, to a family in need or to make a child smile, Hare said.
'The holiday season is about giving and supporting your family, church and charities,' she said. 'It makes you thankful for the blessings you have received through the year and hopes that the coming year will be better and you are thankful for what you have received.'

title: Food giveaways aplenty in lead-up to holiday
author: Trisha Murphy
description: There are a lot of do-gooders in Putnam County working to make sure local residents, especially those in need, have a chance to eat turkey and a slice of pie this Thanksgiving.
content:
Body
There are a lot of do-gooders in Putnam County working to make sure local residents, especially those in need, have a chance to eat turkey and a slice of pie this Thanksgiving.
Giveaways and other charitable events will be occurring throughout the area starting this week and extending into next week.
Some of the events are listed below:
– Epic-Cure will hand out free turkeys along with other food items from 1–3 p.m. Friday at Refuge Church, 614 N. 18th St. in Palatka.
Food giveaways are held every Friday.
– On Friday, Beulah Baptist Church and Epic-Cure will distribute holiday food boxes starting at 12:30 p.m. until the food is gone at 106 Beulah Church Road in Crescent City. The church hands out food boxes every Friday at the same time.
'We usually give out between 180 to 200 boxes each week,' Beulah Pastor Roger Phillips said. 'We don't have a space to store food, so we try and distribute all the food. Nobody leaves without something.'
–Church members at Beulah Baptist will also prepare a Thanksgiving meal with turkey, ham, dressing, all the side dishes and desserts Saturday. This will be the fourth year the church has opened the doors of its fellowship hall, 106 Beulah Church Road in Crescent City, for everyone to partake in the free Thanksgiving meal. Takeout plates are also available.
'Last year, we served about 300 people, including takeouts,' Pastor Roger Phillips said.
According to Phillips, his church wants to be known as a congregation that meets people where they are and ministers to their needs.
'We are glad to be able to provide the food for this celebration meal of Thanksgiving and praise,' he said. 'We welcome our guests to come for fellowship, music and a Thanksgiving devotional.'
Phillips said his church's desire is to serve the privileged and underprivileged.
'Thanksgiving has a tradition of celebrating the blessings of our almighty God,' he said. 'May God grant that he finds us grateful every day for all of his gifts, spiritual and material. God is good and every good gift comes from him.'
– Clayton Homes in East Palatka is partnering with iHeart Realty Inc. to hand out 100 free turkeys weighing 12-14 pounds. The giveaway will be at 9 a.m. Saturday at 316 S. U.S. 17 in East Palatka. One turkey per household will be given out while supplies last. The event is open to everyone.
According to Richard Harris, the general manager of Clayton Homes, the giveaway is a way to say thank you to customers for a great year and to give something back to the community.
'No ID is necessary, just a smile,' he said. 'We saw this as a perfect opportunity to help families who might be struggling, ensuring they can enjoy a holiday meal. It's a way for us to show gratitude to our neighbors and make a positive impact during the season of giving.'
For details, call 386-325-8013 or visit www.claytonhomesflorida.com.
– Lakeside Baptist Church in Hawthorne, in association with Bread of the Mighty Food Bank, will host a drive-thru food giveaway from 10 a.m. Saturday until it's all gone. Food items will include turkeys and chickens.
Volunteers are needed to help with the giveaway, which will take place at the church, 22027 SE 65th Ave. For details, call 352-358-3334 or 352-284-8535.
– The Bread of Life soup kitchen will provide meals to those in need Monday through Wednesday from 11:30 a.m. – 12:30 p.m. at 320 N. Fifth St. in Palatka.
On Wednesday, there will be a memorial meal in honor of a former client who died in October. The food that day will consist of the traditional Thanksgiving meal as well as shepherd's pie, the client's favorite. The public is invited.
– Creative Cuzinz, which was started by Lakesha Session and Marion Session, will serve free Thanksgiving meals with all the fixings through its Feed the Neighborhood program.
The event will start at noon Tuesday at the Price-Martin Community Center, 220 N. 11th St. in Palatka, and will continue while the food lasts. Meals will be in take-out containers but tables will be available for those who want to stay and eat.
Lakesha Session said the meal distribution is a chance to give back to the community.
'Thanksgiving is about family and people around those you love,' she said. 'Everyone who needs a hot meal is welcome to come.'
Creative Cuzins will also hand out care packages along with other community partners.
Along with friends, family and members of the Church of Recovery, Creative Cuzinz officials fed about 385 people last year. The event has been taking place for 13 years.
– The Interlachen Soup Kitchen, which is run by Dave Yonts and his team of volunteers, will offer a holiday meal to anyone who stops by from 11 a.m. – 1 p.m. on Nov. 28, Thanksgiving Day, at 155 N. County Road 315.
The meals are free to everyone.
– In Melrose, residents will celebrate Thanksgiving in the Park and everyone is invited to partake in a free meal and fun.
The celebration will be from 11 a.m. – 1 p.m., or until the food is gone, on Nov. 28, Thanksgiving Day, at Melrose Heritage Park, 300 State Road 26.
Meals will be passed out at the park and there will be tables and chairs set up for those who want to dine there. There will also be games for children.
The meals will be catered and in ready-to-go boxes to take home. The menu includes turkey, potato salad, stuffing and gravy, green beans, a bottle of water, and dessert.

title: CC student 1 of 12 college fellowship finalists
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The hard work and dedication of a Crescent City student have put her in the running to receive thousands of dollars to help pay for college.
content:
Body
The hard work and dedication of a Crescent City student have put her in the running to receive thousands of dollars to help pay for college.
Mithila 'Mia' Paul, a senior at Crescent City Junior-Senior High School and a Take Stock in Children mentee, is one of 12 Take Stock seniors in Florida to be considered for the Asofsky Foundation's Leaders For Life Fellowship.
'Thank you, guys, all so much,' Paul said Monday after being surprised in her English class with balloons, flowers and congratulatory signs. 'It's a little embarrassing, but I thank you. I appreciate it very much, and it's a wonderful opportunity.'
The fellowship would grant Paul up to $10,000 per year during college if she attends a four-year public university in Florida, according to Take Stock in Children, a mentorship program that supports low-income students in their quest to succeed in college and beyond.
If she receives the fellowship, Paul will also get leadership training and professional development assistance, according to Take Stock in Children.
Just six seniors statewide are granted the endowment, and Paul will find out in January is among the winners.
Take Stock leaders, high school employees, other Putnam County School District officials and Paul's family were among the people to surprise her Monday with news of her being a finalist.
Paul's mentor, Latina Hardy, had no doubt she would be among the final 12 and believes she will be one of the lucky six.
'This is such a special young lady,' Hardy said while holding a bouquet of roses for her mentee. 'She works so hard and is continuing to work hard. And I just want her to know I'm very proud of her, and I know she's going to be one of those six to receive that scholarship.'
Paul's English teacher, Adam Mitchell, spoke highly about her character, hard work and dedication.
He submitted a recommendation letter on her behalf to fellowship officials. He had a copy with him Monday and read it to everyone who stopped by to support Paul.
'She is a freethinker: the kind of person who is unwilling to look away from the problems and who instead finds new ways forward,' Mitchell read aloud.
Paul is the daughter of parents who immigrated to America from Bangladesh to start a new life. Because of her parents' hard work, Paul represents the best of society and the potential people have to succeed, Mitchell said.
'Far too often, I have taught students who were afraid to dream as life had taught them that dreams are unattainable,' Mitchell wrote. 'Mia, however, is a true dreamer; she knows the challenges she may face in pursuing higher education, but she will not let them deter her.'
Paul, too, credits her parents for influencing her to become a leader. In one of her application essays, Paul said that if her parents had not entered the U.S. Diversity Visa Program, she would not be who she is today.
'My journey as a leader began in the quiet corners within my own home, where I took on the role of translating the world for my family,' Paul wrote. '… Each time I spoke up for them, I felt the weight of responsibility along with a tinge of pride for being their voice.'
Paul has a 3.99 unweighted GPA and a 4.67 weighted GPA, according to her fellowship application. She already completed her coursework to obtain her Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education diploma, according to Take Stock in Children officials, and is currently enrolled in dual enrollment classes.
Paul has already qualified for the Bright Futures Scholarship Program, according to Take Stock officials.
While handling her coursework, Paul served as part of the district's Chief Science Officers program, which promotes science, technology, engineering and math initiatives in the district. She is a member of the National Honors Society and Superintendent Student Council while holding down a job at Winn-Dixie in Crescent City.
Paul said she is a product of love and the lessons she has learned from her family and other loved ones. The senior wants to attend the University of Florida to become an occupational therapist.
Paul said in one of her application essays that she is fluent in Bengali and could connect with other areas of the world where health care is limited.
'I am compelled in my endeavors by my immigrant parents' journey from Bangladesh, a third-world country, to succeed,' Paul wrote. '… Their determination through complexities of a new culture, determination through language barriers and financial crisis have ignited my passion for people. My parents inculcated the importance of kindness to others in a world surrounded by unknown people.

title: Tour to offer glimpse at historic Palatka structures
author: Trisha Murphy
description: The countdown is on for area residents to get a chance to go inside five private historic homes and one home-turned-bed and breakfast throughout Palatka.
content:
The countdown is on for area residents to get a chance to go inside five private historic homes and one home-turned-bed and breakfast throughout Palatka.
Sponsored by the General Federation of Women's Clubs Woman's Club of Palatka, the second annual Christmas Tour of Homes, which will occur Saturday, will see all of the participating locations decorated for the holidays.
The tour will take place from 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. and begin at the Woman's Club at 600 S. 13th St. in Palatka. At the Woman's Club, participants will pick up their wristbands and programs, which highlight local attractions, including Ravine Gardens State Park.
The tickets are $25 while they last and will be available at the door. Tickets can be purchased at www.gfwcpalatka.com/event-tickets, by emailing gfwcpalatka@aol.com or by calling 386-937-3196.
The tickets are also available at Lemon Street Market & Mercantile, 715 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka, and The Urban Farmhouse, 701 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka.
Proceeds from the event will support local charities and future community projects.
One of the featured places on the tour is Grand Gables Inn Bed & Breakfast owned by Tate and Jessie Miller.
The house has been described as perhaps the most palatial home in all of Florida, according to a news release from the Woman's Club.
'This three-story house has eight bedrooms, six-and-a-half baths and is a stunning example of Queen Anne architecture by famed New England architect Rufus Sargent,' according to the news release. 'The bed and breakfast also has 12-foot ceilings, a grand staircase and a sweeping veranda where guests can luxuriate in rooms steeped in American history.'
The Millers purchased the property in 2017 from the late Pauline Pellicer and opened the inn in November of that year.
The property was the inspiration for what the Millers have turned it into today.
'It called out for someone to open it as a bed and breakfast,' Tate Miller said.
There is nothing in the state quite like the bed and breakfast house, which still has its 140-year-old solid cherry wood China cabinet still fully intact.
'All rooms are decorated in period-correct style,' he said.
Another point of interest in the house is an underground tunnel, which at one time went all the way from the basement to the St. Johns River.
'It originally went 150 yards from the house to the river,' Tate Miller said.
He believes it was in 2000 that Pellicer took on a nine-year remodel and she had workers fill in the tunnel and seal it up.
'It took us nine months to find the location of the tunnel,' he said. 'We opened up the first 10 feet so visitors could see this interesting feature.'
This is the first time the bed and breakfast has been in the Tour of Homes, Tate Miller said.
'This house is a very important part of Palatka history,' said Tate Miller, who lives next door to the bed and breakfast with his wife. 'People are stunned when they see the house and hear its history.'
According to Lucy May, the Tour of Homes chairwoman, those on the tour will be able to see the six showcased historic places that will immerse them in the charm and history of Palatka.
'This tour of homes has a wealth of information and history that Putnam County residents will especially find interesting,' she said. 'It's amazing to hear about all of the interesting facts.'
Another place on the tour is a home that was owned by well-known local residents, including a renowned doctor, who was the namesake for Crill Avenue in Palatka and later a chief engineer with Hubbard Hart's steamship line.
Tour-goers might also want to take note of another home that was owned by a funeral home proprietor who served as a city commissioner. That home, which was owned by a man who was a partner in the Palatka-Jacksonville Steamboat Line, is one of the oldest buildings in Palatka and was remodeled as a Colonial Revival-style home.
Finally, the tour will showcase a home that dates way back to the 1800s. It was owned by a former mayor, a superintendent of the Putnam County School District, a local sheriff and the owner of the Howell Theatre.
May hopes the public will take time to visit these historic places through the self-guided walking tour.
'We are looking for another successful home tour this year,' said May. 'Most of the homes on the tour are located in the North (Historic District) and South Historic District and are decorated for the season to get everyone in a festive, holiday mood.'

title: The Joy of Giving
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Palatka Housing Authority employees partnered with a local civic organization to provide Christmas gifts to families who live in the city.
content:
Body
Palatka Housing Authority employees partnered with a local civic organization to provide Christmas gifts to families who live in the city.
The Rotary Club of Palatka continued its yearly trend of sponsoring a holiday gift giveaway at the housing authority headquarters, something the civic organization has been doing for more than 10 years, according to Daily News records. Rotary has also been sponsoring other local gift giveaways for more than 50 years.
On Wednesday, mothers and other family members bagged a heap of gifts for each family and expressed their gratitude as they did.
'I just want to say thank you all for giving these gifts out to us mothers,' resident Dishara Bullard said. 'It's a blessing.'
Rotary board member Yvette Jones is happy the civic group partners with the housing authority every year for this opportunity, calling it a blessing just to be able to help the residents.
'It always touched my heart when I heard their stories,' she said. 'It makes you feel good.'
Volunteers from a local organization, The Charmettes, wrapped nearly 100 toys and other gifts the Rotary Club donated, said Carol Coffie, the housing authority's director of resident services.
Property Manager Joy Tincher said she's grateful for Rotary's continued partnership, which allowed 25 families to receive assistance this year.
One gift recipient said she has been spending her year raising a young child who was found alone behind one of the housing authority properties, and it's been a struggle to provide with limited funds.
Another recipient called the gift giveaway a nice surprise for her and her family.
For one resident at Wednesday's giveaway, the year brought more challenges than previous ones.
Beleria Leonard spent the past year working to obtain a bachelor's degree in psychology from Colorado Technical University. Leonard said that on Dec. 26, she plans to start working on obtaining a master's degree in psychology and counseling with a focus on mental health and wellness from Grand Canyon University.
'I want to say thank you,' she said, 'because this year, I wasn't able to do as much as I normally do for them.'
