content:
Authorities believe the fatal shootings that took place in front of the Palatka Daily News on Christmas night could have stemmed from a party in St. Johns County that moved to Palatka.
As of Thursday afternoon, two people were killed and another person remains in critical condition after they were shot in front of the newspaper building, 1825 St. Johns Ave., at 9:40 p.m. Wednesday, according to the Palatka Police Department.
Assistant Chief Matt Newcomb said Thursday morning he could not release the identities of the victims. However, he disclosed that one person died at the newspaper building and another person died at a hospital after being taken from the scene, he said.
Newcomb declined to list the trauma facility where the third victim was taken out of caution for their safety.
'We are still trying to make identification and notify the next of kin,' Newcomb said.
Police believe many of the people at the scene prior to the shooting were originally at a St. Johns County Party that had been shut down. After that party ended, Newcomb hypothesized, many of those attendees moved to Palatka to continue the event.
Newcomb said he didn't know the exact location of the St. Johns County festivities.
He said the shootings took place in the Daily News parking lot and under the building's awning near the front door. Newcomb said the crime scene extends past the newspaper to behind Palatka Flooring Center, 1813 Reid St.
'I don't believe there's a threat to the community,' Newcomb said.
He could not confirm if the shootings were gang-related, but the police hope to release more information about the ongoing investigation later this evening.
Numerous vehicles believed to belong to some people gathered by the building at the time of the shooting were parked in the Daily News parking lot and towed away Thursday, Newcomb said. Not all of the vehicles belonged to the victims, he said.
There were at least 73 evidence markers at the scene to pinpoint firearm rounds, a bullet hole through the Daily News mailroom and other pieces of evidence.
Officers had already been near the scene at the time of the shooting Wednesday evening to try to disperse crowds gathered at Dollar & More, 114 N. 19th St., Newcomb said.
Detectives are considering the possibility of a fourth person involved, but Newcomb said that information has not been verified.
'If there is another person that's involved, we're working to identify that person,' Newcomb said. '... That's what we're trying to figure out.'
The Daily News building will be closed today to foot traffic. The office is closed until further notice as the building is an active crime scene and part of the ongoing investigation. The business will reopen to phone calls only as soon as we can.
In a statement issued Thursday morning, Daily News Publisher Jennifer Moates expressed her sadness over what transpired Wednesday night. While newspaper employees were not at the building during the shooting, she said, the events that occurred are no less tragic.
"No Palatka Daily News employees were working at the time,' Moates said in the statement. 'Our prayers are with the families who tragically lost loved ones, and we are grateful to the first responders who acted quickly to assist all involved. As journalists, we will continue to follow this investigation closely and provide updates to our community. As members of our community, we grieve the loss.'

title: Palatka sports icons honored with facility renamings
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Families and other loved ones gathered at Booker Park-Lefty Turner Field in Palatka earlier this month to celebrate the legacies of three local sports and community heroes.
content:
Body
Families and other loved ones gathered at Booker Park-Lefty Turner Field in Palatka earlier this month to celebrate the legacies of three local sports and community heroes.
On Dec. 21, the complex's basketball courts were named the Jarvis Eric Williams Sr. Basketball Courts. The softball fields were designated the John L. Williams North Softball Field and Johnson Session Sr. South Softball Field.
All three honorees have played integral parts in the community.
'Thanks to the city of Palatka for allowing me, Jarvis and Johnson to be part of this community the way I feel like it's necessary to be a part of and continue success from this point on,' John L. Williams said during the renaming ceremony.
Former Mayor Terrill Hill hosted the renaming ceremony as part of a project to revamp Booker Park he had been working on since 2022. The city received a brownfields grant from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to clean up the park, but Hill said there is still more work to be done.
The naming ceremony at Booker Park, 701 N. 10th St. in Palatka, added three more local sports legends' names to the facility to accompany Lefty Turner, a Negro League baseball player who has a field at the park named after him.
Earlier this year, the sports complex section of the park was dedicated as the John Henry 'Pop' Lloyd Sports Complex in honor of the Palatka native and shortstop who broke color barriers during his 27-year career, according to the National Baseball Hall of Fame. He was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1977.
The renaming ceremony focused on celebrating the impacts of honorees, three sports titans whose roots go back to Palatka.
'Those guys were intricate parts of the fabric of Palatka,' Hill said.
Turner, Lloyd, Jarvis Williams, John L. Williams and Session all had humble beginnings, Hill said. And when they left Palatka and made it big, they gave back to the place they called home.
'The naming of the fields … it all goes back to the same concepts,' Hill said.
Lasting legacies
Families of Jarvis Williams, John L. Williams and Johnson Session Sr. attended the renaming ceremony to represent their loved ones, Hill said.
The Central Academy class of 1964 joined Session's family to celebrate their classmate, who passed away at age 75 in 2021.
Session was a coach and umpire in Palatka. He started coaching in the 1960s during segregation and didn't stop until 2016.
Hill said Session raised and coached many kids from Palatka and nearby. When the youth sports teams were underfunded, Session took money out of his own pocket to help, Hill added.
'For 50 years, he had a hand in every aspect of youth life,' Hill said.
Not only did Session coach baseball, football and basketball, but he helped families who were struggling and mentored the youth to make sure they stayed in school and kept up their grades, Hill said.
The complex will also keep alive the memory of another Palatka sports icon, Jarvis Williams, who grew up on Seventh Street in Palatka, just one block away from Turner, Hill said. In 1983, Jarvis Williams graduated from Palatka High School, where he played varsity football, contributing to the team winning the state championship in 1981.
He played for the University of Florida Gators from 1984 to 1987, winning an All-American award in 1987. He later moved on to the NFL, playing for the Miami Dolphins from 1988 to 1993 and the New York Giants in 1994.
At 46, Jarvis Williams died in May 2010 after football practice at Interlachen High School. When the Palatka City Commission voted in May 2024 to name the fields after the three honorees, Hill said Jarvis Williams accomplished so much for Palatka.
'Jarvis died doing what he loved, and that was coaching football,' Hill said in May. 'On the day he died, he'd just left practice before he passed and he left us with so many memories.'
While most of the people whose names grace facilities at the park are deceased, John L. Williams was able to celebrate the renaming in person. He thanked city officials for the honor and expressed his appreciation for his fellow sports legends.
'I love you,' John L. Williams said. 'Thank you, and continue the support that we have been doing.'
He also played for the Gators from 1982 to 1985 after graduating from Palatka High School in 1982, also contributing to the 1981 championship win.
He was a first-round NFL draft pick by the Seattle Seahawks in 1986 and played for them from until 1993. His pro football career came to an end after his stint with the Pittsburgh Steelers from 1994 to 1995.
The men whose names were added to Booker Park were athletes, but their dedication goes beyond any sports arena, which is why they deserved this honor, Hill said.
'The common theme with all of them is they put God first,' he said. 'They were all servant leaders, and they were all committed to their community.'

title: 5 candidates competing for Welaka mayoral seat
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Eight candidates are seeking seats on the Welaka Town Council, with five of them hoping to be the town's next mayor.
content:
Eight candidates are seeking seats on the Welaka Town Council, with five of them hoping to be the town's next mayor.
Welaka's elections occur in March, rather than November with every other municipality. This year's election, in which only people who live within Welaka's town limits can vote, will be March 4.
There are two open council seats, one of which is vacant and the other Councilwoman Tonya Long currently occupies. The mayoral position will be up for grabs as former Mayor Jamie Watts resigned from the position to run for a spot in the Florida House of Representatives.
Watts was defeated in the Aug. 20 primary.
Welaka Town Council President has been acting as the mayor, as required by the town's charter, since November, but declined to run for mayor in the March 4 election. Finch submitted her intent to resign from her councilmember position but did so after plans were underway for the March election.
'This letter is to provide you with a written notice of my resignation for my council seat, effective March 4, 2025,' Finch wrote in her resignation letter to Supervisor of Elections Charles Overturf III.
As Finch, who was first elected to the Welaka Town Council in 2018, transitions out of office, there are plenty of people vying for positions on the council.
First elected in 2021, Long is running for reelection to her position. Sandra Walker, who ran for a council seat in 2023, and political newcomer David Jeltes are also competing for the two councilmember positions.
The people in the running to be Welaka's next mayor are Courtney DeSouza, Watts' girlfriend; Councilwoman Kim Dugger, who declined to seek reelection to her councilmember seat; Kevin Finch, Jessica Finch's ex-husband; Brad Kay; and Pam Olson. Overturf said he doesn't remember ever seeing this many mayoral candidates in one race in Putnam County.
'Normally you might have two or maybe three but not five,' he said. '... Usually Palatka, it might be two or three. … Pomona Park didn't have anybody run except for one candidate. Interlachen, we didn't have anybody run except the one candidate.'
Two people ran for the mayoral position in Crescent City during the 2024 election, he added. Overturf said five candidates might be getting close to a record.
Welaka's mayoral and council seats are up for grabs every two years, per the town's charter.
Jessica Finch's resignation from her councilmember seat after plans were already underway for the March election requires the town to have another election later in the year to fill the vacancy she will leave behind. Overturf said no date for that election had been chosen as of Wednesday.
As of Wednesday, Welaka had 693 eligible voters, said Overturf, who hopes there is a large turnout in March and at the election to replace Councilwoman Finch.
'The elections are important,' he said. 'But, of course, the people voting, to me, is the most important because that's their given right.'

title: FloArts professor's works to be shown at Larimer
author: Trisha Murphy
description: People who don't know or aren't even familiar with Florida School of the Arts professor Dan Askew are unaware he has sense of humor.
content:
Body
People who don't know or aren't even familiar with Florida School of the Arts professor Dan Askew are unaware he has sense of humor.
The East Palatka resident, who has taught at the school since fall 2011, said his humor can be a tad macabre.
'You can also call it dark humor,' Askew said.
He will be featured in the exhibit 'Punchlines from the Doghouse,' which opens Friday from 6–8 p.m. at the Larimer Arts Center, 216 Reid St. in Palatka. Admission is free to the public is invited. Refreshments will be served.
The exhibit will be on display through Feb. 24 and available to be seen during events at the Larimer, including when the River City Players presents 'The Mousetrap' next week.
Special viewing of Askew's exhibit can be seen by calling him at 432-230–1712.
According to Askew, he has been involved in art since he was a little kid.
'When I was in kindergarten through 12th grade, I always assumed I'd be some kind of engineer,' said the father three. 'I started college as a psychology major because I was interested in parapsychology.'
But Askew didn't feel psychology was his calling.
'Art always came easy to me, and it seemed where I might belong,' he said. 'So, I became an art major around 1986.'
Askew explained the title 'Punchlines from the Doghouse' has different interpretations.
'There is sometimes a political bend to my work,' he said. 'Being very progressive, I feel like my ilk has been sent to the doghouse. It also has to do with something very personal.'
Askew has served as the volunteer curator for the Arts Council of Greater Palatka since 2021.
Askew said his upcoming show will be his first solo show since his show at FloArts in 2012. For details on Askew's work, visit danaskew.net.
Askew's work often includes the use of found objects, fabrication in a variety of materials, video, ceramic elements, kinetic components, painting, photography, graphics and 3D printing.
The show leans a little heavy on ceramics, he said.
'With a love for pure function and the patina that comes from prolonged use, my works hint at vague mythologies surrounding the vast plethora of apocalyptic scenarios, both imagined and 'legitimately' prophesied,' he said. 'Black humor, along with a chaotic mash-up of media process becomes the lens through which to view a confused reality. The range of influences are evidence of a re-adolescent skeptic with more questions than answers.'
Askew hopes people will take away of piece of art from the opening.
'It's all for sale,' he said. 'Other than that, I imagine there will be a lot of head-scratching and a few laughs. I play around with a lot of juxtaposition. I don't usually create my work with a clear intended message. I tell my students that you don't have to make art from a soap box. A lot of times, I create my work as an interrogative. I want to know what it means too. I create the work as a means to answer the questions.'
Askew said the show will be a great opportunity for something to do on a Friday night while also seeing art a little outside the norm of what might be expected.
Askew said it sad that no one has offered him a solo show in a while, so he has had to do it himself.
'These days,' he said, 'I guess it's OK to be self-serving and toot one's own horn.'

Image
Body
The Friends of Ravine Gardens is hosting Spill the Tea Party at the Ravine Gardens State Park, where guests who make the trek through the 1.8-mile loop through the park are sure to see a variety of the featured plants in various colors.
Spill the Tea Party will be from 5:30–7:30 p.m. Saturday at 1600 Twigg St. in Palatka.
The event is free to the community and will feature teas, snacks, games, prizes and a chance to hear the latest scoop, according to SallyJan Smith, park service specialist.

title: County judge contest gets another contestant
description: A third contestant has entered the race to win an elected judicial position in this year's election. Earlier this month, Constance Daniels filed her paperwork to seek the Putnam County Court Judge…
content: A third contestant has entered the race to win an elected judicial position in this year's election. Earlier this month, Constance Daniels filed her paperwork to seek the Putnam County Court Judge Group 1 position, according to the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office. The race is nonpartisan. Daniels will be facing off against Judge Anne Marie Gennusa, who was appointed to the position in 2023, and fellow challenger Alex Sharp. Whoever is elected will begin serving their first six-year term as a Putnam County judge. Unlike candidates of other local election races who qualify in June, the judge candidates must qualify to continue running for office from April 22-26. This year's primary is Aug. 20, and the general election is Nov. 5. For more information, call the Elections Office at 386-329-0224 or visit soe.putnam-fl.com.

title: Presenter's illness spurs finale cancellation
description: Palatka Daily News The One Book One Putnam season is coming to an end this year without its usual grand finale. Organizers canceled Thursday's event because the featured presenter, Dianne Jacoby,…
content: Palatka Daily News The One Book One Putnam season is coming to an end this year without its usual grand finale. Organizers canceled Thursday's event because the featured presenter, Dianne Jacoby, became sick, One Book One Putnam Committee Chairman Bob Lee said. He found out Tuesday she was ill and decided the finale could not go on without her. 'Diane Jacoby is renowned as a wonderful historical dramatist,' Lee said in a text message. 'It's unfortunate that she is unable to participate in this year's finale due to illness.' One Book is a countywide reading initiative that encourages local residents to read that year's selected work and participate in events having to do with the book. This year's book was 'A Land Remembered' by Patrick D. Smith. It was the first novel chosen for One Book when the program began 20 years ago. Jacoby is a historical reenactor who had planned to help event attendees relive old Florida history given that the novel first takes place in 1858 Florida. 'We will certainly keep her in mind for future OBOP events,' Lee said.

title: Panther Pride on Parade
description: Palatka Junior-Senior High School students and employees lauded one of their administrators Friday during a parade and pep rally in honor of him being named Florida's Assistant Principal of the Year.…
content:
Palatka Junior-Senior High School students and employees lauded one of their administrators Friday during a parade and pep rally in honor of him being named Florida's Assistant Principal of the Year.
Michael Chaires remained humble and grateful after being notified he'd been named the state's top assistant principal. School employees and students packed the Palatka High gymnasium, plastered his face around the school and led him on a parade through the halls to celebrate his award.
'Attention's not my favorite thing, but I do appreciate all the love and support that I'm getting from everybody,' Chaires said. 'It's overwhelming.'
Faculty and staff members wore shirts and pins that bore his face and read, 'Ain't no (assistant principal) like the one I got.' Others held signs with his picture and congratulatory messages on them.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – Palatka Junior-Senior High School Assistant Principal Michael Chaires signs a poster one of his students made about Chaires' Assistant Principal of the Year award. Students made their own posters to display during the pep rally. One student even asked Chaires to autograph a poster the student created.
Chaires said he was surprised to see state officials in the school's front office to deliver the news in person.
'(Principal Cathy Oyster) tricked me to get me into the front office (by) telling me we were meeting with a parent,' Chairs recalled. 'And as soon as I turn the corner, I see cameras.'
The assistant principal has worked at the school for 19 years, Oyster said. Chaires, a Palatka High graduate, should be considered one of the school's legends, she added.
'I was over-the-moon excited for him,' Oyster said. 'He is a quiet, behind-the-scenes worker – head down, doesn't want recognition, doesn't want the attention. For people to actually give him that, it was very hard for him. It was hard for him to accept, but, ultimately, I'm very proud of him.'
BRANDON D. OLIVER/Palatka Daily News – Palatka High Principal Cathy Oyster, left, and Chaires disembark from a golf cart at after Chaires was paraded around the school Friday afternoon. She said Chaires connects with the students and their families, invests in students' futures no matter who they are and makes sure to help pupils get on the right track, whether that be scholarships or anything else that could boost their futures, she said.
Chaires taught social studies and was a school counselor before becoming an assistant principal. Oyster said he puts his background as a counselor to great use, and his knowledge helped ease the school's transition from ninth through 12th grades to a school that accommodates grades seven through 12.
'He knows what they need and is able to have so many more conversations with families about the opportunities moving forward,' Oyster said.
SARAH CAVACINI/Palatka Daily News – A cutout of Assistant Principal Michael Chaires' head is pasted onto the wall of the Palatka Junior-Senior High School during a pep rally in his honor. Tenth grader Tre'Myia Watts has been at the school for two years, and although she's never interacted with him one-on-one, she has benefitted from his hard work. She described Chaires as a fun assistant principal who deserves the local and state recognition he received this week.
'He's very nice,' Watts said after the pep rally. 'He's just a good person to be around. I'm very happy for him and proud.'
The people who packed the gymnasium were also proud of Chaires. Oyster said she was glad his hard work was recognized at the state level.
BRANDON D. OLIVER/Palatka Daily News – Palatka Junior-Senior High School Assistant Principal Michael Chaires walks in the school gym, where students and employees partook in a pep rally Friday in celebration of him being named the state's Assistant Principal of the Year. Among 67 nominees for Assistant Principal of the Year, Chaires was selected alongside Kristin Stevens and Holli Winter, assistant principals in Lee County and St. Johns County, respectively, as finalists earlier this month.
Oyster, who is nearing the end of her first school year as principal at Palatka High, said Chaires has been a blessing who has helped her transition into her current position. He knows the school's ins and outs and helped her learn what works and doesn't work so the administrative team can solve problems and not repeat ineffective tactics, she said.
'I can't say anything bad about him,' Oyster said. 'I don't know that you will ever find anybody who will say anything bad about him. He is a wonderful human being.'

title: Former commission hopeful enters school board contest
description: A Palatka resident has filed his intent to run for office in the hopes of unseating a two-term member of the Putnam County School Board. Leon Edenfield filed his candidacy paperwork May 29 to compete…
content:
A Palatka resident has filed his intent to run for office in the hopes of unseating a two-term member of the Putnam County School Board. Leon Edenfield filed his candidacy paperwork May 29 to compete in the contest for the nonpartisan District 2 board seat, according to the Supervisor of Elections Office. He will be facing off against David Buckles, who was first elected to the board in 2016 and won his reelection bid in 2020. While this is Edenfield's first time seeking a Putnam County School Board seat, he ran for the District 2 Board of County Commissioners office in 2018. He lost in the primary to Jeff Rawls. If Edenfield and Buckles are the only candidates in the District 2 school board race by the time qualifying ends at noon June 14, the winner will be decided in the Aug. 20 primary. If there are more than two candidates, the primary hopeful who receives 50% of the vote plus at least one additional vote will win the school board seat. If no candidate wins that many votes, the two with the most votes will compete in the Nov. 5 election. Because school board seats are nonpartisan, all voters can vote in the school board races during the primary. For more election information, call the Elections Office at 386-329-0224 or visit soe.putnam-fl.com.

title: Community steps up to support girl with liver cancer
description: When Putnam County residents know there is a need in the community, they get busy making plans and finding out how to help. Such was the case when Pilot Club of Palatka member Lynda Fitzstephens and…
content:
When Putnam County residents know there is a need in the community, they get busy making plans and finding out how to help.
Such was the case when Pilot Club of Palatka member Lynda Fitzstephens and Jim Miller, an ultra-runner and Global Ambassador for the American Liver Foundation, heard about 3 year-old Whitlee Mullins.
The Palatka girl has battled liver cancer half her life and underwent a liver transplant on March 14 at AdventHealth in Orlando where she spent 12 hours in surgery.
Learning of the news, Fitzstephens and Miller brainstormed the idea of having Walks With Whit as a fundraiser for Mullins.
Today's participants are asked to meet at 10 a.m. at Beef ‘O' Brady's parking lot, 201 N. First St. in Palatka, where they will take a scenic 2-mile walk or run across Memorial Bridge.
To participate, people are asked to donate $10, and they can pay the day of the event or at walkswithwhit.org.
Miller said fundraisers are instrumental to Mullins' family because she still has to have follow-up treatments and tests. The girl must travel to Jacksonville and Orlando for many of these treatments and stay overnight.
'Our intent is to raise $8,000 to help the family with all the extraneous expenses they will incur,' Miller said. 'If just 150 people each donated $10 we would hit our goal.'
For those who can't participate, but who would like to donate, they can also contribute to the cause online.
The website includes an expansion of Whitlee's Story, a video message from Miller and an endorsement from Lorraine Stiehl, CEO of the American Liver Foundation.
With June being the month filled with celebrations for graduations, Father's Day, weddings, birthdays, parties, gifts and more, Miller said it could be a time for a new connection by taking part in the last of the five Walks With Whitlee to help with her ongoing treatment.
'We all know that any of our celebrations are going to involve spending well beyond $10, so this little donation would allow for celebration and connection to a good cause,' he said.
According to Miller, a venture like Mullins' takes not only a village, but the full support of a beautiful community.
'We already know that Palatka is such a community,' he said.
Organizers held five walks in all, and the number had a specific meaning, Fitzstephens said.
'We chose to do five walks representing the approximately 500 kids under 5 years of age waiting and praying for a liver transplant on any given day in the U.S,' she said.
The previous Walks With Whit were held May 4, May 11, May 25 and June 1.
As of Friday, organizers have raised $7,500 for the family, just $500 short of their goal.
Fitzstephens said she is so
pleased to see the community's involvement in the Pilot Club of Palatka's fundraisers, who have a motto of ‘Do More. Care More. Be More.'
'It has been amazing to see the community rallying around little Whit and her parents, Kelsee Largacci and Austin Mullins and baby sister, Wrenlee,' she said.
Fitzstephens invites everyone out today to show their support for Whitlee and her family.
'As a community, let's come together to help Whitlee and her family,' she said.

title: Officials aim to reroute heavy semitrailer traffic in Palatka
description: County, city and state officials unveiled Tuesday what they hope to be a solution for diverting semitrailer traffic away from Palatka neighborhoods. The Florida Department of Transportation installed…
content:
County, city and state officials unveiled Tuesday what they hope to be a solution for diverting semitrailer traffic away from Palatka neighborhoods.
The Florida Department of Transportation installed signs across Putnam County to establish a new truck route and deter semitrailer drivers from driving on Crill Avenue. Department officials, Rep. Bobby Payne, R-Palatka, county commissioners, Palatka Police Department leaders and city officials showed off one sign that stands along State Road 19 in front of the Winn-Dixie shopping plaza.
The sign directs truck drivers traveling north on State Road 19 to continue driving straight until they reach State Road 100, instead of turning right onto State Road 20/Crill Avenue at the intersection near RaceTrac, 4011 Crill Ave.
State Road 100 merges into U.S. 17.
'The overall goal is certainly to deter the truck traffic going on Crill Avenue, which is a residential neighborhood,' Commissioner Leota Wilkinson said.
If a semitrailer is traveling west into Putnam County over Memorial Bridge in Palatka, officials want drivers to continue along U.S. 17/State Road 100 and not turn at S. Ninth Street, according to a department map. Drivers should travel U.S. 17 until they reach the left turn to continue on State Road 100 toward State Road 19, the map shows.
Department public information officer Hampton Ray said the agency's District 2 area, which covers Putnam County, received a lot of complaints about Crill Avenue.
Department public information officer Hampton Ray said the agency's District 2 area, which covers Putnam County, received a lot of complaints about Crill Avenue. 'I think what's really important about this project is that it's really FDOT responding to the needs of the community,' he said.
Payne has heard about the issue since getting elected in 2016. He said he knows how dangerous it can be for semitrailers to drive through the Crill Avenue underpass and the risk truck travel poses to residents.
'We're trying to do things to protect our citizens, everything from mailboxes that have been knocked down to head-on collisions that have happened on (Crill Avenue),' Payne said.
The road is only two lanes, has tight turns and the new route would be better for amenities like fuel stations and restaurants, the department advocates in its campaign to deter traffic.
Payne said he is fortunate to work with the state, and he said the signs are a great way to start advocating for the route change. According to the department, the signage cost $10,000.
The official truck route on Google Maps still shows the Crill Avenue route, but the state and county want to work with trucker associations and others to change the known route.
Wilkinson said trucks that continue to use Crill Avenue will not be fined or reprimanded right now because state and county officials only want to increase awareness.
'We're going to be making a consolidated effort to let everybody know and … the companies who receive products,' Wilkinson said, 'and we'll be targeting truck companies in the next few months.'

title: Local attorney appointed judge
description: A Crescent City Junior-Senior High School graduate and legal council for Crescent City is taking the bench after being appointed judge Wednesday. Robert Pickens III was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis…
content:
A Crescent City Junior-Senior High School graduate and legal council for Crescent City is taking the bench after being appointed judge Wednesday. Robert Pickens III was appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to serve as Judge on the Seventh Judicial Circuit Court, which oversees Flagler, Putnam, St. Johns and Volusia counties. 'I was in shock,' Pickens said in an email. 'It took awhile for the reality of the situation to set in, but I am looking forward to taking the bench.' Pickens replaces Judge James R. Clayton, who retired in April, according to a press release from DeSantis' office. In 2021, Pickens was hired by Homes & Young P.A., a Putnam County-based law firm that has offices in Palatka and Crescent City, but also serves clients in the other three counties in the circuit, according to the firm's website. On behalf of the firm, Pickens also provides legal services to the Crescent City Commission. Pickens said he wanted to serve the community as a member of the judiciary. He graduated from Florida Coastal School of Law in 2017 and was admitted to the Florida Bar in September 2017, according to his profile on the Florida Bar website. He remains in good standing to practice law, has no disciplinary history and sat on the Judicial Circuit Grievance Committee, according to the Bar. Pickens previously served as an assistant state attorney for the circuit court, according to the governor's office. 'While serving as an assistant state attorney, I was able to gain valuable courtroom and trial experience that I feel will be beneficial to me once I take the bench,' he said. He thanked everyone who supported him throughout his career and during the process toward becoming a judge. Some of his biggest supporters came from city officials. Mayor Michele Myers said they are all very proud of him. 'He has set the example that dreams are achievable through hard work and determination,' she said. Pickens went to college, obtained experience and came back home to help the community. She said becoming a judge is an honor for him. 'We know he'll be successful,' Myers said, 'and he will truly be missed in our commission chambers.'

'While serving as an assistant state attorney, I was able to gain valuable courtroom and trial experience that I feel will be beneficial to me once I take the bench,' he said.
He thanked everyone who supported him throughout his career and during the process toward becoming a judge.
Some of his biggest supporters came from city officials. Mayor Michele Myers said they are all very proud of him.
'He has set the example that dreams are achievable through hard work and determination,' she said.
Pickens went to college, obtained experience and came back home to help the community. She said becoming a judge is an honor for him.
'We know he'll be successful,' Myers said, 'and he will truly be missed in our commission chambers.'

title: Community recognizes family's service to Palatka
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The history of a prominent family was put on display Saturday when a kiosk was dedicated to the family's landmark downtown businesses.
content:
Body
The history of a prominent family was put on display Saturday when a kiosk was dedicated to the family's landmark downtown businesses.
Despite the 90-degree weather, people congregated around the home of former Palatka Commissioner Mary Lawson Brown and St. Mary's Episcopal Church to celebrate the Lawson legacy. The kiosk stands on the corner of where Mary Lawson Hospital used to be.
The Lawson family operated the hospital near the intersection of Ninth Street and St. Johns Avenue from 1918 to 1958. E.W. Lawson & Son Funeral Home, 109 N. Ninth St., continues its operation today across the street from the former hospital.
'It started out with four people coming here,' said Lawson Brown, the granddaughter of Mary Lawson. 'They came and they wanted to start a new life, a new business, and they came to Palatka and thought it was just the place to be.'
The facility was the first hospital to serve Black and white patients when it opened in 1918, according to the kiosk that was unveiled Saturday. The 35-bed health care facility was used after the city's white hospital began to get overcrowded, the kiosk states.
'It was the overrun of the Glendale Hospital, and they gave (Mary Lawson) one patient,' Lawson Brown said. 'And she did so well with them (that) somebody else came and somebody else came.'
Lawson Brown's grandmother was a registered nurse, and when the family arrived in Palatka, there were no Black hospitals or funeral homes, according to the kiosk. Mary Lawson's husband, E.W. Lawson, was a licensed funeral director who opened the funeral home in 1915.
In 1915, Mary Lawson studied embalming and funeral direction, eventually becoming the first Black woman licensed to perform funerals in Florida, the kiosk states.
The hospital shut down in 1958 when what has become HCA Florida Putnam Hospital, 611 Zeagler Drive in Palatka, was constructed, according to the kiosk.
Many of the people who showed up to watch the kiosk unveiling were born in the Mary Lawson Hospital, Lawson Brown said. One of those people was former City Commissioner Allegra Kitchens, who showed up with a copy of her birth certificate to prove where she was born.
It was overwhelming and heartwarming to be where the hospital once stood, Kitchens said in an email. The building no longer stands, but the base of where it once sat is now the back of Lawson Brown's house.
'Being a part of the unveiling of the kiosk in memory of Mary Lawson Hospital holds a special place in my heart because I was born there,' Kitchens said. 'Mary Lawson Brown showed me where the delivery room had been, and I was able to stand on the exact spot where I was born. How many people get to do that?'
Although the hospital building is gone, Lawson Brown still doted on how the former health care facility helped residents in Palatka and surrounding areas. She never knew her grandparents to turn anyone away simply because they couldn't pay.
The Lawson family also went out of their way to help the community and trained their employees to continue the business or start their own careers, Lawson Brown said.
'When they got into business, they didn't get into business for themselves,' she said of her grandparents. 'They wanted to make sure others would go along with them.'

A person whose substantial interests are or may be affected has the right to request an administrative hearing by filing a written petition with the St. Johns River Water Management District (District). Pursuant to Chapter 28-106 and Rule 40C-1.1007, Florida Administrative Code (F.A.C.), the petition must be filed (received) either by delivery at the office of the District Clerk at District Headquarters, P.O. Box 1429, Palatka FL 32178-1429 (4049 Reid St, Palatka, FL 32177) or by e-mail with the District Clerk at Clerk@sjrwmd.com, within twenty-one (21) days of newspaper publication of the notice of District decision (for those persons to whom the District does not mail or email actual notice). A petition must comply with Sections 120.54(5)(b)4. and 120.569(2)(c), Florida Statutes (F.S.), and Chapter 28-106, F.A.C. The District will not accept a petition sent by facsimile (fax). Mediation pursuant to Section 120.573, F.S., may be available and choosing mediation does not affect your right to an administrative hearing.
A petition for an administrative hearing is deemed filed upon receipt of the complete petition by the District Clerk at the District Headquarters in Palatka, Florida during the District's regular business hours. The District's regular business hours are 8 a.m. – 5 p.m., excluding weekends and District holidays. Petitions received by the District Clerk after the District's regular business hours shall be deemed filed as of 8 a.m. on the District's next regular business day. The District's acceptance of petitions filed by e-mail is subject to certain conditions set forth in the District's Statement of Agency Organization and Operation (issued pursuant to Rule 28-101.001, Florida Administrative Code), which is available for viewing at www.sjrwmd.com. These conditions include, but are not limited to, the petition being in the form of a PDF or TIFF file and being capable of being stored and printed by the District. Further, pursuant to the District's Statement of Agency Organization and Operation, attempting to file a petition by facsimile (fax) is prohibited and shall not constitute filing.
The right to an administrative hearing and the relevant procedures to be followed are governed by Chapter 120, Florida Statutes, Chapter 28-106, Florida Administrative Code, and Rule 40C-1.1007, Florida Administrative Code. Because the administrative hearing process is designed to formulate final agency action, the filing of a petition means the District's final action may be different from the position taken by it in this notice. Failure to file a petition for an administrative hearing within the requisite time frame shall constitute a waiver of the right to an administrative hearing. (Rule 28-106.111, F.A.C.).

title: State agency bestows new moniker on iconic fish
author: Carter Mudgett
description: Florida's most popular freshwater game fish has a new name.
content:
Florida's most popular freshwater game fish has a new name.
Instead of the largemouth bass, they're now called Florida bass, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission announced Wednesday.
Though the name change will affect how these fish are referred to in regulations and other communications, it won't impact anglers fishing for the iconic freshwater sport fish, according to the state.
The American Fisheries Society established the Florida bass as a separate species, meaning what was known as largemouth bass in most of Florida, except for the western Panhandle, now has a new name.
'This new understanding of black bass diversity, distribution and classification provides a critical foundation for better managing and conserving these important and iconic fish,' the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission wrote in a press release Tuesday. 'It will aid in ensuring their continued conservation and sustainable use for future generations.'
The range of Florida bass is now known to be larger than once thought, including parts of Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, according to research published by Yale University.
Florida bass have also taken the scientific name Micropterus salmoides, which was previously used to identify largemouth bass. Now, largemouth bass are known as Micropterus nigricans, according to the release.
To learn more about the Florida bass, go to MyFWC.com, click on 'Freshwater Fishing,' select 'Black Bass Management' and click on 'Florida Bass.'

title: 2 groups bringing Christmas cheer ahead of schedule
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Locals may not be hearing the familiar holiday tunes 'We Wish You a Merry Christmas' or 'Jingle Bells' just yet, but those looking to get an early start finding unique gifts for family and friends
content:
Body
Locals may not be hearing the familiar holiday tunes 'We Wish You a Merry Christmas' or 'Jingle Bells' just yet, but those looking to get an early start finding unique gifts for family and friends are in for a treat.
Christmas in July will be at two locations this weekend in Palatka and will be an opportunity for shoppers to find some unique, one-of-a-kind deals.
Shoppers can find four rooms of the Palatka Art League's historic Tilghman House filled with handcrafted items from more than 20 local artists. The public is invited to the sale, which will be from 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. Friday and Saturday, noon – 4 p.m. Sunday and 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. July 27 at 324 River St. in Palatka.
A few blocks over, the St. Monica Catholic Church Parish Enrichment Center, 410 Oak St., will host its event from 8 a.m. – 1 p.m. Friday and Saturday.
A lunch of soup, sandwich, salad and drink will be available for $10 from 11 a.m.–1 p.m. Friday. Desserts will be $2 each.
The church sale will feature handmade crafts, specialty items and tasty baked goods such as pies, cakes, bread and more.
New this year at the two-day event will be award-winning children's book author Victoria Scudder with her 'Jack's Garage' series of books available for purchase.
According to Marcia Dixon, secretary of the Palatka Art League, Christmas in July shoppers at Tilghman will find handcrafted items made by many of her group's talented members.
'It gives shoppers a taste of what's to come in November,' she said. 'We usually have around 30 artists participate in our Holiday House, and we fill the whole house, upstairs and downstairs, with unique handcrafted Christmas gifts and decor.'
The chairman of the event is Art League member David Forest. Proceeds from sales will go towards community outreach programs such as Pink Out Putnam and an annual scholarship for an art student.
Items at the sale will also include jewelry, pottery, soft sculpture, stained glass, wood carvings, fairy gardens, bird feeders, paintings and photography.
'Everything is handcrafted by our members,' Dixon said.
The St. Monica sale will benefit various charities as a fundraiser for the Ladies Guild of St. Monica, said member Kimberly Delacruz, crafter.
'I have been a part of this event for seven years,' she said. 'We've got lots of handmade items, including a vintage Christmas ceramics chess set with ornaments.'
The chess board was made by Joe Iovino, a Ladies Guild member's husband whose work will be paired with Delacruz, who made the ceramic chessmen from 1965 vintage slip cast molds.
Other items for sale are bird feeders, bird craft, bee and butterfly waterers, crocheted items, ceramics, wood pieces, garden items such as relishes, bags for walkers, Diamond Art items, bath salts, sports team items, baskets, bears, bunnies and other animals.
Rita Smith, the president of St. Monica Ladies Guild, said fall was a busy time of the year, so her group decided to try Christmas in July.
'Our first event was a success so we are trying a second time,' she said. 'Our event is a community outreach where we invite our neighbors to join us in fellowship.'
Proceeds from the St. Monica event will go toward various women's and children's nonprofit programs, including the Lee Conlee House, A Woman's Resource Center and St. Gerard's House.
Dixon said she's not sure when the Art League's Christmas in July started, but it's become a tradition group members and the public look forward to every year.
'It's been a long time though,' she said. 'We like to give our customers a chance to get a head start on their Christmas shopping and to purchase gifts and home decor for all occasions.'

title: Superintendent contenders address voters ahead of primary
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible.
The incumbent and a county commissioner are facing off in the race to become the Putnam County School District superintendent.
Paul Adamczyk, who currently occupies the District 5 seat on the Board of County Commissioners, is competing to unseat Superintendent Rick Surrency.
Whichever of the two Republicans prevails in the primary will advance to the general election to face write-in candidate Pat Wilson.
Adamczyk and Surrency have answered questions from the Palatka Daily News ahead of the primary. Below, the candidates lay out why they think they're the best person for the job.
What are some of the first goals you hope to accomplish once taking office if you are elected?
Adamczyk: Prioritizing third-grade reading is a major goal, working to get our children reading above grade level as currently we rank in the bottom 5% at 64th statewide. We will work to get out of last statewide in chronic absenteeism, as we cannot properly educate students who are not there. We will have school resource officers in every school, currently we are short, we will not pick and choose which schools deserve protection. We will become fiscally conservative, not ballooning budgets over 260% in eight years. We will put our students first with every decision made.
Surrency: Our students showed great improvement in learning gains throughout the district. Increasing learning gains year after year is how we increase the number of students meeting proficiency. Our goal is to continue those practices that create learning gains and improve district achievement scores. We need 678 points to be a 'B' district and we earned 630 points in 2024. In 2016, we earned 467 points, which was barely in the 'C' grade range. What we are doing is working, and consistent systems and leadership at the district and school levels will be key in meeting this goal.
The obligation bond to build new elementary schools with taxpayer dollars is already in effect. What are your thoughts on the bond, and are there any changes you hope to make in terms of the construction or renovation of elementary schools?
Adamczyk: A political action committee pushed the idea for the district of building six new schools with $300,000,000. This PAC was partially funded by Institutional Construction Management, whose officer, William Rutherford, is the R in CRA Architects. CRA is the design manager for all ongoing builds and the architecture firm on two builds. They also donated to the campaign of my opponent, yet another donor exceeding contribution limits under investigation by the election commission. Only three new elementary schools will be built, and the donors will make millions by mortgaging our citizens. All should stop with an investigation.
Surrency: I am proud that our community voted to fund the construction, renovation and replacement of public schools, including implementation of safety enhancements and instructional technology upgrades. Our revitalization plan includes bonds for elementary and state special facilities funds for junior-senior high projects to ensure every Putnam County School District student attends a safe and modern school. We will accomplish this by building four and completely renovating two elementary schools. Construction is underway, and two new elementary schools will be ready for 2025-2026. Our students and staff deserve the best, and our community supported that vision by passing the bond referendum.
The Putnam County School District is partnering with the state to build three new junior-senior high schools. What are your thoughts on the partnership?
Adamczyk: Partnering with the state is great if it did not involve closing middle schools, directly impacting every student in our county, only to provide the appearance of having crowded schools. The first of these three builds was way underestimated, much like the elementary builds, resulting in the need to go beg the state for more funds. Until a recent budget, meeting the match, which will come from the 1.5 mills capital improvement funds on your tax bill as another $35+ million liability on top of the school bond, which was pretty much hidden. All should stop with an investigation.
Surrency: We are grateful to the Florida Department Of Education for awarding the Putnam County School District funds to completely rebuild Crescent City Junior-Senior High School. The process to secure these funds is competitive, and our team successfully navigated that process. Once the CCJSHS project is complete, we will apply for Interlachen and then Palatka Junior-Senior High Schools, thus completing the nine school projects of the revitalization plan. Our team has built a positive partnership with FLDOE, and I believe consistent leadership in the coming years will positively impact future funding, ensuring updated secondary schools in all areas of the county.
What makes you the best candidate to serve as the Putnam County School District superintendent?
Adamczyk: My sole purpose is 'Putting our students first.' No decision will ever be made unless there is a measurable means by which we can establish success by directly benefiting our students. We will be fiscally conservative with your funds, as school funds, whether local, state or federal, are yours. We will make the teaching profession, and every role that works directly with our students, everything it can be in Putnam through pay, benefits, supplies, and support, as we cannot put students first without taking care of those who work with them. Students (are) not special interests.
Surrency: I am the only candidate with experience to successfully serve as superintendent. I hold the degrees expected for superintendent, and I'm the 2023 Florida Superintendent of the Year. I've served 46 years in education – 38 of those years in Putnam County. I was born and raised in Hawthorne. I know the importance of every employee because I've held positions at every level. The Putnam County School District is Putnam's largest employer, with over 1,500 dedicated staff serving over 10,000 amazing students. I'm trusting our community to choose me – the only candidate with experience to lead this great organization.
How will you work to maintain transparency with district employees and the public?
Adamczyk: We will hold school board meetings in evening hours that work for teachers, students, parents and stakeholders to attend. Not forcing people to take time off of work to attend a meeting. We need to overcommunicate clearly with parents, students, teachers and stakeholders on important items. We will reach out to involve our civic groups, neighborhoods and churches in our schools, better utilizing our resources to benefit everyone. We will have an open-door policy for everyone. We will have a beneficial strategic plan, focused on 'Putting our students first'.
Surrency: Community collaboration is a significant part of our 2021-2026 Strategic Plan. We've implemented many options to best communicate with our staff, families and community, including the Superintendent's Student Advisory Council, Bond Oversight Committee, Community Forums, online tools to broadcast meetings/events, upgraded apps for families to stay connected and multiple media channels to share district/school news. Maintaining transparency is, and will continue to be, a priority for me. I believe in servant leadership, and I welcome feedback from our students, staff, families and community. This feedback is needed when building a culture of collaboration, which is crucial for success.

title: College stalwart looks back as he bids farewell
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A 27-year St. Johns River State College employee is moving on to a new opportunity in a neighboring county, but he and others won't forget the lasting impact he made on the college.
content:
Body
A 27-year St. Johns River State College employee is moving on to a new opportunity in a neighboring county, but he and others won't forget the lasting impact he made on the college.
Gilbert Evans Jr., a former English teacher, vice president for student affairs and vice president of legal affairs for the college, worked his last day at the Palatka campus Aug. 8.
'You know, I'm not even a crybaby, but I found myself even shedding tears an hour ago because this has been my life, professionally,' Evans said on his last day.
He sat in his office last week flipping through old photos of him on his first day teaching English in 1993 and him talking to a Palatka High School class when he was responsible for outreach programs.
Evans is leaving SJR State to be the new Volusia County School Board legal counsel.
'It's bittersweet because I've spent (27) years (here),' Evans said Aug. 8. 'It just hit me today. … I've seen many people come and go, and now I'm going.'
Evans said he could definitely see himself returning someday. Evans' ties to the community ran deep, as he is a member of the Rotary Club of Palatka, chairman of the Palatka Housing Authority's board of commissioners and bishop of the Palatka House of God Church.
His time with SJR State began before 1993, having attended the college – when it was still St. Johns River Community College – the summer he graduated from Crescent City High School in 1988. While attending SJR State, he was vice president of the student council and president of the Florida Future Educators of America program.
Evans obtained his associate degree from SJR State, he said, before attending Florida State University, where he earned a bachelor's in English and a master's degree in administration.
Evans thanked his former high school teachers Rita Hooten and Gail Williams for inspiring him to pursue his degrees.
Evans said he worked as an English teacher at SJR State for six years. He obtained a Ph.D. in higher education administration from the University of Florida while working at the college, and eventually earned his law degree in 1999 from the University of Florida Levin College of Law.
The former teacher practiced law in Orlando for three years until he got a call from former SJR State President Robert L. McLendon Jr., who asked Evans to return.
'I already worked here for six years prior to going to law school, and Dr. McLendon told me to come home,' Evans said. 'And when Dr. McLendon gives you a command … you come.'
He called McLendon, who served as president for 36 years, his role model.
'(McLendon) was one of the greatest academicians and leaders I've ever worked with,' Evans said.
Following Evans' return to the college, he served for 18 years as vice president of student affairs, where he covered everything from recruitment to retention to financial aid and counseling services, he said.
'No two days were the same, and student affairs is about meeting the needs of the students,' he said. 'It's a very unique animal. It takes a special person to run student affairs. … It's about meeting the student where they are and helping them to resolve their problems.'
Evans became the vice president of legal affairs in 2021. He's seen plenty of employees come and go, one of which is his retired administrative assistant, Sharon Silcox, who worked with him for 18 years.
She said Evans was one of the best bosses she has ever had.
'Everybody was like family with him,' she said Wednesday. 'You could go to him about anything.'
While he enforced rules, Silcox said, Evans had an open-door policy and took the time to listen to anyone who walked through his door. He also understood the importance of family, she said.
'It was always, 'Your family comes first. That's what we're here for,'' Silcox said.
She made sure to visit him on his last day on campus. The retired assistant said she hated to see Evans go but knows he has a great opportunity in Volusia County.
SJR State President Joe Pickens said Evans's opportunity in Volusia County is unique, and he respects his desire to pursue it. The president wishes Evans nothing but the best and knows he'll succeed.
'Dr. Evans is one of the finest human beings that I have ever met,' Pickens said. 'His dedication to the college for almost three decades is something I'll always treasure.'

title: House hopefuls state objectives for time in office
author: David Shoar
description: The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News submitted questionnaires to candidates who are on the ballot for the Aug. 20 primary. Candidates were asked to limit each answer to 100 words. Out of fairness, Daily News journalists cut answers that went over the limit to be as close to 100 words as possible.
A member of the Legislature and a former sheriff are two of the candidates trying to be the Republican nominee for the District 7 state Senate seat.
Trying to emerge victorious in the Florida primary are Gerry James, state Rep. Tom Leek and former St. Johns County Sheriff David Shoar. With early and mail voting already occurring, the three Republicans hope to be the winner Tuesday.
Leek and Shoar completed the questionnaire the Palatka Daily News sent all primary candidates for the House and Senate. James did not reply by the deadline given to all of the Senate candidates.
Below, Leek and Shoar explain why they're the best candidate for the job, what they plan to accomplish and how they will get it done. Other than editing for clarity, the answers are in the candidates' own words.
What inspired you to run for a seat in Florida's Senate?
Leek: As a member of the state Senate, I would like to continue serving the people of Northeast Florida by establishing Florida as the most law enforcement-friendly state in the union, and by working on many of the recent conservative advances in school choice, economic development and important social issues that strengthen the family. My experience as a state House member these last eight years in leadership positions has given me the unique opportunity to build upon these historic achievements and best represent the people of Senate District 7.
Shoar: At eighteen years of age, I raised my right hand and after taking the oath, served the next forty-one years in public service, forty years of law enforcement in St. Johns as Chief of Police and Sheriff and twenty-four years of service in the U.S. Army retiring as a Major. I decided after much thought to stand for election to the Florida Senate when it became clear to me there was not a pro-Trump conservative in the race who would fight for our community, not the special interests in Tallahassee.
What makes you the best candidate to step into this role?
Leek: As a conservative member of the Florida House, I have served as a committee chairman and on the leadership team of the last three Speakers in the Florida House. I served with House Speaker Paul Renner as Chairman of the House Appropriations Committee and previously chaired the Public Ethics and Integrity Committee, the Pandemics and Public Emergencies Committee and the Redistricting Committee. This experience allows me to effectively and immediately serve the constituents of Senate District 7 on day one and continue my valued partnership with State Rep. Bobby Payne.
Shoar: I am proudly endorsed by President Trump. I am a lifelong conservative Republican and will always fight for our values. I have a record of protecting this community over my 40+ year law enforcement career. I believe we could use more common sense in Tallahassee and get back to the basics of limited government and returning as much power and authority back to local government as possible. I have a long history of telling folks what I thought they needed to hear, not what they wanted to hear regardless of the possible repercussions.
There seems to always be development occurring in counties surrounding Putnam County. How will you help Putnam County bolster its infrastructure to be ready to accommodate whatever development and growth that may occur?
Leek: I share the position of my friend and colleague, State Rep. Bobby Payne, that addressing infrastructure needs in Putnam County is critical if we are to remain competitive in the region, addressing bridges and roads for transportation needs, as well as expanding broadband and connectivity services. There should also be a balanced approach between sensible development and our environmental needs so the district may preserve its uniqueness. These are decisions that should be made at the local level.
Shoar: We need to have smart growth to protect our quality of life and work to ensure funding is available for the necessary infrastructure. The growth of the neighboring counties adds pressure to Putnam County and I believe and many do that Putnam County is going to experience strong growth now and in the future. I think working with our locals and not just writing one-size-fits-all edicts from Tallahassee regarding growth and development and forcing them on local government would be a great start.
How do you plan to work with your colleagues on the other side of the aisle to accomplish great things for Florida residents, especially in Putnam County?
Leek: As a trusted member of House leadership, I have worked on many of the conservative advances of the past few years in school choice, economic development and important social issues that strengthen the family. In working with colleagues on the other side of the aisle, there are many things that unite us rather than divide us, and together we have reached consensus on many issues that make Florida and (Senate)District 7 the best place to live, work, play and raise a family.
Shoar: I have always been part of team throughout my career and led many of them. If we all focus on the health, safety and welfare of our constituents instead on so much of the nonsense and noise out there, we can get a lot done. A great issue to collaborate on might be the state of our Mental Health system in Florida. I worked with stakeholders of all parties as Sheriff and know how to work with and listen to people whose views differ from my own. While I believe in collaboration, I will not compromise my conservative values.
How will you ensure Florida is fiscally responsible while also providing resources and programs to make this state the best in the nation?
Leek: A challenge we face in Northeast Florida is in providing a strong economy, as it relates to families making ends meet and allowing businesses to thrive in recruiting and retaining a talented workforce. As chair of the House Appropriations Committee, overseeing negotiations between the House and Senate for a $117 billion budget in the nation's third largest state, my motto is 'start with zero, justify the rest' in every allocation. These are our dollars, not the government's. We need to be prudent in spending and ever mindful in returning funds to the people of Florida with a balanced budget approach.
Shoar: One of the best ways to start is to carefully assess the current programs, are they programs that are effective and more importantly, are they programs that government should not even be involved in? Most citizens do not know that 'earmarks' exist in state government but they do they are just called something else; this needs careful analysis as well. Fortunately, we are required to maintain a balanced budget in Florida. I will prioritize our key needs – public safety, education, and infrastructure, root out waste, and also cut taxes for our families.
Much attention has been paid to diversity, equity and inclusion programs and resources. What are your opinions on those items, especially as it relates to the millions of people who benefitted from them?
Leek: I believe in merit-based systems over DEI-driven policies, focusing on diversity and inclusion can often undermine meritocracy and result in hiring and admissions policies that are not based solely on qualifications and merit. DEI initiatives promote a divisive and ideological agenda that emphasizes identity politics and creates a discriminatory environment. I agree with Governor (Ron)DeSantis that DEI programs in schools and universities often lead to indoctrination – not proper education. DEI initiatives are an example of government overreach. As a conservative, I oppose any attempt to impose specific values on individuals that infringes on personal freedoms and liberties.

title: Community remembers 9/11
author: Carter Mudgett
description: Putnam County gathered Wednesday morning to remember the lives lost to the deadliest terrorist attack on U.S. soil.
content:
Putnam County gathered Wednesday morning to remember the lives lost to the deadliest terrorist attack on U.S. soil.
Officials led the crowd in a moment of silence at 9:59 a.m., marking the time that the World Trade Center's south tower fell in New York City.
The 2001 terrorist attack and all the anniversaries that have followed are a sobering reminder for fire rescue officials about how dangerous the job can be and how brave the emergency responders were on that day, said Nat Gill, a firefighter at Station 14.
'Twenty-three years ago, I was a two-year kid on the job here – no idea what I was doing, no idea what my future held,' Gill said. 'But that moment, we watched our world in fire rescue take a completely different approach from that moment on. It changed us. It changed how we do things. It changed how we operate.'
The Sept. 11, 2001, attack resulted in the single largest loss of life from a foreign attack on American soil, killing 2,977 people in New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania. That includes the deaths of 441 first responders, which is the greatest loss of emergency responders on a single day in U.S. history, according to the 9/11 Memorial & Museum.
The ceremony was a time of reflection and remembrance of 9/11, a day now known as Patriot Day. Shortly after the moment of silence, Putnam County Fire Chief Richard Back rang a chrome-plated bell in honor of the firefighters' lives lost during the terrorist attacks.
Three sets of five measured strikes of the bell is the signal for a firefighter dying in the line of duty, Gills said.
That bell is personal for Gill, who told the crowd he and Fire Rescue Lt. John Allender polished it themselves when they were both at Station 23.
Gill said they've heard that bell ring 'a thousand times,' whether it be when other firefighters walked into their station or when their truck was going down bumpy roads.
'There's something different when it's in a solemn atmosphere like this and what that bell represents,' he said.
For the many county officials and residents who participated in the ceremony, it was a day of thanks for first responders, including law enforcement.
Board of County Commissioners Chairman Larry Harvey spoke during the ceremony and was joined on stage by Commissioners Terry Turner, Bill Pickens and Leota Wilkinson.
'I was thinking this morning as I was getting prepared to come down here,' Harvey said. 'Twenty-three years ago, a lot of people prepared for their day, too. And it didn't work out the way they thought it would. We need to remember that every day that we get up. We need to say a prayer and thank God that we can come home.'
Harvey thanked the first responders who'd gathered for Wednesday's ceremony for their service in the past and in the future.
'You rush in as we rush out,' he said. 'You rushed into New York City. You rushed in on (the crashed) flight (in) Pennsylvania. And you rushed in at Washington D.C. And you rush in here every day.'
Deputy County Operations Administrator J.R. Grimes remembered being a college student on Sept. 11, 2001, when a librarian walked in and told him and his classmates a plane flew into the trade center. They thought it was an accident.
'Ten minutes later, she walks back into the classroom and tells us somebody hit the second World Trade Center and that our nation was under attack,' he said. 'I thank the good Lord that we're not there again.'
Nearing the end of the ceremony, the Honor Guard lowered the American flag at the Palatka riverfront to half-staff. Atop the St. Johns River Center, the Putnam County Sheriff's Office performed a 21-gun salute.
On Tuesday, county commissioners passed a resolution to recognize Sept. 11 as Patriot Day and a day of prayer, calling upon residents to honor the lives and memories lost that day.
'I do have a heart and I have a calling but I'm not trained to do what you do,' Harvey said Wednesday morning. 'I will offer my services, as meager as they are, so you can rush in as we rush out. … May God rush in with you each day so you can walk out.'

title: Cancer doctor takes ownership of radiation services
author: Trisha Murphy
description: A radiation oncology service at the Cancer Center of Putnam in Palatka changed names Tuesday to someone with whom many local residents who have sought cancer treatments are familiar.
content:
A radiation oncology service at the Cancer Center of Putnam in Palatka changed names Tuesday to someone with whom many local residents who have sought cancer treatments are familiar.
The service is now owned and under the direction of Dr. Anand M. Kuruvilla.
Kuruvilla Oncology is the new name the doctor will operate under, where he will provide radiation oncology treatments for cancer patients. It will remain at the cancer center, 600 Zeagler Drive in Palatka.
For details or to make appointments, call 386-325-8140.
Kuruvilla, 72, who specializes in radiation oncology, graduated with honors in 1977 from T.D. Medical College-University of Kerala in India and has almost 50 years of diverse experience. He has been affiliated with HCA Florida Putnam Hospital in Palatka since 1991 and is the current chief of staff.
He is also a member of the American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine.
'Since the cancer center opened in 1991, we have offered medical and radiation oncology services,' he said. 'Now, the hospital will not be a part of the services offered at the center. I'm taking over the management and overseeing the radiation oncology.'
Kuruvilla said that many times when a potential patient has cause for concern, such as a lump or other symptoms, it could be cancer. And those potential patients don't know where to begin and have lots of questions.
'We will offer a free service workup and help them figure out what they need to have done,' Kuruvilla said. 'I will coordinate all that.'
Part of that workup for Kuruvilla will be advising patients whether they need surgery, radiation, chemotherapy or even hospice care.
'I will evaluate the patient and supervise the treatment with the radiation technologist and office staff,' he said.
Kuruvilla is happy to begin his latest venture in being totally in charge of radiation services.
'Many times people have no clue about their health concerns,' he said. 'Our goal is to help people in need and give them a sense of direction.'
Kuruvilla was instrumental in starting the Putnam First Cancer Fund, a local organization that assists patients who cannot afford to see a doctor for an early diagnosis. From 2014 to 2023, the Putnam First Cancer Fund has provided $475,524 to 397 Putnam County residents dealing with cancer.
The organization doesn't pay for cancer treatments but helps with other expenses, such as transportation costs, living expenses, in-home care and co-pays, for those who qualify.
For details on the Putnam First Cancer Fund, call 386-972-7323.
Kuruvilla is happy he has been associated with the Cancer Center of Putnam since it opened more than two decades ago.
'The center is highly recognized to be in the forefront of cancer care, diagnosis and treatment in Northeast Florida,' he said. 'We utilize state-of-the-art techniques such as image-guided radiation therapy, intensity-modulated radiation therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery. We also (have) a new treatment plan where patients have access to have a CT scan every day.'
Dr. J. Wynn Sullivan is a medical oncologist in Palatka and currently practices at Florida Cancer Specialists & Research Institute at the center. He is also affiliated with HCA Putnam.
'I can send a patient to hospital A, B or C,' he said. 'Here, I'm confident they will get the best care available. We are blessed in Palatka because we have plenty of experts we can choose from where I can coordinate and get them the best care they need.'
Kuruvilla is happy to be a part of a network of facilities and doctors who put patients first and make sure they get the treatment they need in a timely manner.
'It has been a privilege for me to take care of the needs of Putnam County citizens battling cancer at the center since it first opened,' he said.

Laura Berardi
Staff Assistant II
