Now that they are of age, many high school seniors across Putnam County are preparing to vote in their first election.
Some upperclassmen from Interlachen, Palatka and Q.I. Roberts junior-senior high schools have been registered to vote in Putnam County for more than a year, while others registered just in time to qualify to vote in the Nov. 5 general election.
Teenagers can register to vote as young as 16, according to Putnam County Elections Supervisor Charles Overturf III, but they cannot actually vote until they are 18. Even someone who turns 18 on Election Day can fill out a ballot as long as they registered to vote by the registration deadline.
'That's the advantage we try to tell the kids,' Overturf said.
Early voting started last week and will continue from 8:30 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. daily until Saturday. Election Day hours are from 7 a.m. – 7 p.m. Nov. 5.
Early voting can be done at one of the three polling locations set up in Crescent City, Interlachen and Palatka, but residents must vote at their assigned polling place on Election Day.
The Palatka Daily News sat down with eight high school students, who range in age from 18-20, to find out why they are taking the initiative to participate in an election before they walk across the commencement stage.
Everyone questioned had their own reasons for registering and voting, but the common theme among them all was the desire to shape a better future for themselves and their communities.
– Why did you register to vote at such a young age?
Jordan McCullough, 18, from Q.I. Roberts: 'It's very important to my family because they're very vocal about it. And they've been educating me since over at least a year now, and they're very eager for me to vote.'
Gavin Miles, 18, from Q.I. Roberts: 'I've been involved with politics from a pretty early age, and I've always been interested in it. I kept up with everything. I'm the type of person – this sounds boring – but at 13 years old, I wasn't watching cartoons. I was watching C-SPAN.'
Aaleeyah Hill, 19, from Palatka High: 'I registered this school year. I feel like everyone's vote should be heard, especially if it depends on how it affects our country.'
– Why do you want to vote this year?
Hunni Simpson, 18, from Interlachen High: 'I care about people. In this election, I feel deeply tied to who I am as a person and my rights. And, you know, I care about those.'
Sierria Burl, 20, from Palatka High: 'Right now, with the things that are going on, if we don't change it now, it's going to be a very bleak future.'
Rashean Jones, 18, from Q.I. Roberts: 'I think it definitely matters when you want to talk about the future, most definitely. Now it sets up for how … when we get into the workforce, how that's going to be.'
– Do you think your vote really does count?
Hill: 'Of course. There's a saying: 'It only takes one.' So if my vote can help change the whole country, can help … determine what will happen later on, I would be happy that I'm the reason why it changed.'
Jeffrey Pauley, 18, from Palatka High: 'I always believe that. To me, it doesn't matter if you're old, young or right between. Your voice always matters because we give the power to the officials of what they can and cannot do. Sometimes the biggest things in history have happened from small towns, so we can make a difference if we put our minds to it.'
Simpson: 'I feel it's more important than ever. I feel our country is going down. It's important. I think a lot of people are going to get hurt if I don't try to involve myself with the community.'
– What do you have to say regarding people, especially young people, who don't think their vote matters?
Aurorabelle Duck, 18, from Palatka High: 'It's better than sitting around doing nothing because if you do nothing, then definitely nothing's going to change. It is your own personal decision (to register). But it's probably a good idea and especially a good idea if you don't like the way the country is now.'
Simpson: 'It's unfortunate. I don't think they get it – you know what I mean – because a lot of the people I talk to (think) it won't affect them directly or it won't affect them as much as other people.'
Miles: 'It's amazing to me because I talk to young people and they have such novel perspectives on what we need to be doing as a country. They have these ideas that can break from the antiquated mind of tradition to bring this fresh perspective on things. They have these fresh perspectives, these amazing ideas. And for some reason, it's incredibly sad to me that we don't see a lot of them actually showing up to vote. So, I'm going to do my part in that.'

title: FloArts students to explore ‘Motion' at upcoming show
description: Submitted to the Daily News
content:
Body
Submitted to the Daily News
Celebrating the creativity of student choreographers is what Florida School of the Arts students plan to do Nov. 22-24 when they present the 'Falling Into Motion' dance concert.
The essence of the show is an exploration of momentum – embracing its fluidity, weight and transformative power. Through movement, the students capture a stage in time where transition and change are at the forefront, according to dance instructor Jessica Mayhew-Borrero.
'Through a diverse range of dance styles, viewers will enjoy and resonate with the art forms of contemporary dance, street jazz, tap, and ballet,' she said. 'This production highlights the artistry of student choreographers, who submit their works to an adjudication panel consisting of guest artists and FloArts faculty. Selected pieces are showcased in the choreography concert, allowing students to experience a professional creative process.'
Showtimes are 7:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday, with matinees at 2:30 p.m. Saturday and Sunday, on the main stage theater at the St. Johns River State College, 5001 St. Johns Ave. in Palatka.
Admission is $10. Tickets can be purchased in advance at floarts.org or at the box office one hour before showtime.
Under the mentorship of directors and dance faculty members, Mayhew-Borrero and Andrea Montez, students gain hands-on experience with essential production elements, such as lighting, costume and sound design.
In addition to the student pieces, the concert will feature guest artists and faculty choreography.
For details about the production, call 386–312–4300.

title: SJR State celebrates fall 2024 graduates
description: Submitted to the Daily News
content:
Body
Submitted to the Daily News
When Riley Speaks' two younger siblings first underwent speech therapy, she had no idea it would lead her toward her future career path. But after witnessing their progress, the 20-year-old Palatka resident said she had found her calling.
'There were many words and sounds they could not say, and it was hard for people other than our family to understand what they were saying,' Speaks said. 'I was able to attend some of their lessons, and watching the instructor use different techniques and exercises to increase their vocal abilities astonished me. It was amazing to slowly notice their improvement and how their hard work has paid off. Seeing the kind of impact that this speech therapist had on my siblings made me very interested in the vocation.'
Speaks is among more than 350 students who graduated Thursday from St. Johns River State College. With her associate degree in hand, Speaks will transfer next year to the University of Florida, where she will begin pursuing her bachelor's degree in communication sciences and disorders and will embark on a path to earn her master's degree in speech language pathology.
Prepared to begin UF as a junior, Speaks said beginning college at SJR State taught her how to manage her time wisely and efficiently.
'When first starting college, I did not designate my time very wisely and would often be stressfully cramming in a bunch of work at the end of the week,' Speaks said. 'The greatest thing that I learned about myself at SJR State is time management.'
Also among the graduates was Palatka resident Denver Fulghum, 25, who, like many, is proof that slow and steady wins the race.
After high school, Fulghum knew his future needed direction and skill sets, so he began working on his associate degree. However, halfway through his academic journey, he experienced a drop in motivation and withdrew from the college.
'I left SJR State after I let my grades drop,' Fulghum said. 'I just didn't care about school anymore.'
But after much encouragement from his family and friends, and the realization that an education can improve career prospects and personal fulfillment, he reapplied to the college.
He advises to anyone who may be 'stuck' to reach out for assistance and use the resources available to them.
'It has taken me about five years to complete (my associate degree),' Fulghum said. '… Don't be afraid to ask people for help.'
Fulghum said campus advisers helped put him on the track to not only complete his degree but also find his next step.
'They helped me find what I want to do in life and to get the rights classes for the future.'
With his associate degree now complete, Fulghum is considering transferring to the University of North Florida to study sports management.
Fulghum said the most significant thing he has learned about himself during his collegiate journey is confidence.
'It helped me know that I can do anything I put my mind to,' he said.
A portion of the ceremony was dedicated to the Paul 'Dee' Causey President's Award. Each year, the award honors the memory of the SJR State alumnus whom SJR State President Joe Pickens described as not only his mentor but a fearless athlete, dedicated family man and successful businessman.
'Dee Causey loved the underdog, and he loved nothing more than helping the underdog succeed,' Pickens said.
This year, Pickens presented the award to Abegayl O'Hara, a nursing student from the St. Augustine campus.
'Abbey exemplifies unparalleled strength, resilience, and determination qualities that have not only shaped her life but have also prepared her to excel as a compassionate and dedicated nurse,' said nursing instructor Wendy Thomas, who nominated O'Hara for the award.
According to Thomas, O'Hara was thrust into responsibilities far beyond her years.
'At just 8 years old, she became the primary caregiver for her mother, who struggled with physical and mental issues,' Thomas said. 'This role required her to act as a parent, providing care and stability under extremely challenging circumstances … further complicated by the absence of her biological father.'
Despite these formidable challenges, O'Hara displayed extraordinary perseverance. She made the courageous decision to return to school and earn her high school diploma.
Tragically, O'Hara's mother passed away when O'Hara was 20 and expecting her first child. Determined to create a better life for herself, her husband and two children, O'Hara began nursing school and continued to distinguish herself as a compassionate, driven and highly capable individual.
'Her experiences have endowed her with a deep empathy and an unwavering commitment to patient care,' Thomas continued. 'She understands firsthand the challenges that patients and their families may face and brings a unique perspective and passion to her work, using her own journey to inspire and uplift those around her.'

title: Publishing schedule altered due to holidays
description: Amid closures throughout the holiday season, the Palatka Daily News will undergo temporary changes to when it will be released.
content:
Image
Body
Amid closures throughout the holiday season, the Palatka Daily News will undergo temporary changes to when it will be released.
There will be only two publication days during this and next week, with the paper coming out on Tuesdays and Saturdays both weeks.
Christmas and New Year's Day fall on Wednesday both weeks, and the U.S. Postal Service, which delivers the Palatka Daily News to its subscribers, will be closed. The company that prints the publication will also be closed on both holidays.
The front office will be closed on Christmas and New Year's Day, but Daily News journalists will continue to cover breaking news that occurs.
The Daily News will return to its regular publication schedule the week of Jan. 6.

title: March, festival celebrate King's life, impact
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: People throughout Putnam County braved the cold in Palatka on Monday to celebrate the life of a civil rights giant who dreamed of freedom and equal rights for all.
content:
Body
People throughout Putnam County braved the cold in Palatka on Monday to celebrate the life of a civil rights giant who dreamed of freedom and equal rights for all.
Like in previous years, the Martin Luther King Jr. Day festivities kicked off with a march in the streets toward a meeting spot, where a festival in his name took place. However, this year's events saw slight changes from their previous counterparts.
Instead of taking place downtown, the march started at the Jenkins Community Center and ended at the Calvary Family Life Center, the site of the festival.
Justin Campbell – the president of the African-American Cultural Arts Council of Putnam County, the group that hosted the events – said the alterations to this year's festivities were to showcase and enhance Jenkins and the life center, two well-known facilities on the city's north side.
The march echoed back to how the marches took place before they were downtown.
'Historically, the march has always started from Jenkins, and it used to go to Booker Park,' said Campbell, who is also city commissioner.
The Martin Luther King Jr. Day Festival featured music, vendors, raffle prizes, games and a food truck, among other items. People could give back to the community in various ways, like participating in a cleanup that took place around and near the life center grounds.
Pamela Brown, the vice president of the cultural arts council, stressed the importance of having a King Festival every year to inform the community, especially the youth, about the works of King and other historical figures.
She highlighted people, like retired Putnam County educator Cynthia Asia, who marched with King when he visited St. Augustine. It's easier to teach lessons, Brown said, when there are real-life, local people to reference.
'The importance of keeping (the King Day events) going is for students to know the history and impact that Dr. Martin Luther King made on society as a whole,' she said. 'So, when you think about that and we begin to have these (local) people share their stories, then young people can relate to it and not just look at those people as historical figures.'
Sharing stories and other lessons with younger people is a way to ensure key pieces of history aren't lost to time, Brown said.
She expressed her desire to have more young people attend events like the King Festival. Considering how some states are changing the way history can be taught in school, she said, children need somewhere to learn about history so King's impact isn't minimized.
'In our educational system, when we're having book bans and all those things and our history is pretty much being erased, it's very important that we as members of this community and African Americans share all the history that we can with our young people so they will know it and we will not forget it,' Brown said.
As Monday's festival got underway, Campbell said he looked forward to more people showing up to learn about the past and converse with each other.
He encouraged people follow King's teachings by reaching out to people outside of their usual group of family, friends and acquaintances.
'Get out and meet somebody who you don't generally talk to on a day-to-day basis,' he said. 'That's what Dr. King did.'

title: Media Companies on the Move
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Two Palatka media organizations are packing up shop as they plan to move to a downtown building in the coming months.
content:
Body
Two Palatka media organizations are packing up shop as they plan to move to a downtown building in the coming months.
The Palatka Daily News and Bass Capital Radio will be leaving their respective buildings to move to the 200 block of St. Johns Avenue.
The Daily News building, 1825 St. Johns Ave., went up for sale Friday for $1,490,000. Bass Capital, 1428 St. Johns Ave., has not yet been listed on the market, said Charlie Douglas, who owns the newspaper and radio station.
An exact moving date has not been set, but the move for both companies will be an ongoing process. Daily News Publisher Jennifer Moates said this will be a new chapter for the newspaper.
'Although moving from the building we have been in for so many years is bittersweet, we are happy to be going back to our roots downtown,' she said.
The Daily News used to operate out of a Second Street building until the paper moved to its current location in April 1967, according to Daily News records. The newspaper building expanded in 1986 to accommodate the press that was added that year.
The radio station has been in its current location for about 50 years. An official from the radio station declined to comment.
The newspaper has undergone a few changes lately, such as getting a new owner and no longer printing in-house.
In June, Douglas, a Putnam native, acquired the Daily News from Community Newspapers Inc., a Georgia-based media company that had owned the newspaper since 2000.
From the early 1970s until 2000, the New York Times owned the Daily News.
Douglas said last year he purchased the Daily News to keep the paper local and avoid it being purchased by a larger media conglomerate with no ties to the area and no firsthand knowledge of the paper's importance to Putnam County.
Media giant Gannett owns the Gainesville Sun, St. Augustine Record and Daytona-Beach News Journal.
Last summer, the paper shut down its printing press, which had been installed in 1986, and relied on a company in Callahan for printing.
Moates said the newspaper no longer needs a building as big as the 19,488-square-foot structure out of which it currently operates.
'With the size of our current location no longer needed after our printing operation has been consolidated elsewhere, the downtown location will be ideal for our employees and readers,' Moates said.
While the newspaper is moving after nearly four decades in the same building, Moates said the merging of the newspaper and radio station will bring a synergy of news for Putnam County.
It also brings the media entities geographically closer to ongoing efforts to spruce up the city, including the reworking of the St. Johns River Center, 102 N. First St., which Douglas owns.
'We are proud to be a part of the revitalization of downtown Palatka,' Moates said.

title: Teacher leading Christie mystery play
author: Trisha Murphy
description: Courtney Johnson is known to jump feet-first into projects she is passionate about and, at times, tends to offer a bit extra with details even when not solicited.
content:
Courtney Johnson is known to jump feet-first into projects she is passionate about and, at times, tends to offer a bit extra with details even when not solicited.
Another leap will take place for the 48-year-old East Palatka resident when the River City Players theater group opens its next show, 'The Mousetrap' by Agatha Christie, on Wednesday at the Larimer Arts Center, 216 Reid St. in Palatka.
Johnson has been cast as Mollie Ralston, a newlywed who has opened her family home as a guest house.
'I was very lucky to have an amazing drama teacher, Sarah Munday, in high school,' she said. 'She and Mr. (Jim) Pignato, who at that time was the band director, gave us so many wonderful opportunities to perform in shows like 'Oklahoma,' 'My Fair Lady' and 'West Side Story.' They were a brilliant pair who started me on a path that eventually led me to becoming a teacher.'
'The Mousetrap' will run through Feb. 9, with performances at 7 p.m. from Jan. 30 to Feb. 1 and Feb. 6-8, as well as matinees at 2 p.m. Feb. 2 and 9. There will be a Feb. 5 show, the proceeds from which will benefit Guardian Ad Litem. The tickets are $20 per person.
The opening night performance and the Feb. 2 and 5 shows are sold out, but for those interested in attending shows on these dates, there is a waiting list. For details or tickets, call 386-244-7886 or visit rivercityplayers.ludus.com.
Amy Cornwell, who is the co-director of the show, said there is a level of suspense that is sure to keep the audience on the edge of their seats as they watch the story of 'The Mousetrap' unfold.
'Throughout the story, you are not only trying to uncover the truth about the tragic events on Culver Street, but you also unravel the darkest, most secretive moments in these characters' lives.
According to Cornwell, the murder mystery play takes place in the 1950s about an hour away from London. The story centers around Monkswell Manor, a guest house owned by characters Mollie and Giles Ralston.
'All of the guests have come to this guest house for various reasons, and it is up to the audience to determine the significance of the guest house and the intentions of the people who stay there,' Cornwell said.
'It's a classic whodunit with many twists and turns along the way,' Co-director Sara Story said. 'It gives the audience a chance to try and unravel the mystery before it is revealed.'
Cornwell said Johnson is a joy and a light to be around.
'She adds charm and energy to her character, Mollie Ralston,' Cornwell said. 'She comes in prepared and is great at trying new ideas to bring this show to life. She always has a smile on her face and is ready to get to work.'
Johnson finds there is a certain joy in revisiting a classic like 'The Mousetrap,' which opened in London during the 1952 season and is still going today.
'Show-goers, I hope, are going to feel that giddy oh-my-gosh feeling, and this is certainly a show to have a friend ride with you to see it,' she said. 'There is such a potential of needing to rehash the details and scenes to see if your friend picked up on something you may have missed.'
Johnson said the setting for the upcoming show is like the start of a scary story.
'Twas a snowy, cold evening in an isolated English manor house,' said Johnson. 'A blizzard is setting in when the doorbell rings. … I cannot give anything away. There are such great nuances and character arcs, but my lips are sealed.'
Johnson said her character is excited about the venture she is embarking on with her husband, Giles, played by actor Stephen Lowe.
'Working with the directors and the cast members is the best part,' she said. 'I love collaborating on projects, and the people I have been able to work with over the last two shows have rekindled in me a love of performing. When I say the other performers in this piece are jaw-dropping, I am not exaggerating. I am so grateful to work with such talented artists.'
Cornwell hopes the public will go to the show and enjoy solving the murder mystery.
'We hope to make the show interactive and give our patrons a new experience,' she said.
Johnson finds a feeling of quiet excitement right before she steps onstage, and then everything feels calm.
'Especially when you are working with a cast who brings such great energy to a show,' she said. 'It reminds me of standing on a diving board and getting ready to jump, knowing that it is going to be fun and that you have friends cheering you on. Then you just jump. The rush is amazing.'

title: Special primary voter turnout lagging below 5%
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: The vast majority of the local electorate has shied away from the polls as Putnam around surrounding counties have been tasked with picking the partisan nominees competing for a seat in Congress.
content:
Body
The vast majority of the local electorate has shied away from the polls as Putnam around surrounding counties have been tasked with picking the partisan nominees competing for a seat in Congress.
Putnam County residents have until polls close Saturday to vote early for Republican and Democratic candidates for Florida's 6th Congressional District, which comprises all or parts of Putnam, Flagler, Lake, Marion, St. Johns and Volusia counties. Primary day is Tuesday.
At 3:10 p.m. Friday, only 1,224, or 3.24%, of 37,793 eligible voters, had cast a decision either in early voting or via mail ballot, according to the Supervisor of Elections Office's website.
'That's not great, but it's better than where we were,' Elections Supervisor Charles Overturf III said, adding that barely any mail-in ballots had returned.
The primary candidates are competing to succeed former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Waltz, who resigned Nov. 25 when President Donald Trump selected him to be the national security adviser.
This is a closed primary, meaning only Democrats and Republicans can vote for a candidate. The winner of each party's primary will be on the April 1 special election ballot.
The Republicans on the primary ballot are Aaron Baker, Randy Fine and Ehsan Joarder, while the Democrats up for election are Ges Selmont and Joshua Weil.
None of the contestants are from Putnam, something Overturf said could be why not many people have voted so far.
'Both parties are sitting there like, 'I don't know who (this candidate) is,'' he said.
On Thursday, Overturf said he expects a 4% turnout. The state average for special primaries is 10%, he said. He would love to see a 20% turnout from Putnam voters, he knows it won't get close to the 80.5% percent turnout Putnam saw for the 2024 general election.
'It's not gonna be a Nov. 5 or anything like that,' Overturf said.
Early voting hours Saturday will be from 8:30 a.m. - 5:30 p.m. at the following locations:
– The Supervisor of Elections Office, 2509 Crill Ave., Suite 900, in Palatka.
– The Interlachen Community Center, 135 S. County Road 315.
– South Putnam Government Complex, 115 N. Summit St. in Crescent City.
On primary day, Republicans and Democrats must vote from 7 a.m. – 7 p.m. in the polling place listed for their residence.
All eligible voters can participate in the April special election, which will feature the Republican and Democratic primary winners, as well as Libertarian, no party affiliation and write-in candidates.

title: Putnam, district voters select party nominees
description: Voters from Putnam and surrounding counties have chosen their party nominees in Tuesday's special primary to compete to fill a congressional vacancy.
content:
Body
Voters from Putnam and surrounding counties have chosen their party nominees in Tuesday's special primary to compete to fill a congressional vacancy.
Putnam had a 9.91% voter turnout in the special primary, with 3,744 of 37,793 eligible voters going to the polls via mail, early voting or primary day voting, according to the Putnam County Supervisor of Elections Office website.
State Sen. Randy Fine of Melbourne ran away with the Republican victory in Putnam County. Unofficial election results on the Supervisor of Elections website show Fine receiving 2,674 votes (87.39%) compared to Aaron Baker's 338 votes (11.05%) and Ehsan Joarder's 48 votes (1.57%).
The Democratic race in Putnam was a closer contest. Josh Weil won 354 votes (54.29%) while George A. 'Ges' Selmont received 298 votes (45.71%), according to the Elections Office.
The special primary, as well as the April 1 special election, are necessary to find someone to fill the void left behind by former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Waltz, who represented Florida's 6th Congressional District. In addition to Putnam County, the 6th Congressional District is made up of all or parts of Flagler, Lake, Marion, St. Johns and Volusia counties.
Districtwide, Fine won with 33,883 votes and Weil claimed victory with 9,713 votes.
Those two will go up against Libertarian candidate Andrew Parrott, no party affiliation hopeful Randall Terry and write-in contestant Chuck Sheridan in April's special election.

title: Student-athlete 1 of 8 selected for NFL award
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A Crescent City Junior-Senior High School flag football player will represent her school at the Super Bowl after her own athletic feats caught the attention of the NFL.
content:
Body
A Crescent City Junior-Senior High School flag football player will represent her school at the Super Bowl after her own athletic feats caught the attention of the NFL.
Senior Paola Cruz-Ramos, 17, was one of eight students nationwide selected to be a finalist for this year's NFL Latino Youth Honors Award, which is sponsored by Procter & Gamble and has partnered with the Hispanic Heritage Foundation.
Of the 64 male and female Latino football and flag football players across the nation who were each nominated by one of the 34 NFL teams, Cruz-Ramos, whom the Jacksonville Jaguars nominated, was one of the eight chosen.
'It means a lot to me to be able to represent who I am, you know, where my family comes from in a sport that is barely starting to grow,' she said Tuesday. 'I think it's very cool to be able to represent my heritage.'
Family, peers, Putnam County School District officials and a representative from the Jaguars lauded Cruz-Ramos' accomplishment during a ceremony Tuesday at the school.
As part of the award, all eight finalists will receive a $5,000 scholarship, according to the NFL, and the top male and female winners will receive a $25,000 scholarship.
Those two will be announced at Super Bowl LIX on Feb. 9. Cruz-Ramos and her sister are traveling to New Orleans during the week of the Super Bowl to meet the other finalists and participate in special events.
The events are aimed to provide mentorship, guidance and resources to the finalists to pursue careers in professional sports, according to the NFL.
Cruz-Ramos was the Daily News' Player of the Year in flag football in 2024 and nabbed spots on the Jaguars' All-Prep Team and the All-State Second Team, according to the NFL. She scored seven touchdowns and made 17 interceptions in the 2024 season, the Daily News reported.
The senior, who also plays soccer for Crescent City High, said she committed to play flag football at Bethel College in North Newton, Kansas, after her high school graduation.
Keenon Henry, Cruz-Ramos' flag football coach at Crescent City High, said he has never seen a program like this, but if anyone deserves the recognition, it's Cruz-Ramos.
'This is something very special to me,' Henry said. '... Watching her (from) her first year and watching her grow is just real special. And she's a great kid. I'm very proud of and excited for her.'
He said Cruz-Ramos excels on and off the field. She is part of the National Honor Society and Crescent City High's honor guard, and she maintains a 4.0 GPA.
'She has great character in the classroom,' Henry said. 'She's just all-around a great kid. The main thing is she keeps getting blessed because she is so humble.'
During her celebration, Cruz-Ramos said she wasn't used to being in the spotlight. However, with the opportunity she has been given, she said she'd like to shine even more light on Crescent City High, especially if that means winning one of the two big prizes.
'It would mean a lot to represent my school,' she said, 'because you don't really hear about athletes from here.'

title: Open for Business
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Editor's note: The St. Johns River Center is under the ownership of Charlie Douglas, who also owns the Palatka Daily News.
content:
Editor's note: The St. Johns River Center is under the ownership of Charlie Douglas, who also owns the Palatka Daily News.
The smell of roasted coffee beans wafted along the Palatka riverfront Tuesday as an established business settled into its second day operating in a new location in the city.
Palatka Coffee Co. Owner Aashton Hodge said having the coffee shop at the River Center, 102 N. First St. in Palatka, is humbling.
'It feels like we're on the ground level of bringing life back to downtown Palatka,' Hodge said. 'It's been dead down here for so long, and (we're) very happy to be part of that.'
The river center location is open from 7 a.m. – 5 p.m. Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. – 2 p.m. Saturday. The location is closed on Sundays for now, but Hodge said that after the Florida Azalea Festival, which will be Feb. 22-23, the shop will be open from 8 a.m. – 2 p.m. on Sundays.
The riverfront branch of Palatka Coffee Co. is Hodge's second location in Palatka, the first being at 3711 Crill Ave.
He also owns Hastings Coffee Co., 308A N. Main St. in Hastings. Hodge plans to sell the Hastings location next month, but it will remain a coffee shop under the new ownership, he said.
Hodge said his family is supportive of the company's new venture. He opened the Crill Avenue location about five years ago because establishing a coffee shop was something he always wanted to try.
Hodge likes interacting with the public, and because he and his wife used to own Tangles Hair Salon at the Crill Pointe Plaza, they thought it would be a good fit to open a coffee shop next door to the salon.
'Two of my kids are employees,' Hodge said. 'They all love it.'
When he found out in March about the opportunity to open a new location in the river center, Hodge said, he couldn't pass it up.
On Tuesday morning, locals continued to flow in and out of the center to get their coffee, with Hodge estimating he had about 50 customers at that location on opening day. Patrons were treated to music from Blue Crab Development employee Sandy Robinson, who played piano Tuesday morning.
Holly Haring, who works at NiCole's Salon & Spa, 210 St. Johns Ave., said she has been a frequent Palatka Coffee Co. customer since the Crill Avenue location opened in 2020.
'They're a great company,' said Haring, who was getting coffee at the river center Tuesday morning. 'I love that it's local. They have really good coffee, and I think they'd just be a good asset downtown.'
The shop brews Kookaburra coffee, which comes from St. Augustine, and the Palatka shops are known for ham and cheddar scones, cinnamon rolls and sausage biscuits, Hodge said.
The river center location has tables inside for patrons to enjoy their coffee, and Hodge said they are also working to make rooftop access available to customers.
Hodge, who grew up in Palatka, said the city's downtown used to be bustling when he was younger. He remembered JCPenney and a popular drug store along St. Johns Avenue and said there always used to be much to do in the 1970s and 1980s.
He hopes more businesses like his will draw people back to the area.
'I always felt like the river was just underutilized in this town because of how beautiful it is down here,' Hodge said.

title: PDN claims 14 awards for writing, photography
description: The Palatka Daily News won big over the weekend as three of its journalists took home awards for their work in various categories.
content:
Body
The Palatka Daily News won big over the weekend as three of its journalists took home awards for their work in various categories.
The Florida Press Club awards banquet took place Saturday in Ocala, where the organization honored journalists from around the state for their works spanning from June 1, 2023, to May 31, 2024. Three of the Daily News' journalists won a total of 14 awards in areas ranging from sports to the environment to business and more.
Lifestyles Editor Trisha Murphy took home a first-place honor in the Health News and Light Features Writing categories, while Sports Editor Mark Blumenthal won first place in the Sports Writing category.
Reporter Sarah Cavacini secured a second-place victory in the Environmental Writing category.
Publisher Jennifer Moates expressed her pride in the Daily News' award-winning journalists and the comprehensive work they produce.
Murphy, Blumenthal and Cavacini have continued the newspaper's trend of talented journalists being recognized for incomparable work, she said.
'Congratulations to all of the winners,' Moates said. 'I am very proud of the work you all do; it is much appreciated. Your hard work and dedication deserves this recognition.'
Also taking home second-place honors were Blumenthal in the Sports Action photography and Sports Column writing categories. Murphy had second-place wins for writing in the Community News, Business News, General News and Serious Features categories.
Murphy also came in second for the Lucy Morgan Award for In-Depth Reporting.
She won third place for writing in Education News and Religion News, and Blumenthal came in third for Sports Columns.
Editor Brandon D. Oliver commended the three winners for their stellar writing and photography skills. While only 14 of their works were honored this weekend, their portfolios are filled with amazing stories, pictures, interviews and designs that prove why they are invaluable assets to the Daily News and Putnam County.
'I'm so proud of Trisha, Mark and Sarah for their never-ending commitment to telling the stories of Putnam County and the people who live here,' Oliver said. 'I hope Putnam residents know how tirelessly these three esteemed journalists work to accurately and fairly report on different aspects of life in Putnam County.'

title: Family feuding in honor of late loved one
author: Trisha Murphy
description: When February rolls around, most people look forward to special gift-giving to celebrate their love for their family and friends on Valentine's Day.
content:
When February rolls around, most people look forward to special gift-giving to celebrate their love for their family and friends on Valentine's Day.
However, the Marshall family, all of whom are natives of Palatka and graduates of Palatka High School, found a different way to show their love.
The Marshall clan wanted to celebrate the memory of a beloved aunt who was a passionate viewer of the TV game show 'Family Feud' and who often dreamed of being on the show but never had the chance.
Pauline Lee is that aunt who lived in Palatka and died of cancer in August 2022 shortly before her family got word they had been selected to audition for the show, according to her niece, Audrey Mitchell Gainey, who lives in Gainesville.
'I submitted the application on April 26, 2022, hoping to fulfill her dream of being on the show,' Gainey said. 'We received the invitation on Dec. 26, 2022, to audition.'
Because of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic at the time, there were no in-person auditions, Gainey said. Instead, she said, the family participated in a virtual audition, bringing the same excitement, energy and enthusiasm as if they were there in person.
The Marshall Family's episode of the show, which was filmed in April, will air on WJAX and WNBW at 7 and 7:30 p.m. Feb. 14.
'It was a long wait before we were finally booked to tape for season 26,' Gainey said. 'The anticipation was truly worth it.'
Other airtimes on Valentine's Day include 5:30 and 7:30 p.m. on WUTV, 7 and 7:30 p.m. on WBFS, and 3 and 7 p.m. on WFTV.
To verify air times, visit familyfeud.com and type in a zip code for additional station information.
Darius D. Seay Jr., Gainey's son, was a part of the family team and remembers how much his aunt loved watching 'Family Feud' every day.
'She was an avid fan of it, and we wanted to honor her by being on the show,' he said. 'For our family to be a part of it, it was an honor and a dream come true.'
Traveling to Atlanta to visit the Tyler Perry Studios and meet show host Steve Harvey in person was an incredible opportunity, Gainey said.
'When Steve introduced us as The Marshall Family from Palatka, Florida, we felt immense pride even though he couldn't help but think the city's name and location was quite amusing,' she said, laughing. 'Everyone will have to tune in to see how he reacted to that unforgettable shout-out.'
Aside from Gainey and Seay, the latter of whom lives in Daytona Beach, those representing the Marshal family on the game show were Leonard E. Marshall of Buffalo, New York, Daryl G. Medlock of Lauderhill, and James A. Bailey Jr. of Orlando.
When asked how the family fared in winnings, Gainey wouldn't say. She also couldn't remember the name of the family they were up against.
'We had to sign an agreement with Family Feud that prohibits us from sharing specific details about the show until it airs,' she said.
Gainey recalls submitting one of her late aunt's funny Christmas videos as part of the application packet to demonstrate the humor in the family.
'Our aunt was the life of every party and she would have been thrilled about our appearance on the show,' she said. 'Had her life been extended, she would have been right there cheering us on.'
Gainey can't wait to watch the show on Valentine's Day, saying she feels she may need to pinch herself to remind herself she's not imagining it.
'It was surreal,' she said. 'It also required a lot of energy.'
Gainey knows she and her family were given a rare opportunity to honor their aunt when they were selected for the show.
'Being under the lights and in a real live studio was a once-in-a-lifetime experience,' she said. 'I know it will be real when I hear those famous words, 'Survey says?' I can't wait.'

title: Guests to be honored with Night to Shine
author: Brandon D. Oliver
description: Volunteers have spent the week making sure a Palatka venue looks great in anticipation of the party being thrown today for a group of people who may otherwise not have such an experience.
content:
Body
Volunteers have spent the week making sure a Palatka venue looks great in anticipation of the party being thrown today for a group of people who may otherwise not have such an experience.
For the second year, Night to Shine, a product of the Tim Tebow Foundation, will take place in Palatka. The event, which will occur at 5:30 p.m. today at Calvary Missionary Baptist Church's Family Life Center, 1414 Bronson St. in Palatka, is a formal dance for people with disabilities.
Calvary, Peniel Baptist Church and First Baptist Church of Palatka partnered to produce today's event, and student volunteers from Peniel Baptist Academy in Palatka have been decorating the life center since Monday. Meanwhile, volunteers from the three partner churches were decorating other areas of the venue or finishing landscaping projects outside.
On Thursday morning, Peniel art teacher Casper De la Torre oversaw students decorating the dining and dancing room for Friday's event. De la Torre volunteered last year as a decorator and enjoyed his time at Palatka's inaugural Night to Shine so much that he volunteered this year as the lead ballroom decorator.
'Last year was a lot of fun, and then I was also a volunteer buddy last year,' De la Torre said in between giving instructions to his students. 'So, this year, I wanted to amplify that and amplify that wow factor.'
Night to Shine isn't simply a dance, organizers said. The event is meant to give its attendees, referred to as 'honored guests,' an elegant night they won't forget.
Aside from the dining and dancing room, there are hair and makeup, shoeshine, karaoke, sensory and photobooth rooms. There is a room for volunteers – including volunteer buddies, who accompany honored guests for the evening – and a room for caregivers to relax while honored guests are having the time of their lives.
The event will start with honored guests getting spruced up in the hair and makeup and shoeshine areas before taking a ride around the area in limos. They will then reenter the Family Life Center by making their way down the red carpet with paparazzi-like photographers capturing their special moments.
'And at the end of the night, all the honored guests get crowned prom king and queen,' De la Torre said.
Peniel students and employees volunteered this week as part of February being the church's Mission Month. Among the volunteers was sophomore Abbie Alford, who said she wanted to contribute to Night to Shine to help the 125 honored guests have the perfect night.
Although the workload was heavy, Alford said, having many of her classmates with her made the tasks feel lighter.
'It's been fun, actually,' she said. 'It was a little hard, but it's for a good cause. So, it makes it fun.'
In addition to the 125 honored guests expected at today's event, 470 volunteers are expected to attend, said Christa Smith, the Night to Shine Palatka chairwoman.
The event is for caregivers as much as it is for honored guests, said Smith, who is also the disability ministry manager for the Tim Tebow Foundation. Having a room designated specifically for caregivers gives them a chance to relax while guests enjoy themselves.
'This is an opportunity for us as a community to love on all members dealing with disability,' Smith said. '(The caregiver room is) a chance to give their parents an opportunity for respite, for love.'
Smith expects tonight's event to be bigger and better than its first year in Palatka. There was a great community response last year, she said, and the community has contributed even more this time around.
Smith said Calvary, First Baptist and Peniel have been working together to make sure the event – from volunteers to donors to honored guests – reaches all areas of the community rather than be contained in one restricted bubble.
'Our community has come out in full force (in its) financial support, volunteering and giving,' Smith said.
For more information about Night to Shine Palatka, visit www.lovepalatka.com.

title: Preteen arrested in connection to bus bomb threat
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: A Palatka child is said to have caused panic after claiming there was a bomb on his school bus Wednesday afternoon.
content:
Body
A Palatka child is said to have caused panic after claiming there was a bomb on his school bus Wednesday afternoon.
The 11-year-old was arrested and charged with a second-degree felony for making a false report about a weapon of mass destruction, according to a Facebook post from the Putnam County Sheriff's Office.
White had been on his way home from school when he remarked that he saw a bomb on the bus, authorities said.
The bus had been traveling along U.S. 17 North near West River Road when White said he saw a bomb, according to the sheriff's office.
Deputies searched the bus after receiving a call from the Putnam County School District's Transportation Department, authorities said.
After investigators confirmed White was responsible for the fake threat, he was taken to the Putnam County Jail and then to a Florida Department of Juvenile Justice facility in Daytona Beach, according to the sheriff's office.
Sheriff Gator DeLoach said his agency has a zero-tolerance policy about these types of threats so he and his deputies can keep students and district employees safe.
'These actions are not funny and cause undue stress and panic for our children,' DeLoach said in the Facebook statement. 'I will continue to pursue and arrest any student or adult that makes these types of threats. If there is an underlying cause to this young man's behavior, I hope he gets the help he needs."

title: District gifted $73K for grants to benefit students
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: Putnam County students are getting a boost from a local nonprofit organization that donated a sizable sum toward their education.
content:
Body
Putnam County students are getting a boost from a local nonprofit organization that donated a sizable sum toward their education.
The Education Foundation of Putnam County gifted the Putnam County School Board $73,050 during Tuesday's board meeting. The money is being divided into four grants that are to be used for dual enrollment opportunities, technology for students, and programs related to science, technology, engineering and mathematics.
School board member Holly Pickens thanked the foundation, five members of which were at the meeting to present the check, for their efforts to help students.
'They work tirelessly for our students and, you know, just everything they raise, they give back to our children,' she said. 'And, so, we need to support them whenever we can.'
Foundation board President Les Sims said the organization reaches out to community members, state sponsors and companies nationwide to raise money for the county's students, he said.
One grant worth $4,500 to be funded with the money donated Tuesday is the Rural Careers Pathway Grant. St. Johns River State College donated the money to the foundation, and the district by proxy, to keep parents and students better informed of dual enrollment opportunities between the local high schools and the college, Sims said.
Clay Electric Cooperative donated $9,450 to the foundation to be used for the Clay Electric Operation Roundup Grant. Sims said the money is to be used by teachers and other district employees to purchase STEM supplies.
Money for the third grant, Decreasing the Digital Divide Grant, was given to the foundation on behalf of AT&T. The grant allows the district to purchase 150 electronic tablets for students in kindergarten through eighth grade, Sims said.
The $51,000 for the final grant that will fund STEM learning was donated by local resident Tom Hunter, a school district alumnus, retired nuclear engineer and member of the Bond Oversight Committee, which oversees the spending of the obligation bond the district is using to build and renovate schools.
Sims said $48,000 will benefit all district STEM programs. Crescent City, Interlachen and Palatka junior-senior high school principals will receive $1,000 each to use for STEM opportunities at their own discretion, Sims told school board members.
He said his own education experience inspired him to get involved with the organization to help students.
'We were poor growing up,' he said. 'Education was not afforded to me.'
Sims went into the military right out of high school, but he said there are more opportunities for students today that he did not have.
'One of my passions in life is to make sure each and every child in our community has some form of opportunity, whether it's college (or) vocational education,' he said. 'That's just one of my passions, and it always has been.'

title: Town council hopefuls address community
author: Sarah Cavacini
description: With the town's election less than three weeks away, Welaka Town Council candidates let community members know their political stances this week.
content:
Body
With the town's election less than three weeks away, Welaka Town Council candidates let community members know their political stances this week.
On Wednesday, former candidate Sandra Walker and political newcomer David Jeltes answered residents' questions during a political forum at Shrimps R Us & More.
Councilwoman Tonya Long, who is running for re-election, could not attend the forum because of a family obligation, she said in a letter that was read during the forum.
'I will address … questions before the election,' she said in the letter.
The three candidates are competing for two slots on the council. Another seat will be vacant after the March 4 election because Jessica Finch, who was the council president before being appointed as acting mayor, does not wish to return to office.
She became the acting mayor after former Mayor Jamie Watts resigned last year amid an unsuccessful bid to serve in the Florida House of Representatives.
Finch's last day will be March 4.
Finch did not submit her letter of resignation soon enough for her position to be included on the March 4 election ballot. Officials from the Supervisor of Elections Office said the special election to fill Finch's vacancy will likely be in the spring, but no specific date has been announced.
Wednesday's event was the second of two political forums in Welaka, the first being for the five mayoral candidates. People can watch the mayoral and council member forums on the Friends of Welaka's Facebook page.
Two questions of the questions and the candidates' answers are included below:
Where do you stand with the form of government for the city (sic) of Welaka? Which route would you (favor): a strong mayor (form of government) or a city manager?
Jeltes: 'I'm in favor of a town manager. … I believe we need strong, long-term leadership for this town. It's a full-time job, and working part-time is not going to happen. It's not going to work. … The disadvantage to the strong mayor (system, where the mayor is also the town's administrative leader) is (Florida) Sunshine Laws. The town council members cannot speak to the mayor except during a once-a-month, maybe twice-a-month, meeting to get business done with the mayor. I think that's a huge hindrance.'
Walker: 'I'm in favor of a strong mayor. … Now, down the road, if something changes, or the town's growth is expanding more than we anticipated and we see that we need a city manager, I will be open to looking back into it. But as of where we are now, I support the strong mayor.'
Welaka has three police officers and a police chief. Do you support the Welaka Police Department?
Jeltes: 'I am definitely for the police department. … In my opinion, we don't need to grow any larger than that for (a) town of this size. It's nice to know they are out and about.'
Walker: 'I think we do need the police here, the chief and the officers. I talked to a lot of people about complaints or issues with the amount of police that we have. But, in an emergency … we need our own officers. So, with that being said, I spoke to the chief, and he has an open-door policy.'

The City Commission of the City of Palatka will meet in a closed executive session to discuss collective bargaining negotiations on June 11, 2024 at 5:00 PM, at City Hall, 201 N. 2nd St., Palatka, FL 32177. In attendance will be: Mayor Correa, Commissioners McCaskill, Campbell, Borom, and Jones, City Mgr. Bell, Asst. City Mgr. Griffith, Attorney West, Clerk Krantz, Chief of Police Shaw, Asst. Chief of Police Newcomb, Finance Director Carty, and Human Resources employees Ms. Jones and Mr. Hunter. • This closed executive session is not open to the public. • The closed executive session is expected to last approximately 90 minutes. • Under the provisions of Section 447.605(1), Florida Statutes, a limited exemption from Section 286.011, Fla. Stat., exists for discussions between the chief executive officer of a public employer and the labor negotiating committee, including the legislative body of the public employer relative to collective bargaining. The agenda for the meeting is as follows: 1. Call to Order, 2. Discussion/Direction Collective Bargaining Negotiations with the Police Benevolent Association, 3. Adjourn Section 447.605, Florida Statutes provides that discussions between the chief executive officer of the public employer, or his representative, and the legislative body of the public employer relative to collective bargaining shall be closed and exempt from the provisions of s. 286.011 and provides as to the Public Record Act that work products developed by the public employer in preparation for negotiations, and during negotiations, shall be confidential and exempt from the provisions of s. 119.07(1), Florida Statutes Please govern yourselves accordingly, Sunni Krantz, CMC, City Clerk Legal No. 00102718

Failure to respond will result in a determination of ineligibility by the Supervisor and your name will be removed from the statewide voter registration system. If you attempt to vote at an early voting site or your normal election day polling place, you will be required to vote a provisional ballot. If you vote by mail, your ballot will be treated as a provisional ballot. In either case, your ballot may not be counted until final determination of eligibility is made.
